Bizarre as it sounds, we've now heard that they are calling the Assembly  members back.
So it appears that the Assembly leadership will at least make  a run at this.
We are getting more information and mobilizing industry.
Some key considerations:  The Governor is putting immense pressure on the Legislature to get something  done.
The Legislature is fearful of getting blamed by the Governor for having "done  nothing."
Becauase the Assembly has thus far "done nothing," the only thing it has in  front of it is 78.
The Assembly could not agree to the Speaker's bill because it felt the bill  was too far to the left; but 78 is even more one-sided.
So there's a  reasonable likelihood that 78 would have to be amended considerably in order  to get the support necessary to get voted out.
Once voted out of the Assembly, it would have to go back to the Senate, where  the Senate would have to approve it.
Again, the Senate has adjourned, so Burton would have to round them up and  call them back for a vote, and there's no indication at this time that  Burton's inclined to come back.
In addition, Burton has said that he's not interested in making any changes  to 78, that "it's 78 or nothing."
Consequently, for the Sentate (i.e.,  Burton) to vote it out, it would first have to agree to the Assembly's  amendments.
Thus far, the Assembly and the Senate have not seen eye to eye  on the issues.
All that said, this Legislature is far from rational, and nothing can be  counted out.
We're therefore operating under the assumption that 78 could  move.
Will report back as information becomes available.
Best,

First of all, tell me what the difference is between "overcharges" and "excessive" charges. If there isn't one, give me your opinion on why this analyst would say such a stupid thing.
Second, give me one reason why the lead is journalistically incorrect, and one why it is grammatically unattractive.

Kate

Subject: Words That Aren’t What They Seem: Debridement and Other Misleading Terms

Hi Team,

I wanted to share some thoughts on the importance of language clarity in healthcare, especially regarding terms like “debridement.” On the surface, these words might sound technical but neutral—however, their true meaning and implications can often be quite different and even intimidating for patients.

For instance, “debridement” refers to the removal of dead, damaged, or infected tissue to improve the healing potential of the remaining healthy tissue. While the term itself sounds clinical, it doesn’t reveal how significant or uncomfortable the procedure might be for the patient. Other examples include “negative pressure therapy” (which might sound unpleasant but is actually a common wound care practice), or “conservative management” (which often means ‘watchful waiting’ yet could be misunderstood by families expecting more aggressive intervention).

I encourage everyone to be mindful of these potentially misleading terms and take a moment to clarify their meaning when discussing care with patients and families. Clear explanations can help build trust and ensure everyone is on the same page.

Feel free to share your own experiences or other tricky terms you’ve encountered!

Best,  
[Your Name]
source_text:
debridement (di-BREED-ment, day-) noun     Surgical removal of dead, infected tissue or foreign matter from a wound.
[From French debridement, from debrider (to unbridle), from Middle French desbrider (de- + brider).]
"Voluminous clinical studies also indicate that hypnosis can reduce the    acute pain experienced by patients undergoing burn-wound debridement,    children enduring bone marrow aspirations and women in labor."
Michael R Nash, The Truth And the Hype of Hypnosis, Scientific American    (New York), Jul 2001.
Here is a pop-quiz: how many light-years does it take for an astronomer to change a light bulb?
Answer, of course, is none.
She knows a light-year is a unit of distance, not time.
The red-herring word `year' in this term tries to mislead us.
This week brings together words whose meaning is not the first thing that comes to mind.
-Anu

- The order requires that all terms, rates, and conditions be filed with FERC.
- The original order recognized GridSouth as the sole provider of transmission service on its grid, so all transmission uses must take place under the GridSouth tariff.
- The RTO applicants asked for clarification on whether FERC was requiring unbundling of retail rates. They planned to move their bundled retail load under the GridSouth tariff for terms and conditions, but not rates.
- The rehearing order does not claim jurisdiction over bundled retail rates. However, because GridSouth is now the sole provider of transmission service, all applicants must take these services—including those for bundled retail service—from GridSouth.
- As a result, all terms, conditions, and rates must be on file with FERC. Specific rate issues will be addressed later when GridSouth files a Section 205 filing. This leaves the door open for GridSouth to potentially propose different rates for native load and for FERC-jurisdictional transmission services.
- It’s not yet clear how FERC will address this particular issue.
- Initially, GridSouth will operate three control areas. Joint Protesters had requested integration and netting of loads and imbalances across all control areas, but the Commission denied this because Order No. 2000 doesn’t require a single control area.
- However, to streamline things for users, the Commission is requiring a single agreement that can include the necessary information for each delivery zone. Compliance with this is required in 10 days.
- While netting over all control areas isn’t required right now, the order encourages GridSouth to consider, in consultation with stakeholders, RTO-wide solutions for minimizing energy imbalances—using operational or trading tools.
- The Commission is deferring decisions related to ancillary services and the Hourly Imbalance Charge until a supplemental filing is made.
- The rehearing request from Santee Cooper—which asked FERC to find that unlimited passive ownership might compromise RTO independence—was denied. Instead, the Commission found that passive ownership proposals should be reviewed case-by-case, ensuring that while passive owners’ financial interests are protected, they cannot control RTO decision making.
- Existing GridSouth members will have the right of first refusal to buy new equity interests issued by the Board until the Initial Public Offering. This protects members from dilution of their interests if new equity is issued at a low price.
- The Commission emphasized that its goal remains the formation of a single RTO in the Southeast. Issues of scope and configuration will be handled separately as part of the review of the May 14 filing.
- EPMI’s requests for a settlement judge proceeding and for rehearing on making market-based rate authority conditional on RTO participation were denied.
- The Commission also denied EPMI’s request to clarify that GridSouth cannot incur significant start-up costs before the independent Board is in place, noting that GridSouth has said it will not spend significantly on software or hardware related to real-time balancing until the independent Board approves it.

If you have any questions or would like more detail on any of these points, please let me know—I’m happy to help!

2000 did not require a single control area.

Martin,

Following my last email, I discovered an additional detail that may help explain why ENCE prefers to purchase the Chilean E. globulus species over the Brazilian species for pulp production.

It appears that the E. globulus species performs better than various Brazilian species during the refining process. While most papermakers typically don't refine hardwoods and softwoods with the same equipment, many smaller European mills cannot afford the capital investment of a second refiner and therefore use a single refiner for all grades. This is particularly common among Italian mills.

Since hardwoods cannot withstand the intensive refining required for softwoods without losing their papermaking characteristics (opacity, etc.), these papermakers need to use the hardwood species best suited for this type of processing. The globulus species (which is also the predominant species in the Iberian Peninsula) performs much better under this type of heavy refining than any other eucalyptus species.

I hope this provides additional insight into this issue. Please feel free to contact me with any questions you might have.

Thanks.
Karen

Welcome to another episode of “As the Market Turns,” where drama is high, optimism is rationed, and coffee is absolutely essential.

Right now, the market seems determined to look on the dark side—kind of like your friend who just can’t watch a movie without Googling the spoilers. The war on terrorism is expected to be not just long, but “are we there yet?” long, with economic impacts deeper than the couch cushions you lost your remote in back before September 11th.

But don’t despair! The administration is spending at a pace that would impress even the most ambitious holiday shopper, which could just help us speed past this downturn faster than you can say “stimulus package.”

So, as always—hang in there. Remember, it’s a marathon, not a sprint (but marathoners do get to celebrate at the finish line).

*Upgrade to 2-Buy, Compelling Valuation*  
We’re bumping MTB up from “just okay” to “go ahead and buy it”—on account of solid fundamentals. Our estimates and price target aren’t changing (because if it’s not broken, don’t fix it), but we expect MTB to deliver 11% EPS growth—that’s beating the group’s average of 8%. Hey, in this market, every extra percent counts!

**Banks – Citibank – Henry Chip Dickson**  
*Citi Previews Stronger than Expected 3Q*  
Despite everything but the kitchen sink being thrown at it—including a $0.12-$0.14 hit from the September 11th disaster—Citi is tackling expectations like a pro, aiming for $0.77 for Q3, topping consensus. We’ve had to trim estimates a little—think haircut, not head shave—but our rating stays at 1 (Strong Buy) with a $70 target. Citi trades right around the large cap bank average, proving even banks can be average and ‘super’ at the same time.

After last week’s tragic events, we’re leaving most of our price targets unchanged, mostly because we don’t have a crystal ball. The big oil companies look cheap enough that even a coupon-hunter might take notice, but we think as the market recovers, the oil sector might be left at the dance—again.

For now, oil is the quiet, sensible pick in your portfolio—little drama, sure, but maybe not the life of the party. Eni and TotalFinaElf get some extra sun in the Middle East/North Africa, but for Repsol YPF we’re cutting our target, and ENI and TotalFinaElf get downgraded—think of it as swapping your gold medal for silver and your silver for a nice participation ribbon.

*Outlook: Shares in Light of Development*  
Recent events haven’t changed our overall cautious view. The E&P sector is still more anxious than a kid in the dentist’s waiting room, but we’re keeping an eye out for deals. Oil prices could be higher in the near term, but slowing economic activity could lead to a natural gas glut—which, for prices, is about as fun as a water balloon with a hole in it.

E&P shares took a 1-6% dip Monday, so we’re hunting for bargains like it’s Black Friday. EOG Resources and Noble Affiliates both look at least 10% below our fair value estimates—so, there’s some “fill your cart” opportunity out there.

The meeting Don and I had with Kinder/Morgan to discuss his Price Risk Management Product went really well. We met with Park Schaper (CFO), Anthony Lannie (President of Power Group), and Jay Hopper (VP and General Manager), who was on the phone from Denver. The group was highly engaged and demonstrated significant interest, particularly in the idea of potentially replacing long-term tolling agreements with this innovative product. During our discussion, they asked thoughtful questions about the structure and mechanics of the Price Risk Management Product, indicating that they have already been exploring alternatives to their standard tolling agreements.

We explained in detail how Enron could provide a five-year toll, and the product would begin in the sixth year, running through year 15 or even year 20. Both Park and Anthony seemed receptive to the flexibility this structure could offer, especially given the current volatility they are experiencing in the energy market and the increasing demands from their financial partners for more predictable revenue streams. They expressed that having a hedge product with duration past five years could be a significant differentiator for their development plans.

We talked very little about their existing projects, specifically Little Rock and Michigan, but we did touch briefly on their current development status. They have already secured all the necessary permits for the Little Rock site, which is a major milestone indicating the project is progressing. For the Michigan site, they are moving forward aggressively but still do not have any tolling agreements in place for either of those projects, making the timing for our proposed product especially relevant.

The ball is currently in their court and they are going to get back with Scot in regards to the projects and with Tom on the PRM Product. Their level of interest and specific follow-up requests suggest that they see real value in Enron’s offering, and this could potentially open doors for similar engagements with other Kinder/Morgan ventures down the road.

Thanks!

10) A question for insurance - Does our Business Interuption insurance  protect us in any of these instances?

Greetings Evening MBAs!
Sign up for one of the most worthwhile organizations at Haas.
Join Challenge for Charity TODAY!
WHAT IS CHALLENGE FOR CHARITY?
Challenge for Charity (otherwise known as C4C), is our official  philanthropic endeavor where Haas, along with 5 other major west coast  business schools, raises money for Special Olympics.
Haas' chapter of C4C  donates significant sums of money and volunteer hours to Special Olympics  every year.
In previous years we've raised as much as $70,000 for Special  Olympics and we hope that this year will be just as successful!!!
C4C is one of the largest organizations at Haas and plays a major role in  organizing almost all of the most popular student functions including the  Halloween Ball, Ski Weekend, Charity Auction, Talent Show, Sports Weekend  at Stanford, and much more.
Stop by our booth at Club Night this Thursday  9/5 from 5pm to 8pm to get more involved with any of these fantastic events!
WHAT DO I GET WITH MY C4C MEMBERSHIP?
As an Evening MBA student, your C4C membership dues are only $150!
Not  only does your membership support a fabulous cause, it also entitles you to  so many great benefits including a really cool new baseball cap and free  access to some of the most popular social events at Haas!
Ticket prices for non-C4C members typically range about $40 per person for  EACH of our most popular events.
This means that your membership brings you  a ton of fun at significant savings!
Anyone who has attended any of our  events can tell you that this is a deal!
So, sign up today!
CAN MY SIGNIFICANT OTHER JOIN C4C TOO?
As you may have noticed, significant others are just as much a part of the  Haas family as the students, so don't forget your significant other is  eligible for C4C membership as well.
We realize that significant others are  not always able to attend as many events as Haas students, so significant  others' membership dues are only $75.
That means you and your honey can  join for a mere $225!
If your S.O.
can only attend two of our many events,  it will more than cover the cost of his/her membership!
HOW DO I SIGN UP?
To join C4C, simply submit a check payable to Challenge for Charity  indicating the name(s) of the new C4C member(s).
Please place your checks  in Linda Ng's mailbox in the MBA Lounge at Haas or stop by the C4C table at  Club Night this Thursday 9/5 from 5pm to 8pm.
We will also be holding a  membership drive during the coming weeks, so look for us in the Haas  courtyard during break.
Remember that membership is only $150 per Haas  student and only $75 for Haas significant others.
WHAT IF I'M ALREADY A MEMBER?
C4C membership is only for the academic year, so if you joined C4C last  year, you must sign up again this year.
If you've already joined C4C this  year, you need to pick up your brand-spanking new baseball cap.
Please stop  by the C4C table at Club Night this Thursday or during our membership drive  at break during the coming weeks.
Thank you for supporting C4C and the Special Olympics!
Sincerely,

Tana mentioned you need guidance on which Enron entity should book trading transactions with various counterparties. While a few general rules apply in most cases, exceptions arise when the transaction is linked to another Enron deal (e.g., financing or equity investment), the counterparty prefers a specific Enron company, a product is exclusive to a certain Enron entity, or the counterparty is based in a different jurisdiction. In such cases—or if local laws restrict trading—consult Legal.

Here are the general guidelines, primarily driven by tax considerations:

1. If no master agreement exists between the counterparty and an Enron company, the trade should be booked through the Enron entity located in the same country as the trader at the time of execution. If further trading is anticipated, alert Credit and Legal to negotiate a master agreement. For cross-border deals, consult Legal beforehand, as some countries have special restrictions or prohibitions.

2. If a master agreement is in place with ENA or Enron Canada, and the trader is in the U.S. or Canada, trade through the Enron entity party to the agreement. If the trader is outside these countries, different rules may apply.

3. If a master agreement exists with ECT International (often for European counterparties) and the trader is in the U.S. or U.K., the trade should be booked through ECT International. For U.K. traders, note that trades are arranged by Enron Europe Finance and Trading Ltd. on ECT International’s behalf due to U.K. regulations. If the trader is elsewhere, refer the trade to a U.S. or U.K.-based colleague for execution and consult Legal or Tax for specifics.

These rules determine which Enron entity serves as the legal counterparty, not where the economic risk is housed. If risk should reside in a different Enron entity than the contractual counterparty, an intercompany transaction (likely via RMT) should be booked to allocate risk appropriately.

Lucy:  Tana tells me you are looking for some guidance as to which Enron entity  should be used for booking trading transactions with various counterparties.
There are a couple of general rules that apply to "normal" trading  circumstances and I'll spell them out below, but remember that these are not  hard and fast rules and may go straight out the window when circumstances  vary (even just a little bit) from "normal."
For example, abnormal  situations exist where the trading transaction is in connection with another  transaction with an Enron company (e.g.
a financing or equity investment),  the counterparty has a legally justifiable desire to trade with a certain  Enron company, the product being traded is only traded by a particular Enron  company or the counterparty is in a jurisdiction outside the country where we  are trading (except as spelled out below).
Having said all that, the  following rules (generally tax driven) can be used as general guidelines:  1.
If there is no master agreement in place between the counterparty and an  Enron company, the trade should be entered into on behalf of the Enron  company based in the country where the Enron trader is when the trade is  concluded and, if there is any hope of further trading with the counterparty,  Credit and Legal should be notified to negotiate a master agreement.
Of  course, if the counterparty is outside the country where we are trading,  Legal should be consulted ahead of time (there are some countries where  derivatives are actually illegal, special procedures must be followed or  can't be done by us from the U.S.).
2.
If there is a master agreement between the counterparty and either ENA or  Enron Canada, and the Enron trader is in the U.S. or Canada, the trade should  be entered into by the trader on behalf of the Enron company that is party to  the master agreement.
If the trader is outside of the U.S. or Canada, other  rules may apply.
3.
If there is a master agreement between the counterparty and ECT  International (usually only European counterparties), and the Enron trader is  in the U.S. or the U.K., the trade should be entered into by the trader on  behalf of ECT International.
Note that there are special considerations if  the trader is in the U.K. based on U.K. regulatory issues (the trade is  actually "arranged" by Enron Europe Finance and Trading Ltd. on behalf of ECT  International).
If such a master exists but the trader is not in the U.S. or  U.K., the trade should be handed off to a trader located in one of those two  countries for final negotiation and execution.
It would be a good idea to  consult with Legal or Tax if this comes up for more specific advice.
These general rules relate to which Enron entity should be the legal  counterparty to the transactions.
This doesn't determine where within the  Enron family the actual risk should ultimately reside.
If we want the risk  to be in an Enron company other than the Enron counterparty for contractual  purposes, an intercompany transaction should be booked (probably through RMT)  to get the risk in the right place.

10.2 Effect of Force Majeure.
If a Force Majeure event affects Seller's ability to Deliver Scheduled Energy from the Facility, the following procedures and conditions shall apply:
(a) Seller shall as soon as reasonably practicable use commercially reasonable efforts to fulfill its obligations to deliver Scheduled Energy from Market Sources until notice is provided pursuant to Section 10.2(b) below.
(b) Not later than ten (10) Days following the onset of the Force Majeure event, Seller shall (i) issue a notice to Buyer stating whether Seller will continue to fulfill its obligations to Buyer hereunder from Market Sources until the Force Majeure event is terminated or (ii) declare Force Majeure and relieve Buyer from its obligation to pay the Demand Charge during the time that Seller is unable to meet its obligations hereunder, computed on a daily basis.
If Buyer does not Schedule Energy during the ten (10) day evaluation period and Seller declares Force Majeure, then Buyer's relief of the obligation to pay the Demand Charge shall commence as of the date of the Force Majeure event.
(c) If, during the ten (10) day evaluation period referenced above, Buyer Schedules Energy and Seller continues to Deliver Energy, but then declares Force Majeure, Buyer's relief from the obligation to pay the Demand Charge shall commence on the date of the declaration of Force Majeure and not on the date of onset of the Force Majeure event.
If, during the ten (10) day evaluation period Buyer Schedules Energy and Seller initially Delivers Energy but subsequently fails to Deliver, Buyer shall be relieved of the obligation to pay the Demand Charge from the date Seller fails to Deliver Energy, and not on the date of onset of the Force Majeure event.
Such relief from the Demand Charge shall be computed on a daily basis.

In the event of a Force Majeure affecting Buyer's ability to receive Energy from Seller, payment of the Demand Charge shall continue.
10.3 Termination Due to Force Majeure.
If an event of Force Majeure continues in effect for twelve (12) consecutive Months, then the Party not declaring Force Majeure may terminate this Agreement upon providing written notice of such termination to the other Party (but if such event of Force Majeure terminates before any such termination notice is provided, then this Agreement shall continue in full force and effect).

John and Randy, I got a call from Bob Sevitz regarding a change I made to the EECC revisions to the Co Op City EPC contract.  
Specifically, I deleted language he had added to the waiver of consequential damages.  
Bob had added a provision that said that the waiver was "subject to" the indemnification section of the contract. For example, under Bob’s proposed language, if the Owner brought a claim against the Contractor for consequential damages arising from a third-party injury covered under the indemnity section (such as a resident slipping and falling due to construction debris), the Owner could potentially bypass the waiver and hold the Contractor liable for consequential damages, including things like loss of rent, extended project delays, or reputational harm.  
I felt this was too broad of a carve out, especially from the contractor's point of view. This type of language could open up the Contractor to significant exposure for consequential damages, which the waiver was intended to exclude.  
Any tweaking of the indemnity language (to blatantly reconcile it with the waiver) can occur during the drafting process. For instance, if we want to clarify that indemnity is limited to direct damages or explicitly state that consequential damages remain waived even in the context of indemnified claims, we can address that as we work through the next draft.  
Just wanted to pass this along.  
Kay

Subject: Enron Amsterdam, UBS & European Discussion

Dear Colleagues,

I wanted to initiate a discussion around the intertwined themes presented in the subject line, given their historical significance and ongoing relevance in the financial landscape.

The collapse of Enron, with its tentacles reaching internationally to entities like Enron Amsterdam, serves as a powerful reminder of complex financial engineering, corporate governance failures, and the critical role of accounting transparency. Enron Amsterdam, in particular, often comes up in discussions about the company's international web of Special Purpose Entities (SPEs) and how they were used to obscure debt and manipulate financial statements, presenting a unique European angle to the scandal.

In parallel, major global financial institutions like UBS operate within a constantly evolving regulatory environment, profoundly shaped by events such as Enron. While not directly involved in the Enron scandal, the lessons learned from Enron – concerning auditor independence, corporate accountability, and the scrutiny of structured finance – have undoubtedly influenced how banks like UBS and other European institutions conduct their operations, manage risk, and comply with international and regional regulations. The post-Enron era brought about significant shifts in corporate governance and financial reporting standards across Europe and globally.

I am particularly interested in exploring the following:
*   What specific aspects of Enron's European operations, like those in Amsterdam, shed light on the broader scandal's international reach and methods?
*   How did the fallout from Enron influence regulatory changes and risk management practices within major European banks like UBS, particularly concerning derivatives, off-balance sheet financing, and corporate governance?
*   What are your perspectives on the lasting impact of the Enron scandal on European financial markets and regulatory frameworks, and how have institutions adapted?

Ladies and Gentlemen:

As a follow up to Jim Schiro's note, I am personally reaching out to you in the hope of gathering your most candid insights regarding the future of the Global Business Council. The path we are charting together is not only critical for our organization but may ultimately shape how we collaborate on a global scale for many years to come. Your feedback is not just valuable—it will be the foundation upon which we build the Council’s purpose, identity, and impact.

The decisions we make now will define the GBC’s role in championing progress, driving innovation, and strengthening our collective voice in a rapidly changing world. I recognize you each have demanding schedules, but I am asking you to pause—just briefly—to share your perspectives. Even a few lines, or an initial thought, could spark the ideas that define our future and, quite possibly, the futures of those we serve and lead.

Specifically, your reflections on the following will help us construct the framework of the Global Business Council:

ROLE   
- What do you believe are the primary objectives and defining activities of the GBC?
- What specific actions should the GBC boldly pursue—and, just as importantly, what should remain outside our scope?

STRUCTURE   
- Who do you see as essential members of the GBC, and how large should the Council be to remain effective and inclusive?
- What recommendations do you have for 1) the membership selection process, 2) membership terms, and 3) orientation, to ensure we have the strongest team possible?

GOVERNANCE   
- What should our leadership structure look like, to inspire confidence and accountability?
- How should we select leaders, and for what duration, to ensure both continuity and fresh perspectives?
- How frequently should the GBC convene to sustain momentum and connection?
- What are your thoughts on the ideal meeting format—face-to-face, rotating locations, or virtual—to maximize energy and engagement?

PROCESS   
- How can the GBC truly operate to achieve its aspirations—through working groups, special projects, ongoing interactions?
- Who should be at the table for these meetings (WEF members, GBC only)?
- What is the most effective way for the GBC to interact with other councils and consultative groups, so our work has real resonance and reach?

PERFORMANCE   
- How will we hold ourselves accountable—both as a group and as individuals—to the vital responsibilities in our charter?
- How can we foster open communication, vigorous discussion, and true consensus?
- How should we measure the effectiveness of our Council: our focus, our attendance, our level of preparation, and our meaningful participation?

There will never be a more crucial moment than this to share your vision and concerns. Your voice has the power to shape the direction and success of the GBC, and by extension, to affect change far beyond these walls.

We will incorporate your feedback—no matter how brief—into a draft charter and share it for your review next week. Your thoughts are urgently needed, and profoundly appreciated.

Thank you for your dedication, your honesty, and your leadership in helping to shape our collective future.

Sincerely,

Subject: Exploring Day Trading Systems

Dear [Recipient Name],

I'm writing to share some thoughts on day trading systems, a topic of significant interest for many active traders.

A day trading system is essentially a predefined set of rules or algorithms designed to identify entry and exit points for trades within a single trading day. The primary goal of these systems is to bring consistency to trading decisions, reduce emotional biases, and potentially capitalize on short-term price movements.

These systems can range from simple, manual strategies based on a few technical indicators (e.g., moving averages, RSI, MACD) to highly complex, automated algorithms that execute trades without human intervention. Common components often include:
*   **Technical Indicators:** For identifying trends, momentum, and overbought/oversold conditions.
*   **Price Action Analysis:** Studying candlestick patterns and support/resistance levels.
*   **Volume Analysis:** To confirm the strength of price movements.
*   **Risk Management Rules:** Defining stop-loss levels, profit targets, and position sizing.

While a well-designed system can offer a disciplined approach to trading, it's crucial to understand several key considerations:
1.  **No Guarantees of Profit:** No system can predict the market with 100% accuracy, and past performance is not indicative of future results.
2.  **Rigorous Backtesting:** Any system should be thoroughly tested against historical data to evaluate its potential efficacy.
3.  **Forward Testing/Paper Trading:** Practicing with the system in a live market environment (without real capital) is essential before deploying it with actual funds.
4.  **Adaptability:** Markets are dynamic, and a system that works today may need adjustments or become less effective over time.
5.  **Robust Risk Management:** This is arguably the most critical component. Even a system with a high win rate can lead to significant losses if risk is not properly managed.
6.  **Understanding Limitations:** Systems typically don't account for sudden news events, geopolitical shifts, or "black swan" events.

The effectiveness of a day trading system often depends on the trader's understanding of its underlying logic, their discipline in adhering to its rules, and their ability to manage risk effectively. It's a tool that requires ongoing refinement and a deep understanding of market dynamics.

If you have any specific systems in mind or would like to discuss this topic further, please feel free to reach out.

Best regards,

[Your Name]

Headline:  "Unocal, Tesoro, Pioneer, Equiva, Reliant Among Energy Companies Providing Opening-Day Insights at Interactive Energy 2001"  HOUSTON, TEXAS, November 19, 2001 - The opening-day program for Interactive Energy has been set with presentations from SAP, Booz Allen Hamilton and case studies and panel discussions from management from such companies as Reliant, Equiva, Tesoro, Unocal and SAIC.
Les Amidei, VP of business development for process from SAP America, will open the session to discuss how energy companies are working to gain maximum returns from their current investments.
Many of the larger companies committed to SAP's enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems during the past 15 years, and new innovations must interface with SAP to access and uplink enterprise data.
"With all the great promises of the internet, the energy industry has made numerous investments in information technology," notes Amidei.
"The reality is that while many have delivered, many [others] have not.
As a result, the overall climate has changed dramatically where any investment in technology will be driven by measurable and quantifiable ROI.
Leveraging existing investments such as ERP into new arenas will be critical in assuring maximum value is delivered.""
A panel of senior technology officers, including Xavier Flinois, president, Schlumberger Network Solutions; Tom Halbouty, CIO, Pioneer Natural Resources; Paul Cuneo, CIO, Equiva Services LLP; and Ray Cline, CTO, SAIC, will follow Amidei's presentation.
Each panelist will be asked how he or she is prioritizing IT spending and levering from investments made in previous years to maximize profitability.
Accenture Partner Jeff Sakaguchi will direct the discussion.
Then, Eduardo Alvarez, partner of Booz Allen Hamilton will wrap up the morning with a presentation on how some energy companies have managed innovation more effectively and what can be learned from their strategies.
In the afternoon, the conference will feature the results of an IT survey conducted by Booz Allen Hamilton and Zeus Development Corporation, which investigates how the upstream, refining and gas and power sectors are prioritizing IT spending.
The two firms have joined in the research project to interview information officers at many of the world's leading energy firms to understand how they are currently managing IT investment.
The report will enhance and build upon the earlier presentations, providing a broader industry perspective.
Then, four case studies will be presented: The first entitled, "Dropping the 'E:' Moving E-Business to Just Business" by Tim Pownell, general manager, e-procurement project, will discuss how  Unocal is in the process of fully integrating their e-business systems into the mainstream practices of the company.
The second, entitled "Rapid ERP Integration: A New Supervisory Application to Reduce Training Time and Improve Inventory Accuracy," which will be presented by Mark Evans, CIO, Tesoro, will discuss how Tesoro was able to integrate its marine logistics unit into the broader SAP ERP to improve performance, inventory accuracy and employee satisfaction.
The third and fourth presentations will be made by management from Reliant Resources Inc. to describe how they are using IT to prepare for Texas' forthcoming deregulated marketplace.
Will Symmes, director - energy information systems, will describe how Reliant has developed an internet-based energy information and analysis portal for large industrial customers, entitled "Energy Commander."
Then, Ron Orsini, vice president - eBusiness, will discuss how Reliant is investigating home automation technology to better serve residential and small business accounts.
"We're very pleased with the lineup for Wednesday and believe it provides a most important full-day forum for the opening discussion of Interactive Energy," said Nimocks.
"In the final analysis, our job is to facilitate the exchange of information and ideas so advancements can be made more efficiently, and this lineup promises to do that."
About Interactive Energy Interactive Energy will be held at Houston's George R. Brown Convention Center, Dec. 4-7.
The annual conference and exhibition covers information technology (IT) advancements in the energy industry and features numerous case studies of technology implementations, new software demonstrations, business plans and special workshops.
To register, please phone Mel Ladin at 832-200-3704 or go to www.interactiveenergy and click on "Register Now".
Conference Sponsors of Interactive Energy 2001 already include Enermetrix (www.enermetrix.com) SAIC (www.saic.com), AT&T (www.att.com), Microsoft Corporation (www.microsoft.com), Luminant Worldwide (www.luminant.com), Unisys (www.unisys.com), Conchango (www.conchango.com), Proclarity (www.proclarity.com), Silicon Energy (www.siliconenergy.com), Avocent (www.pixelvision.com), documentum (www.documentum.com), appropria (www.appropria.com) and Oracle (www.oracle.com).
Supporters include PR Newswire, Energy Central, TIPRO, Techxans and the Houston Business Journal.

Lesson Number One
*****************
A crow was sitting in a tree, doing nothing all day. A rabbit saw the crow and asked, "Can I also sit like you and do nothing all day?" The crow said, "Sure, why not." So the rabbit sat on the ground and rested. Suddenly, a fox appeared and ate the rabbit.

Management Lesson: To do nothing without consequences, you need to be very high up.

Lesson Number Two
*****************
A turkey was talking to a bull. "I wish I could get to the top of that tree," sighed the turkey, "but I don’t have the energy." The bull said, "Try eating some of my droppings—they’re full of nutrients." The turkey nibbled on some dung and had enough strength to reach the first branch. The next day, after eating more dung, he reached the second branch. After two weeks, the turkey was at the top of the tree. A farmer saw the turkey and shot it down.

Management Lesson: Bullshit might get you to the top, but it won’t keep you there.

Lesson Number Three
*******************
When the body was first made, all the parts wanted to be Boss. The brain said, "I should be Boss because I control everything." The feet said, "We should be Boss because we carry the brain." The hands said, "We should be Boss because we do all the work and earn the money." The heart, lungs, and eyes all gave their reasons. Then the asshole spoke up. Everyone laughed at the idea, so the asshole went on strike and stopped working. Soon the eyes crossed, the hands clenched, the feet twitched, the heart and lungs panicked, and the brain got a fever. Finally, they all agreed the asshole should be the Boss. All the other parts did the work while the Boss just sat and passed out the shit.

Management Lesson: You don’t need brains to be a Boss—any asshole will do.

Lesson Number Four
******************
A little bird was flying south for the winter. It was so cold, the bird froze and fell to the ground. A cow passed by and dropped dung on it. Lying in the dung, the bird realized it was warm, and it began to sing for joy. A cat heard the song, found the bird, dug it out, and ate it.

Management Lessons:
1) Not everyone who drops shit on you is your enemy.
2) Not everyone who gets you out of shit is your friend.
3) When you're in deep shit, keep your mouth shut!

During the past few days several people have approached us wondering why we=  are continuing to do college recruiting and continuing with the floor buil= d out given the state of the company today.
We appreciate people's concern= s about adding people and spending money at a time when we ought to be redu= cing unnecessary expenses.
Let us begin by saying that we share these conc= erns and are not hiring people or undertaking significant capital expenditu= res without a great deal of thought.
We would also encourage people to tal= k to their manager or either of us if you don't understand why we are doing=  certain things.
In short, we have decided to continue with the college re= cruiting, although we have not yet decided how many, if any, we will hire.
=  We have decided to delay the beginning of the floor build out for a couple=  of weeks.
Why Are We Continuing With College Recruiting?
During the last few years we have made tremendous progress establishing a p= resence for Enron broadly and the Portland office specifically with leading=  schools in the northwest.
This past year we finally reached critical mass=  and had tremendous success in our recruiting efforts.
Although we are unc= ertain about our hiring needs this year, we feel that it is in our best lon= g term interest to continue having a presence with the schools in the north= west.
We have already made presentations and done initial screenings at mo= st schools.
We have identified the best people from each school and have a= lready made plans for them to come to our office for two super Saturdays.
= The cost to us to finish this process is not large compared to the benefit = that we gain from honoring our commitment to the schools and students as pa= rticipants in their on-campus recruiting programs.
We also realize that it=  is a hard year to be coming out of school looking for a job.
It is our be= lief that students would rather interview with us even if the possibilities=  of employment may be somewhat diminished.
Finally, we would like to empha= size the point that we have not yet committed to hiring anybody.
We will i= nterview people, identify the best candidates, and make hiring decisions ba= sed on the needs of the office.
Before extending offers we will consider t= he potential impact that it could have on people in this office and Enron e= mployees in other offices who have been redeployed.
Stated another way, we=  don't intend to hire a bunch of new people if there are people within Enro= n who could fill positions or if it would put the jobs of the people alread= y here at risk.
We may end up postponing hiring decisions until we are mor= e certain about the state of affairs in the company.
How Will the Floor Move Play Out?
We have decided to postpone the floor build out for a few weeks.
While we = still think that it makes sense for the office, we have decided to pause fo= r a couple of weeks before we start to spend significant amounts of money o= n this.
When talking to the build out team today it became clear that dela= ying would accomplish several goals.
First, it allows us to get final arch= itectural plans in place and firm quotes from contractors so that we can mo= re precisely peg down the costs before moving forward.
Second, it gives th= e build out team breathing room to iron out more of the details of the move= .
Finally, it buys us a little more time to decide whether or not it makes=  sense to do this project given the state of affairs of the company right n= ow.
While we still think that we are going to move forward with this proje= ct, it seems like buying a couple of weeks of time is the right thing to do=  right now.
In about two weeks we will reconvene with the build out team w= ith firm budget numbers and make a decision to either move ahead, cancel, o= r delay again.
=20  As always, we will try to keep people updated on things as soon as new, rel= iable information becomes available.
We recognize that this is a very hard=  time for everyone.
Please try to stay focused on the job at hand and keep=  up the success of this office.

I spoke with Oscar Wyatt this afternoon on Crown and subsequently to Tom Bachtell, an attorney in Utah who is attempting to organize shareholders to replace existing management.
Crown has an asphalt oil sand production facility in northeast Utah and an asphalt distribution company.
Bachtell owns about 4-5% of the stock.

We have written down our carrying value to nil.

MCNIC has interests in the asphalt assets and is a lender to Crown.
MCNIC attempted to foreclose on certain Crown assets and Crown in turn counter-sued for $100 million.
The arbitration hearing will be held July 23 - August 10.
If Crown obtained an award from the arbitration, some value could be restored to our investment.
We will get further information from Bachtell on the details of his plans and recommend what position Enron should take in this matter.

Most folks probably listened in to the press conference, but for those that  didn't here's a summary of the ISO's proposal to FERC.
The description of  the proposal was vague and general, and Winters tends to speak in run-on  sentences, so if I've gotten anything wrong, please chime in.
$100 cap for "old" generation; "new" generation would be exempt.
FERC would require generators and SCs to contract forward for at least 70% of  their power.
For those that meet the 70% requirement, they will be exempt from the $100  cap, and the $250 cap will apply.
Winters believes that the 70% requirement, coupled with utility-controled  gen, will result in the IOUs scheduling about 85% of load into the forward  market.
Load and supply that deviate from schedules and go to the real time market  will be penalized (details to be "ironed" out).
The ISO is supposed to make the filing at FERC today.

Phillip, I'm embarking on a project to bring unprecedented clarity and precision to our financial hedging strategies. I'm building a robust, personalized daily tracking sheet designed to provide real-time insights into each individual's positions and P&L. Each day, it will automatically pull in the previous day's position and price curve to calculate the mark-to-market. Following this, daily transactions can be entered to accurately determine the P&L of closed positions and establish new open positions.

Initially, I thought that daily P&L could be calculated by simply adjusting the P&L whenever a transaction was made by the difference between the bid/offer of the closed out position by the offer/bid of the new position (of course time value and storage costs would be included). However, this only works if the person is 100% hedged, meaning they do not have any open positions which require marking. As the seller of synthetic storage utilizing 100% hedging, I should be able to do this, except for the fact that I will have size limits on transactions that will probably leave me open here and there. The main question I have is simply, "Should I be calculating the P&L for each person's storage book for open and closed positions?" Then beyond that, if we do calculate the P&L's from the buyer side, it seems that if their storage is not hedged, I will have to develop the market value of the storage in the ground and the remaining capacity to mark to market it. So, I guess I could apply the model for that purpose. Does this make sense to you? Any comments are appreciated. Thanks. Mat

Then beyond that, if  we do calculate the P&L's from the buyer side, it seems that if their storage  is not hedged, I will have to develop the market value of the storage in the  ground and the remaining capacity to mark to market it.

Does this make sense to you?
Any comments  are appreciated.
Thanks.
Mat

Hi!
I just got back from Germany!
It was a pleasant trip but things in Frankfurt are just so expensive.
I went there for a distributor's meeting, and had the opportunity to meet the people that we are having correspondence with over fax and e-mail in the past.
Our account officer is a pretty girl and she is only 23 years old.
The downside is that she is married for one year already.
Oh well, life's tough.
I think one of the other distributors noticed me flirting with this girl.
Well, a quarter of the way around the world should be fair game.
Anyway, I was surprised that Frankfurt wasn't that big of a city.
You can walk from the main parts of the city in a few minutes.
Mostly, they only have Churches (every five blocks there seems to be one), slaughterhouses, and castles.
In fact, they have been preserving so many allegedly historical buildings.
These are ugly ass buildings that have no apparent architectural appeal.
Due to this, the new European Central Bank buildings has to be built at the back of one of these alleged historical sites.
The building is long and takes up too much prime space with no apparent purpose whatsoever.
This seems to be a prevalent site in most of Frankfurt.
A pleasant surprise during my trip was that the company paid for my hotel room.
I was prepared to pay for it, but I wasn't charged when I checked-out.
Our meeting lasted from Monday to Thursday, which left Friday and Saturday free for me before my flight on Sunday.
I decided to join a city tour by bus to Rothenburg.
Well, I was initially set on going to Heidelberg but I met this American Chinese girl who was travelling alone and I decided to just accompany her to Rothenburg.
She works in Santa Clara for some upstart IT company.
I told my girlfriend about it because nothing really happened aside from us spending the whole of Friday and Saturday together.
Then again, I am not sure what I would have told her if something did happen ;-)  I'm seriously thinking of taking my Masters in Finance here in the University of the Philippines.
However, the application forms would only be available every May and the exam would be in August.
It would be a one-year course starting September, which would time my graduation right about when Claudine finishes her local board exams.
I guess I don't see a bright future here in the Philippines, and I may just follow her when she specializes in the States or Canada.
Unless something drastic happens and our country just progresses rapidly, or my stars change, I think that this would be the plan that I would take.
I guess her petitioning me for a Canadian citizenship would help a lot in getting a job in Canada or the US.
I'm pretty sure that the US economy would pick-up after two years.
You guys never stay down!
My country is sinking because of the ever-divided people.
There is no unity and I would suggest for us to just divide the goddamn country - one for the Muslims, one for the Chinese, and one for the Spanish people - then we call it the Divided States of the Philippines!!!
Oh well, I'm just ranting right now.
Just write when you have the time.
Have you spoken to Khan lately?
Tell his ass to write me!
I haven't heard from him for quite some time now.
I hope he is okay.
Send him my regards.
Cliff

Subject: Court Ruling Invalidates 2003 Prozac Patent—Implications for Generic Fluoxetine Launch

Dear Team,

I am writing to inform you about the recent court ruling declaring the 2003 Prozac (fluoxetine) patent invalid due to double patenting. This decision effectively removes the primary barrier to market entry for generic versions of fluoxetine.

Key Implications:
- The invalidation means generic manufacturers can now legally launch their fluoxetine products without risk of infringing the 2003 patent.
- This is expected to lead to a significant increase in competition and a rapid decrease in the market price of fluoxetine.
- Market exclusivity for the branded product will cease, and we should anticipate changes in prescribing trends and payer formularies as generics become available.

Please let me know if you need further details or a more comprehensive analysis of this development.

Best regards,  
[Your Name]
source_text:
We learned today that the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit has modified its opinion of August 9, 2000 in which it found the 2003 Prozac patent invalid for double patenting.
In essence, the Court has again ruled that the patent is invalid for double patenting, but has used a different analysis to reach this conclusion.
We intend to seek legal review of today's decision.
Although it is possible that the legal review process could delay Barr from entering the market on August 3, we continue to plan for Barr launching generic fluoxetine at that time.

I interpret Wednesday's NGPL order (RP00-18-002) as applying solely to NGPL, given their unique restrictions and tariff rules. I do not believe it forces the rest of the industry to use the floor rate as the reserve price for negotiated index rate bids and ordinary recourse rate bids.

Instead, I think we can still determine the reserve price on prearranged deals, like the ENA deal, based on our good faith valuation of the index mechanism's upside. This means we can value the index mechanism at "x cents" for such a deal and, consequently, require a discounted recourse rate bidder to bid more than the floor plus "x cents" to win. Agreed?

DF

I think we  can still determine the reserve price on a prearranged deal like the ENA deal  based on our good faith valuation of the upside provided by the index  mechanism.
I.e., on that type of deal, we can determine that the index  mechanism is worth "x cents" to us and require a discounted recourse rate  bidder to bid more than the floor plus x cents to win.

There are 2 open issues on Dresdner Bank:

1. Netting - they are saying that operationally they cannot net across product lines. Are you okay with this?

2. Calculation Agent - they want to be the Calculation Agent. Since we have no CSA with them, this means that they would be doing all of the calculations required under each transaction that we enter into with them. Specifically, the CA does the following:
   - calculates the Floating Price and the Floating Amount, Fixed Amount or Cash Settlement Amount payable
   - gives notice of Settlement and Payment Dates
   - determines whether a Market Disruption Event has occurred

Also, my notes indicate that we agreed to increase the Guaranty cap to $25,000,000 from $15,000,000. Is that okay with you? They had initially requested no cap.

On Reliant Energy Services, Inc., you were going to think about the following credit issues:

1. Specified Transaction - they want to include physical energy deals. You were going to think about this and whether we needed a cap. They wanted to amend the definition of Specified Indebtedness to deal with this, but I think you and I felt that it should be dealt with in the definition of Specified Transaction.

2. Cross Default threshold - is 3% of equity okay?

3. On Credit Event Upon Merger, they want to define "materially weaker" as either (1) being below investment grade by either S&P or Moody's or (2) failing to be rated by either S&P or Moody's.

4. On setoff, they did not have the "affiliate" language.

5. In the CSA, they want the collateral that is posted to secure both financial deals and physical gas and power deals entered into between ENA and Reliant Energy Services, Inc.

6. In the collateral threshold, they have proposed a matrix of S&P and Moody's ratings, with the threshold amount being the lower of the 2 ratings:
   AA-/Aa3 and above        $20,000,000
   A-/A3 to A+/A1           $15,000,000
   BBB/Baa2 to BBB+/Baa1    $10,000,000
   BBB-/Baa3                $5,000,000

Also, they have defined MAC to be going below BBB- by S&P or below Baa3 by Moody's or a failure to be rated by either S&P or Moody's.

7. In the LC provisions, they have different cure periods for each of the types of Letter of Credit Defaults that can occur. Here is a summary of the events and the time periods for transferring substitute collateral:
   - If issuer's credit rating is downgraded - 1 business day after written demand by the Secured Party
   - If issuer fails to comply with its obligations under the LC or disaffirms or rejects the LC - 1 business day after the pledgor receives notice of dishonor
   - If LC fails to be in full force and effect or issuer declares bankruptcy - 3 business days after written demand by Secured Party

In our form, we require substitute collateral to be posted within 2 business days of the occurrence of the above events, except for a downgrade where the time period is 5 business days.

On SG Interests, you were going to talk to them about certain credit issues.

Please let me know when you can where you stand on the above.

Thanks.

Mark,

We sent Chisholm an electronic copy of the LOI and received comprehensive feedback with several key concerns that need to be addressed before we can move forward.

**Issue #1: "Obligation" Language in Paragraph 2**

In paragraph 2, Chisholm has raised significant concerns about our use of the term "obligation," specifically noting that we never clearly define what constitutes our "current obligation." During our follow-up call with their legal team, they emphasized that this vague terminology raises compliance red flags and could create ambiguity in contract interpretation. Their general counsel specifically mentioned that without clear definition of what obligations we're referencing, they cannot assess the full scope of what they're agreeing to.

We explained extensively that the existing NDA and all its conditions, including confidentiality provisions, data protection requirements, and disclosure limitations, would remain fully in place and enforceable throughout this new agreement. However, Chisholm's legal team indicated they need this continuity to be explicitly stated in clearer, more definitive language rather than implied through the broad term "obligation."

Is there a way we can revise the language to more transparently articulate the continuation of our existing NDA framework without using the problematic "obligation" terminology? Perhaps we could specify: "All terms, conditions, and provisions of the existing Non-Disclosure Agreement dated [DATE] shall remain in full force and effect" or similar explicit language.

**Issue #2: Non-Solicitation Clause Incompatibility**

The non-solicitation clause has emerged as another significant point of contention that requires immediate resolution. During our detailed discussion with Chisholm's project management team, we learned that their current operational structure fundamentally conflicts with our proposed non-solicitation terms.

Specifically, Chisholm has provided evidence that they are:
- Currently utilizing graduate students from their engineering program to develop an internal proprietary system for similar applications
- Already engaged in active negotiations with at least three other vendors (they provided a list of companies including TechSolutions Inc., DataFlow Systems, and Advanced Analytics Corp.)
- Committed to a multi-vendor evaluation process as part of their standard procurement policy
- Required by their institutional guidelines to maintain competitive bidding processes for technology implementations exceeding $50,000

Given these documented existing relationships and institutional requirements, Chisholm's procurement director has confirmed that our standard non-solicitation clause simply will not work within their operational framework and could potentially violate their institutional procurement policies.

**Proposed Solution: Notification Clause**

After extensive discussion with their team, we have collaboratively developed an alternative approach that addresses both parties' concerns. Instead of the restrictive non-solicitation language, we propose implementing a comprehensive notification and transparency clause.

The suggested language would read: "Chisholm agrees that it will provide written notification to Enron within ten (10) business days if and when it decides to enter into formal negotiations, issue a letter of intent, or execute a binding agreement with any third-party vendor for services substantially similar to those outlined in this agreement. Such notification shall include the general scope of services being considered and anticipated timeline for vendor selection, while respecting any confidentiality obligations Chisholm may have with other parties."

This approach provides us with:
- Advance notice of competitive activities
- Transparency into their vendor selection timeline
- Opportunity to adjust our proposal strategy accordingly
- Maintained relationship integrity without restricting their business operations

**Next Steps Required**

Please review these proposed modifications and let me know your thoughts. I believe these changes will address Chisholm's legitimate concerns while still protecting Enron's interests. We should also consider whether these revised terms could serve as a template for similar situations with other institutional clients.

Give me a call if this doesn't make sense or if you need additional clarification on any of these points. I'm available this afternoon after 2 PM or tomorrow morning before 10 AM for a detailed discussion.

Thanks.
Make It A Great Day!!

Lorie E. Hernandez
Specialist - E-Commerce Transaction Development

If you didn't believe us before, I'm sure it is by now painfully clear that  negotiating master swap agreements is a very lengthy process.
My impression  is that the commercial team in Portland is anxious to begin trading  financially.
If this is correct, it would be possible, at least from a legal  point of view, to begin trading now under the existing documents.
In each  case where a master agreement is already in place, trades entered into before  the amendments we want will certainly be binding on both parties.
Our only  issues with trading under these agreements are where we need more restrictive  credit provisions and that resumption of trading before an amendment is  signed reduces to some extent our negotiating leverage.
As to the credit  issue, only the credit group can decide whether or not to permit trading  under the existing terms.
As for the negotiating leverage, if the commercial  people want to resume trading immediately, my suggestion would be to let them  go ahead.
If it turns out that additional leverage is needed, we can always  stop trading.
Where no master swap agreement exists, we have documentation available to  enable trading on a limited basis until the master is signed.
The so-called  "omnibus" confirmation will work for any normal commodity derivative  transaction and can be customized to include necessary credit provisions -  even where multiple trades exist with the same counterparty.
Tana has unsuccessfully tried to get you access to our Lotus Notes database  so you could determine the status of any negotiation on an up-to-the-minute  basis.
She will be sending a monthly report of our progress until you get  the necessary software to access the database.
Of course, if any issues come  up in the meantime, please continue to feel free to call.

Victor LaMadrid will manage the Southeast Logistics team and will report directly to Scott Neal.

Dear Ken,

I am a second-year associate with the RAC underwriting group. Over the past few days, I have observed fellow staff members packing their personal items in anticipation of a massive layoff. At the same time, some employees have begun legal action against the company—perhaps understandably, given the circumstances.

In light of these events, I believe it is important for all of us to offer ideas and suggestions on how best to handle the situation, regardless of how unorthodox these ideas may seem. While you and the leadership team have likely considered and perhaps even rejected many suggestions already, I wanted to share a thought that may be worth revisiting.

Specifically, I wonder how feasible it would be to persuade our creditors or debt holders to convert a significant portion (if not all) of their debt holdings into preferred equity, with an option to convert to common equity. Such a move could improve our credit rating, reduce cash outflows on interest payments, and provide us with greater flexibility to borrow as needed. Additionally, offering creditors a favorable conversion ratio—especially if they make a concurrent cash infusion—could be defensible, even in the event of bankruptcy.

Admittedly, banks and other creditors are typically reluctant to accept equity positions. However, given the current circumstances, this approach might become more palatable, particularly if it serves to protect their investments in the long term.

I understand this is a challenging time, and that you have many urgent matters to address. Nevertheless, I hope to share ideas with you from time to time, for as long as I remain here. I have absolute confidence in the capabilities of our leadership team and trust that you are all doing your utmost to improve the situation.

Best regards,

I know it is a tough time and you have a lot of better things to do rather than reading emails, however, I will be pitching my ideas to you from time to time (as long as I'm around).

Subject: Summary of Recent FERC Draft Orders - NYISO and ISO-NE Market Rules Updates

Dear Team,

Please find below a summary of key FERC draft orders impacting NYISO and ISO-NE operations:

**NYISO Market Rules & Bid Caps:**
- FERC approved modifications to energy bid cap methodology, raising the system-wide offer cap from $1,000/MWh to $2,000/MWh during scarcity conditions
- New demand curve parameters for installed capacity markets effective for the 2024-2025 capability year
- Enhanced price formation rules to better reflect operational constraints and scarcity pricing

**ISO-NE Updates:**
- Approval of Forward Capacity Market (FCM) rule changes including new capacity accreditation methodology for intermittent resources
- Modifications to real-time reserve pricing to improve market efficiency
- Updated transmission cost allocation for reliability projects

**Virtual Bidding:**
- FERC maintained existing virtual bidding rules for both RTOs with minor refinements to position limits
- Enhanced monitoring and reporting requirements for virtual transactions
- Clarification on portfolio bidding restrictions

**Interconnection Costs:**
- New cost allocation methodology for network upgrades in generator interconnection queue
- Streamlined study processes to reduce interconnection timeline delays
- Updated financial security requirements for interconnection customers

**Calpine Complaint Decision:**
- FERC denied Calpine's complaint regarding capacity market mitigation rules
- Upheld existing buyer-side mitigation framework
- Reinforced cost-of-new-entry calculations for competitive capacity offers

These changes will take effect over the coming months. Please coordinate with your respective market operations teams for implementation planning.

Best regards,
[Your Name]

Today FERC issued the following draft orders:  NYISO TEP and Bid Cap (ER01-3001):  Commission granted NYISO's request to extend the currently effective $1000/MWh Bid Caps on certain NYISO adminstered markets, and to extend its Temporary Extraordinary Procedures for Correcting Market Design Flaws and Addressing Transitional Abnormalities, until the Northeastern RTO is operational.
The Commission ordered NYISO to narrow the scope of the TEP, and to file tariff sheets doing so within 30 days.
NYISO proposed virtual bidding procedures (ER01-3009; ER01-3153):  Tariff changes to implement virtual bidding were approved.
The changes would allow market participants to bid non-physical generation and load into the day-ahead market and settle the bids in the real-time market.
Also accepted were NYISOs Market Mitigation Measures to address gaming or market power strategies that might emerge as a result of the virtual bidding.
NYISO - Cost responsibility for new interconnections.
(ER01-2967):  Tariff changes allocating cost responsibility for interconnection facilities.
The provisions allocate to developers 100% of the cost of facilities necessary to physically interconnect the project.
Additionally, developers are allocated the coswts for transmission system upgrades that would not have been made "but for" the interconnection, minus the cost of any facilities that the NYISO's regional plan dictates would have been necessary anyway for load growth and reliability purposes.
ISO-NE - Interim Bid Caps (ER01-3086):  Commission approved extension of bid caps until the Northeastern RTO is operational.
Calpine v. ISO-NE (EL01-124):  Commission granted complaint by Calpine and Mirant, finding that ISO-NE has amended Market Rule 5 to exclude external contracts from setting the energy clearing price, in violation of a Commission order.
If you need further information, please let me know.
Susan Lindberg x30596

4.  **Unsustainable Valuation Disparity & Potential Scenarios:** We consider the current gap between public and private market valuations unsustainable, projecting three possible outcomes: 1) Stock prices could rebound, correcting the disparity; 2) IPPs might reduce new plant capital allocation, opting for share buybacks or acquiring other IPPs; or 3) Domestic/foreign traditional utilities or external entities might acquire IPPs.

Regards,

Rick/Bill/David, Generally, we have managed to keep our main counterparts transacting, but things are tight.
We are signing netting agreements and agreeing to collateral threshholds, but we are negotiating hard where we think that we will be so close to collateral lines in the next few months that we would actually have to post.
As we go into this week, we need to hold on to those we have, incrementally open up a few more, and start to get people to business as usual.
Amongst the things that continues to be missing are the OFFICIAL STORY (we have access to the newspaper here, too), good communication regarding global relationships, and calendar and status of new developments regarding credit facilities, equity issuance/raising.....  Not that some of it is getting through, it just comes through random channels and we know very little more than our counterparts that have a subscription to the Wall Street Journal.
To that end, it has been suggested here that Houston (PR?)
with RAC/Finance develop a daily script of talking points for the masses.
We have traders and credit people talking all day to counterparts - they really could use a strong story to tell without have to think about it.
I am very confident that I can tell a reasonable story myself, but I am concerned that I do not have all the facts at my disposal and my guess is that the average trader/credit specialist is probably at a greater disadvantage.
Thoughts?
Ted

Subject: Upcoming Amendment: Allowing Cash as Eligible Collateral Under BMO ISDA – Procedural and Cost Considerations

Dear Team,

I hope this email finds you well. I am writing to inform you of an upcoming amendment to our BMO ISDA agreement that will allow cash to be utilized as eligible collateral for our derivative transactions.

**Key Changes:**
- Cash (USD, CAD, EUR, GBP) will be added to the list of eligible collateral types
- Minimum transfer amounts and thresholds will be adjusted accordingly
- Interest rates on cash collateral will be based on overnight benchmark rates less applicable spreads

**Procedural Considerations:**
- Legal documentation requires execution by both parties within 30 business days
- Operations team must update collateral management systems to accommodate cash postings
- New daily cash sweep processes will need to be established
- Enhanced reporting requirements for cash collateral positions

**Cost Implications:**
- Estimated one-time implementation costs: $15,000-$25,000 (systems updates, legal review)
- Ongoing operational costs: $5,000-$8,000 annually (enhanced reporting, reconciliation)
- Potential funding cost savings through improved collateral efficiency
- Reduced haircuts on cash vs. securities may lower overall collateral requirements

**Next Steps:**
1. Legal review and approval by December 15th
2. Systems testing scheduled for January 2024
3. Staff training on new procedures in early January
4. Go-live target date: February 1st, 2024

Please review this information and provide any feedback or concerns by December 8th. I will be scheduling a team meeting next week to discuss implementation details.

Best regards,
[Your Name]

What's Next for Enron Federal Credit Union

Over the years, Enron Federal Credit Union has been proud to share the Enron name and support many wonderful employees and their family members around the world. As we all know, it's been quite the ride!

Here are some of the exciting changes slated for the Credit Union in the coming months (and no, we're not going anywhere).

**New Name**
We believe it's time for a fresh start with a new name – you know, something that doesn't make people do a double-take when they hear it! Our new name will reflect everything that we actually stand for: trustworthiness, outstanding service, innovative products, value and convenience. (All the good stuff, basically.)

You can expect to hear about our official new name later this month. We promise it'll be much easier to explain at parties.

**Expanded Field of Membership**
Since being the exclusive credit union for Enron Corp. has become, well, a bit limiting, we're expanding our field of membership! We'll continue to welcome and serve current Enron employees and their families (we're not abandoning ship), but we're also rolling out the welcome mat for individuals and businesses that live, work or worship in Downtown Houston and the surrounding areas.

**Additional Location**
We're also putting down some new roots! We've made plans to open an additional full-service facility located conveniently close to the Enron Building in the downtown area. Think of it as our way of staying in the neighborhood while branching out.

More details about our new digs will be announced as soon as we have them. In the meantime, our current office will remain open and ready to serve all our members.

We're genuinely excited about the changes that 2002 will bring and look forward to sharing this adventure with each of our members. Thanks for sticking with us!

We create television programming focused on politics and public policy that broadcasts in state capital cities. Our current operations span Pennsylvania and Ohio, with planned expansion into New Jersey, Maryland, and Delaware.

Our innovative approach centers on this concept: the television program primarily targets the guest rather than the viewing audience.

Lobbyists face challenges securing meetings with politicians and regulators, and even when successful, they struggle to obtain meaningful intellectual engagement from government officials. We have resolved both issues.

Politicians and appointed officials are eager for television appearances and consistently accept our invitations. When they inquire about discussion topics—such as telecommunications competition or electricity deregulation—they request background materials, which they thoroughly review to ensure strong on-air performance. We achieve similar results by including journalists, radio hosts, and television commentators on our panels.

Phase three: Provide briefing documents and/or conduct pre-recording briefings

Hey Guys.
The ISO cutting our off-peak imports from PV has been an ongoing problem.
Now that we are doing congestion wheels again we can finally do something to avoid these cuts using congestion wheels.
Normally the ISO will cut our Import and shift our load from NP15 (PGE1&2&3) across the path to relieve the congestion.
If you submit a congestion wheel there cannot be $30 cong,  thus they will not cut your schedule going in at PV.
Instead of shifting your load the ISO will award your congestion wheel and everybody will be happy.
It is important to make your wheel larger then your import to ensure that part of your import not getting cut.
I would recommend to put in the max number of MW's you think you can buy in the North and get rid of in the Desert.
Go big in the off-peak, we submitted 200MW wheels Saturday and I think its safe to do similar size most nights.
Geir

Hello All—

Human Resources Department

She  said she would do further research, given the difficult fact that—because of regulatory restrictions—Utilicorp, the GP, simply cannot furnish a Guaranty. I made it clear to her just how important this is to us. At the very least, we would need Utilicorp to be designated a "Specified Entity" so that they're directly tied to the credit-related Events of Default in the ISDA Master. I stressed how critical this is: whenever the counterparty is an LP and your comfort really comes from the GP’s credit, it’s absolutely essential to make the GP a "Specified Entity"—otherwise, if something disastrous happened to them, like bankruptcy, we’d be left completely exposed. This is our line of defense. Please call me if you have any questions—this is not something we can afford to mishandle.  
carol

Southern Trails proposed, at an estimated cost of $155,000,000, a pipeline  project consisting mostly of 693 miles of crude oil pipeline acquired from  ARCO.
Ten percent of the project would be new construction and the remainder  would be conversion of the crude oil line to gas service.
The pipeline  system would be divided into an East Zone and a West Zone.
The East Zone,  which will begin in the San Juan Basin and end at the California border, will  have 87,500 Dth/d of available capacity.
The West Zone, wholly within  California, will have 120,000 Dth/d.
Southern Trails received certificate authority for the project on July  28,2000.
An optional certificate application does not require any showing of  market need; however, Southern Trails did hold an open season from Sept. to  Oct. 1998 during which it received 22 bids totalling 810,000 Dth/d of  demand.
The order issuing the certificate did not say how much of the  capacity had been subscribed, only that Southern Trails had contracted with  its affiliate, Questar Energy, for 30,000 Dth/d of firm capacity in theh East  Zone for 5 years and one month, and taht firm transportation service  agreements of 5 and 10 year terms are "being negotiated" with prospective  shippers which, if executed, would subscribe the balance of the capacity in  both the East and West zones.
TW is an intervenor in this docket so I have received everything that has  been filed.
I have no further information about any further subscription of  capacity.
I also have no information regarding any progress that has been  made on construction.
If you need a more detailed summary of the proposal that was filed at FERC,  or if you have any other questions, please let me know and I'll see what I  can find.
I've got the entire environmental report in my office if we need  that for any reason!
