Last month, I sat across from Maria Santos, a veteran project manager who'd spent three years trying to get permits for a clean energy facility in Riverside County. Her folder was thick with rejection letters, environmental impact studies, and appeals to various agencies. "It's like trying to solve a Rubik's cube blindfolded," she told me, exhaustion evident in her voice. "Every time I think I'm close, another agency wants a different study, a new assessment, or raises a concern nobody mentioned before."


Maria's story isn't unique—it's emblematic of California's power plant siting crisis.


Overall, we respect the effort, but California failed to get the ball over the goal line: On Siting Intentionally or not, California has designed power plant siting laws that make it excruciatingly difficult to construct power plants in the state.


Folks seem to have lost sight of the need to balance growth and environmental quality in California. That's why nothing's been built in the state for a decade and developers are going outside the state to build power plants. Maria herself recently accepted a position in Arizona, where her company finally decided to focus their efforts.


Tinkering around the edges won't help; and (with all due respect) the legislation passed yesterday tinkers. Real reform is required if California hopes to build the supply necessary to keep pace with Silicon Valley and a high tech culture and tame the price spikes.


If developers continue to have to navigate through a maze of a half a dozen—or more—state and local agencies, California's supply problems will persist, and we'll see more talented professionals like Maria taking their expertise to states that actually want to solve their energy challenges.

Dear Mr. Lay,

I am one of many long-time employees who has lost my life's savings and my kids' college fund.  
Today I am receiving my 15 Years of Service Award and having my anniversary luncheon.  
Would you like to attend?  
My department would appreciate a candid explanation of how this could have happened to such a great company.  
I have gone through tough times and many good times with Northern Natural Gas, InterNorth, and Enron.  
I was always so proud to be a part of this company.  
Should I have seen this coming?  
I was just another sheep, following and believing everything our leaders, including Skilling, said regarding the probability of Enron's stock splitting.  
I didn't play the market, but looked at my 401(k) stock purchases as long-term retirement and continued to put money into the 401(k) even when we (my family) were struggling to do so.  
I, too, grew up on a farm in Missouri.  
I was raised under the same Midwest-rooted values and the strict convictions of my father: that you did not take charity or borrow money.  
He also preached that to sue was not the way to correct a wrong.  
I was always a little prideful that you, too, were a Midwesterner, with those rooted values of high integrity, compassion, and honesty.  
Life goes on.  
I hope to continue my employment through all of this and will continue to be a great employee, only now for Dynegy.  
This is also a concern since I am in my late 40s.  
My job, my kids' education, and my retirement weigh heavily on me, along with the atmosphere we are all currently living in.  
This reality is a struggle, with many unanswered questions and devastating concerns for the future.  
I would appreciate your thoughts.

Respectfully yours,

The following e-mail is to confirm my understanding of several verbal assurances provided to me—assurances delivered across a series of meetings in offices shadowed by boxes and dry-erase boards hastily wiped clean, as Enron’s gas and power trading business prepared for transition. My questions echoed in half-empty conference rooms, the muted hum of uncertainty in the air, as legal pads and Styrofoam coffee cups gathered on the long walnut tables.

If a new entity purchases the Enron trading business and the contingent employment agreement executed on January 5, 2002 becomes a valid and binding agreement, Enron's management will not initiate a lawsuit to recover the 2001 performance bonus payments. This was stated in firm voices while the winter light filtered through the blinds and rows of cubicles stood quieter than usual.

Enron and/or the purchaser of the Enron trading business will seek approval from the bankruptcy judge of the 2001 performance bonus payments to eliminate any future uncertainty with respect to the validity of those payments—a measure emphasized during tense discussions with legal counsel, their laptops casting a cold glow on anxious faces as they reviewed page after page of documentation.

To the extent the total retention $'s available for the Enron trading business employees is increased above current levels (from the leading bidder as of January 5, 2002), the intent of Enron's senior management is to make an upward adjustment to the individual employees who have committed to the new entity, such that the employee maintains a substantially similar percentage of the total "pool" of retention $'s. This assurance was reiterated as managers paced along the glass-walled hallways, stressing their commitment even as footsteps echoed, signaling a business and its people on the brink of major change.

Dear Stakeholders,

I am writing to address the significant implications of Southern California Edison's potential bankruptcy filing on Independent Power Producers (IPPs) operating within California's energy market.

**Immediate Concerns:**

The potential bankruptcy filing creates substantial uncertainty for IPPs currently under Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) with SCE. Key risks include:

- **Contract Security**: Existing long-term PPAs may face renegotiation or potential rejection under bankruptcy proceedings
- **Payment Delays**: Outstanding receivables and future payments could be subject to extended collection periods
- **Credit Risk**: Increased counterparty risk for all SCE contractual obligations

**Market-Wide Implications:**

This development extends beyond direct SCE contracts, affecting:

- **Energy Pricing**: Potential market volatility as supply agreements face uncertainty
- **Financing Challenges**: Lenders may tighten requirements for California-based renewable projects
- **Regulatory Response**: CPUC intervention could reshape existing market structures

**Recommended Actions:**

1. Review all SCE-related contractual agreements immediately
2. Assess exposure levels and implement risk mitigation strategies
3. Engage legal counsel specializing in utility bankruptcy proceedings
4. Diversify counterparty exposure where possible
5. Monitor CPUC proceedings and regulatory developments closely

We will continue monitoring this situation and provide updates as developments unfold. Please contact our team with any immediate concerns regarding your specific exposure.

Best regards,

[Your Name]
[Your Title]

The following additions and modifications to Stack Manager will be effective as of Saturday September 8, 2001.
Stack Manager Modifications  Inactivate All Stack - In addition to the individual Activate/Inactive Stack buttons, there is now an Inactivate All Stack button.
Similar to the Suspend All button, this button will inactivate the trader's stack on all active products.
Any existing top of stack limit orders will continue to post to the website and remain transactable.
See screen shot below: Inactivate All Stack button on far right.
Please note that we have switched the positions of the suspend and inactivate buttons in Stack Manager.
Fill Order - If a product is set up as either Restricted Top of Stack or Top of Stack the trader now has the ability to automatically fill any order that is at the top of the stack.
In order to fill a limit order that is at the top of the product's stack, which will appear in pink, the trader should right click anywhere on the stack window and choose "Fill order".
The volume filled on an order will be that which is offered by the trader.
In order to fill the complete volume of the order, the trader will need to adjust the volume in his stack.
Floated Stack windows - If the stack is inactive on a product, the price and volume fields on the my products tab will continue to be blank.
On the depth window and floated stack window of these products the trader's prices will be in gray and italics.
Children of products that have inactive stacks will not be gray and italicised in the floated stack windows and will not see the calculated prices.
No Auto Inactivate Stack - It is now possible to keep a product active even if the trader is not logged into Stack Manager.
If the trader wishes to enable this functionality on the upper right corner of the product properties page the trader should choose "No Auto Inactivate when Stack Manager is down".
Changes regarding Suspension of products  Stack Manager will inactivate products rather than suspend them in the following cases:  ?
Market Close - If a product is active at the end of its trading hours its stack will automatically become inactive rather than suspending.
In order to keep a product's stack active past the set trading hours, the trader should choose "Keep Awake" next to the trading hours section of the product properties page.
?
Auto Suspend now inactivates stack - On a product with the Auto Suspend function enabled to monitor the price changes on the product, the product's stack will be inactivated if the Suspend at level is reached.
This feature can be used by checking the Enable box on the product properties page under the Auto Suspend section.
?
Logging Out of Stack Manager- When you log out of Stack Manager without inactivating or suspending your products, the system will now inactivate your products rather than suspending them.

Subject: Enron's Flexible Model vs. Energy Companies' Asset-Heavy Approach

Dear Team,

I wanted to share some thoughts on the fundamental differences between our business model and that of traditional energy companies.

While conventional energy firms focus on owning physical assets - power plants, pipelines, and refineries - our approach emphasizes flexibility and market positioning. We've built our success on trading capabilities, risk management, and creating innovative financial instruments around energy commodities.

This asset-light strategy allows us to:
- Respond quickly to market opportunities
- Avoid the heavy capital expenditures required for infrastructure
- Generate returns through market intelligence rather than operational efficiency
- Scale our business without proportional increases in fixed costs

Traditional utilities are constrained by their physical assets and regulatory oversight. They generate steady but limited returns on their substantial investments. Our model, by contrast, allows us to capture value from market volatility and inefficiencies.

The question we should continue asking ourselves is: How can we further leverage this flexibility advantage while maintaining our competitive position in the evolving energy marketplace?

I'd welcome your thoughts on how we can continue to optimize this approach.

Best regards,
[Name]
source_text:
Dave, I still believe that the most flexible model that provides high ROCE  and has growth not constrained by capital is the one being employed by  Enron.
I think the cash on cash returns on these Genco's in the short run  will be good; however, I think it will be difficult for these companies to  move quickly to react to market opportunities given their need to protect  their long position (not unlike our friends in the oil & gas producing  sector).
The returns and value provided by these companies will be primarily  be based on the timing of new production and their asset base and they will  realize (on a relative basis) very little from the trading.
It is not a bad model just a different one.
Either way, they will be  a strong bid for assets given their story to Wall  Street.
Regards

in this uncertain world, how do we set priorities when everything feels urgent and the path ahead is constantly changing? It’s a challenge many of us face, both personally and professionally.

One effective approach is to anchor ourselves in core values and a clear mission. When decisions are grounded in what truly matters to us or our organization, it becomes easier to filter out the noise and identify tasks that align with our ultimate purpose. Ask yourself: "Does this task move me closer to my most important goals or values?"

Another crucial step is to differentiate between urgency and importance. Not everything that screams for immediate attention is truly important, and many important tasks are not urgent. Tools like the Eisenhower Matrix (Urgent/Important, Important/Not Urgent, Urgent/Not Important, Neither) can be incredibly helpful in categorizing tasks and dedicating resources appropriately. Prioritizing important but not urgent tasks often leads to long-term success and prevents future crises.

Finally, embrace flexibility and iterative planning. In an uncertain environment, rigid, long-term plans can quickly become obsolete. Instead, focus on shorter planning cycles, regular reviews, and a willingness to adapt. This allows for continuous learning and adjustment, ensuring your priorities remain relevant even as circumstances evolve.

By combining a strong values compass, a clear distinction between urgency and importance, and agile planning, we can navigate uncertainty more effectively and ensure our efforts are directed where they will make the biggest impact.

We have identified an increasing number of instances where unique or non-standardized descriptions are being applied to DRN/DRN fields as data flows through our automated pipelines. *   Pipeline failures and errors.
*   Increased manual intervention and troubleshooting time.
*   Inconsistent reporting and data analysis.
*   Delays in data availability and processing.

Dear market participants: methodology for nyiso virtual bidding credit requirements:

This email provides an overview of the credit methodology used to determine financial security requirements for virtual bidding activities in the New York Independent System Operator (NYISO) markets.

Virtual bidding participants must maintain adequate credit to support their market positions. The credit requirement calculation considers the following key components:

1. Maximum potential loss exposure based on historical price volatility
2. Portfolio diversification benefits across different locations and time periods
3. Stress testing scenarios including extreme market conditions
4. Collateral requirements updated daily based on open positions

The credit methodology employs a Value-at-Risk approach with a 99% confidence interval over a 7-day holding period. This calculation incorporates:

- Historical price data spanning the previous 12 months
- Correlation analysis between different pricing nodes
- Seasonal adjustments for demand patterns
- Transmission constraint impact factors

Participants must post initial credit equal to 110% of the calculated requirement. Additional margin calls may be issued if positions exceed predetermined thresholds or if market volatility increases significantly.

Credit instruments accepted include cash deposits, letters of credit from approved financial institutions, and investment-grade corporate guarantees. All credit postings must be maintained throughout the settlement period.

For questions regarding specific credit calculations or acceptable collateral forms, please contact the NYISO Credit Department at creditrisk@nyiso.com.

Best regards,
NYISO Market Operations

Dear Market Participants:  Methodology used in developing the NYISO Virtual Bidding Credit Requirements:  Day Ahead Market Hourly Zonal LBMP and Real Time Market Integrated Hourly Zonal LBMP values were used as the data source for developing the NYISO Virtual Bidding Credit Requirements.
These values are available on the NYISO web site.
The time period of June 1, 2001 through August 31, 2001 was used.
Peak hours are defined here as the hours of 6am (06:00) through and including 10pm (22:00).
The absolute value of the difference of the DAM and R/T price was calculated for each peak hour.
The 97th percentile of these series of prices was calculated for each zone.
The maximum of these zonal 97th percentiles was calculated to be $159.33.
The data manipulation and calculation was performed in MS Excel.
The attached spreadsheet contains the data used in the June 2001 to August 2001 calculations.
(See attached file: Virt Bidding Credit Req data.xls)   Please contact the Customer Relations department with any questions.
Regards,

Hello , my name is Tori Kuykendall (One Pass BJ927934).
My husband, Patrick(  One Pass VF751282), and I have been One Pass members for a few years now as  well as elite members on several occasions.
We also use Chase Continental  Visa exclusively, and my husband is a President's Club member.
I have made  Continental my airline of choice for as long as I can remember booking my own  travel arrangements and have been a very satisfied customer in the past.
This morning, however, I had a very bad experience.
I booked tickets for a  vacation back on September 4th for a trip from Houston to New York on  December 1.
Since I booked the ticket, I became pregnant and found out from  my doctor last week that I will still be unable to travel on December 1st due  to complications with my pregnancy.
My doctor indicated to me that I may not  be able to fly at all during my pregnancy, which is due to end in June.
I  spoke to Leroy Peterson this morning to explain the situation, and he  indicated that all he could do was give me credit that would expire on  September 5th, 2001 and that a $75 service would be charged to me next time I  book a ticket for me or my husband.
I understand that this is the same  policy that you would have given me if I had just decided that I didn't feel  like taking a vacation this weekend.
In my opinion, this is an unacceptable  policy in the event of medical complications.
As you can see with my  situation, it is unlikely that my husband and I will be able to plan a  vacation by September of 2001 considering we will hopefully have a 2 month  old child.
I repeatedly asked Leroy if there was anyone else who could help  me or anyone I could talk to in order to get some kind of exception to your  policy.
I indicated that I could provide a doctor's note if necessary.
He  was very rude to me, stating "You don't have to ask me 7 different times for  the same thing - I already told you NO!"
I had to cancel a flight for work  about a month ago on Southwest airlines for the same reason, but I was hoping  that I would be able to fly again by now.
For your information, your  competitor was very helpful.
They accepted my doctor's note, gave me a  credit good for one year, and will allow me to change the ticket to another  person's name if I am still unable to use it.
That ticket was also booked as  a non-refundable fare.
Although I have always used Continental  for my  personal travel, the treatment I have had in this difficult time has  definitely made me second-guess my future choices.
If there is anything you  can do to help, I would greatly appreciate it.

Sara,

The east and west power trading desks are implementing different pricing methodologies for floating price language in certain power pools, creating a potential operational inconsistency.

**Key Difference:**
- West desk: Averages negative prices as zero
- East desk: Includes all prices (positive and negative) in calculations

**Issues:**
- Neither desk has provided a clear business rationale for their preferred approach
- ENA may take either side of these deals, making the methodology choice particularly important
- The confirm desk must now track deal sources to apply correct pricing language
- Potential online trading system complications remain unclear

**Recommendation:**
We need to establish a unified approach. I recommend requiring both desks to justify their methodologies before allowing this divergence to continue, as it creates operational complexity and potential confusion.

Thoughts?

Sara
source_text:
The east and west power desks are creating slightly different floating price  language for some of the power pools.
The west desk wants "negative prices"  to be averaged in as "zeroes"; the east desk wants to average in all prices  "positive or negative".
I'm inclined to let the traders do as they wish.
I  can't seem to get an explanation for the difference in approach (in each  instance ENA may take either side of the deal).
The confirm desk will have  to pay attention to the source of the confirms to use the correct pricing  language.
I don't know if this will create an on-line trading issue.
What do you think?
Sara

Bryan and I commenced the annual task of adorning our home with Christmas decorations this week. On Sunday, the Christmas tree was retrieved from storage and subsequently erected in the living room. Our strategy involved dedicating a segment of each evening to this endeavor, with the objective of achieving a fully adorned residence by Thanksgiving.

On Monday, Bryan meticulously affixed the lights to the tree. Subsequently, I began the process of unwrapping various ornaments, initially for the purpose of examination. Following the complete unwrapping of all ornaments, we collectively resolved to finalize the tree's adornment. Bryan adopted a somewhat deferential stance, permitting me to largely manage the decorative endeavors. Nevertheless, I observed that among the initial ornaments he placed was my heart-shaped Nicole ornament. Upon completion, we reclined amidst the luminous ambiance cast by the large-bulb lights, appreciating our adorned tree.

It was at this juncture that Bryan apprised me of my oversight in locating a novel ornament. He indicated that a new item had been placed on one of our two Christmas trees—specifically, either the smaller 'Charlie Brown' tree situated in the bedroom or the prominent main tree in the living room. My initial search of the 'Charlie Brown' tree yielded no discovery, prompting me to direct my attention to the main tree.

After a brief reconnaissance of the main tree, an intuitive, almost childlike impulse suggested, "Search for a ring, search for a ring." However, my more pragmatic inclination urged, "Locate the ornament." Precisely at that moment, I discovered a resplendent diamond ring suspended from the heart-shaped Nicole ornament. My engagement ring had been present on the tree throughout the entire duration. My profound focus on the decorative process had rendered me oblivious to its presence.

Bryan has subsequently jested that a typical individual would have immediately discerned the presence of a diamond ring on the tree.

I am delighted and eager to formally announce that Bryan and I are now engaged to be wed. As of yet, specific details regarding the date, time, venue, or even the city for the ceremony remain undetermined. Nevertheless, my eagerness to share this news precluded any further delay. I anticipate maintaining a pronounced expression of joy for a considerable duration.

Regards,
Nicole

That is part of this Word of Testimony.

Dear Team,

source_text:
I've gotten a bit more educated about IT revenue crediting since you asked  your question yesterday.
"IT revenue crediting" is an industry term used to  describe a requirement (brought about either by a FERC order or a rate case  settlement) that IT revenues in excess of a certain dollar amount will be  credited back to all firm shippers in the next rate proceeding or thru some  refund mechanism.
Transwestern is currently not under any IT revenue  crediting obligation, and I would be very hesitant to negotiate any such  obligation with any individual shipper because then we would have to do the  same for all firm shippers on a nondiscriminatory basis.
If you need more info, let's talk.

**URGENT: El Paso's Oversubscription Crisis Demands Immediate Action and Fair Compensation**

Last week's critical discussions regarding El Paso's systematic oversubscription of the Socal Topock Point revealed a pattern of mismanagement that has cost producers millions and threatens the integrity of our entire system.

**The Financial Crisis is Real and Escalating**
The devastating impact cannot be ignored: Border cuts have inflicted $3 million in direct losses on Amoco and Burlington alone, while forcing an additional $15 million in fuel costs when mainline fuel was reduced and gathering fuel increased. Producers are rightfully demanding a minimum of $17 million in compensation – a figure that represents only the beginning of El Paso's financial obligations.

**The Core Problem: Dangerous Oversubscription**
The facts are undeniable: 1.2 bcf/day is being nominated at Socal Topock, which can only deliver 540,000 mmbtu/day. This represents a staggering 220% oversubscription that threatens system reliability and producer operations.

While SoCal Gas claims this crisis will resolve when their system becomes unbundled under Gatekeeper (pending CPUC approval for October 1, 2001 implementation), we cannot afford to wait. Under Gatekeeper, only 540,000 mmbtu/day will be accepted at Socal Topock and must match intra-state transport requirements.

**SoCal Gas's Proposed Solution Shows a Path Forward**
SoCal Gas has presented a logical framework: divide the 1.2 bcf/day nominations based on original capacity intent – 400 to Mohave, 540 to Socal Topock, and 180 to PGE Topock. They've demonstrated flexibility by accepting less than 540 at Topock (minimum 300 for core needs) with appropriate compensation and agreeing to maintain status quo until Gatekeeper implementation.

Williams has shown leadership by offering to examine CD reduction, reduced take requirements, or alternate points with rate adjustments.

**El Paso's Counter-Proposal Falls Short**
El Paso's interim solution, while addressing some concerns, still forces producers to accept devastating 37% cuts. Their proposal includes:

1. Block 1 Capacity permanently alternate to Socal Topock (198,000)
2. Block II Capacity restrictions at PGE Topock (614,000)
3. Amoco and OneOk contract modifications (45,000/d each)
4. Expansion shipper capacity redistribution
5. Final Socal Topock allocation totaling 851,000 with 540÷841 = 37% cuts

**Producers' Justified Resistance**
The 37% cut proposal is unacceptable. Producers correctly argue that any transport sold after their September 28 complaint should be terminated first, particularly El Paso's merchant services Block 3 capacity. This principle of "last in, first out" is both fair and industry standard.

**The Path Forward Demands Action**
Separate meetings among Topock shippers demonstrate the urgent need for collective action. El Paso must be held accountable for their oversubscription practices and provide immediate, fair compensation while implementing a solution that doesn't penalize existing shippers for El Paso's mismanagement.

The time for half-measures has passed. We need decisive action that protects producer rights and ensures system integrity.

Steve and Lindy, as I mentioned in our staff meeting, it is probably not going to be possible to solve our max rate cap dilemma by making a tariff filing unless we can 1) get FERC to change its mind about its policy that recourse rates always be available as an alternative to negotiated rates or 2) prove that Transwestern lacks market power and should therefore be allowed to charge market based rates.

The following is a very brief outline of what would be required to prove lack of market power. A warning: lack of market power is very difficult to prove. Koch, a pipeline that most in the industry would agree does lack market power, tried and failed. The deck is already stacked against us in TW's case given the withholding of capacity by El Paso's affiliate and the price conditions in California. 

However, we do need to analyze the possibilities for TW, if not to the Cal. border, then on other parts of our system. Additionally, we need to discuss acceptable incentives for shippers to pay negotiated rates if we do not end up changing our tariff.

Would you be available on Tuesday to discuss this? Please let me know. In the meantime, here is a summary of FERC's policy on market based rates.

*** To obtain authority to charge market based rates, TW would first have to request a declaratory order, and in its application provide information showing it meets the requirements outlined below. If the Commission finds all requirements have been met, it will issue an order and TW would then make the appropriate tariff filing to put market based rates into effect.

Application for declaratory order must include:

1. Detailed description of the services proposed for market-based rate treatment. I assume in our case it would be firm transportation service.

2. A statement defining the relevant product and geographic markets necessary for establishing the applicant lacks market power with respect to the services at issue. The Commission requires a narrow definition of the market ("firm transportation" is probably narrow enough, but for our purposes we might want to narrow it down more (i.e., firm transportation East of Thoreau). We have to define substitute services available to shippers (other pipelines are a "good substitute" only if shippers can obtain the same quality of service on a timely basis, and if the other pipelines offer such service at a price that would deter TW from raising its prices more than 10%). All relevant "origin markets" must be defined (Panhandle; West Texas) as well as "destination markets," and alternatives for shippers in those markets identified. Transportation alternatives are only good alternatives if they provide a netback to shippers that is roughly the same as if they used TW. Note that the Commission has rejected capacity release as a good alternative since it does not guarantee a shipper its desired contract quantity.

3. Market share and HHI calculations; discussion of other relevant competitive factors. Commission looks at size of market share, mitigating factors such as ease of entry, and market concentration as measured by HHI. Market concentration has to be calculated for each relevant receipt point and delivery point. HHI is calculated by adding up the total market share and squaring it. There is a presumption of no ease of entry for transportation services because of the expense involved in constructing facilities.

4. Proposal for accounting for costs and revenues.

Over the past few days, several people have come to us asking why we are still conducting college recruiting and moving forward with the floor build-out, given the current situation of the company.  
We appreciate everyone’s concerns about adding staff and incurring expenses when we should be trimming unnecessary costs.  
First, we want to say that we share these concerns and are not hiring or committing to significant capital spending without careful consideration.  
If you are unclear on the reasoning behind certain decisions, we encourage you to speak with your manager or either of us directly.  
In summary, we have elected to proceed with college recruiting, although no final decisions have been made on the number—or whether—we will hire at all.  
We have chosen to postpone the start of the floor build-out for a few weeks.  

Why Are We Continuing With College Recruiting?  
Over the past few years, we have made significant progress establishing Enron’s presence, and specifically the Portland office, at top schools in the northwest.  
This past year, we finally reached a critical mass and achieved excellent results in our recruiting efforts.  
While we are not certain what our hiring needs will be this year, we feel it is in our best long-term interest to maintain our presence with these schools.  
We have already done presentations and initial screenings at most schools.  
We have selected the top candidates from each school and have scheduled them to visit our office for two super Saturdays.  
The remaining cost to complete this process is relatively small compared to the benefit we gain from honoring our commitments to the schools and students as part of their campus recruiting programs.  
We also recognize that this is a challenging year for new graduates seeking jobs.  
We believe students would still prefer the opportunity to interview with us, even if the prospects for employment are somewhat limited.  
It’s important to note that we have not committed to hiring anyone yet.  
We will interview candidates, identify the strongest ones, and make hiring decisions based on our office’s needs.  
Before making offers, we will factor in the potential impact on current staff in this office and Enron employees elsewhere who may be redeployed.  
Put simply, we do not plan to hire new people if there are existing Enron employees who could fill those roles or if doing so would jeopardize current employees’ positions.  
We may even postpone hiring decisions until we have greater clarity on the company’s outlook.  

How Will the Floor Move Play Out?  
We have decided to delay the floor build-out for a few weeks.  
While we continue to believe that this project makes sense for the office, we have chosen to pause for a couple of weeks before incurring substantial costs.  
Discussions with the build-out team today made it clear that a delay would achieve a few important objectives.  
First, it lets us finalize the architectural plans and get firm bids from contractors so we can more accurately determine the costs before proceeding.  
Second, it gives the build-out team more time to work through additional logistics of the move.  
Finally, it gives us a little extra time to assess whether this project still makes sense, considering the company’s current situation.  
Although we are still leaning toward moving forward with the build-out, it seems prudent to buy a couple more weeks before making any major commitment.  
In about two weeks, we will meet again with the build-out team, review finalized budget numbers, and then decide whether to proceed, cancel, or delay further.  

As always, we will keep everyone updated as soon as new, reliable information becomes available.  
We know this is a difficult period for everyone.  
Please try to remain focused on your work and continue contributing to the office’s success.  

Tim Belden and Chris Calger

Lisa and Liz: The fluorescent overhead lights hum quietly in the office as we pore over the binder-thick EEI master agreements from Great Bay, El Paso Electric, and LG&E Power, their stiff paper fraught with legal fine print. Each of them has issued us Letters of Credit that now sit in our file cabinet, time-stamped by the last courier delivery. A drawing condition hangs in the air like tension before a storm: they’ve failed to provide alternate security, and less than 20 days remain before the LC’s expiration dates flicker ominously on our compliance calendar. 

Another drawing condition lingers in the dense legal text: a "default" under the EEI. For both the LG&E and Great Bay EEI masters, the definition of default is precise, almost chilly—if a party fails to establish, maintain, extend, or increase Performance Assurance as required under the Agreement, default is triggered. Yet as we press our fingers to the page, the definition of Letter of Credit in each Master is frustratingly spare; there’s no language ensuring that it has to be acceptable to us.

El Paso’s master, in contrast, lays out its own path. There, the notion of default springs to life when a party fails to meet the collateral requirements of Article 8. Flipping to that section, it’s clear: in that Master, the LC must be “acceptable to us,” giving us at least one strand of something solid.

So with the seconds ticking down, can we argue that this failure to renew—this silence where a new Letter of Credit should be—constitutes a “default” strong enough for us to terminate and draw?

New e-platform opens market to producers
EnergyGateway.com yesterday launched a new platform, allowing gas producers to conduct online transactions with variable service levels. The platform opens the online marketplace to small and medium producers, EnergyGateway.com said.

Producers can choose their service level (swing, interruptible, or firm) with each offer. This allows buyers and sellers to transact for any term, elevating the platform beyond a simple day-trading tool, according to EnergyGateway.com.

"Wholesale trading platforms often ignore the highly customized needs of producers and consumers. All market participants value liquidity, competitive processes, and access to strategic information, not just trading companies," said EnergyGateway.com CEO Mark Jergens. "Such platforms essentially prohibit the sale of natural gas in the way it's produced, flowed, and transacted."

By allowing more producers to compete online, EnergyGateway.com expects its program to create savings. "To build the best portal for buyers and sellers, we must have direct contact with the producer community," Jergens explained. "This program allows us to serve producers nationwide who want to participate in e-commerce but are blocked by wholesale entry barriers."

Columbus, Ohio-based EnergyGateway.com is an independent developer of e-communities, offering transaction services and strategic market information to large natural gas and electric suppliers and consumers. The company also plans to offer small business and residential customers a nationwide preferred provider network of natural gas and electric suppliers in 2001.
VM

I have a couple REMINDERS for all staff on the 24 Hour Desk.

1. There MUST be a cut note created for each occurrence of a curtailment and posted on the Discussion Forum in Lotus Notes. This includes any reduction in scheduled power deliveries, whether due to transmission constraints, equipment failures, or grid reliability issues. The cut note should specify the MW amount reduced, duration, affected delivery points, and reason code. Post these immediately when curtailments occur, not at shift end.

2. The Shift Note should also be posted on the Discussion Forum each morning by 8:00 AM. Include overnight trading activity, market conditions, any operational issues, weather impacts, and key information for the incoming day shift. Use the standard shift note template in the shared folder.

3. Make sure you get a good hand-off from the departing staff, Day or Night Shift. Spend at least 15-20 minutes going over: current desk position (long/short by hour), active deals and their status, counterparties who are actively buying/selling, any transmission constraints or outages affecting our delivery points, pending confirmations, and any unusual market conditions. Don't just rely on the shift note - have a verbal discussion.

4. Keep good personal notes on trades using the desk log template. Record counterparty name, contact person, MW quantity, price, delivery period, delivery point, product type, and confirmation status. Update these notes throughout your shift and file them in the shared drive before leaving.

5. Identify what type of product you are buying/selling for each trade: Non-firm (interruptible), Transmission Contingent (subject to available transmission capacity), TLR Contingent (subject to Transmission Loading Relief procedures), or Firm. Always specify the MW amount and price (e.g., "50 MW Non-firm HE 16-20 @ $45/MWh" or "100 MW TLR Contingent real-time @ $65/MWh"). Document the specific transmission path and any contingencies.

6. Continue to import power into PJM in the morning until future notice. Focus on the 6 AM to 10 AM window when PJM prices typically spike. Target 200-300 MW of imports during HE 7-9, primarily from MISO and NYISO when price differentials exceed $10/MWh after transmission costs.

7. Hammer the phones during high-volatility periods (6-10 AM and 4-8 PM). Call utilities that you don't normally call - try smaller municipal utilities, co-ops, and industrial customers who may have flexible load or generation. Explore new deal structures like hourly shaping products, weekend/weekday swaps, and weather-contingent deals. Consider reverse flows during low-load periods when prices invert.

The winter is not far away, therefore we must be ready to profit from the morning and late afternoon volatility. Peak winter demand can drive prices to $100-200/MWh during morning ramp and evening peak. Build relationships now with counterparties who will trade during these critical periods.

Give me a call on my cell phone (555-0123) if you have any questions, market opportunities above 100 MW, or if prices exceed $75/MWh.

Thanks,

Listening in by phone is so much better than traveling to these meetings.
It greatly reduces one's exposure to the toxins of this process.
1.
A learned expert on Secured Transactions  from Mike's firm gave an opening address on the principles of granting and receiving the grantation of security interests.
Almost completely irrelevant.
The guy up and suggested that for a given transaction, the parties might consider giving a security interest in an office building, ie.real estate,  as collateral.
2.
A cannabalized EEI Credit Support Annex  was tabled by Deedee Russo of Reliant and muddled through.
The format was typically:      Mike:  "Okay guys, why don't you explain to me what you want."
Member:  "We think we need this...blah blah blah, "    Mike:  "Okay, we'll put that into our next draft and have a conference call in December and a meeting in   January and remember, none of this is binding, its all optional."
3.
At the very end, a lawyer from PacifiCorp managed to raise the vital issue and Mike got his hackles up very quickly.
The PacifiCorp guy was basically saying that the WSPP was becoming more and more like the EEI and that this made it more and more difficult for parties to decide which agreement to use.
His implication was that the WSPP should try to remain different or throw in the towel and be just like the EEI.
Small reacted from a position of religion, dogmatically and loudly asserting that the two agreements were fundamentally different.
Here is where he left himself open to the shining light of rational analysis:  if someone, had the time,  and we thought it mattered enough, the approach to take would be this:    Dispassionate Spokesperson:  A question has been raised:  is the WSPP agreement becoming more or less like the EEI?
To fairly answer this question one needs to look at all the changes that have been made by  the WSPP in the last three years, comparing each change to the EEI agreement.
(prepare comparison document).
If we look at the evidence do we see convergence or divergence?
The answer will be overwhelmingly convergence.
If this objective study could be placed before the "Membership" it would speak for itself.
Nobody would have to utter a word.
The comparison document would do the job.
If we are going to bother playing with these guys, this is what we should do.
It would take some time, but if we circulated it to the membership and then merely raised the question of future direction, we might deal this tedious process a mortal blow.
Believe it or not, the solution to  this process is to follow the same process that went on when the King James Bible was put together in 1611.
Various scholars took various views on how various Hebrew passages should be translated, and it took a committee of draftsmen, appointed and sent to Geneva  by King James  to pound out the form that has stood the test of time for centuries.
The Joint Drafting Committee's time on the historical stage is finally arriving.
I am going to talk to this Pacificorp fellow and Brenda Anderson at BPA and see what happens.
----cgy

The agreement is currently designed to cover master agreements and transactions specifically between Enron North America Corp. ("ENA") and/or Enron Power Marketing, Inc. ("EPMI") and two major American Electric Power ("AEP") trading affiliates: American Electric Power Service Corporation as Agent for the AEP Operating Companies ("AEP"), which represents AEP's suite of regulated utilities such as Appalachian Power Company, Indiana Michigan Power Company, and others; and AEP Energy Services, Inc. ("AEPESI"), which handles unregulated trading activities.

The Netting Agreement explicitly enumerates the enabling agreements between these entities that cover the purchase and sale of both physical and financial commodities. This includes, but is not limited to, master purchase and sale agreements for physical natural gas (using NAESB contracts), master power purchase and sale agreements for physical and financial electricity (employing EEI agreements), and ISDA master agreements for OTC financial swaps on power and gas. For example, physical gas deals transacted through NAESB contracts executed in 2001-2002, physical power exchanges under the EEI Master Agreement, and financial swap structures such as fixed-for-floating, heat rate, and spark spread swaps entered into between ENA/EPMI and either AEP or AEPESI are specifically contemplated for netting within this agreement. 

Earlier today, the Enron Credit group advised that ENA trades (using General Terms and Conditions or “GTCs”) not only physical coal but also physical synthetic fuel (“synfuel”) products with American Electric Power Service Corporation. This typically involves structured contracts for delivery of Central Appalachian coal and synfuel to AEP generating stations, with monthly invoice settlements subject to setoff and netting under the proposed agreement.

Please contact me with any questions.

-- David

Subject: Evaluation of LNG Terminal and Pipeline Feasibility in Freeport

Dear [Recipient’s Name],

I am writing to provide an initial assessment regarding the feasibility and competitiveness of constructing an LNG terminal and associated pipeline infrastructure in the Freeport area, based on projected market conditions and estimated costs.

Market Outlook:  
Global LNG demand continues to grow, especially in Asia and Europe, driven by the energy transition and the search for stable, diversified supply sources. While competition among LNG exporters remains strong, the U.S. retains cost advantages due to abundant domestic natural gas and well-developed infrastructure.

Site Considerations:  
Freeport’s strategic location on the Gulf Coast offers proximity to existing gas supply networks, shipping channels, and skilled labor. Environmental and permitting regulations must be reviewed, but preliminary indicators suggest the location is favorable compared to less developed alternatives.

Cost Projections:  
The capital investment required for a new terminal (liquefaction, storage, and berths) and the supporting pipeline infrastructure is estimated at $8–12 billion, varying with capacity and technological choice. Construction costs remain volatile due to labor availability and materials pricing, but Freeport’s deep industry base may help mitigate inflationary pressures.

Competitiveness:  
Under current forward price curves, U.S. LNG remains competitive, particularly for buyers seeking long-term contracts versus spot exposure. The ability to secure sufficient offtake commitments is critical to project viability. Key risks include potential cost overruns, regulatory delays, and future shifts in global LNG pricing dynamics.

Next Steps:  
A detailed pre-FEED study is recommended to refine cost estimates, assess technical requirements, and further analyze regulatory, commercial, and environmental factors. Engaging with potential offtakers and local authorities early will be essential for derisking the project.

Please let me know if you would like to discuss these findings in further detail or schedule a meeting with the project team.

Best regards,  
[Your Name]  
[Your Position]

Jaime: Just wanted to update you on the call that I had this morning with Jose and Pablo.

The conversation started in my home office, the faint whoosh of the air conditioning blending with the soft hum of my computer. Outside, I could hear the distant sounds of the city waking up—trucks rumbling, birds calling from sun-dappled branches, occasionally a shout or laugh from the street below. The aroma of my coffee—deep, rich, faintly bitter—hovered near as I reviewed my notes before dialing in.

As the call began, there was a faint crackle over the line before Jose’s voice came through, warm and measured, layered with the background buzz of an office somewhere in Mexico City; papers shuffled, a printer whirred to life, and once or twice I caught the quick clack of someone’s heels on tile. Pablo joined in with a softer tone and the murmured background of colleagues chatting near him—occasionally punctuated by spurts of laughter and the aroma of cologne and strong brewing espresso wafting through their office.

As a general matter, after a few moments of polite small talk, the conversation turned practical. There was the scratch of pens on pads as we discussed our approach. I felt the smooth, slightly cool edge of the printed materials in my hand: glossy brochures, textured letterhead, slick plastic tabs of presentation binders. José noted that they are in the process of reviewing the online documents—likely sitting at his desk right now, the faint citrus scent of cleaning spray lingering on the surface, the paper slightly rough under his fingers.

They will get back to me sometime next week with any thoughts or recommendations. One area that we will need to be careful in is in how we market Enron Online; José’s tone grew sharper at this point, the low rattle of a nearby air vent underscoring his caution. There are restrictions in connection with the offering of “securities.” While it is fairly clear that commodity-based derivatives are not securities, there may be other products where it is not so clear-cut. 

I think that it would be very helpful if you would send to Jose and Pablo the online materials (i.e., brochures, etc.) that we would plan to send to prospective counterparties, so that we can make sure that our marketing efforts don’t violate any restrictions that we would be subject to. As I said this, I ran my thumb along the crisp edge of a freshly printed pamphlet, smelling the faint tang of ink and paper. 

Here is their address:

Subject: Concerns About UH Faculty Member's Public Commentary

Dear [Recipient],

I am writing to express my concerns regarding recent public statements made by a University of Houston faculty member. While I understand and support academic freedom and the right to personal expression, I believe some recent commentary may not align with the professional standards and institutional values we expect from our faculty.

I would appreciate the opportunity to discuss this matter further and understand what processes exist for addressing such concerns. I believe it's important to maintain open dialogue about how we balance individual expression rights with our collective responsibility to uphold the university's mission and reputation.

Thank you for your time and consideration of this matter. I look forward to your response.

Sincerely,
[Your name]

Hi, Ken:  I'm a former ECT VP who is just down the street, back at Ryder Scott Company which was my home before my six-years with Enron.
A great six-ears, in fact, I learned much and enjoyed the Company and the company, but it does feel better to be back in the "oil patch".
I still have stock and will continue to be a stockholder as I know the company will continue to be innovative and dynamic.
My reason for this email is a recent op-ed piece in the Houston Chronicle by Robert Buzzanco decrying the current campaign against terrorism.
His editorial was at best silly, fraught with inaccuracies (as a geological engineer I rely on facts - minorities make up 34.4% of the combined arm forces - not the opposite as suggested in Buzzanco's piece) and intended only to protract his personal agenda which has nothing to do with peace.
This may be more about selling his anti-American books than current events.
I could really care less about this person, he certainly has the right to conduct his protest, many have fought and died for his right and more may die in the coming days.
I do object to this guy using the University of Houston to lend credibility to his cause.
That's like an Enron employee (purely an example) marching in protests wearing the logo and identifying him or herself with Enron.
He is a private citizen when he writes an editorial or marches in protest.
He used his position at UofH  to get his piece in the paper.
I know you are an alumnus, and I ask you to read his editorial (10/8) and respond according to your hear.
Keep the ship on course, Ken.
Respectfully  Thomas M. Talley

Ken,  As you'll recall, during the September 10th advisory board meeting, we discussed the need for strong, senior-level support to ensure an opportunity for Xcelerator's success.
At the conclusion of the meeting, we agreed you and Greg Whalley would discuss the support level with the Management Committee on the 13th.
Of course, the sad events of the 11th understandably delayed that timeline.
Since September 10th, I've revisited the Xcelerator with several members of the Management Committee including Louise Kitchen, John Lovorato, Jim Fallon, John Sheriff, and Andy Fastow.
In summary, they are supportive contingent on support from you and Greg.
Additionally, other Xcelerator board members are supportive - specifically Jeff Donahue and Kevin Garland - but all agree the sincere support from you and Greg will be necessary for success.
Greg Whalley and I have also discussed the Xcelerator on two occasions.
Greg is concerned that I will be unable to attract good talent from within Enron to this "risky" initiative, especially given the trajectory of the economy and scarcity of new jobs within the company.
I agree with him.
Greg asked if I would try the Xcelerator understanding that most if not all of the full-time team members would need to be hired from the outside.
Although not optimal, I think it is doable and told him I'd be willing to proceed under those circumstances.
While Greg was quite supportive, he was appropriately distracted by the upcoming board meeting and close of the quarter.
As a result, he and I are planning on discussing the future of the Xcelerator this Tuesday.
(Of course, the earnings announcement may delay that discussion to next week.)
As I mentioned in the Xcelerator's board meeting, I am excited about this opportunity and am committed to giving it my all, with the support of the senior team.
This effort could create tremendous value for Enron.
However, I have no delusions about how difficult it will be and the patience it will require.
If we are successful over '02, we will definitely create value for our shareholders, but are almost certain to be a drag on earnings -- albeit a small one.
If you and Greg are not able to be supportive, then let's acknowledge that and discontinue the Xcelerator's operations.
As we discussed on the 10th, lukewarm senior support will not be sufficient for success.

Andy,  Just finished meeting with Nelson from gas fundies and Martin Lim from power fundies to discuss getting the Exotica libraries migrated ASAP.

The best I can get from them is "hopefully tomorrow" as far as a date for migration. They are dealing with the validation of calculation routines between the UBS libraries and the Exotica libraries since Exotica will play a role in pnl calculation. According to Nelson, they've identified several discrepancies in the pricing models that need to be resolved before they can sign off on the migration. Martin mentioned that the power derivatives team has been running parallel tests for the past three days, and while most vanilla products are matching within acceptable tolerance levels, some of the more complex structured products are showing variance issues that could impact daily P&L reporting.

I will follow up on this again tomorrow, but wanted to give you a more detailed picture of what's causing the delay. The validation process involves cross-checking approximately 200 different calculation routines, and they've only completed about 60% of the testing so far. The remaining 40% includes some critical volatility surface calculations that are essential for our options pricing.

I told them that "hopefully tomorrow" was not the answer I was looking for so I would help out in any way. Nelson suggested that if we can provide additional resources from our quant team to help with the validation testing, it could accelerate the timeline. He specifically mentioned that having someone familiar with our current pricing models could help identify the root causes of the discrepancies they're seeing.

They recognize that we need these libraries loaded on our machines regardless of their validation. Martin confirmed that the technical infrastructure is ready and the installation process itself would only take about 2 hours once they get the green light. The holdup is purely on the validation side, not the deployment logistics.

Also, Nelson showed me a list of the products that are scheduled for 'day 1' and power options are not on that list. The current priority ranking has gas swaps, gas options, and basic power forwards in the first tier, with power options relegated to 'day 2' or potentially 'day 3' depending on how the initial rollout goes. This could significantly impact our power trading desk's ability to price and risk-manage their book during the transition period.

There are a lot of people working with that list to prioritize support so this is just a heads up for you. I saw representatives from at least four different trading desks in the meeting, all lobbying for their products to be moved up in priority. The final decision apparently needs to go through the trading floor steering committee, but Nelson indicated that power options might get bumped up if we can demonstrate critical business impact.

Later.
Rob

Dear [Recipient Name],

I hope this message finds you well. I am reaching out to share my intention to write a comprehensive book chronicling the history of Enron, from its early days to its eventual collapse and the far-reaching impact it had on the business and regulatory landscape.

Given your expertise and experience in [relevant field/industry], I would greatly appreciate your thoughts on this project. Additionally, if you have any insights, resources, or contacts who might be valuable for my research, I would be grateful for your recommendations.

source_text:
Dear Ken:   When the timing is right, I would like to visit  with you (and Linda if appropriate) to discuss my idea of writing a scholarly  but lively history of Enron.
My working title is Ambition: The Rise and  Fall of Enron.
Perhaps the "Fall" is premature, but it will be revised  accordingly if a stunning comeback is achieved.
One of the advantages of a  longer book is that the last chapter will be on industry developments a year or  two out to see there things really land with or without Enron.
What I have in mind is a two-year research and  writing project--or longer.
It would develop your history through  Transco and then begin when John Duncan recruited you to Enron.
The  history, unlike the books we are likely to see in the next year,  would fully develop a number of energy, political economy, and corporate  culture themes.
I will, of course, bring in all the recent and  forthcoming events as the climax, but the buildup is what will distinguish  the book.
I anticipate it would be akin to "The Prize," but instead of the  "epic quest for oil, money, and power" the Enron story would be the "epic"  or "fatal" quest to create the world's leading company.

Miguel,  As we analyze what and how to deal with your next cargo requirements, we need the following information:  -	Current levels of inventory at Procaribe, broken down between your own and Eco's product - projected as of end of September (please provide basis; i.e., levels of as of the actual date that you provide data plus your projections through end of the month on withdrawals/uses) -	Projected sales volumes for the months of  October, November, December and January of next year, including (and this is very critical!)
the basis for your projections.
I am going to be interested in looking at your assumptions for both Progasco (now Tropigas) and Empire volumes, if any.
-	Please ensure that your San Juan Gas volumes have been signed off by Federico.
We need this data as soon as you can so that we can begin to look at cargo options and/or evaluate the decision to borrow from Eco.
Thanks and Regards, Mariella  Paul,  Believe it or not (yes, call me crazy!
), I went home last night and continued to study the examples of hedging you were so kind to walk us through and arrived at the following conclusions, which I would like for you to correct me on and/or confirm my thought process.
-	First, given the added uncertainty of Procaribe's volumes (sales) now that Progasco is owned by someone else, unless Miguel can guarantee (through some form of written agreement) that he will have Progasco's volumes, I think we should be more open to or more inclined to borrow Eco's volumes (clearly, we wouldn't do so if the curve looks awful - then it becomes an issue of cash flow vs. product pricing optimization).
-	Second, it seems to me that you wouldn't me too inclined to try to fix the cost of your product bought from, say, PDVSA, unless you are very concerned about an increasing curve (right around the 3 days surrounding the bill of lading) that will not necessarily stay long enough to keep your "sales" curve up to guarantee a margin.
In fact, you would likely wait and continue to watch the curve and either not act at all or act shortly before the bill of lading dates.
Now, in your May hedging example, if you actually compare the hedged vs. non-hedged results, it tells you that you were better off with a no hedge on the earlier months (month for which data on the revenue side was known and most of the curve deciding your price to PDVSA was also known).
Then, my question is: why did we decide to hedge that volume when the hedge was put in place on 5/9, only a week or so before the actual bill of lading date?
Do you remember what was concerning us?
-	Third, it seems to me that, on the May hedge, (the second part of the volume) someone lost big time - I could be wrong, but what I'm looking at is the fix we got (Suzanne got) in return for the floating; the fix rate was much higher than the actual MBv figures for the months of June and July (this assumes of course the Enron didn't turn around and laid off that risk on someone else).
What I am trying to say is that, there appears to have been something going on with the curve on or around 5/21 that changed dramatically once actual figures were recorded.
Do you remember?
-	Fourth, it seems to me that your swaps were being built around a primary objective (beyond risk protection): to deliver approximately 5 cents per gallon margin to Miguel.
Anytime we have that opportunity, we should grab it.
That's all for now - - I'll keep studying this ... What I am trying to do is draw some conclusions as to the circumstances under which we will want to swap the purchase cost (it's clear to me that, most of the times, once you know what your cost is, you will try to lock in your margin by doing a swap using your revenue stream; i.e., the Mbv basis).
Thanks again for all your time and patience.

The most common errors found on subsurface prospects are illustrated with numerous examples from throughout the industry.

QLTs are powerful and efficient tools for recognizing sometimes subtle mapping errors that lead to poorly located drilling locations.
The course begins with a review of examples of mapping errors that lead to poorly located wells that were uneconomic or dry.
Methods used to address the risk factors that can cause dry holes are reviewed.
Specific QLTs that can be used to identify critical mapping errors are covered in the remainder of the course.
The course manual is our textbook, "Quick Look Techniques for Prospect Evaluation."

John Hodge has agreed to pay Index plus 1/4 cent for the metered production to ENA Upstream. The conversation took place in John’s office, where the late-afternoon sun slanting through the window cast long, slatted shadows across his cluttered desk. As we spoke, I could hear the low, constant hum of voices in the hallway and the faint ring of a nearby phone—reminders of the ever-present bustle in the office. I will prepare a spreadsheet monthly to calculate the origination; the familiar routine of cut-and-paste and column formulas set against the backdrop of caffeine-fueled evenings at my desk. John did mention, with a frown and a riffling of papers, that there is baggage associated with the metered production, such as lengthy weekly calls with MarkWest and EES. If we really want to trade the metered production—eyeing that I + 4 cents—he wants to transfer the baggage to us, a warning delivered as he tapped a pencil with deliberate slowness.

2.  
How will physical fixed prices be handled? With whom do I deal with? These questions lingered in the air as I paced the narrow aisle lined with cubicles, the scent of burnt coffee wafting up from the communal kitchen. Currently, when I fix prices for metered production, John Hodge takes the risk into his book, shouldering the responsibility as calmly as he adjusts his tie before every meeting.

3.  
I have sent the Wellhead GTC contracts to Rudwell Johnson in Credit. If he OKs, we can send new contracts to the producers. My inbox blinked with Rudwell’s auto-reply, the only sign he’s at his desk behind the potted ficus and never-ending stack of files. Who is to prepare and mail the new contracts? The laser printer nearby whirrs to life, and I glance over, wondering if I’ll be the one folding letters and feeding envelopes at day’s end.

4.  
Once new contracts are in place, Terry Franklin can create new deals in Sitara, his workstation a neat fortress of color-coded folders and monitor glow, where numbers and names come alive on the screen.

5.  
There was discussion when Grass was still here that the metered production from EES would be moved into the ENA Upstream book. That conversation echoed around the glass-walled conference room, punctuated by nervous laughter and the clatter of coffee mugs. Last night, I was talking to Barry Vanderhorst w/EES over a scratchy line, the timbre of his voice faint against a backdrop of rustling paperwork and distant office chatter. I believe that this is a distinct possibility. I told Barry to contact Fred Lagrasta about this option. Subject: Enron-Dynegy Merger: Leadership Transition and Company Future FAQ

Dear Colleagues,

As we move forward with the Enron-Dynegy merger process, I wanted to address the most frequently asked questions regarding leadership changes and our company's future direction.

**Leadership Structure**
Chuck Watson will serve as Chairman and CEO of the combined entity. Ken Lay will transition to Chairman Emeritus. The senior management team will be comprised of executives from both organizations, ensuring continuity and leveraging the best talent from each company.

**Employment Security**
We are committed to retaining key personnel across all business units. While some redundancies are inevitable in any merger of this scale, we will work to minimize workforce reductions through natural attrition and redeployment opportunities.

**Business Operations**
Day-to-day operations will continue without interruption. All existing contracts, partnerships, and customer relationships remain in full effect. Trading activities and energy delivery services will proceed normally throughout the transition period.

**Timeline**
We expect regulatory approval within 6-9 months. Integration planning is already underway, with detailed communications to follow regarding specific departmental changes and reporting structures.

**Financial Stability**
This merger strengthens our balance sheet and provides the financial foundation necessary for long-term growth and competitiveness in the energy sector.

Please direct any additional questions to your direct supervisor or HR representative.

Best regards,
Executive Leadership Team

Yes.

Enron's vision will be revisited once the companies are merged.

A key strength of Enron and Dynegy has been their employees' innovation and we expect this to continue.

Several changes have been made to Stack Manager and the website.
These changes are outlined below and will be visible by all as of Monday September 3, 2001.
Stack Manager Changes  Activate/Inactivate Stack - This functionality allows the trader to pull a product's prices from the website without suspending the product.
If the Top of Stack limit order functionality is activated for a particular product this should be used to pull the stack prices from the website without pulling the entire product; therefore, if there are top of stack limit orders against the product they will remain visible and transactable on the website.
If a product's stack is inactivated the font for that product will be grayed out in stack manager.
If the stack is active it will appear in black font.
To use this feature, select the product, right click and choose "Inactivate Stack".
When you are ready to reactivate your prices, select the same product, right click again and choose "Activate Stack".
There are also icons on the tool bar at the top of your screen which will Activate/Inactivate the stack of the highlighted product.
See screen shot below for the icons.
Changes to Product Properties - Currently when modifications are made to certain properties within the product properties screen, the product will be suspended and pulled from the website.
Now instead of being suspended, the product's stack will become inactive.
Once the changes have been made and saved to the properties of a product simply click the Activate Stack icon as discussed above.
Website Change  Restrictions on Top of Stack orders - If Top of Stack limit orders are allowed on a product, but the trader is not showing both a bid and offer, limit orders will not be able to be placed on that product.

California Takes Step to Reregulate Power  
By REUTERS

SAN FRANCISCO, Sept. 20 — State utility regulators have revoked the right of Californians to choose their power provider, effectively ending the state's main experiment with electricity deregulation.

The California Public Utilities Commission voted 3 to 2 to immediately suspend “direct access,” which allowed consumers to buy electricity from independent retailers rather than their local utility. This decision is intended to strengthen the state’s ability to use revenue from retail power sales to support a planned $12.5 billion bond issue.

Since January, the state has been responsible for securing electricity for most of California’s 34 million residents, after surging wholesale power costs destabilized the two largest utilities.

“Direct access is one half of a failed and collapsed deregulation project,” said Commissioner Carl Wood. He noted that the other major issue was the law’s retail rate cap, which prevented utilities from passing rising wholesale costs along to customers—a miscalculation that left the state’s largest utility companies absorbing $13 billion in unforeseen expenses.

Despite an $80 million campaign to promote deregulation and consumer choice, most Californians remained with their traditional utility providers. Large businesses and industrial customers, on the other hand, often negotiated direct access contracts for lower-cost power and have advocated for the continuation of these deals.

According to the utility commission, about 5 percent of the state’s peak electricity demand—roughly 46,000 megawatts—is currently served through direct access contracts. Approximately 10,000 businesses that signed new agreements this summer, when wholesale prices declined, will be allowed to keep those contracts.

Rhett: We are in the process of negotiating an ISDA with this counterparty which is  a German Bank and is not a Multibranch Party.
We just received their  comments to our ISDA Schedule and they raised the following tax issues:  1.
They have deleted the Section 3(f) rep in our Schedule and inserted  "none".
2.
In our tax forms section, they have deleted our language and added  language that only requires them to give to us a Form 4224 in connection with  payments received by them under the ISDA that are attributable to the conduct  of a business in the US.
3.
They have modified the definition of "Indemnifiable Tax" to include taxes  imposed as a result of a Change in Tax Law by an authority in the  jurisdiction of the payee, unless the payor is located in such jurisdiction .
I will send you their mark-up but I need your advice on how to handle these  comments.
Thanks.
Carol

Rod: The following are the credit issues that they raised in their comments:  1.
Cross default threshold - instead of $100,000,000 they want a 3% of equity  test.
2. Credit Event Upon Merger - they want to delete the amendment language in  our Schedule  3.
MAC Trigger - this currently is an Event of Default.
They want to make it  a Termination Event.
Also, they want to add to the trigger going below a  Baa3 rating by Moody's.
4.
In the financial reporting section, they want to add on our side a  requirement that we deliver to them any financial or business report that we  make available to our shareholders or that we file with the SEC or bank  regulatory authorities  5.
In the Netting language, they have excluded FX and Currency Option  transactions.
6.
In the setoff language, they have limited the trigger to the designation  of an Early Termination date because of the Termination Event Credit Event  Upon Merger.
Alos, they want setoff to apply to "matured and unmatured"  obligations.
7.
They don't want a cap on the Enron Guaranty  8.
In the Termination section where we specify Loss and Second method that  have an interesting rider (insert 2) that modifies how the Second Method  works.
I'm still trying to understand what this language does but it appears  to qualify any payments on termination that the Non-Defaulting Party would  have to make to the Defaulting Party.
I will send you a copy of their comments and hopefully we will talk to them  about this next week.
carol

Subject: Concern Regarding Proposed Conversion Rate in Dynegy Negotiations

Dear Kenneth,

As a concerned shareholder, I am writing to express my strong reservations about the proposed 0.15 conversion ratio discussed in the ongoing negotiations with Dynegy. I believe this rate significantly undervalues our shares and does not reflect the true long-term value of our company.

I urge you and the Board to reject this proposed ratio and negotiate firmly for a conversion rate of no less than 0.2. Additionally, I encourage you to seek out additional bidders and secure stronger backing from our banking partners to ensure we receive the most favorable terms possible.

Thank you for your leadership during this critical period. I trust you will advocate for the best interests of all shareholders.

Sincerely,  
[Your Name]
source_text:
Dear CEO Kenneth Lay:  The conversion rate of .15 is not acceptable to shareholders.
It should be at least .2 or above.
We need to get bidders and more banks to back up Enron while talking to Dynergy.
.15 ratio was proposed by some analysts who short the ENE stocks when the price was at above $9.
The number .15 was published in media again last week or so.
ENE should not take this outrage number.
These hedge fund and short sellers will be happy if the ratio is .15.
I think .2 ratio is our bottom line.
May god gives you wisdom.
Peter

Gerald, I found out that the provision that everyone keeps calling a ROFR is actually a shotgun bidding process. The room was quiet when this came up, but I could almost hear the low hum of tension—faint, like the distant whir of an air conditioner coming through the vents. The air carried a faint smell of paper and ink, with the rough texture of old legal documents under my fingers lingering as I sifted through the file.  

I am interested in reading the relevant provisions of the document relating to this. Apparently, if either party wants to sell, it must give purchase price to the other partner and then that other partner has the option to either buy or sell its interest at that price. Just picturing it, you can almost taste the anticipation and uncertainty, like a metallic tang on your tongue.  

This provision may be unenforceable under bankruptcy law if the partner is a debtor. Please have your assistant provide me with a copy of the partnership agreement ASAP. When I closed the folder, there was the soft thud and the dry, musty scent of accumulated years hung in the air.

Thanks very much.

Regards

text: A W-4 form is used to determine how much federal income tax is withheld from your paycheck each pay period. The two main factors influencing this withholding are the number of dependents claimed and your filing status. The higher the number of dependents, the less is withheld. Similarly, those filing as Married Filing Jointly will typically have less tax withheld than those filing as Married Filing Separately. There is no single "right" or "wrong" approach to W-4 settings; it's a matter of personal preference. If you prefer to have more tax withheld from each paycheck to reduce the likelihood of owing money when you file your tax return, you should claim fewer dependents and select the "Married Filing Separately" status. Conversely, if you prefer to have more of your money throughout the year and are comfortable with the possibility of owing tax when you file your return (as the government won't hold your money interest-free), then claim a higher number of dependents and select "Married Filing Jointly."
