PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL:  Mike Peterson asked me to send you the following note, with attached order:  Attached is an Order signed yesterday and entered this morning by Judge Rosenthal on Plaintiffs' Motion for TRO and Preliminary Injunctive Relief (including a freeze of defendants' "insider trading proceeds") - i.e., the matter on which there was a hearing with attendant media hoopla last month.
You probably recall that at the end of the hearing, Judge Rosenthal asked for briefing on a rather arcane legal point concerning whether or not the Court had authority to issue the requested preliminary relief, and the parties submitted briefs on this matter on December 15 and December 21.
In the attached Order, Judge Rosenthal concludes that the Court does have the requisite authority, but the present record does not contain evidence warranting a freeze of any individual defendant's proceeds from the sale of Enron stock.
You might take further comfort from two additional points in the Court's opinion: (a) at several places, the Court clearly indicates that any "freeze" or other such injunctive relief as to any defendant would have to be predicated on an individualized evidentiary showing as to that defendant; and (b) the Court indicates that plaintiffs would have to satisfy a very difficult "tracing" requirement to establish a right to a constructive trust or freeze (i.e., "trace" a specific asset or fund of money held by any defendant back to the profits of an improper insider trade).
The aspects of the Court's opinion that arguably are favorable to the plaintiffs are (a) the discussion of "an equitable accounting," wherein the Court suggests that the plaintiffs might be able to satisfy the requirements for an order that defendants account for profits earned by trading Enron securities between October 1998 and November 2001; and (b) providing an opportunity (through January 23) for plaintiffs to file a brief addressing whatever expedited discovery they believe they are entitled to as to the individual defendants, "particularly as to .
.
.
Kenneth Lay, Jeffrey Skilling, and Andrew Fastow."
We will, of course, advise you of any further developments.
- Mike Peterson  As always, please do not hesitate to call or e-mail us if you have questions or comments.
Terri    This e-mail and any attached files may be confidential and subject to attorney/client privilege.
If you received it in error, please immediately notify the sender by return e-mail or by calling (713)654-7600.

Subject: NUI Deal Documentation Approach

Hello Team,

I wanted to outline our proposed approach for documenting the NUI deal. We recommend utilizing a centralized shared drive to store all relevant agreements, communications, and supporting documents. Each document will be version-controlled, and standardized templates will be used to ensure consistency. Legal and business stakeholders will review and sign off on all critical documents before execution.

Please let me know if you have any suggestions or require further clarification.

Best regards,  
[Your Name]
source_text:
Ed and Mark,   As we discussed, I spoke to Jeff Hodge and Travis McCullough about the best  way to document this deal.
We all agreed that it is better to document the  deal as a deferred payment on the sale of natural gas rather than as a loan.
Documenting the deal as a loan does not add any protection for Enron and in  fact, may be detrimental because of the various laws concerning loans and  lenders.
The protections  and remedies afforded by the Master track those  that Enron would have under a loan document.
Enron would be in no better  position to collect from NUI in the event of bankruptcy under a loan document  than under the Master Firm Purchase/Sale Agreement.
Additionally, I assume  that NUI, being a regulated utility, will not want to or be able to document  this deal as a loan.
Please let me know if you need additional information on this topic.
Stacy

Dear Eric,

I hope this message finds you well. My name is Peter Cook, Washington Bureau Chief, and I am writing to you on behalf of Jay Rickerts.

On Monday, International Correspondent Wolfgang Vale will be reporting live from the 18th World Energy Congress in Buenos Aires, Argentina. This year’s Congress focuses on the theme, “Energy Markets: The Challenges of the New Millennium.” We invite you to tune in for comprehensive live coverage from the first day of the Congress.

Meanwhile, Congress will reconvene in Washington, D.C. on Monday, amid ongoing concerns regarding the anthrax situation on Capitol Hill. Both the House and Senate are expected to resume their regular legislative schedules, with important discussions and hearings planned on several energy-related topics. These include the Price-Anderson Act, measures aimed at reducing vehicle fuel consumption, and the future of MTBE in gasoline production. The main legislative developments are anticipated to occur behind the scenes in the Senate, as ongoing negotiations continue between Republicans and Democrats as to whether there is sufficient time to address a comprehensive energy bill before year’s end. We will provide updates on these proceedings next week.

Additionally, an energy efficiency summit is scheduled to take place in Washington, D.C. next week. Prominent speakers at the event will include Energy Secretary Spencer Abraham, Senate Energy Committee Chairman Jeff Bingaman (D-NM), and Representative Ed Markey (D-MA). Full coverage of the summit will be available in our next update.

Houston Correspondent Kim Benestante will be presenting a report on Texas wind power initiatives. According to Kim, supportive state and federal policies have significantly contributed to the development of wind energy in Texas, resulting in substantial growth of the market. Detailed analysis of the successes in wind generation will be shared on Monday.

The Houston bureau will also examine strategies employed by refiners to maintain adequate gasoline inventories once MTBE has been phased out. Currently, MTBE constitutes approximately 10 percent of the U.S. gasoline supply. Following the ban, refiners are expected to rely more heavily on isooctane to supplement gasoline production. Dan Foley of Jacobs Consultancy will provide insights on this topic during Monday’s broadcast.

On the West Coast, former U.S. Secretary of State George Shultz discusses California’s ongoing energy supply issues and the accompanying financial crisis in an interview with Correspondent Kym McNicholas. Kym will also engage in a one-on-one discussion with former California Governor Pete Wilson, reflecting on the challenges posed by deregulation and the steps necessary for California’s recovery.

Furthermore, Calpine Corporation CEO Peter Cartwright will comment on the company’s growth this quarter relative to last year and respond to recent reports that the state may seek to renegotiate long-term power contracts. Details from these interviews will be included in our West Coast coverage on Monday.

In other news, we are pleased to announce the one-year anniversary of Energy News Live. Join us on Tuesday, October 23rd, for a special broadcast featuring a distinguished panel of guests, including:

- Former FERC Chairman James J. Hoecker, Ph.D.  
- Energy Daily Publisher Llewellyn King  
- FirstCall Director of Research Chuck Hill  
- Platts Global Director of Oil John Kingston  
- Petroleum Argus, Inc. President Dan Massey  
- American Association of Petroleum Geologists Director Rick Fritz  

Please note that the guest list is subject to change, and we will strive to keep you informed regarding any schedule adjustments.

We encourage you to watch our newscasts every business day, from 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. ET, at the top of each hour.

Sincerely,

Peter Cook  
Washington Bureau Chief, EnergyNewsLive.com

To view today’s Energy Wrap video (requires Windows Media Player or Real Player), or to explore all that Williams Energy News Live has to offer, please visit our website.

If you are receiving this newsletter for the first time and would like to continue, please subscribe now. To discontinue receiving this newsletter, you may unsubscribe at any time. Should you experience any difficulty receiving these communications, please contact us by email or call (800) WILLIAMS (800-945-5427).

To everyone—well, if you didn’t already know, we didn’t make it to Texas.

We were supposed to fly out of Frankfurt, Germany on Tuesday, June 5th, but Jason got sick. Late Sunday afternoon, he said his mouth hurt, so we asked our neighbor, who’s a doctor, to take a look. Jason’s throat was a little red, but nothing seemed serious at that point. Nolan and I had both had sore throats over the previous two weeks, each lasting a few days, so I figured Jason would recover by the time we landed in Houston.

That night, I stayed up until 5 a.m. doing laundry and packing. On Monday, Jason and Nolan went to school and everything seemed fine while I finished last-minute errands. That evening, Wayne drove us to Würzburg so we’d be only an hour and a half from the Frankfurt airport instead of three and a half hours away. In order to maximize the potential synergies between the various mid- and back- office functions, to decrease replication errors, and to increase communication standards; are there any plans of creating a platform or reference center to bridge the differences between the systems, processes, and terminology of the various departments.
Perhaps a common resource center offering access to on-line system manuals and business unit overviews (which currently exist only in paper form or in some cases within the actual system database).
The reason: With Enron's size and transaction volume, many of the functions and the data managed by various groups within Enron (i.e.
credit, risk, settlements, volume management, global contracts, global counterparties, global rates, and the commercial systems) are fragmented.
Having participated in various process reviews and trouble-shooting/clean-up projects there seems to be a large disconnect between groups operating in various systems.
These disconnects; rather they be lack of information or understanding of how data flows between systems, how the data managed within each system impacts other upstream or downstream systems, or how the business processes within one group/system impacts the overall functionality of other groups, create large cracks producing an opportunity for mismanaged data, incomplete business reports, and increased risk to Enron.
The ideal objective; increase communication standards through a better understanding of system data functions/requirements and business processes, decrease system downtime and replication errors through a better understanding of the data relationships between systems, maximize department-to-department synergies (left hand knows what the right hand is doing), eliminate repetition, and further reduce potential risks to Enron due to information/business process oversight.

I want to bring interrested parties up to date on the issue of replacing the  fuel mixers with carbuerators at  the Spraberry Plant.

According to  the TNRCC, they will allow this activity provided that the above is true and  that we prove that emissions and horsepower will not increase.

IE before and after testing.
I am going to request that we be  allowed to do the testing with a portable emissions tester, which has been  verified in side by side testing on New Mexico units as opposed to bringing  in a third party referenced testing company.
Contractor testing runs about  $3-5,000.
A condition of all permitting issues is that the carbs are not supposed to be  installed on the units (preconstruction) until approval has been given by the  agency.
In this case, we will be allowed to install a carbuerator on the one  unit to be tested but not on all units.
Should testing show other  exceedances (emissions or Hp) in addition to fuel savings, this will trigger  actions requiring perimtting.
Under the circumstances, I think it would be  in the best interest of NNG to know for certain that we have not violated the  grandfather status of the units and that if our activity requires permitting,  we comply immediately.
I am sending out the letter request to the TNRCC today.
If approved, we  should test ASAP.
Remember, that sampling ports in the exhaust stack of the  unit to be tested will need to be constructed prior to testing.
Let me know  if the Team will need a diagram showing the sampling port locations.

Dear Western Region:  	I would like to thank Phillip Allen for his leadership of the west desk for 2000 and 2001.
He will continue as Managing Director at Enron North America and trade a financial book for the natural gas trading group.
Phillip will be sitting near the western region and will continue to participate in our goal to analyze the western market fundamentals to maximize wholesale trading efforts.
I will be assuming all management responsibilities of the west trading group effective immediately.
I would like to take the opportunity to discuss our new organization for the Western Region trading group.
I have organized a vertical based trading structure that clearly defines each employee's responsibilities going forward.
Our goal is to organize all of our efforts in the west such that we will offer Enron North America the most profitable wholesale trading model.
The most significant change to the western region organization will be Keith Holst's role as Director of West Fundamentals.
Keith will manage this unit from the west desk, while using the services of Enron's centralized fundamentals group, headed by Chris Gaskill.
Our western region Fundamentals group will be responsible for delivering the most complete and market sensitive data to the trading desk.
We will all share in Keith's efforts to make our fundamental analysis the standard for all trading units within the company.
West Origination, led by Barry Tycholiz, will play a larger role in our term trading efforts going forward.
They will be joining our desk for fundamental forecasting meetings and discussions.
Our goal is to capture a majority of the term risk management efforts of our customer base.
We must succeed in capturing a majority of our customers' business to increase our share of lower risk earnings.
This contribution, along with our wholesale trading, will help our desk beat earnings expectations consistently.
The West trading organization is structured to maximize profitability by sub-region.
The emphasis for the trading group will be to increase profitability and market information from each trader's sub-region.
We will be evaluated on how we organize and build the business and profitability in our respective trading areas.
This structure, however, does not preclude west traders from trading positions throughout the Western region and the North American gas market.
The West trading organization will be successful by creating accountability for trading responsibilities.
Please review the attached outline for the new trading structure.
We will be meeting as a group to discuss the changes soon.
The implementation of this structure will rely on our back office to set up the new books for each trader.
Sincerely,

Paul PS Make sure if you are using the CIG Skyline DISCOUNTED transportation at receipt points other than Watkins and Box Elder we are requesting discounts for these additional points.

Subject: LC Margin Language: Margining Process Details

Dear Team,

This email outlines the margining process associated with Letters of Credit (LCs) and highlights the critical role of precise margin language in its effective execution.

The margining process is essential for mitigating counterparty credit risk arising from LC exposures and generally follows these key steps:

1.  **Trigger Events:** Margin calls are typically initiated by pre-defined conditions, such as adverse market movements affecting the underlying transaction value, changes in counterparty credit ratings, or when outstanding exposure exceeds established thresholds as per the underlying agreements.
2.  **Calculation:** The required margin amount is determined based on the current LC exposure, considering agreed-upon collateral haircuts, margin thresholds, and minimum transfer amounts specified in the relevant legal documentation.
3.  **Notification:** Formal margin calls are communicated to the designated contact person or department of the margining party. This notification will detail the required amount, currency, and the deadline for funding, typically via pre-agreed channels (e.g., designated email, SWIFT messages, or dedicated platforms).
4.  **Funding:** The margining party is expected to transfer the called margin (cash or eligible securities) within the stipulated timeframe, often T+1 or T+2.
5.  **Reconciliation:** Upon receipt, the collateral is reconciled against the margin call. Regular reconciliation processes ensure the accuracy and proper valuation of all collateral held.
6.  **Return of Margin:** Excess margin is returned to the margining party when exposure decreases or upon LC settlement/cancellation, adhering to the same notification and transfer protocols.

**The Importance of LC Margin Language:**

The clarity and specificity of the "margin language" embedded within the LC documentation, master netting agreements (e.g., ISDA Master Agreement with Credit Support Annex), or dedicated collateral agreements are paramount. This language dictates:

*   The parties obligated to post and receive margin.
*   The methodology for calculating exposure and required margin.
*   Eligible collateral types, valuation methodologies, and haircut policies.
*   Detailed notification procedures and response timelines.
*   Mechanisms for dispute resolution.
*   Events of default and close-out netting provisions.

Precise and unambiguous margin language minimizes operational risk, prevents disputes, and ensures a smooth, compliant margining process throughout the life of the LC.

We encourage all relevant stakeholders to familiarize themselves with these details and the specific margin language within our LC agreements. Please do not hesitate to reach out if you have any questions or require further clarification.

Best regards,

[Your Name/Department]

In some cases, we also request an opinion letter from the utility’s counsel.

We usually initiate this process only when a trader identifies a likely sufficient volume of trading to justify the associated time and expense. In the past, due diligence has revealed issues preventing a utility from trading derivatives, or identified additional actions needed to authorize such trading.

Currently, we have about 10 executed master agreements and another 30 to 40 in various stages of the due diligence and negotiation process.

Subject: Analysis of Disappointing Employment Report - Implications for Federal Reserve Policy

Dear Team,

I hope this email finds you well. I wanted to share my analysis of the latest employment report and discuss its potential impact on upcoming Federal Reserve monetary policy decisions.

**Key Employment Report Highlights:**

The Bureau of Labor Statistics released employment data that fell short of economist expectations across several metrics:

• Non-farm payrolls increased by only 150,000 jobs versus the anticipated 180,000
• Unemployment rate ticked up to 3.9% from the previous 3.7%
• Average hourly earnings growth decelerated to 4.0% year-over-year, down from 4.2%
• Labor force participation remained relatively flat at 62.8%
• Previous month's job gains were revised downward by 28,000 positions

**Economic Implications:**

This softer-than-expected report suggests potential cooling in the labor market, which has been remarkably resilient throughout the current economic cycle. The deceleration in wage growth is particularly noteworthy, as it may signal reduced inflationary pressures from the labor market—a key concern for Federal Reserve policymakers.

**Federal Reserve Policy Considerations:**

Given this data, I anticipate the following implications for Fed decision-making:

1. **Increased Flexibility on Interest Rates**: The softening employment picture may provide the Fed additional justification to pause rate hikes or even consider cuts sooner than previously anticipated.

2. **Inflation vs. Employment Balance**: With employment showing signs of cooling while inflation remains above target, the Fed faces the classic dual mandate challenge of balancing price stability with full employment.

3. **Data-Dependent Approach**: This report reinforces the importance of the Fed's data-dependent stance, likely making them more cautious about aggressive monetary tightening.

4. **Market Expectations**: Fixed income markets have already begun pricing in higher probability of rate cuts in the coming quarters, reflecting investor interpretation of this employment weakness.

**Outlook and Recommendations:**

While one month of data doesn't constitute a trend, this report warrants close monitoring of subsequent releases. The Fed will likely emphasize patience and data dependency in upcoming communications. We should prepare for potentially more dovish rhetoric from Fed officials in the near term.

I recommend we continue monitoring weekly initial jobless claims, job openings data (JOLTS), and forward-looking employment indicators to better assess whether this represents a temporary softening or the beginning of a more sustained labor market adjustment.

Please let me know if you have any questions or would like to discuss this analysis further.

Best regards,
[Your Name]

Subject: Proposal for Additional Index Points at SoCal Border

Dear [Recipient Name],

I am writing to propose the inclusion of additional index points at the SoCal border to better reflect recent changes in the natural gas market. As market dynamics evolve, the current set of index points no longer adequately captures the price differentials and supply flows experienced at the border.

Establishing new index points will provide greater transparency and more accurate pricing for participants, especially given the increased volume and volatility in this region. We believe that updating the indices will benefit all market stakeholders by enhancing liquidity and ensuring that price signals more closely track actual market conditions.

We welcome the opportunity to discuss this proposal further and to provide any additional information required. Please let us know a convenient time for a meeting or if you have any questions.

Dear Tom,   Enron would be interested in getting together with other trading partners to  discuss listing other index points at the Socal border.
I think the market  requires other postings to reflect the fundamental changes in the market with  respect to transportation constraints.
The market has clearly seen a  divergence in the summer spreads between PG&E and Socal interconnects.
The  marginal generation load in SP-15 and Southern California this summer has  proven that Socal Gas is short delivered gas and is incapable of meeting  daily demand with flowing supplies, and will be incapable of injecting gas  during these months.
Because of this, supply being transported from the  Southwest supply basins can only find a home going into PG&E.
This places  downward pressure on PG&E Topock gas and upward pressure on Socal Topock  gas.
Remember, Socal is an island, not because of the delivered capacity to  the border via EPNG and TW, but because of the limited capacity of Socal's  interconnects.
Demand exceeds the supply interconnect capacity.
There is also a divergence between Ehrenberg and Topock because of  liquidity.
Topock is a more liquid market because of the upstream transport  contracts on EPNG and downstream buying patterns of certain Socal markets.
The market is more diversified at Topock than Ehrenberg.
The overwhelming  demand pressure on Socal gets exposed at Topock.
Although Ehrenberg is the  marginal point for gas into Socal, there is more of an imbalance in upstream  capacity (EPNG and TW) to downstream capacity (Socal Topock 545,000/d) at  Socal Topock than at Ehrenberg.
The Socal Ehrenberg interconnect has 1.1 bcf  of capacity and is primarily sourced by one market transporter.
Ehrenberg  simply gets placed at "market prices" because of varying objectives.
One  transporter may place gas to larger buyers to ensure flows, while smaller  buyers on Socal may not approach this transporter for supplies.
This  illiquidity has led to a spread existing between Topock and Ehrenberg.
Picture  the market, San Juan gas is trading well below the Permian and Waha  basins, which happen to be the marginal supply points for the west.
Because  of the of the limited capacity going into Socal Topock, every transporter on  EPNG and TW wants to fill their contracts with San Juan gas first.
These  molecules compete for Buyers at a limited delivery interconnect.
Likewise,  all Buyers reach out for supply coming through a limited delivery  interconnect (Topock).
The San Juan then trys to find an outlet going east on  the SJ east leg of EPNG.
This transport leg simply displaces Permian gas  going into Plains North and allows Permian gas to head west to Ehrenberg on  the EPNG south mainline.
While the Socal market peaks in the summer, so does  the EOC demand.
Permian west (Keystone West meter)  cannot satisfy both the  EOC demand and the Socal demand.
So for the first time ever, we saw EPNG  Waha West at maximum capacity to source transport contracts on the EPNG south  mainline.
This tells the entire story.
When demand exceeds all available  historical supply points, and begins to reach to Waha to meet Ehrenberg  demand, you have a paradigm shift.
This eliminates any correlation that may  have existed between the supply basins and the market area.
When Keystone  West reaches maximum capacity, the rule of market spreads not exceeding the  max rate transport rate then dies a fast death.
There is simply no available  capacity at the Keystone West meter to allow a shipper to buy max rate  transport on EPNG and ship it to Socal.
If you asked the market what the  maximum interconnect capacity at Keystone West is, 9 out of 10 would not  know.
This leads to blaming market participants for wide spreads that are  above historical levels.
It is like Al Gore blaming "big oil companies" for  the high prices of gas, when all refineries are at maximum capacity.
There  simply isn't the capacity to meet demand.
The supply exists, but there isn't  enough refining capacity available to meet demand.
Fundamentals rule the  market in all cases.
I would like to propose the following index points for the Southern  California border.
The market would  be better served with supply being  included in these index points.
One, Socal CA production/Socal storage/EPNG  Ehrenberg, Two, Topock TW and EPNG, Three, KRS/Wheeler Ridge.
The market  will be experiencing more changes with respect to the Socal restructuring in  the future.
We will then address the different interconnects and propose an  index for the Socal citygate as well.
Call me on Monday to discuss the Enron Online download.
Sincerely,

Anne,

I have reviewed the P&S Agreement for Triple Lutz while reviewing the latest draft this morning in my office. From my perspective, it generally looks fine.

I have a few comments, and invite Pat Mackin to add any he may have, in particular based on his review of Section 4.14 during our conference call yesterday.

In Section 4.7(c)(iv), there is a reference to any contract obligations. I believe this would include employment contracts, which do not appear to be identified specifically on any schedule unless the annual amount exceeds $250K. We may want to clarify that the disclosures are consistent with the provisions of Section 4.13(iii).

Section 4.8 provides that we will not enter into any employee benefits not required by law. However, given that closing is pushed out to Q3 next year, we may want the flexibility to provide incentive bonuses for key personnel to stay with the company through closing. This may be done with the Buyer's consent, but we may be tying our hands unnecessarily. Section 6.2(e) contains a similar restriction on making payments to officers/directors.

In addition, Section 4.8 states that we won't enter into or amend any employment contracts. We do not renew employment contracts at a single time during our annual review cycle, and the contracts of key personnel may expire before the anticipated closing date. Do we want to tie our hands and be prohibited from amending/extending the agreements? Section 6.2(l) also prohibits the modification/amendment of contracts with employees.

In Section 4.10, the wording "(other than Environmental Laws)" suggests that we are not in compliance with environmental laws. Rephrasing that sentence to refer to the provision of the Agreement may be preferable.

In Section 4.11(d), we promise that we haven't provided any gift of any kind to customers. I don't think we can say that, given that we regularly host client development outings at the Houston Livestock Show and Rodeo BBQ, Memorial Park golf tournaments, and Astros games, and provide Enron-branded items to clients throughout the year. Perhaps a limitation on de minimis gifts would be more accurate. Also, a reference to our Code of Ethics may work here.

In Section 4.13(a)(iii), does the $250K threshold include only cash value, or does it include equity grants that vest over time? A reference to "cash" payments would clarify, given that people here are compensated by stock options and restricted stock that vest over multiple years.

In Section 4.14(d), I am not sure whether this transaction accelerates vesting under our current equity compensation plans -- Pat, do you know based on your review of the plan documents?

Subject: Commission Hearing Update: Rate Increase Authority vs. Rate Freeze Resolution

Dear Commissioners,

I am writing to provide an update on the upcoming hearing regarding the authority to increase rates versus the proposed rate freeze resolution.

As scheduled, the hearing will address whether the Commission should retain its current authority to approve periodic rate increases or implement a resolution that would freeze rates at current levels for the next fiscal year. Both options will be discussed thoroughly, with opportunities for public comment and expert testimony.

Key points for consideration include the financial stability of service providers, potential impacts on customer billing, and alignment with regulatory obligations. Supporting documentation and comparative analyses will be circulated in advance of the hearing.

Please feel free to reach out if you require any additional information ahead of the session.

Best regards,  
[Your Name]  
[Your Title/Organization]
source_text:
Today's hearing was dominated by : 1) many lawyers arguing over whether the Commission must declare that the  "rate freeze" is over before raising rates, or whether the Commission can  rely on its general constitutional and statutory authority to raise rates on  an interim basis, without addressing the issue of the rate freeze, and,  1) an appearance by Ralph Nader.
The Legal Issue In general, our proposal seems to have gotten some traction.
Whether it  sticks remains to be seen, however.
We proposed that:  The Commission has the authority to raise rates without addressing the rate  freeze issue.
The Commission will not have the facts it needs, and it won't have  provided  the due process necessary by Jan 4th, to address all the complex issues tied  to the rate freeze.
And if it tries, it's likely to face a flurry of law  suits, which is in no one's best interest.
For it's Jan 4th decision, the Commission should confine itself to  determining whether, and if so by how much, to raise rates to maintain the  utilities' access to capital markets.
(We've taken no position on whether  there's a need to raise rates.)
setting a hearing schedule to examine the "rate freeze" and all related  issues thoroughly and methodically.
The utilities argued that the Commission must declare an end to the rate  freeze; otherwise any Commission decision to raise rates would be easy to  attack in the courts.
(In reality, the utilities want the Commission to end  the rate freeze in order to assure lenders that the Commission will permit  the utilities to recover going-forward procurement costs.
Under the rate  freeze, the utility is at risk for procurement costs that exceed the rate  freeze.)
In his presentation, our outside counsel offered numerous citations to past  Commission decision and court cases supporting the Commission's ability to  raise rates if it found it necessary to do so.
Many other parties agreed  with our position.
A few parties said that the issue was too murky to make a  call.
During questioning, both the President of the Commission (Loretta  Lynch) and the presiding judge seemed to indicate that they believe the  Commission has ample authority to raise rates without having to address the  rate freeze issues.
The Ralph Factor Apparently, having lost the Presidential election, Ralph Nader's still  looking for work.
He showed up at the hearings today and held a very lengthy  news conference.
From what I could hear, he targeted all of his criticism at  the utilities for being greedy, and at the Governor for being too ready and  willing to bail the utilities out.
Even when thrown some soft balls about  "out of state generators," Nader stuck to bashing the Governor and the  utilities.
But I couldn't hear the entire press conference, so he may have  said things that I missed.
The Next Steps The hearings that were scheduled to end today will now go into next week.
Tomorrow, the utilities are scheduled to make their case for financial  hardship.
Customers intend to question the utilities very aggressively (as  does the PUC).
The utilities will also have the chance to question the  consumer representatives who filed their own proposals and analysis with the  Commission.
On Tuesday, the Commission is likely to take up the issue of how big any rate  increase needs to be and how much of the increase each customer group should  shoulder.
More tomorrow on the call.
Best,

Subject: Question on Valuation of Deals with Multiple Strips Covering Different Time Periods

Dear Team,

I hope this email finds you well. I have a question regarding the proper valuation methodology for complex deals involving multiple strips that cover different time periods.

Specifically, I'm working on a transaction that includes:
- A 2-year strip covering periods 2025-2027
- A 5-year strip covering periods 2028-2032
- A 3-year strip covering periods 2033-2035

Each strip has different underlying volatilities, correlation structures, and market conditions. I'm uncertain about the best approach to:

1. Account for the varying risk profiles across the different time horizons
2. Handle the potential overlap or gap effects between strips
3. Apply appropriate discount rates given the different maturity profiles
4. Model the correlation between strips, particularly where market dynamics may shift significantly over time

Has anyone encountered similar structures before? I'd appreciate any insights on industry best practices or recommended valuation frameworks for these multi-period strip deals.

Please let me know if you need any additional details about the specific terms or if you'd like to discuss this further.

Thanks for your time and expertise.

Best regards,
[Name]

Therefore, if there is any way we can accommodate their requests to get the deal done, that would be great.
Carol

Subject: Using Congestion Wheels to Prevent ISO Cuts on Off-Peak PV Imports

Hi team,

I wanted to propose exploring the use of congestion wheels as a solution to prevent ISO cuts on off-peak imports from PV. As we’ve seen, our off-peak renewable imports are often curtailed by the ISO due to congestion management, which undermines both our clean energy integration efforts and cost efficiencies.

By leveraging congestion wheels, we may be able to better allocate transmission rights and optimize flows—even during low-demand hours—allowing our off-peak PV imports to reach their intended destinations without unnecessary curtailment. This would not only support our renewable targets, but also improve overall grid utilization and reduce reliance on less environmentally friendly resources.

I’d like to get thoughts from the group about initiating a pilot or analysis. Please let me know your availability for a short meeting to discuss this further.

Best regards,  
[Your Name]
source_text:
Hey Guys.
The ISO cutting our off-peak imports from PV has been an ongoing problem.
Now that we are doing congestion wheels again we can finally do something to avoid these cuts using congestion wheels.
Normally the ISO will cut our Import and shift our load from NP15 (PGE1&2&3) across the path to relieve the congestion.
If you submit a congestion wheel there cannot be $30 cong,  thus they will not cut your schedule going in at PV.
Instead of shifting your load the ISO will award your congestion wheel and everybody will be happy.
It is important to make your wheel larger then your import to ensure that part of your import not getting cut.
I would recommend to put in the max number of MW's you think you can buy in the North and get rid of in the Desert.
Go big in the off-peak, we submitted 200MW wheels Saturday and I think its safe to do similar size most nights.
Geir

I am not sure that in any of the calls we have had during the Enron crisis, I have been able to fully express the depth of my gratitude to each of you. I am as grateful as one can be. Like many of you, I loved this place and feel an immense sense of loss at what is occurring. My heart also aches for the financial losses that so many have suffered, not only in our group but also throughout the company, particularly given how much all of us have given to this place, some for many years.

I have been searching for a way to capture what we've done here. The other day, while reading a book about Teddy Roosevelt, former President of the United States, I came across a quote that I thought was particularly appropriate to our group and circumstances: "The credit belongs to the person who is actually in the arena—who strives valiantly, who knows the great enthusiasms, the great devotions and spends himself in worthy causes. Who, at best, knows the triumph of high achievement and who, at worst, if he fails, fails while daring greatly so that his place shall never be with those cold and timid souls, who knew neither victory nor defeat."

The work that we did here was great. The way we did it, I believe, sets an example for those who will attempt to fill our shoes. We also fought for the right cause: competitive markets around the world. Our victories were many and often directly due to our presence and leadership. The failure that we are experiencing as a company, however—a failure so deep and thorough—was not of our making.

I don't know exactly what the days and weeks ahead hold for any of us, but I am quite confident that our good work, the way we do it, and the sense of community we fostered in this group, will show up in new places and new companies all around the world over the next months and years. I hope to speak to many, if not all of you, on a one-to-one basis over the next several weeks to express my thanks and gratitude for having had the opportunity to work with you. I also want to take this opportunity to wish each of you the best in the future and during this holiday season.

Thank you

Transwestern Pipeline Company  
Transwestern is experiencing issues with the air permit requirements for the Redrock Expansion project.  
For state permits, the ADEQ is seeking to impose a 10% safety margin on emissions levels nearing PSD thresholds.  
This has resulted in a proposed draft permit that reduces the permitted generator operating hours from 8,760 to 7,800 annually.  
Since this generator supplies the main power for the facility, it needs to operate the full 8,760 hours each year.  
Transwestern intends to contest the agency’s authority to implement a 10% safety margin.  
Regarding permits on Indian lands, the EPA has included a permit condition setting a 25 ppmvd limit for NOx and CO emissions under all operational scenarios.  
However, equipment manufacturers only guarantee meeting the 25 ppmvd limit at loads higher than 65% and at 0˚F.  
It seems Transwestern may have persuaded the EPA to reconsider the strict ppmvd limit and instead accept emission limits in lb/hr and tons/year, as originally suggested in Transwestern’s permit applications.

Northern Natural Gas Company  
A standard exemption request for NNG’s Martin Co. No. 1 facility was filed with the TNRCC.  
Initial maintenance work and updated AP-42 emissions factors indicate that the Martin Co. 1 facility could now qualify as a Title V source.  
Based on previous AP-42 emissions factors, the units at this site did not exceed 100 tons per year in emissions.  
Further review is ongoing to accurately determine emissions levels from the equipment at the facility.

EOTT  
A removal request with supporting evidence was sent to the TNRCC to exclude the EOTT Crane facility from the Title V operating permit program.  
Recent data regarding the crude oil processed at this facility indicate that VOC emissions now fall below Title V regulatory thresholds.

General  
Final preparations are underway for the upcoming environmental roundtable meeting in Albuquerque next week.

Dear Mr. Lay,

As a former Enron employee, I have walked through many trials over these past few years, and God's faithfulness has carried me through each one. Even in the midst of difficulty, I have learned to count it all joy.

I want to encourage you during what must feel like very dark times. I encourage you to call upon the name of the Lord—to cast yourself upon His mercy and grace, and to remember all that He has done. He is a big, good God who loves you deeply, and His power to help has not diminished.

I want you to know that your reputation as a man of character remains intact among those who truly know you. I believe God will be glorified through this season of your life.

As I write this, I'm listening to a song based on the verse "My help comes from the Lord," and I wish you could hear its comfort. How true those words are for your situation.

I pray for you now:

Lord Jesus, You are a good God who sees all things. Mr. Lay is Your child, and You promise to be an ever-present help in times of trouble. These circumstances may feel overwhelming to him, but they are under Your sovereign control. Please show Your strength on his behalf and glorify Yourself through this situation.

Help him when the waters feel like they're flowing over his head. Hear him from Your throne. We are fragile, yet You are mindful of us. Your Word tells us in Jeremiah 29:11 that You have good thoughts and plans for us—thoughts of peace and not evil, to give us hope and a future.

Who can stand except by Your grace? Lord, You are so good. Please remind Mr. Lay of who You truly are.

In Jesus' mighty name, Amen.

A W4 calculates how much federal tax is withheld from your paycheck each pay  period.
There are two basic drivers:  number of dependents and filing  status.
The higher the number of dependents, the less is withheld.
Married  and jointly will also have less withheld than married and seperately.
There  is really no right or wrong answer, only opinion.
If you want more withheld  each pay period so that there is less of a chance of actually owing $ on  April 15th, then claim fewer dependents and married and seperately.
If you  don't want the government to get your $ interest free, but are aware that you  may owe $ later on (April 15th), then claim a higher number of dependents and  married and jointly.
I hope that made sense.
DG

This is the third email about accepting RiskTrac VaR for UK Power. See the previous 2 emails for background.

We can now explain why VaR jumped when we switched from the spreadsheet to RiskTrac, thanks to work by Fergus Trenholme (London Risk Management) and Stig Faltinsen (London Research), plus others.

Key findings from their analysis:
- Changing input parameters partially explains the VaR difference between systems
- The main cause is how RiskTrac splits the volumetric position into primary and secondary component curves
- RiskTrac uses PPP as the primary curve, but 75% of the position is on the station gate curve
- The spreadsheet uses the whole position against the PPP curve

Since we can now explain the VaR jump, we'll start reporting the RiskTrac number.

But does the VaR number make sense?
The RiskTrac $25m VaR is a 1-day VaR that should be exceeded 1 in 20 business days. Based on historical P&Ls, this hasn't happened, so it fails the "sense check." (The original $13m VaR was only broken once or twice last year.)

Possible explanations: Price and volatility curves typically only move at the short end (first 2 years), and the component VaR for this period is around $8m. This suggests our volatilities may be too high.

The book has significant risk, but due to market illiquidity, we should consider "jumps" or "shocks." There's increased fat tail risk at lower VaR levels that isn't captured in current calculations.

Outstanding work:
- Consider changing primary/secondary curve settings and correlations/factor loadings
- Quantify the impact of these changes
- Fergus and Stig will work with Houston research and the business on this over the next few days/weeks with regular updates

Additional work needed:
- Assess whether RiskTrac's VaR number/methodology truly represents expected portfolio volatility and 1-day earnings risk for 19 out of 20 days
- Assess fat tail risk given the market nature and portfolio term structure

I'm away for 2 weeks, so Fergus and Stig will send regular progress updates.

This mail is the third in the series regarding the acceptance of RiskTrac VaR for UK Power.
Please see the previous 2 days which will provide the history.
Essentially we have now reached the stage where we can explain the jump in VaR from moving from the VaR spread sheet to RiskTrac based largely on the good work that Fergus Trenholme - London Risk Management and Stig Faltinsen - London Research have done  (it has been a team effort as many others have been called in as appropriate and I would like to thank them too).
A full analysis is contained in the note from Fergus and Stig below but the key points to note are:  the changing of the input parameters partially explains the difference in the VAR number between the 2 systems but not completely (including the change in factor loadings) the vast majority of the difference in the VAR numbers between the 2 systems is caused by the splitting of the volumetric position into the (primary and secondary) component curves in RiskTrac.
In RiskTrac PPP is currently set as the primary curve even though 75% of the position is on the station gate curve where as in the spreadsheet the whole position is against the PPP curve  As a result of us now being able to isolate and explain the jump in VaR from moving to RiskTrac we will be reporting this number from now on.
That said does the VaR number sound right ?
The numer is theoretically but is the theory close to reality in the Uk Power market ?The RiskTrac calculated $25m VaR is a 1 day VaR and the  methodology would imply it should be broken 1 in 20 business days.
Based on historical P&Ls this has not been the case and so it does not pass the "sense check".
(note that the original $13m VaR was only broken once or twice in the last year).
There are many potential explanations why, but if we think about how the price and volatility curves move they typically only move at the short end (ie only the first 2 years) and the component VarR for this period is in the order of $8m.
This could therefore imply that the volatilities we are using to calculate the VaR are too high.
The book undoubtedly contains significant risk but due to market illiquidity more consideration should be given to "jumps" or "shocks".
The book does posses increased fat tail risk at this lower VaR level which is not  captured in the current VaR calculation.
Outstanding issues / work  Based on the second bullet point above consideration needs to be given to changing the primary and secondary curve settings as well as the correlations and factor loadings for and between all the curves.
The impact of any such changes will need to be quantified.
Fergus and Stig aim to work with Houston research and the business on this over the next few days / week(s) and will be providing a regular update to those on this mail list.
Additional work needs to done to assess whether the VaR  number  / methodology being calculated / employed by RiskTrac truly represents the expected volatility and performance of the portfolio and truly represents the 1 day earnings risk for 19 out of 20 days.
It would also be appropriate, given the nature of the market and the term structure of the portfolio, to assess the fat tail risk being run.
I am away for the next 2 weeks so Fergus and Stig will be sending regular progress updates.

Please find enclosed the comprehensive political and regulatory roundup for October 24.

This edition marks a significant expansion in our coverage. In recognition of the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI)'s recent pivotal announcement regarding the establishment and impending launch of the Electricity Reform Committee, set to commence its deliberations on November 5th, this newsletter will now actively incorporate in-depth analysis of regulatory developments in energy policy, alongside our traditional focus on national political issues. This strategic broadening of scope reflects the increasing interlinkage between economic policy, energy security, and environmental sustainability within the national agenda.

Contents:

1) **National Political Issues: Legislative Priorities and Parliamentary Dynamics**
    *   **Anti-terrorist Bill Consumes Parliamentary Session:** The Diet's current session has been largely dominated by intense debate surrounding the proposed anti-terrorist legislation. This critical bill aims to enhance national security measures and bolster international cooperation in combating terrorism, particularly in light of evolving global threats. Discussions have been robust, focusing on issues of civil liberties, the scope of surveillance powers, and the definition of terrorist activities, leading to prolonged deliberations and significant public scrutiny from both ruling and opposition parties.
    *   **Supplementary Budget Issues Next on Agenda:** Following the resolution of the anti-terrorist bill, the parliamentary focus is expected to shift immediately to the pressing matter of a supplementary budget. This substantial budget package, anticipated to address urgent economic stimulus needs, disaster recovery efforts, or other unforeseen contingencies, will likely face scrutiny regarding its allocation of funds and its projected impact on the national debt, setting the stage for further intense legislative discussions and potential political maneuvering.

2) **Energy Deregulation and Environmental Policy: Key Regulatory Developments**
    *   **Electricity Reform Committee to Start Deliberations November 5:** The Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) has confirmed the formal launch of the Electricity Reform Committee's deliberations on November 5th. This highly anticipated committee is tasked with reviewing and proposing fundamental reforms to the nation's electricity market structure. Its mandate includes evaluating the potential for greater market liberalization, promoting fair competition among power generators and retailers, addressing grid unbundling challenges, and ultimately aiming to achieve a more efficient, resilient, and consumer-centric electricity supply system. Key stakeholders, including major utilities, new market entrants, consumer advocacy groups, and industrial users, are expected to contribute extensively to these crucial discussions, shaping the future of the nation's energy landscape.
    *   **Environment Ministry Opens Committee to Discuss Merits of Carbon Tax:** In parallel with energy market reforms, the Ministry of the Environment has established a new expert committee to thoroughly evaluate the merits and implications of implementing a carbon tax. This initiative underscores the government's commitment to addressing climate change and achieving emissions reduction targets. The committee will examine various aspects, including the potential effectiveness of a carbon tax in incentivizing decarbonization across industries, its economic impacts on businesses and households, and potential mechanisms for revenue utilization, such as investment in renewable energy and green technologies. This marks a critical step in assessing the viability of market-based instruments for environmental policy and represents a significant policy exploration towards sustainable economic development.

Subject: Enron's Legacy: A Breakdown of Investor Confidence and Transparency Failures

Dear [Recipient Name],

I hope this email finds you well.

I wanted to provide a concise overview of the profound impact Enron's collapse had on investor confidence and the critical issue of corporate transparency. Enron, once a darling of Wall Street and a seemingly innovative energy trading company, became a symbol of corporate malfeasance due to its deceptive accounting practices and lack of forthright disclosure.

At the heart of Enron's downfall was a deliberate obfuscation of its true financial health. The company extensively used Special Purpose Entities (SPEs), particularly partnerships like LJM and Raptor, to hide massive debts and inflate earnings. These SPEs were often managed by Enron executives, creating significant conflicts of interest and allowing the company to keep vast liabilities off its balance sheet, thus presenting a deceptively robust financial picture to the public and investors.

This pervasive lack of transparency shattered investor confidence. Shareholders, who believed they were investing in a legitimate and profitable enterprise, suddenly found their investments worthless as the truth about Enron's hidden debts and manipulated profits came to light. The sheer scale of the deception, involving top management and its auditor (Arthur Andersen), led to widespread distrust not just in Enron, but in corporate financial reporting as a whole. Investors questioned the validity of financial statements across the board, demanding greater accountability and clearer, more honest disclosures.

The Enron scandal served as a stark reminder of the paramount importance of transparent financial reporting, ethical leadership, and robust independent auditing. It directly led to the passage of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, a landmark piece of legislation designed to improve corporate governance, enhance financial disclosures, and increase the accountability of corporate executives and auditors.

Enron's story remains a crucial case study in the perils of unchecked corporate power and the devastating consequences when transparency and ethical considerations are sacrificed for short-term financial gains.

Sincerely,

[Your Name]

Hi Adam and Stan,

Just wanted to give you an update after my follow-up chat with Gary Fitch about Enron Wind's aviation.

Gary shared some helpful insights: He mentioned that the aviation budget numbers look pretty comparable to operator standards (around $1,900/hour, with a 600-hour estimate). The plane has a market value of $1.8 - $2.0 million, though its book value is $2.2 million. Also, turbo prop charters for Tehachapi trips would be over $1,100/hour and might be tricky to book, as there are only two qualified operators. It turns out the Cessna is actually the only jet suitable for Tehachapi due to its runway length and altitude requirements. Gary also plans to do a site visit before the end of the year.

Looking at the numbers, if we assume only 400 of the budgeted 600 operational hours would require a charter, that charter cost would be about $0.5 million out of the $1.2 million total budget. When you combine this with the flexibility of using the plane for longer hauls (like to Houston), it really makes good economic sense.

So, my recommendation is that, considering everything, we hold onto the aircraft for now.

Best,
Tod

Hi!
I just got back from Germany!
It was a pleasant trip, but things in Frankfurt are just so expensive.
I went there for a distributor's meeting, and had the opportunity to meet the people we've been corresponding with over fax and email in the past.
Our account officer is a bright young woman—she’s only 23 and already very professional.
She’s already married, though.
Such is life!
I think one of the other distributors noticed me chatting with her quite a bit.
Anyway, being a quarter of the way around the world definitely puts things in perspective!
I was surprised that Frankfurt wasn’t as big as I expected—you can walk through the main parts of the city in just a few minutes.
There are a lot of churches (it seems like there’s one every five blocks), some industrial buildings, and a few castles.
They work hard to preserve a lot of historical sites, even if many of these buildings don’t have the same architectural style as the modern ones.
For example, the new European Central Bank building had to be constructed right behind one of these historic sites.
It’s a long building, taking up a lot of space—I’m still figuring out its purpose!
This kind of mix of old and new is pretty common all over Frankfurt.
A pleasant surprise for me was that the company covered my hotel room.
I was ready to pay for it, but I wasn’t charged at check-out!
Our meeting was from Monday to Thursday, so I had Friday and Saturday free before my flight home on Sunday.
I decided to join a bus city tour to Rothenburg.
Originally, I planned to visit Heidelberg, but I met an American-Chinese traveler from Santa Clara who works for an IT company, and decided to join her instead.
We spent Friday and Saturday exploring together.
I told my girlfriend all about it—nothing happened except for us hanging out.
But if something had happened, I’m not sure what I would have told her ;-)
Anyway, I’m thinking of taking my Master’s in Finance at the University of the Philippines.
Applications open in May and the exam is in August.
It’s a one-year course, so I’d graduate around the time Claudine finishes her local board exams.
I’m not sure about my future here in the Philippines, and I may follow her to the States or Canada if she specializes abroad.
Unless there’s some sudden positive change in the country, this seems like my best plan.
If she petitions me for Canadian citizenship, it might really help me get a job in Canada or the US.
I’m optimistic that the US economy will pick up in a couple of years—you all never stay down for long!
Meanwhile, things in my country aren’t going well.
There’s a lot of division; people just can’t come together.
Sometimes I joke we should divide the Philippines according to our various communities and call it the Divided States of the Philippines!
Oh well, just venting here.
Write back when you can.
Have you spoken to Khan lately?
Tell him to drop me a line—I haven’t heard from him in a while.
Hope he’s doing okay.
Send him my regards.
Cliff

The sound was so infectious, so visceral, that not only did HE have to flee the intense, hot glare of the set, his face a vivid flush of red, but half the crew stumbled away, their shoulders shaking with uncontrollable mirth, tears streaming down their faces.

Dear [Recipient],

I wanted to share my thoughts on the Nissan Pathfinder after having the opportunity to thoroughly evaluate this midsize SUV.

**Overall Performance:**
The Pathfinder delivers solid performance with its 3.5L V6 engine producing 284 horsepower. The CVT transmission provides smooth acceleration, though some may find it less responsive than traditional automatics. Fuel economy is competitive at approximately 24 mpg combined.

Nissan's Safety Shield 360 comes standard, including automatic emergency braking, blind spot monitoring, and rear cross-traffic alert. The ProPILOT Assist semi-autonomous driving feature works well on highways.

With 16.3 cubic feet behind the third row and 84.5 cubic feet with seats folded, cargo space is adequate for family needs. The power liftgate is a convenient feature.

The CVT can feel sluggish during highway merging, and road noise is somewhat noticeable at higher speeds.

**Conclusion:**
The Pathfinder offers good value as a family SUV with strong safety ratings, comfortable seating, and practical features, making it a solid choice in the competitive midsize SUV segment.

Best regards,

Thorough identification, cataloging, and professional valuation of all assets within the estate or trust, including real estate, investments, business interests, and personal property.

Hey everyone, a quick update on some important developments! This memo is to keep our EPMI and EES commercial teams in the loop about the status of retail competition here in Texas, especially in those non-ERCOT regions that include areas served by:

*   Southwestern Electric Power Company (SWEPCO) and West Texas Utilities Company (WTU) - both in the SPP region
*   Entergy Gulf States (EGSI) - in the Energy-SERC region

As many of you may have heard, the Texas Utility Commission has been taking a close look recently at whether these areas are truly ready for retail competition. The Public Utility Commission of Texas (Staff) even filed petitions to figure out if our market institutions are prepared to kick off retail competition in these regions on January 1, 2002. There's a bit of a worry, shared by the Commission and many others, that these non-ERCOT-Texas regions might not be quite ready for prime time. This concern mostly stems from two key things:

*   Not enough of a lively, efficient wholesale market in these regions, which means new REPs can't easily access other suppliers fairly.
*   The retail pilot programs in 2001 didn't really take off – no alternative suppliers joined, and customers didn't switch at all! A recent hearing sadly confirmed that most REPs aren't too keen on these regions right now.

**SPP Update**

Last week, the Public Utility Commission decided to push back the start of competition in SPP Texas. Or, as they prefer to say, "delay customer choice." We, Enron, were asked to share our thoughts and argued against any delays, pointing out that while SPP might not be a "perfect market," REPs could still operate there just like other marketers do. We don't have final dates yet, but it's looking like the delay could be anywhere from 12 to 18 months. The good news is that the Commission has outlined some clear steps and goals to hit before retail competition rolls out:

*   Helping SPP get its wholesale market operations off the ground, which means fine-tuning and upgrading some existing systems, like settlement.
*   Updating SPP Tariffs and bringing in market-based congestion management.
*   Keeping the pilot program going, encouraging new competitors to join, and ultimately opening up the market.

To help with all this, the Commission has set up a Southwest Power Pool Market Readiness Implementation Project (Docket # 24869). This project will work on the necessary steps for a smooth transition to full competition, identify key milestones, keep an eye on progress, and report back to the Commission regularly. And yes, Enron will be pitching in to support this important work!

**SERC Situation**

The SERC regions are seeing a similar push to delay competition from the Commission, much like SPP. The big difference here is that the existing utility, EGSI (an Entergy subsidiary), has been a strong advocate for implementing competition on schedule. The Commission's concern is that Entergy might end up in a "monopolistic" position if other REPs aren't present. While no final decisions have been officially made, Entergy Gulf States, along with the Commission Staff and other interested parties, has been working through a settlement process. The proposal is to delay retail competition until September 15, 2002. This is still under review by the Commission, but we're anticipating they'll approve the Settlement Agreement, which would mean competition would indeed be delayed until September 15, 2002.

**ERCOT – On Schedule?**

Interestingly, all this talk about delays has been centered *only* on non-ERCOT Texas. While there are a few whispers and ongoing chats about potentially delaying competition in ERCOT-Texas (which is still set for January 1, 2002), we have good reason to be optimistic. For example, Nancy Hetrich from Enron will be attending the Legislative Oversight Committee this Friday, November 2nd, representing us as Chair of the RMS Sub-Committee. Unlike the non-ERCOT areas, there's widespread support from most industry players to launch retail competition on time here. Plus, the pilot results were really promising, and ERCOT is expected to offer a robust wholesale competition environment. So, unlike SPP and Entergy, we don't anticipate any significant reasons or worries that would push back retail competition in ERCOT-Texas. We'll definitely keep you updated as more information comes in!

Subject: Enron Americas' Estate Management Strategy

Following its dramatic bankruptcy, Enron Americas' estate management strategy centered on a complex, multi-year liquidation process under Chapter 11. The primary objective was to maximize asset recovery and distribute proceeds equitably among creditors, a task complicated by the company's vast, interwoven structure, global operations, and significant litigation.

Key strategic pillars included:

1.  **Asset Identification & Valuation:** Meticulous efforts were undertaken to locate, categorize, and value a diverse range of assets, including energy trading contracts, physical infrastructure (pipelines, power plants), subsidiaries, real estate, and intellectual property. Many assets required significant legal untangling due to pre-bankruptcy transactions and securitizations.
2.  **Orderly Liquidation & Sales:** Assets were sold through a combination of auctions, private sales, and structured divestitures. The strategy aimed to optimize timing and market conditions where possible, though often dictated by court mandates and creditor pressures.
3.  **Litigation Management:** A significant component involved prosecuting and defending thousands of legal claims, including clawbacks from former executives, directors, and counterparties, as well as resolving disputes with various creditor classes. This was crucial for asset recovery and defining the estate's liabilities.
4.  **Creditor Management & Distributions:** Developing and executing a confirmed plan of reorganization involved extensive negotiations and legal wrangling to classify creditors, determine allowed claims, and establish distribution mechanisms, ensuring compliance with bankruptcy law.
5.  **Wind-Down & Administrative Efficiency:** Managing the remaining corporate infrastructure, including accounting, legal, and administrative functions, while minimizing administrative costs, was a continuous challenge throughout the protracted process.

The strategy consistently faced obstacles such as market volatility for energy assets, the sheer volume and complexity of legal claims, reputational damage impacting asset values, and the difficulty of recovering assets tied to international entities. The process, overseen by appointed trustees and a dedicated legal and financial team, resulted in the eventual dissolution of most Enron entities and significant, though partial, recoveries for creditors over more than a decade.

crabwise (KRAB-wyz) adjective     1.
Laterally.
2.
In a careful or indirect fashion.
[From the lateral movement of crabs.]
"John Smith continues to advance laterally toward modernity."
John Major's Last Year?, The Economist (London), May 15, 1993.

Having a child at home is truly a gift.
As the parent of a four-year-old, I endeavor to respond to my daughter Ananya's endless inquiries about the moon and earthworms and clouds and trees and bears as honestly as possible.
Our explorations of these apparently ordinary topics frequently uncover discoveries that serve as educational moments for us both.
However, there are occasions when my mind is distracted and I merely respond to the question "Why?" 
with "Because that's how God created them."
I was unaware I would be outsmarted until the night I discovered the corner of our living room wall decorated with vibrant crayon marks.
When asked why we had that artwork on the wall, she simply responded, "Because that's how God created it."
Well, if we were to inquire why a crab moves crabwise or laterally, that would be an excellent response: because that's how God (or nature, based on your personal convictions) designed it.
Because that's how their limbs bend.
That's how their muscles contract.
That's how they've evolved.
That's how they endure as a species.
And that's how we acquired a synonym for the word `sideways' in our lexicon.
If we were to search for the term `humanwise' in a crab's lexicon, it would likely mean `sideways'.
This week's AWAD showcases additional words originating from animals (the sole animal-derived materials we utilize here).
-Anu

If you didn't believe us before, I'm sure it is by now painfully clear that  negotiating master swap agreements is a very lengthy process.
My impression  is that the commercial team in Portland is anxious to begin trading  financially.
If this is correct, it would be possible, at least from a legal  point of view, to begin trading now under the existing documents.
In each  case where a master agreement is already in place, trades entered into before  the amendments we want will certainly be binding on both parties.
Our only  issues with trading under these agreements are where we need more restrictive  credit provisions and that resumption of trading before an amendment is  signed reduces to some extent our negotiating leverage.
As to the credit  issue, only the credit group can decide whether or not to permit trading  under the existing terms.
As for the negotiating leverage, if the commercial  people want to resume trading immediately, my suggestion would be to let them  go ahead.
If it turns out that additional leverage is needed, we can always  stop trading.
Where no master swap agreement exists, we have documentation available to  enable trading on a limited basis until the master is signed.
The so-called  "omnibus" confirmation will work for any normal commodity derivative  transaction and can be customized to include necessary credit provisions -  even where multiple trades exist with the same counterparty.
Tana has unsuccessfully tried to get you access to our Lotus Notes database  so you could determine the status of any negotiation on an up-to-the-minute  basis.
She will be sending a monthly report of our progress until you get  the necessary software to access the database.
Of course, if any issues come  up in the meantime, please continue to feel free to call.

Thanks,

Subject: The Importance of Kindness and Positive Values in Times of Conflict

Dear Team,

During times of conflict or war, it is easy to become overwhelmed by uncertainty and fear. However, it is precisely in these difficult moments that embodying kindness and upholding positive values becomes most crucial. When we choose compassion and empathy, we not only support those directly impacted by conflict but also foster resilience and hope within our communities.

Acts of kindness—whether small gestures or large-scale initiatives—can bridge divides, ease suffering, and remind others of our shared humanity. By living according to values such as respect, integrity, and solidarity, we inspire others to do the same and contribute to the foundation of a more peaceful and just world.

Let us remember that our attitudes and actions matter. Even in the face of adversity, kindness has the power to heal wounds and build a brighter future.

Warm regards,  
[Your Name]
source_text:
I thought that this is something to think about as we contemplate war...
I have to admit that I am caught between the feelings of needing to act with violence to defend and needing to act with compassion to understand.
> What can you do TODAY...this very moment?
A central teaching in most spiritual traditions is: What you wish to experience, provide for another.
Look to see, now, what it is you wish to experience-in your own life, and in the world.
Then see if there is another for whom you may be the source of that.
If you wish to experience peace, provide peace for another.
If you wish to know that you are safe, cause another to know that they are safe.
If you wish to better understand seemingly incomprehensible things, help another to better understand.
If you wish to heal your own sadness or anger, seek to heal the sadness or anger of another.
Those others are waiting for you now.
They are looking to you for guidance, for help, for courage, for strength, for understanding, and for assurance at this hour.
Most of all, they are looking to you for love.

Hi Kathy,

Here are my suggestions/comments on Rev. 6 Definitions, with some expanded notes and supporting evidence:

- I think we need a clear Business Day definition, and a comprehensive search and replace changing all instances of "business days" to "Business Days" for consistency. For context, most recent agreements standardize this term to avoid confusion, and the absence of a defined "Business Day" can create ambiguity, especially for deadlines around weekends or holidays. See sections 1.12 and 12.3 of the ABC Vendor Agreement for best practices.

- 1.55: The definition of Performance Tests currently reads more like the definition of "performance test reports" rather than the tests themselves. For accuracy and alignment with standard contractual definitions, I recommend creating or revising a definition that also incorporates the specific tests listed on Exhibit E, as these are explicitly referenced as the performance benchmarks. Additionally, the term "installation option" is used within this definition, but after doing a search through the document, I couldn’t locate any section that precisely describes the "installation option". This lack of clarity could leave parties uncertain about their obligations or available choices under the agreement. If it is meant to refer to an option previously discussed in negotiations, it should be spelled out in the definitions or referenced by section.

- 3.14.2.1: Is six months enough time under these circumstances? When comparing similar provisions in XYZ's supply agreement, the typical window is 9 to 12 months to accommodate for unexpected delays (e.g., permitting, supply chain issues). I would like to understand if there is a specific reason for opting for a shorter timeline here, or if there are risks associated with leaving it at six months. Would extending this period have any material impact?

- 4.3: Delete "Each" at the beginning. This appears to be a grammatical holdover, and its removal would improve clarity.

Hi John.
Here is the spreadsheet.
A couple of comments/assumptions:  Only trades done after 8/26/01 are considered (bid week started on the 27th in August). For example, any deals executed prior to August 27th, such as a fixed price trade on August 22nd, are not included in these calculations.
Only North American physical gas products are considered. This excludes any financial instruments (like swaps or options) and physical deliveries outside the US and Canada—for instance, a Nova Scotia gas deal is included, but a UK NBP or Henry Hub swing swap is not.
All numbers are in USD; an assumed conversion of 1.40 CAD/1 USD is used for the Canadian CAD trades. For example, for a sale to Enbridge at Dawn at C$4.20, this is converted to US$3.00.
For index pricing, an index of 3.00 USD is used. This applies whenever the trade references a monthly or daily gas price index, such as NGI or Platts—e.g., a buy at AECO monthly index would be priced at $3.00.

The other two sheets are supporting data. Sheet two lists transactional details, e.g., counterparty, location, volume, price, date, and currency; sheet three contains the raw deal data imported from the system.

**The Three-Party Transfer Process:**


1. **Initial Assignment (Day 1):** Fletcher Challenge assigns their petroleum business contracts to Shell Holdings as an intermediate holder


2. **Immediate Re-assignment (Day 1-2):** Shell Holdings immediately transfers all agreements and ongoing transactions to Apache Corporation


3. **New Master Agreement:** Apache negotiates a fresh ISDA Master Agreement to govern future derivatives trading


**Business Rationale:**

- **Credit Enhancement:** Apache has stronger creditworthiness than Fletcher Challenge, making them a more attractive counterparty

- **Risk Management:** The company wants all trading relationships backed by collateral agreements, regardless of credit quality

- **Clean Transfer:** Using Shell as a brief intermediate holder ensures smooth legal transfer of existing positions


**The Credit Tension:**

While Apache's strong credit profile typically allows trading without collateral requirements, the company maintains a firm policy requiring collateral annexes on all master agreements - creating a negotiation point between Apache's market expectation of unsecured trading versus the company's universal collateral requirements.


This structure is common in corporate restructuring where assets move between entities of varying credit quality, requiring careful coordination between legal assignment mechanics and credit risk policies.
