Early this morning, I met with Jack Steward (president of CMA) and Keith McCrea (CMA's lawyer) to follow up on the meeting Steve and I had with them about the proposal Ken Lay was pushing last week.

At the start, they expressed support for several elements: they like removing Texas from the MOU, they agree with getting DWR out of the power purchase business, and they believe Edison's MOU should be trimmed down. McCrea initially pushed back on the core/noncore concept, questioning why it should be mandatory to go to market. However, after a lengthy discussion, they acknowledged that our core/noncore approach has merit.

Our proposal is that the core/noncore split would take effect in 18-24 months, once markets stabilize and prices decline. Everyone—core and noncore customers—would help pay for DWR's previous purchases since all consumed that power. Core customers would receive IOU generation, QFs, and DWR contracts, eliminating the core’s "net short" position. Noncore customers would go to market and would not pay for DWR's "going forward costs," since the core customers—who receive all the low-cost IOU generation—would take those on. I let them know we are still crunching the numbers to determine the rate impacts and would share those results when ready.

While they are supportive of this approach and willing to help develop it further, they are not convinced there is enough support to get it passed. They are also withholding final judgment until they see the numbers, so we still have work to do. Their overall outlook is pessimistic: they are very skeptical about resolving anything in California and extremely upset about the PUC’s proposed rate decisions from the judge and Loretta Lynch. They have little trust in the Governor or the Legislature.

Interestingly, the recent rate increase decisions, together with calls in Sacramento for an immediate move to core/noncore, make our proposal much more attractive to CMA. Regardless, CMA said they will continue to engage and are willing to keep meeting to try to resolve California’s issues.

Subject: Refining Performance of Chilean *Eucalyptus globulus* for Pulp Production

Dear Colleagues,

I would like to draw your attention to the significant role of the refining performance of Chilean *Eucalyptus globulus* in the efficiency and quality of pulp production.

*Eucalyptus globulus* is a highly valued raw material in the global pulp industry, particularly in Chile, due to its excellent fiber characteristics. However, optimizing its refining process is crucial for maximizing its potential. Effective refining directly impacts the final pulp properties, including strength, drainage, and brightness, as well as the overall energy consumption of the mill.

Understanding the unique fiber morphology of Chilean *E. globulus* and tailoring refining strategies to achieve optimal fiber fibrillation and flexibility is paramount. This not only leads to superior pulp quality, suitable for a wide range of paper and board products, but also contributes to reduced operational costs through lower energy input and improved machine runnability.

Further research and the implementation of advanced refining techniques can unlock even greater value from this valuable resource, ensuring sustainable and high-quality pulp production.

Sincerely,

[Your Name/Department]

While most papermakers generally don't refine hardw= oods and softwoods with the same equipment, many smaller European mills are=  unable to afford the capital investment of a second refiner and accordingl= y do use a single refiner for all grades.
This is particularly true of the=  Italian mills.
Since hardwoods cannot withstand the rigorous refining req= uired for softwoods without losing their papermaking characteristics (opaci= ty, etc.
), these papermakers need to utilize the hardwood species best suit= ed for this type of processing.
Accordingly, the globulus species (which i= s also the predominant species in the Iberian peninsula) holds up much bett= er under this type of heavy refining than any other species of eucalyptus.

Dear [Recipient Name],

I wanted to inform you of a recent change regarding the application of FERC's "Shipper Must Have Title" rule. FERC has updated its guidance on how this rule is interpreted and applied to transactions involving the transportation of natural gas. These changes may impact the documentation and contractual arrangements required for shippers on interstate pipelines.

Either I didn't fully understand the December Texas Eastern order or else  FERC has just put a new and unhelpful spin on it.
The Thursday rehearing  order dramatically changes how the "shipper must have title" rule applies to  acquisitions of upstream capacity.
I thought the Dec. order pretty clearly  allowed a pipe to acquire upstream capacity and then resell that capacity  under the acquiring pipeline's rate schedules.
FERC specifically held that   the "shipper must have title" policy won't be applied if the acquiring pipe  treats the acquired capacity "as though it were part of its own system".
(p.  61,886)  The Dec. order even cited TW's acquisition of park n ride capacity  from PG&E as an example of the type of transaction that (I thought) could be  done without advance Commission approval.
Now, FERC explains that it did  not intend a "blanket waiver" of the shipper must have title policy.
Pipes  can still acquire upstream capacity without advance FERC permission, but only  if the acquiring pipe is going to use the acquired capacity for operational  needs or to resell under the selling pipe's release mechanism.
If the  acquiring pipe wants to use the acquired capacity to support sales of service  under the acquiring pipe's rate schedules, a specific waiver of the "must  have title" policy is required (see FN 20 and text).
We are right back to  where we started.
I guess the orders signal that FERC is  much more likely  to grant waivers of the "must have title" policy than in the past, but I  don't think we are good to go to acquire upstream storage, for example, and  resell it as FDD or IDD until we get permission first.

USA: INTERVIEW-EnronOnline sees volume growth, CEO says.  
By Gelu Sulugiuc  07/17/2001 Reuters English News Service (C) Reuters Limited 2001.  
NEW YORK, July 17 (Reuters) - While most players in a shrinking pool of online energy trading platforms struggle to survive, market leader EnronOnline follows a simple philosophy: If it ain't broke, don't fix it.  
The Internet arm of energy marketing and trading giant Enron Corp., EnronOnline anticipates continued growth in trading volume and believes it can peacefully coexist with the IntercontinentalExchange (ICE), Enron Networks’ chief executive told Reuters on Tuesday.  
As an innovative company, EnronOnline constantly assesses its business environment and is ready to adapt to market demands. However, it is not currently seeking mergers or acquisitions, according to Greg Piper.  
"I would never say never, but we're not proactively looking at acquiring an ownership position in any other exchange platform," Piper said.  
With an average of $3.5 billion in daily trades, EnronOnline boasts the highest volume of any energy electronic platform.  
Most energy trading platforms launched last year have failed to generate profits, but EnronOnline stands out from the crowd.  
Its closest rival is ICE, which regularly surpasses $1 billion in daily transactions.  
However, while ICE operates as a many-to-many exchange matching bids and offers, EnronOnline only allows trading directly with Enron.  
"It's a tool that supercharges our market-making business," Piper said.  
Enron remains the number one natural gas and electricity marketer in the United States.  
Roughly 60 percent of its transactions occur through the electronic platform.  
"As long as we show good prices to our customers, our volumes will continue to grow," Piper said.  
The company is looking to expand its online volume into products such as metals, steel, weather, petrochemicals, and plastics.  
"We're trying to remain the leader in energy and help our other markets gain traction," Piper said. "There is a huge amount of growth that we haven't even tapped into yet."  
Piper isn't concerned about ICE's recent success. The Atlanta-based exchange recently acquired London's International Petroleum Exchange and plans to migrate its open-outcry business online, significantly boosting trade volumes.  
"Maybe six to twelve months from now, the story might be very different," Piper said. "But right now, there is room for both of us."  
He added that Enron traders are not reluctant to trade on ICE. Many of the energy giants that founded ICE and provide most of its liquidity are also among Enron's biggest clients.  
"Enron will seek out a good deal on ICE when there is one," Piper said.  
INNOVATION KEY TO SUCCESS  
Recognized as one of the most innovative companies in the United States, Enron is continuously assessing its position in the market and looking for ways to become more successful.  
"The right thing to do in November 1999 was to launch EnronOnline," Piper said. "But we evaluate it daily, and if it made sense to do something different, you can bet Enron would do it without hesitation."  
One of the company's advantages is that its software is a flexible application, allowing EnronOnline to easily enter and exit different markets and regions.  
It is constantly adding new products to its trading arsenal.  
However, Piper said EnronOnline has no plans to transform itself into a many-to-many exchange.  
"We want to focus on providing our markets to others," he said. "In the near term, we're not changing that."  
The company is considering licensing the application itself, but Piper would not elaborate on who is interested or how much Enron would charge.  
EnronOnline has been so successful that even its competitors tip their hats to it.  
"I've been hearing for two years now that a one-to-many exchange wouldn't work, but Enron just keeps proving people wrong," said Frank Getman, chief executive of online energy exchange HoustonStreet.  
"If you're willing to make tight two-way markets and be the best price in the market, then people will continue to use your site."  
Enron's stock rose 41 cents to $49.53 a share on Tuesday on the New York Stock Exchange.

According to the DOE facilities manager, this rate has been relatively stable over the past six months, but they expressed concerns about potential increases given recent regional energy market volatility. The 5.3 cent figure represents their base energy charge and aligns with what we've seen in other government contracts in the Southwest region.

Tino's consultant claims that factoring in the demand charge yields an effective rate of approximately 7 cents/KWh. The consultant provided a detailed analysis showing that DOE's peak demand charges typically add 1.5-1.7 cents per KWh to their effective rate, particularly during summer months when their cooling loads are highest. This analysis was based on reviewing twelve months of DOE's actual utility bills and usage patterns. The consultant noted that DOE's load factor of approximately 75% is actually quite good for a government facility, but the demand charges still represent a significant portion of their total electricity costs.

Assuming we need to come in at 10% less than the current rate, our bogey is 6.3 cents/KWh. This 10% discount threshold was specifically mentioned by the DOE procurement team as their minimum expectation for considering alternative power arrangements. They indicated that anything less than 10% savings would be difficult to justify given the administrative overhead of switching from their current PNM contract. The 6.3 cent target represents a meaningful but achievable cost reduction that would provide DOE with approximately $280,000 in annual savings based on their current consumption levels.

First, I'd like to welcome you back. While Enron has faced challenging times this past year, I'm confident you will help lead us toward our goal of becoming the world's leading company.

I wanted to bring an important safety concern to your attention. A close friend who works at Enron and lives in Houston's outlying areas has been commuting using what I consider a risky practice. She, along with many other Enron employees and downtown workers, picks up strangers from park & ride lots to access HOV lanes. From what I understand, people literally line up while cars drive by to pick up passengers, with drivers and riders typically not knowing each other.

While I believe most people doing this have good intentions and are simply trying to save time, I'm concerned that someone with bad intentions could take advantage of this situation. I don't want anything to happen to my friend or anyone else.

I'd like to explore whether Enron could help our employees commute downtown more safely. Although I've spoken with my friend about these safety concerns, she hasn't changed her routine, so I'm hoping to find an alternative solution.

My suggestion would be for Enron to create a voluntary list of employees living in the same areas who could form official carpools together. While some might argue this isn't an Enron issue, I believe it is since several of our employees commute this way.

Recent tragic events have reminded me to focus on what truly matters. I simply want to help ensure my friend's safety.

Thank you for your time, and welcome back.

Dan,

I have reviewed the Wildhorse (Mesa) Gathering, Processing, and Transport Agreement and want to clarify the main takeaway: while the agreement is still valid and governs the gas dedication through 2013, it contains several significant issues that create uncertainty and risk for our project. My main concern is that these unresolved issues could delay or potentially jeopardize our ability to move forward, and we should address them with Wildhorse before closing and funding the deal.

Here are the key problem areas:

1. **Gas Quality** – The agreement only requires Wildhorse to transport gas if it meets the downstream carrier’s (Northwest Pipeline’s) specifications. Even if we propose to install a treating plant to meet these specs, the agreement does not allow us to connect a plant between Wildhorse and Northwest. Wildhorse could delay or demand added value from us for this connection, creating a significant uncertainty.

2. **Wildhorse’s Obligation to Perform** – When Northwest Pipeline enforced stricter gas quality specs and refused our gas, Wildhorse shut in Enogex’s production and has done so ever since. Under the agreement, Wildhorse is not obligated to transport gas unless it meets Northwest specs—so Wildhorse is not in breach, and its obligation was suspended. This means we currently have no avenue to require them to resume service.

3. **Unprofitability** – Even if Wildhorse helps us install a treating plant, they can still refuse gathering service if it remains uneconomical for them. In such a case, they can either renegotiate terms, allow us to operate their equipment at our own risk and cost, or release the gas from the agreement. Importantly, there is no deadline for Wildhorse to resolve this, nor any requirement they agree to a specific solution. They could indefinitely delay resolution and leverage this situation to extract more value from us.

**Recommendation:** We should make resolution of these issues with Wildhorse a condition precedent to closing and funding the deal. If Enron proceeds with funding before resolving these matters, everyone should be aware that negotiations with Wildhorse could be protracted, and they will have considerable leverage.

Let me know if you have any questions or would like to discuss further.

Dan,  I have reviewed the Wildhorse (Mesa) Gathering, Processing, and  Transport Agreement.
This agreement is still valid and the gas is dedicated  to this Agreement through 2013.
The agreement present some problematic  issues which I will outline.
1.
Gas Quality -  The gas quality provisions only require Wildhorse to  transport the gas if the gas meets the downstream carriers (in this case  Northwest Pipeline) gas quality specifications.
We propose to put in a  treating plant which would allow the gas to meet the specifications, however  there are no provision in this Agreement which allow us to insert a plant  between Northwest Pipeline and Wildhorse.
Wildhorse could delay are extract  value from us for this connection.
This is an uncertainty.
2.
Wildhorse Obligation to Perform - Based on my understanding of the  facts, at some point during the term of this agreement, Northwest Pipeline  enforced their gas quality specifications and refused to take the gas at the  downstream side of Wildhorse's Gathering System.
As a result, Wildhorse shut  in Enogex's production and it has been shut in ever since.
Wildhorse has a  right to do this under this Agreement (see #1 above) and therefore Wildhorse  has not breached its obligation to transport under this Agreement.
Wildhorse's obligation was suspended when Northwest refused receipt of the  gas.
3.
Unprofitability - Assuming Wildhorse worked with us to install the  treating plant which conformed the gas to Northwest Specifications, they  could refuse to provide gathering service under this agreement if it was  still uneconomical for them to do so.
If they decided it is uneconomical for  them to do so, they have the right to provide Enogex with various potential  solutions which include (i) renegotiating the terms (ii) allowing Enogex to  operate Wildhorse's equipment at Enogex sole cost, expense and risk, or (iii)  release the gas from the Agreement.
The problem here is that there is no  time limit under which Wildhorse must reach a solution with us and no  specific solution they must reach.
Wildhorse could drag this out for some  extended period of time and they could extract significant value.
My  recommendation is that we make Enogex's resolution of these issues with  Wildhorse a condition precedent to closing and funding this deal.
I know the  timing is late.
However if Enron funds this deal and takes on the risk of  negotiating with Wildhorse to resolve either a new deal or a release of the  gas,  everyone needs to understand that such negotiation could take  substantial time and Wildhorse will have significant leverage.

Subject: Enron Stock Moved to OTC Trading Following NYSE Delisting

Dear Shareholders,

We are writing to inform you that effective immediately, Enron Corporation (ENE) shares have been delisted from the New York Stock Exchange and will now trade on the over-the-counter (OTC) market under the symbol ENRNQ.

This delisting follows the NYSE's determination that our stock price has remained below the exchange's minimum listing requirements for an extended period. Trading will continue through electronic quotation systems, though liquidity may be reduced compared to exchange-listed securities.

Current shareholders should contact their brokers regarding any questions about trading or holding positions in the restructured symbol. We will continue to provide updates as our financial restructuring process moves forward.

For additional information, please visit our investor relations website or contact our shareholder services department.

Sincerely,
Enron Investor Relations Department
source_text:
Enron announced today that its common stock will now be traded as an Over-the-Counter (OTC) equity security under the symbol "ENRNQ."
This follows a decision by the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) to file an application to delist Enron's common stock, which means that Enron's common stock and related securities are suspended from trading on the NYSE.
Enron is considering whether to appeal the NYSE's decision.
The NYSE has standard criteria for listing stocks, which can be found on their website at www.nyse.com.
Enron recently fell below the following listing criteria: average closing price of a security less than $1.00 over a consecutive 30 trading-day period.
Quotation service for Enron's stock will now be provided by the National Quotation Bureau, LLC "Pink Sheets."
The NYSE's delisting of our stock will not have an impact on Enron's business, and we will continue to trade in the OTC market.

As I recall, the ABB contract was considered finalized on our end and subsequently signed by ABB *after* I had meticulously secured all necessary internal Global Finance approvals. Specifically, I received your explicit verbal approval on **July 14**, during our scheduled phone call at **11:00 AM** where we also discussed the Moore project. This was further corroborated by Rose's email confirmation sent on **July 15 at 10:30 AM**, and Herman's verbal assent during our team meeting on **July 16 at 2:00 PM**, as documented in the meeting minutes. Furthermore, we had diligently incorporated all specific comments and revisions provided by Rob Taylor via email on **July 13**, ensuring that all legal and commercial parameters were fully addressed and integrated into the final document we presented to ABB for their signature.

Given this comprehensive, multi-level internal review and the incorporation of all requested feedback, I genuinely believed that the Global Finance approval process for the ABB contract was definitively concluded, and the document was ready for execution by all parties. Consequently, the unexpected comments from WestLB, which arrived via fax on **July 19** – just a few days after what we understood to be the final version was out and ABB had signed – came as a significant surprise. We had not anticipated further revisions from external financing partners at such a late stage in the process, especially after the contract had already been signed by ABB based on the terms approved by our team.

Kay

Dear Equity Office Team,

This email addresses your request for documentation concerning a name change for Enron.

It is important to clarify that Enron Corporation did not undergo a conventional corporate name change. Following its collapse and subsequent bankruptcy filing in December 2001, the company entered into a complex dissolution process. Its assets were liquidated, and various divisions or subsidiaries were either sold off, spun off, or ceased to exist.

Therefore, there is no single "name change" document from Enron to a new entity in the traditional sense. Legal documentation regarding Enron's corporate status would typically involve bankruptcy court filings, asset sale agreements, and documents pertaining to the specific successor entities that acquired parts of Enron's former operations or assets.

If your request pertains to a specific asset, liability, or successor entity, please provide further details, and we will endeavor to assist you in locating the relevant bankruptcy court records or public filings.

Sincerely,

A cluttered, untidy, or disrespected space speaks volumes, reflecting poorly not just on the specific team that used it, but on our entire department and, by extension, the company's commitment to excellence and attention to detail. This initial impression can profoundly influence perceptions of our competence, organization, and even trustworthiness in critical business interactions, potentially impacting everything from client confidence to future hiring decisions.

We observed a particularly egregious instance of this last Thursday, following the morning project review in the Aspen Conference Room. Members of our group departed, leaving behind not only multiple empty lunch boxes and food wrappers, but also scattered notes, half-empty coffee cups, and general debris strewn across the table and even under chairs. Please do not put me in the position of having to address this personally with individuals or, worse, escalating this issue further to management. Vince

We learned today that the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit has modified its opinion of August 9, 2000 in which it found the 2003 Prozac patent invalid for double patenting. In essence, the Court has again ruled that the patent is invalid for double patenting, but has used a different analysis to reach this conclusion.

To put this into perspective, imagine two inventors, Alex and Morgan, both with a knack for solving puzzles. Alex creates a clever riddle and patents it; Morgan, seeing the potential, tweaks the wording but keeps the solution the same, and files for another patent. The examiner quickly spots that the second riddle is merely a dressed-up version of the first—essentially the same core idea—and denies it for "double patenting." In the real world, Barr's case isn't about brain teasers, but medications, where the rules apply just as strictly.

We intend to seek legal review of today's decision. Although it is possible that the legal review process could delay Barr from entering the market on August 3, we continue to plan for Barr launching generic fluoxetine at that time.

Joseph and I have begun (barely) to plan for this year's festivities.
But  before we get to far along, tried and true democratic (small "d") principles  call for a wee bit of polling.
Because we're already in the middle of October we need your responses  pronto.

Should we expand to include Western GA or keep it to SFGA?
We choose for dates the 7th or 8th or 14th or 15th of December.
What's your  preference.
Is there a day that just won't work?
Joseph, if I've missed anything, please tack on.
Best,

Jim: We're working on a deal where our company (ENA) sells natural gas to Citizens Gas in Arizona. Citizens Gas will then send this gas to PP&L for their Griffith power plant.

As part of this gas deal, another Enron company, Enron Asset Management Resources (EAMR), needs to operate a pipeline. This pipeline connects other gas pipelines (El Paso and Transwestern) to the main pipeline system that delivers gas directly to the Griffith power plant.

Here's the problem: EAMR thinks they should only be responsible for damages up to $144,000 (which is their yearly fee for operating the pipeline). However, Citizens Gas wants EAMR to be responsible for up to $1,000,000 if something goes wrong.

Citizens and EAMR agree on everything else about EAMR's services, just not this amount of responsibility. While our main gas deal might still happen without EAMR, it's not guaranteed.

I'm trying to find a solution to this problem so our gas deal can go through. This email asks for your opinion on two possible ways to solve the liability disagreement, specifically concerning how much they would cost and if they're even possible:

1) Our company (ENA) could buy an insurance policy to cover the difference in liability, from EAMR's desired $144,000 up to Citizens' desired $1,000,000.
2) EAMR could agree to take on the $1,000,000 liability, but in return, we (ENA) would pay EAMR an extra $120,000 (which is what we expect the insurance in option 1 would cost).

ENA prefers option 2. Our company, Enron, stands to make about $3 million from this overall deal (this information is confidential). We've set aside about $120,000, which is the estimated cost of increasing EAMR's responsibility from $140,000 to $1,000,000.

Please tell me if either option 1 or 2 is practical. If neither will work, I need to know soon so I can look into other solutions. If one of them is possible, which do you think is better?

Citizens Gas representatives will be here today at 3:00 pm. I would really appreciate your feedback by then. To reach me, please call Kim Ward at 713/853-0685, and she will find me. Thanks for your time. Chris

Jim:  As we have discussed, ENA is trying to close a gas supply transaction with Citizens Gas in Arizona to provide gas supply to Citizens for ultimate delivery to PP&L for the Griffith power plant.
As part of this transaction, Enron Asset Management Resources (EAMR) would provide services to operate a pipeline that interconnects El Paso and Transwestern to the pipeline header system that ultimately interconnects with the Griffith power plant.
To date, it has been the reasonable position of EAMR that its liability for services provided to Citizens should be "capped" at the sum of its annual fee of $144,000.
Citizens wants a $1,000,000 limit.
Citizens and EAMR have agreed to all aspects of the services deal except this liability question.
Although it might be possible to close our gas deal without EAMR, this is far from certain.
I have been trying to come up with an approach that would bridge this gap so that the ENA gas deal can be closed.
This e-mail is intended to indicate the value of this transaction to Enron and get your viewpoint as to the feasibility and cost of one of two deal structures:  1)  ENA buys insurance to cover the cost of our buying a policy to bridge th gap in liability from $144,000 to $1,000,000.
2)  EAMR decides to increase the laibiltiy to $1,000,000 in return for increasing their earnings on the deal by the amount ENA would pay fior the insurance product - about $120,000.
ENA's preference is clearly for approach 2.
The attached spreadsheet indicates the value of this transaction to Enron.
ENA will earn approximately $3 million on the deal.
Please keep this number in confidence.
In addition, we have budgeted about $120,000 for the insurance product to increase the liability of EAMR from $140,000 to $1,000,000.
Can you please advise me as to the feasibility of 1) or 2) above?
If there is no way we are going to get there, I need to know fairly quickly so I can explore other options.
If it is possible, which of the above 2 approaches is better from you perspective?
Citizens will be here today at 3:00 pm.
I would greatly appreciate some feedback from you by that time.
To contact me please call Kim Ward at 713/853-0685 and she will be able to find me.
Thanks very much for you time.
Chris

CLFP proposes the following changes to medium and large commercial and industrial customer tariffs for electric service provided by Pacific Gas and Electric Company and Southern California Edison Company.
CLFP proposes the Commission establish an optional summer on-peak, peak period consisting of a continuous 3-hour period during the current summer on-peak period for both utilities.
The 3-hour period would be selected by the customer.
Specifically:   Service Eligibility:  Customers served as medium or large commercial/industrial customers on time-of-use rates and metered accordingly.
Examples - PG&E's E-19, E-20, etc.
and SCE's TOU-8, etc.
Customer Eligibility:  Electric customers processing, handling, distributing or processing perishable food and agriculture products.
(As noted below, since no revenue shift occurs within the class, the Commission may consider opening the option to others.)
Customer Charge Surcharge:  A surcharge of $130 per meter per month for the initial summer period (2001) to offset the utilities cost for changes to billing procedures.
In the case of optimal billing period service customers the surcharge shall correspond with such billing period.
Optional Summer On-Peak Period:  Any continuous 3-hour period during the summer-on-peak period of time.
Hours may be designated by the customer consistent with metering capabilities of the customer or changes to metering capability.
The reason for designation by the food processor or agriculture commodity processing customer is in order to take into account the many factors involved in load shedding.
Labor, harvesting schedules and coordination with growers, delivery schedules, inspection activity, etc.
All bear upon such an effort.
Rate for Optional Summer-On-Peak Period Service:  Energy rates for the 3-hour period would be two times the otherwise applicable charge for summer-on-peak energy.
The other 3 hours of the 6-hour on-peak period would be billed at the non-peak rate and equalized for rate/revenue neutrality.
In the event partial peak periods are retained, the rate for the non-optioned 3-hour period during the on-peak period would be adjusted to retain revenue neutrality.
These rates would apply, as now, workdays of Monday - Friday.
Notice and Service:  An eligible customer must notify the utility in writing, by fax, email, or hand delivered, to both the appropriate account representative and the customer billing department of the request for optional summer-on-peak period service.
The 3-hour period of optional service and the start date for such service shall be specified.
Start dates should coincide with billing cycles, with a minimum of seven days notice prior to such cycle.
Optional optimal billing period customers would be treated accordingly, except as currently provided, a two-day advance notice.
Implementation Issues - TOU Meters and Billing.
It appears the number of customer meters and billing changes potentially required by optional summer on-peak period service is relatively small compared to the total number of meters of the utilities.
In response to CLFP's data request by PG&E and SCE (attached) the following is observed.
For SCE, SIC 20 (food and kindred products) customers account for approximately 163 meters out of about 10,000 meters.
Of the 163, all but 8 can be managed locally by the Customer Data Acquisition System.
The 8 would appear to require a field visit.
For PG&E, out of 11,675 TOU meters on E-19 and E-20 service, 354 or 3% of the total are SIC 20.
Of the 354 nearly half, 175, are hourly interval meters.
The remaining 179 presumably would need a field visit for reprogramming.
Conclusion:  Based upon the data supplied, metering and billing changes required by an optional summer on-peak period program for processors of perishable commodities, there does not seem, in CLFP's opinion, to be a significant barrier to establishing the program.

Dear Mr. Galvan,

Thank you for your recent letter concerning my support of a new basketball arena in Downtown Houston.

I believe that the responsibilities of my position at one of the world's leading companies extend far beyond day-to-day business—corporate leadership today means being actively engaged in the communities where our employees live and work. I am personally committed to helping Houston thrive, not only as a business hub but as a vibrant, inclusive city where all residents feel invested in its future.

Corporate stewardship is a cornerstone of a healthy, forward-thinking community. At Enron, we understand the challenges facing underserved populations in our neighborhoods, which is why each year we contribute one percent of our earnings to charitable causes. Our investments have grown as the company has grown, and now amount to millions of dollars annually. These contributions support a variety of initiatives, including programs that promote cultural diversity, fund educational programming and scholarships, and assist families and individuals as they work to rebuild their lives after hardship.

For example, our education partnerships with area schools have helped hundreds of students access college scholarships and opportunities that would have otherwise been out of reach. Furthermore, our support of organizations such as United Way, Houston Food Bank, and local shelters demonstrates our commitment to addressing issues of hunger, homelessness, and disaster recovery in our backyard. 

Three years ago, Houstonians took the bold step of passing a baseball stadium referendum, ensuring that the Houston Astros would remain in the city. The construction of that stadium ignited new economic growth and revitalization in our downtown district, resulting in increased tourism, more local businesses, and higher property values. According to the Greater Houston Partnership, the stadium has already generated millions in additional annual tax revenue and created thousands of new jobs.

A new downtown basketball arena to house our hometown Houston Rockets and Comets would not only build upon the momentum of these efforts but also serve as a catalyst for further development. Cities such as Denver and Cleveland have demonstrated that new sports facilities create jobs, stimulate local businesses, and attract national events such as playoff games and concerts, which in turn generate significant economic impact. The presence of professional sports teams also enhances civic identity and pride, helping to recruit and retain a world-class workforce by offering the kinds of amenities and excitement that talented professionals seek.

Houston has a vibrant, attractive central business district recognized around the globe. A state-of-the-art basketball arena is of key importance for the continuing revitalization of downtown, for ensuring that the Rockets and Comets remain integral parts of our community, and for keeping Houston competitive with other major cities. If we allow our city to fall behind in these areas, we risk losing not only beloved teams but also opportunities for business investment, tourism, and cultural enrichment.

Enron employs more than 6,500 individuals who live and work in Houston. We all take tremendous pride in being part of Houston's progress and success, and we are deeply committed to its ongoing growth and prosperity. We plan to remain in Houston for many years to come and strongly believe that making sure the Houston Rockets and Comets continue to call Houston home is essential to that vision. 

Downtown Houston is being transformed into an exciting, dynamic destination, and we cannot afford to lose this momentum. I appreciate your engagement on this issue and share your commitment to ensuring Houston remains a world-class city, both on and off the court.

Sincerely,

Today, we announced our third quarter earnings results, which were right on target with analysts estimates for recurring earnings per diluted share of $0.43.
This marks a 26 percent increase over the third quarter of last year, which is due to the strong performance of our core wholesale and retail energy businesses and our natural gas pipelines.
In addition, we also announced that we are on track for our earnings target of $0.45 for the fourth quarter ($1.80 for 2001) and $2.15 for 2002.
We made a commitment to you that we would provide you with timely information about Enron's business strategy and performance, so this email is intended to provide an explanation about our earnings this quarter.
Over the past few months, we have met with analysts to discuss Enron's performance.
We received considerable feedback from investors and analysts that we needed to expand our financial reporting to include details for more of our business units.
In response to that feedback, we have provided results separately for several of our business units.
For example, while we have provided volume figures for North America and Europe, this is the first quarter we have provided financials separately for Enron Americas and for Europe and Other Commodities.
In addition, information about our global assets had previously been included in our numbers for Wholesale Services.
This quarter they are reported separately.
Finally, even though our broadband business is now part of Enron Wholesale Services, we are continuing to report that business separately.
Following are the highlights of our businesses:  Wholesale Services: Total income before interest, minority interests and taxes (IBIT) increased 28% to $754 million in the third quarter.
Total wholesale physical volumes increased 65% to 88.2 trillion British thermal units equivalent per day (Tbtue/d).
Americas: IBIT increased 31% to $701 million.
Natural gas volumes increased 6% to 26.7 Tbtu/d, and power volumes increased 77% to 290 million megawatt hours (MWh).
Europe and Other Commodity Markets: IBIT remained unchanged at $53 million as compared to last year.
While physical gas and power volumes increased, low volatility in these markets caused profitability to remain flat.
Retail Services: Enron Energy Services reported IBIT of $71 million, compared to $27 million a year ago.
So far this year, EES has completed more than 50 transactions with large customers and more than 95,000 deals with small business customers.
Transportation and Distribution: 	Natural Gas Pipelines: IBIT increased slightly to $85 million in the third quarter.
Portland General: We reported an IBIT loss of $(17) million this quarter compared to IBIT of $74 million a year ago.
This loss is due to power contracts PGE entered into at prices that were significantly higher than actual settled prices during the third quarter.
Last week, we  announced an agreement to sell PGE to Northwest Natural.
This transaction is expected to close next year.
Global Assets: This segment includes Elektro, Dabhol, TGS, Azurix and Enron Wind.
Third quarter IBIT remained unchanged at $19 million compared to last year.
Broadband Services: IBIT losses were $(80) million in the current quarter compared to a $(20) million loss last year.
This quarter's results include significantly lower investment-related income and lower operating costs.
Corporate and other: This segment includes the unallocated expenses associated with general corporate functions.
This segment reported an IBIT loss of $(59) million compared to $(106) million a year ago.
In addition, this quarter we announced one-time charges of $1.01 billion.
Over the past few quarters, we have conducted a thorough  review of our businesses and have decided to take certain charges to clear away issues that have clouded the performance and earnings potential  of our core businesses.
These charges include: ?
A $287 million write-down of Azurix Corp. ?
$183 million associated with the restructuring of Broadband Services.
This includes severance costs, a loss on the sale of inventory like servers and routers, and a write-down of the value of our content services contracts due to the bankruptcy of a number of customers.
?
$544 million related to losses from certain investments, primarily Enron's interest in The New Power Company, broadband and technology investments and early termination of a structured finance arrangement.
With our announcements this quarter we accomplished three things:  1) we showed continued strong earnings and earnings growth in our core businesses, 2) we cleared away those things that were clouding this superb performance in our core businesses, and 3) We expanded our reporting of financial results to increase transparency for our investors.
To read the full earnings press release, go to www.enron.com/corp/pressroom/releases.

On December 29, 2000, Enron North America Corp. and Deutsche Bank AG entered into a comprehensive trading relationship by executing an ISDA Master Agreement (Multicurrency-Cross Border) governed by New York law.

**Middle:**
The agreement provides extensive trading capabilities, covering all approved products including foreign exchange transactions. Deutsche Bank AG serves as both the confirming entity and calculation agent, with operational flexibility across nine approved branches: Brussels, Frankfurt, London, New York, Paris, Singapore, Sydney, and Tokyo. The structure includes provisions for Deutsche Bank AG to act as agent for Deutsche Bank Securities when specifically designated in transaction confirmations.

**End:**
The payment structure establishes a dual framework: cross-transaction payment netting applies exclusively to commodity transactions, while non-commodity transactions operate without payment netting provisions, thereby completing the operational parameters for this comprehensive trading arrangement.

We reached a conceptual agreement with government representatives on Sunday night. The main points are as follows:

1. **Rationing Losses:**  
A defined methodology has been established, allowing distribution companies to recover rationing losses incurred from June 1 until the end of rationing in 2002 over the next 36 months. Recovery will include financial compensation. Immediate funding, covering 80% of these losses, will be provided through BNDES with support from Brazilian government funds. The loans will be repaid over three years as tariff increases are implemented. Funding is expected to be in place by December 15th. For Elektro, the EBITDA impact is approximately R$191 million (US$73 million).

2. **April/May MAE Settlement:**  
The market will settle under current rules, as the pre-rationing conditions are confirmed by the procedures used in Elektro’s books. The impact for Elektro is approximately R$18 million (US$7 million).

3. **Parcel “A” for the Future:**  
All non-controllable costs faced by local distribution companies (LDCs)—including power purchases and sector charges—will be passed through to final tariffs, either using a tracking account mechanism or by synchronizing adjustment dates with LDC tariff revision dates. The tracking account will accrue financial compensation from the date these costs are incurred until they are effectively passed through and collected, thereby eliminating a significant risk for the distribution sector. For Elektro, the EBITDA impact from 2002 onward is R$60 million (US$19 million), as accounted for in the 2002 plan. This methodology represents substantial risk mitigation as initial power supply contracts are renewed starting in 2003.

4. **Parcel “A” from the Past:**  
Minister Parente has agreed in principle to recover non-controllable costs that were not passed through to tariffs since late 1999, using the same methodology as for future recoveries. A dedicated team from the Federal Attorney General’s office is working to reach a final solution within ten days. For Elektro, the impact in 2001 is R$145 million (US$55 million). The proposed recovery mechanism will take effect after the 36-month period designated for rationing losses.

We are currently finalizing a memorandum of understanding, while the government team is completing settlements with generators to finalize the terms of the overall agreement. Minister Parente has committed to resolving the outstanding issues affecting investors in the power sector.

These agreements represent a major step forward and significantly enhance the value of our businesses. By resolving the lingering issues related to rationing losses and eliminating the Annex 5 controversy, the MAE should return to normal operations, enabling us to operate Eletrobolt and settle against the pool.

Total benefits for the sector amount to approximately R$10 billion (US$3.8 billion at current exchange rates). Our team has led sector negotiations since the onset of rationing and has been instrumental in convincing the government of the need for these changes.

Folks,

Here are some preliminary comments on the model we are using for Argentina. Please correct me on any misunderstandings!

**Model Overview**
ModReg was written by consultants in Buenos Aires. Documentation is available in Spanish only. All data input is by means of text files, which require column-oriented input—numbers must go into specific columns. Detailed documentation has been provided specifying the data format for each file.

**Technical Specifications**
The model uses a weekly time step with five load blocks per week and a time horizon of one year, typically. Each model run requires about 6 hours of processing. ModReg is a modified version of the model used by the grid operator. It is coded in Fortran and requires a CPLEX licence.

CPLEX is a powerful linear programming solver developed by ILOG. Since the model is written in Fortran, the very good higher-level interface to CPLEX is not available, so the code must access CPLEX at a lower level. We have no documentation describing the model algorithms. Source code is not available at present.

**Model Structure**
ModReg appears to model around 30 buses and 71 lines. Lines are characterized by from bus number, to bus number, maximum MW capacity in each direction, a percentage loss factor, cost of transmission in each direction, and some other details.

Demand data is specified by week and load block for each bus. Thermal plants have a heat rate and maintenance schedule specified, with the possibility of multiple fuels. I understand that hydro generation schedules for each historical inflow condition are an input to the model as they are calculated elsewhere.

**Current Challenges**
From the above it appears that we have an unsatisfactory situation:
• ModReg is difficult to use
• We do not know in detail what the model does
• We do not have documentation describing the algorithm
• Because source code is not available, we are completely dependent on the consultants

**Recommendations**
If Enron is to continue modeling Argentina, we should as a minimum have a model that we understand, is reasonably easy to use, and is documented. A graphical user interface is really needed to make ModReg easier to use. Documentation is, of course, essential. We should not use a model developed by consultants without documentation.

These steps would enable us to have more confidence in model results and shorten the learning curve to enable more people to use the model.

**Alternative Solution**
SDDP is likely to be a suitable replacement. It would require reservoir inflow data rather than the calculated generations. The regional loads could be modeled using the DC loadflow feature with zero impedance lines. Transmission losses in SDDP are a quadratic function of power flows, so some guesses would have to be made for line resistance values.

Setting up an SDDP model to represent all the aspects included in ModReg would be a time-consuming job that would require a good understanding of the data for both models. Some direct cut and paste of data from one model's files to the other will be possible with a suitable column-oriented text editor. However, the end result would be a model with the desirable attributes of documentation, GUI interface, and flexible output.

Tom Halliburton

I've developed a streamlined solution to address the EES sleeve issue in our EOL reporting.

This approach will require just a few additional minutes daily but should significantly improve the relevance and accuracy of our EOL summary. Here's what I'm proposing:

1. You will continue to receive the same EnPower/EOL summary, complete with EES sleeves.
If I take the EES deals out of this table, I have to adjust the total megawatts accordingly.
This could end up taking awhile, and I'm not sure the effect would be worth it.
Again, let me know if you agree, because I'd like this report to be as applicable as possible.

2. I will run the EnPower deal count, excluding EES deals.
I'll compare this count to the original one to determine how many EES deals were done by each desk, then double that number - to account for both sides of the sleeve - and subtract.
I'll enter the altered numbers into the graph, which should produce a more accurate rendering of the day's activities.

I think I made it sound more complicated than it is.
Bottom line, this should solve the EES sleeve dilemma with little ado.

Kate

To make a long story short, I plan to catch the 2:30 p.m. bus home today.
I will be back in tomorrow at 7:00 a.m. and at full speed.
I apologize for any inconvenience this may cause.

Subject: Reorganization of Enron's Human Resources Department

Dear Team,

I am writing to inform you about important changes taking place within Enron’s Human Resources department. As part of our ongoing efforts to streamline operations and enhance organizational effectiveness, we are undertaking a reorganization of our HR functions.

The restructuring will involve the consolidation of certain roles, realignment of responsibilities, and implementation of new processes aimed at supporting both our employees and strategic objectives more efficiently. We anticipate that these changes will strengthen our ability to attract, retain, and develop top talent while also improving our service to all business units.

We understand that such transitions can bring questions and uncertainties. Over the next few weeks, the HR leadership team will provide updates and facilitate sessions to answer your questions and gather your feedback. Our goal is to ensure a smooth and transparent transition for everyone involved.

Your patience and cooperation during this period are greatly appreciated. Should you have immediate questions or concerns, please do not hesitate to reach out to me directly or contact your HR representative.

Thank you for your continued dedication and support.

Best regards,

[Your Name]  
[Your Title]  
Enron Human Resources
source_text:
Greg,  I've been helping the HR team draft this memo.
Cindy asked that I run it by you prior to having it sent out.
Any comments?
As we continue to address a number of issues facing Enron, it is critical that the company remain focused on attracting, motivating and retaining our diverse and talented workforce.
We strongly believe that our workforce is world-class - the best in any industry, so we will continue to develop and reward this tremendous talent base.
Because the lasting strength of our company is determined by the strength of our workforce, we are elevating the role employee-focused functions play within Enron.
We are pleased to announce that effective immediately Human Resources, Employee Responsibility, and Executive and Corporate Compensation will report directly to the Office of the Chairman.
David Oxley, Vice President, will continue to oversee Enron's Global HR function.
The lead HR representatives for the individual business units will report to David in addition to their respective Office of the Chairman.
Besides managing Recruiting, Staffing, Training, Compensation and the Performance Evaluation Process, David will also add Payroll and Labor Relations to his list of responsibilities.
Cindy Olson, Executive Vice President, will have responsibility for Employee Relations and Corporate Responsibility, which includes Social Responsibility, Community Relations, Diversity, Employee Relations, Redeployment, Alumni Relations, Employee Events and Programs, Benefits, Wellness, and Worklife.
Mary Joyce, Vice President, will continue to have responsibility for Executive and Corporate Compensation in addition to Global Employee Information Management and Reporting and Analysis.
David, Cindy and Mary will each report to the Office of the Chairman.
A detailed organizational chart is attached.
Please join me in congratulating them on their new responsibilities.

Dear WTN Members, WTN Associates, and other WTN friends,  On behalf of the membership of the World Technology Network, I wish to express deep, deep condolences to the family, friends, and colleagues of one of our members, Daniel C. Lewin, aged 31, who perished on 11 September on American Airlines Flight 11 as it was deliberately crashed into the World Trade Center in New York.
Over a year ago, Danny (along with, Tom Leighton, his fellow co-founder of Akamai Technologies) was inducted into the WTN membership as a co-Finalist for the World Technology Award for Commerce.
All those who are even nominated for a World Technology Award, such as yourself, are singled out for doing work of "the greatest likely long-term significance."
It is, therefore, even more tragic and non-sensical that a person such as Danny, who so purposefully engaged in a process of hopeful and innovative creativity, should be a victim of an act of such purposeful negation of innocent life.
We mourn all of the victims of the constellation of tragedies that occurred on September 11th and, in particular, we re-salute you, Mr. Lewin.
The world will miss you.
Your life was clearly already marking the future.
I suspect somehow it now shall do so even more.
Onward,  James P. Clark Chairman The World Technology Network

Ken,  I wanted to let you know that I spoke with W.O. King, the Director of External Affairs, at the Baker Institute earlier today. Everything is ready for tomorrow's activities, including the logistics for the award presentation and the security protocols for Chairman Greenspan's visit. There will be a great deal of media coverage for the event from outlets such as The Wall Street Journal, CNN, Reuters, The New York Times, and the Houston Chronicle. Many of these media organizations will be accessing the live video feed of Chairman Greenspan's speech, which is being coordinated by the Baker Institute's AV team and broadcast via their secure streaming platform. However, the media will not be able to interview any participants directly, as per Chairman Greenspan's advance team’s requirements and Baker Institute media policy.

Chairman Greenspan will only answer written questions submitted by the audience (including media), and those questions will be vetted twice: first by the Baker Institute's communications staff and then by Greenspan’s personal aides before being passed to the moderator on stage. I will be receiving the media advisory that has been distributed, which outlines the press restrictions and photo opportunities, as well as the most current media attendee list from the Baker Institute tomorrow morning. I will provide that to you as early as possible once received.

You probably know that, because of his position as Federal Reserve Chairman, Chairman Greenspan cannot accept the prize itself—an engraved crystal sculpture and $10,000 honorarium—but only the "honor" of being named an Enron Prize recipient. For that reason, the Enron Prize will not be present on stage during the ceremony, and there will be no physical hand-off.

Karen Denne, Christie Patrick and I will be attending as Enron representatives, and we will coordinate with Baker Institute staff at the check-in desk near the main rotunda at 9:45 a.m. Please let me know if you have any questions or need additional information prior to the event.

See you there,  
Terrie

Subject: Class Action Lawsuit: Document Request Protocol

Dear [Recipient Name/Team],

This email outlines the established protocol for all document requests related to the ongoing class action lawsuit, [Lawsuit Name/Case Number, if known]. Adherence to this protocol is critical to ensure proper legal compliance, maintain data integrity, and streamline the discovery process.

**Protocol for Document Requests:**

1.  **Centralized Point of Contact:** All document requests, whether originating from internal legal counsel, external counsel, or court order, must be routed exclusively through [Department/Person's Name/Email, e.g., the Legal Department's Discovery Coordinator at discovery@yourcompany.com]. Do not respond directly to requests from external parties without prior internal authorization.

2.  **Request Submission Format:** All requests must be submitted in writing, preferably via email, and clearly state the specific documents or categories of information sought, the relevant date ranges, and the requesting party. Verbal requests will not be processed.

3.  **Acknowledgement and Triage:** Upon receipt, the Centralized Point of Contact will acknowledge the request within [e.g., 2 business days] and initiate a triage process to assess the scope, relevance, and potential custodians.

4.  **Custodian Identification:** The Centralized Point of Contact, in consultation with relevant department heads, will identify potential custodians of the requested information. Legal holds, if not already in place, will be issued or confirmed to all identified custodians.

5.  **Document Collection:** Custodians will be instructed on the secure and compliant method for collecting responsive documents. This may involve utilizing specific e-discovery tools or following designated secure transfer protocols. Personal devices or unapproved storage locations must not be used for document collection or transfer.

6.  **Review and Redaction:** Collected documents will undergo a thorough legal review for responsiveness, privilege, and necessary redactions by [e.g., the Legal Team/Designated Review Counsel].

7.  **Production:** Approved documents will be produced to the requesting party in the format and timeframe stipulated by court order or agreed upon by all parties. All productions will be logged and tracked.

8.  **Communication:** All communication regarding document requests and production schedules will be managed by the Centralized Point of Contact. Department heads and individuals involved in document collection will be kept informed as appropriate, but direct communication with opposing counsel or the court regarding document details is prohibited unless explicitly authorized.

Failure to follow this protocol may result in legal non-compliance, sanctions, or compromise the company's position in the lawsuit. Please direct any questions regarding this protocol to [Centralized Point of Contact's Name/Email/Phone].

Thank you for your immediate attention to this critical matter.

Sincerely,

[Your Name/Legal Department]
[Your Title/Company Name]

Good news! The tariff *does* permit us to nod along to such an alternate point and rate. Even better, it doesn't *require* us to give away the farm! If BP tries to sweet-talk us, let's stick to our guns: "One month, take it or leave it!" (Okay, maybe phrase it a *tad* more politely).

For those who haven't memorized the thrilling saga of the Global Settlement, our ability to approve or deny changes to a customer's primary or alternate paths outside the main route is our secret weapon to recoup those pesky turnback costs. In plain English, by strategically *not* agreeing, we might just snag some incremental revenues to help cover those turnback costs we're now, ahem, 100% on the hook for. Think of it as our chance to turn a 'no' into a 'cha-ching!'

Lorraine, could you work your magic and fill in the Contract No. for me? My crystal ball is a bit foggy on that one.

And with the Dynegy transition keeping us all on our toes, please forward any additional brilliant comments or observations to Bill Rapp. He's eagerly awaiting your wisdom!

Maria

Kern Gets Speedy OK; Breathitt Questions Action  FERC moved with record speed to issue a certificate last week to Kern River  Gas Transmission for its 135 MMcf/d, mostly compression, expansion to the  natural gas-starved California market, but not all of the commissioners were  happy with the expedited manner in which the project was approved.
"The speed with which the Commission has acted in this proceeding is  something which will no doubt be touted as a great effort," but the  "precedent we have created could be a double-edged sword," warned  Commissioner Linda Breathitt in a partial dissent of the decision.
Although  she voted in favor of the certificate in the end, she questioned whether FERC  "should...be willing to sacrifice careful review for speedy action."
Breathitt further said she seriously doubted the so-called California Action  expansion of the 900-mile,Wyoming-to-California Kern River system merited the  "extraordinary regulatory treatment" that the Commission gave it.
Critics  claim that the $81 million project will not flow any more gas to the Wheeler  Ridge Interconnection in California than is currently available there, she  noted, adding that it would simply displace existing gas.
"...[I]t will not necessarily result in any net increase of natural gas in  the California marketplace.
This makes it difficult to understand just how  our approval of Kern River's proposal is going to assist in increasing  electric generation in California this summer," Breathitt said.
If anything,  she noted the project could make the congestion problem at Wheeler Ridge even  worse than it is.
There should have been a "fuller airing of this issue" at FERC before the  project was certificated, she noted.
"It would be counterproductive for this  Commission to act precipitously on projects related to California without  ensuring that they will, in reality, benefit specific markets --- and more

Given the extreme scrutiny and potential liabilities we're currently facing, I immediately thought of you. Do you have *any* recollection or knowledge of these agreements? This could expose us to significant unmanaged risk.
I am absolutely terrified to call the counterparty, as I fear opening a Pandora's Box of unknown liabilities. And to assume 'it probably doesn't even matter at this point' feels incredibly reckless, especially given the current climate.
My immediate impulse is to send these documents to the file room, but without a contract number or any identifying information, they'll simply be lost in limbo, adding to our already precarious record-keeping situation. This isn't just about filing; it's about accountability.
Jeff, we need to address this *urgently*. What do we do? How do we mitigate the potential fallout from these missing, critical documents? Your immediate guidance is crucial.

Subject: Deep Disappointment and Broken Promises

Dear Mr. Lay,

I am writing to express my deep disappointment and anger regarding the events leading up to Enron’s collapse and the devastating impact it has had on me and countless colleagues.

When I joined Enron, I believed in the values and promises that senior leadership, including yourself, publicly championed. You assured us of our company’s integrity, long-term vision, and commitment to employees. At every step, we were told that hard work and loyalty would be rewarded, and that Enron would stand by its people. This trust and dedication have been repaid with unemployment, broken promises, and financial ruin.

In the wake of Enron’s failure, it’s clear that our values—once a point of pride—were cast aside by those entrusted to uphold them. Decisions made by leadership left thousands without jobs, retirement savings, and health insurance. The sense of betrayal is immense. I urge you to reflect on the real cost of these failures, not just for executives, but for every employee whose life was upended through no fault of their own.

I believed in Enron and in your leadership. Today, I am left angry and disillusioned, a casualty of empty assurances and a culture that prioritized profit over people.

Sincerely,  
[Former Employee Name]

Mr. Lay: I am a former Enron employee.
I used to be proud of Enron.
I believed everything that you and EES management said.
I believe that the Vision and Values that you and other senior executives at Enron preached are not worth the paper they are printed on.
Respect, Integrity, Communication, Excellence.
I don't believe you respected the rights of so many Enron employees who sacrificed their family time so that the company would succeed.
I don't believe you have any integrity when it comes to fully disclosing Enron's future.
You obviously have not communicated the truth to employees, analysts or anyone else.
Maybe you should look inside yourself to see if you have the excellence now that you demanded from your employees.
I would like to see you take ownership of the incredible debacle that has fallen upon Enron.
So many of my friends and colleagues are out of work because of the gross mismanagement that you and others have shown.
I believe the least you could do is go on record and address these people at a time of year that is so special to so many.
Do the right thing and show some of the visions and values that you spoke so highly of not so long ago.
Show the men and women of Enron and Houston what you're all about.
Steve Beck

I have sent original contracts for execution, watching as the email with the attachments blinks out of my outbox. Now we have to put the deal in the system, which is never as simple as it seems.

The attached spreadsheet—still open on my screen, numbers glinting under the harsh fluorescent lights—lays out how this deal will work, using June as an example month. The air hums with the faint buzz of computers, and I scrawl notes in the margin: “The only differences between June and future months are:  1)  In the future, we will collect a $.09/MMBtu demand charge, with $.02/MMBtu of this going to EAMR (ENA gets $.07/MMBtu). 2)  In the future, the PG&E discount is $.10, not $.25.”

Across the hall, printers clatter as invoices print for other contracts, but for this deal, we will continue to bill Citizens for the TW Mainline cost on our utility deal. Thanks!

Mark and Greg,

I hope you'll consider these strategic recommendations that could significantly strengthen our operations and financial position.

**1) Establish a Chief Risk Officer with Deal Authority**
We urgently need a single officer empowered to reject deals before they reach your Office of the Chairman. While Rick Buy may be reluctant, someone with his caliber and real authority must fill this role—ideally within each business unit. The key is selecting someone committed to exhaustively exploring ways to improve deals before making the final call to reject them. This single change could prevent costly mistakes and streamline our decision-making process.

**2) EIM Leadership Requires Immediate Action**
EIM needs new leadership now. If Bowen won't accept the position, I strongly urge you to consider Shankman. His exceptional performance at EGM over the past 12 months demonstrates he's ready to lead his own operation. This promotion would capitalize on proven talent while addressing a critical leadership gap.

**3) Eliminate the Dividend—Retain Hundreds of Millions**
We must stop paying dividends immediately. Unlike companies dependent on institutional investors who require dividends, we have the flexibility to retain these hundreds of millions of dollars. This capital could be deployed far more effectively to fuel growth and strengthen our competitive position.

**4) Reduce London Metal Inventory Exposure**
Our London metal inventory represents an excessive capital commitment and operational risk. We should seriously evaluate exiting this inventory-intensive business and redirecting resources to higher-return opportunities with less physical exposure.

These recommendations address fundamental operational and financial inefficiencies that are costing us significant value. I'm confident implementing these changes will deliver substantial returns and position us for stronger performance.

Thank you for your consideration of these critical initiatives.

James C. Lewis  
VP Finance and Structuring EGM

The following terms will be recognized on the ICE System for trading of North American Natural Gas during the upcoming holiday season. Note that these scheduling adjustments reflect market closures and altered trading days for Christmas and New Year’s:

• **Friday, December 21:**  
  - **NEXT DAY = December 22–26**  
  - All NEXT DAY natural gas trades booked on Friday, December 21 will be for gas flow dates covering Saturday, December 22 through Wednesday, December 26.  
  - This consolidates Saturday, Sunday, Christmas Eve (Monday, Dec 24), Christmas Day (Tuesday, Dec 25), and Boxing Day (Wednesday, Dec 26, Canada only) into a single trading term due to market closures on those dates.

• **Monday, December 24 (Christmas Eve):**  
  - **NEXT DAY = December 25–26 (Canada only)**  
  - For Canadian delivery points, the NEXT DAY product traded on Christmas Eve covers both Christmas Day and Boxing Day (Tuesday, Dec 25 and Wednesday, Dec 26). This is due to Canadian market closures on both days.
  - **SAME DAY = December 24–26 (Canada only)**  
  - For certain Canadian hubs, SAME DAY products traded on Monday, December 24 will cover gas flow for the combined period of December 24 through December 26.

• **Wednesday, December 26:**  
  - **NEXT DAY = December 27 (normal)**  
  - Trading resumes to standard schedules, with NEXT DAY transactions for gas delivered on Thursday, December 27.

• **Thursday, December 27:**  
  - **NEXT DAY = December 28 (normal)**  
  - Normal trading terms apply. NEXT DAY products traded on Thursday, December 27 will be for Friday, December 28 flow.

• **Friday, December 28:**  
  - **NEXT DAY = December 29–31 (normal; Friday afternoon trades include Jan 1–2)**  
  - NEXT DAY trades on the morning of Friday, December 28 will be for gas delivery Saturday, December 29 through Monday, December 31.
  - During the Friday afternoon trading session, terms may be available to cover the New Year’s holiday period—specifically, combined flow days of Tuesday, January 1 (New Year’s Day) and Wednesday, January 2, reflecting anticipated market closures or limited scheduling.

• **Monday, December 31 (New Year’s Eve):**  
  - **NEXT DAY = January 1–2**  
  - NEXT DAY products traded on Monday, December 31 will be for gas flow covering New Year’s Day (Tuesday, January 1) and the day following (Wednesday, January 2), due to holiday market closures.

---

If your delivery or trading needs do not match these standard holiday schedules, please utilize the "Bal Month" (Balance of Month) and "Custom Strips" products available on ICE to configure non-standard or partial period trades as needed. These tools allow for scheduling of alternate flow dates beyond those described above.

**A Poem About September 11, 2001**

**Two Thousand One, Nine Eleven**

Two thousand one, nine eleven  
Five thousand plus arrive in heaven  
As they pass through the gate,  
Thousands more appear in wait  

A bearded man with stovepipe hat  
Steps forward saying, "Let's sit, let's chat"  

They settle down in seats of clouds  
A man named Martin shouts out proud  
"I have a dream!" and once he did  
The Newcomer said, "Your dream still lives."  

Groups of soldiers in blue and gray  
Others in khaki, and green then say  
"We're from Bull Run, Yorktown, the Maine"  
The Newcomer said, "You died not in vain."  

From a man on sticks one could hear  
"The only thing we have to fear..."  
The Newcomer said, "We know the rest,  
trust us sir, we've passed that test."  

"Courage doesn't hide in caves  
You can't bury freedom, in a grave,"  
The Newcomers had heard this voice before  
A distinct Yankee twang from Hyannis Port shores  

A silence fell within the mist  
Somehow the Newcomer knew that this  
Meant time had come for her to say  
What was in the hearts of the five thousand plus that day  

"Back on Earth, we wrote reports,  
Watched our children play in sports  
Worked our gardens, sang our songs  
Went to church and clipped coupons  

We smiled, we laughed, we cried, we fought  
Unlike you, great we're not"  

The tall man in the stovepipe hat  
Stood and said, "Don't talk like that!  
Look at your country, look and see  
You died for freedom, just like me"  

Then, before them all appeared a scene  
Of rubbled streets and twisted beams  
Death, destruction, smoke and dust  
And people working just 'cause they must  

Hauling ash, lifting stones,  
Knee deep in hell, but not alone  

"Look! Black man, White man, Brown man, Yellow man  
Side by side helping their fellow man!"  
So said Martin, as he watched the scene  
"Even from nightmares, can be born a dream."  

Down below three firemen raised  
The colors high into ashen haze  
The soldiers above had seen it before  
On Iwo Jima back in '44  

The man on sticks studied everything closely  
Then shared his thoughts on what he saw mostly  
"I see pain, I see tears, I see sorrow—  
but I don't see fear."  

"You left behind husbands and wives  
Daughters and sons and so many lives  
are suffering now because of this wrong  
But look very closely. You're not really gone.  

All of those people, even those who've never met you  
All of their lives, they'll never forget you  
Don't you see what has happened?  
Don't you see what you've done?  
You've brought them together, together as one."  

With that the man in the stovepipe hat said  
"Take my hand," and from there he led  
five thousand plus heroes, Newcomers to heaven  
On this day, two thousand one, nine eleven  

*Author Unknown*

lynn, here's the recipe i was telling you about—it's delicious! I made it again last week and it was a huge hit. It's for a super easy one-pan lemon herb chicken and veggies.

**Ingredients:**
*   1.5 lbs boneless, skinless chicken thighs (or breasts, cut into chunks)
*   2 cups small broccoli florets
*   1 red bell pepper, chopped
*   2 carrots, sliced
*   1 lemon, thinly sliced, plus extra for juice
*   2 tbsp olive oil
*   1 tsp dried oregano
*   1 tsp dried thyme
*   1/2 tsp garlic powder
*   Salt and freshly ground black pepper to taste
*   Optional: Fresh parsley, chopped, for garnish

**Instructions:**
1.  Preheat your oven to 400°F (200°C).
2.  In a large bowl, combine the chicken, broccoli, red bell pepper, and carrots.
3.  Drizzle with olive oil. Sprinkle with oregano, thyme, garlic powder, salt, and pepper. Squeeze half a lemon over everything and toss to coat evenly.
4.  Spread the mixture in a single layer on a large baking sheet. Arrange the lemon slices among the chicken and vegetables.
5.  Bake for 25-30 minutes, or until the chicken is cooked through and the vegetables are tender-crisp. If using chicken breasts, check that the internal temperature reaches 165°F (74°C).
6.  Garnish with fresh parsley, if desired. Serve hot.

It's really that simple! Let me know when you try it out. I think you'll love how easy cleanup is too.

Talk soon,

Sarah
