Center for the Advancement of Energy Markets Newsletter - Year End 2001 Review

What a year 2001 has been for the supporters of energy competition.

For every positive development (such as Pat Wood III, former Texas Public Utility Commissioner and CAEM advocate, being nominated by President Bush to chair the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission in August, and Canada's continued progress toward full retail electricity choice in Alberta and Ontario), we have endured multiple setbacks throughout the year.

In December 2000, who could have predicted:

1. The terrorist attacks of September 11th, which disrupted energy markets and infrastructure planning nationwide.

2. California's electricity crisis, featuring rolling blackouts from January through May, Pacific Gas & Electric's bankruptcy filing in April, and wholesale electricity prices reaching $1,900/MWh.

3. Pennsylvania retail marketer exodus, with over 30 companies withdrawing from residential markets due to unsustainable customer acquisition costs and regulatory constraints.

4. Natural gas price spikes reaching $10/MMBtu in December (compared to $2-3/MMBtu in 2000), despite mild winter weather reducing demand.

5. The Bush Administration's National Energy Policy released in May, which emphasized supply-side solutions while largely ignoring electricity market restructuring reforms.

6. Enron Corporation's bankruptcy filing in December, the largest in U.S. history at that time, undermining public confidence in energy markets.

7. FERC's retreat from its ambitious "Super RTO" vision in July, instead proposing four regional transmission organizations rather than comprehensive market integration.

8. Texas's delayed implementation of retail choice, postponing full market opening from January 2001 to January 2002 due to technical and regulatory complications.

9. The absence of unified industry leadership to address restructuring challenges, with state regulators, utilities, and competitive suppliers offering conflicting solutions.

2001 represents what we believe is the low point for North American energy competition - but also the foundation for future progress.

Looking ahead through our analytical lens (powered by competitive natural gas markets, naturally), CAEM anticipates significant improvements in 2002. Our staff predictions and recommendations for electricity markets (with some applicability to natural gas) follow below.

As always, these are informed opinions from our policy research team, not investment advice. We're a modest think tank with ambitious goals for competitive energy markets.

We persist. We analyze. We advocate.

Happy New Year!
The CAEM Policy Team

P.S. We welcome additional predictions from industry stakeholders. Please email your forecasts with contact information to Hope Duncan at hduncan@caem.org for posting at www.caem.org, clearly indicating which specific market issue you're addressing.

Edgefield is a unique  European-style village, which includes lodging, a pub with a movie theater, fine dining, a winery, a brewery, distillery, golf course, gardens, vineyards, artwork, meeting, wedding and banquet space, and special events year round.
Edgefield, built in 1911, served for several decades as the Multnomah County Poor Farm.
Residents operated a self-sufficient environment, raising hogs, poultry, growing a variety of fruits and vegetables, operating a dairy, cannery and meat packing plant as well as working in the laundry, kitchen and hospital.
In 1947, it was  renamed the Multnomah County Home and Farm and in the late fifties the farm operation was eliminated.
In 1962, the facitity was renamed Edgefield Manor and for the last two decades of operation, functioned as a nursing home and eventually closed in 1982.
McMenamins purchased the property from Multnomah County in 1990.
In phases lasting over four years, the condemned buildings and land were transformed into a place that is quite special.
Edgefield also offers over 100 bed and breakfast rooms creating a unique lodging experience.
Spacious rooms are furnished with cozy and inviting  decor from the turn of the century.

Elizabeth, Jeff forwarded me your questions about capacity options. I've answered them below, focusing on the legal/regulatory issues. If you need anything further please don't hesitate to call.

**Key Questions and Answers:**

**Can a new shipper enter into an FTS-1 contract with zero MDQ to purchase a shipper call option or sell a transporter put option, then transfer the underlying option rights by permanently releasing this contract before the exercise date?**
YES.

**Will we be required to report these zero MDQ contracts on the Index of Customers and/or the Transactional Report?**
YES.

**Can the releasing shipper permanently release a portion of their existing MDQ and choose to keep or transfer the option rights?**
YES. The shipper could even release all of its MDQ (reducing it to zero) and keep its option rights.

**How is it determined whether a contract with an option amendment is within the min/max tariff rate or needs to be filed as a negotiated rate?**
The option fee is converted to a per-Dth, per day rate and added to the transport rate. If the total exceeds the maximum tariff rate, it's "negotiated". Otherwise, our position is that it's not negotiated. We are not 100% positive that FERC will agree with us on this issue.

From the Birmingham Sunday Mercury (7th Jan 2001) Worker dead at desk for 5 days

Bosses of a publishing firm are trying to work out why no one noticed that one of their employees had been sitting dead at his desk for FIVE DAYS before anyone asked if he was feeling okay. George Turklebaum, 51, who had been employed as a proof-reader at a New York firm for 30 years, had a heart attack in the open-plan office he shared with 23 other workers. 

He quietly passed away on Monday, but nobody noticed until Saturday morning when an office cleaner asked why he was still working during the weekend. Throughout the week, staff came and went, assuming George was simply immersed in his work as usual. According to colleagues, George had a reputation for being extremely dedicated to his job, often arriving before anyone else and leaving after everyone had gone home. His commitment and quiet demeanor meant that he was often left undisturbed, even during breaks.

His boss Elliot Wachiaski said, "George was always the first guy in each morning and the last to leave at night, so no one found it unusual that he was in the same position all that time and didn't say anything. He was always absorbed in his work and kept much to himself." Several co-workers admitted they simply thought George was working on a particularly demanding manuscript, given the size of the pile on his desk and the fact that he rarely participated in office chit-chat.

A post mortem examination revealed that he had been dead for five days after suffering a coronary. Medical experts note that symptoms of heart attacks can sometimes go unnoticed, especially in quieter individuals who do not draw attention to themselves. Dr. Lisa Browning, a cardiologist not connected to the case, commented, "It’s not uncommon for early symptoms of heart trouble to be ignored, particularly by people who are highly focused on their jobs. In rare instances, prolonged unnoticed deaths can happen in isolated work environments."

Ironically, George was proofreading manuscripts of medical textbooks when he died, some of which contained chapters on heart disease and its warning signs. This sad event highlights both the importance of workplace camaraderie and awareness of co-workers’ well-being. The incident sparked discussions in the publishing firm about implementing regular health checks and encouraging more social interaction among staff to prevent similar tragedies. 

You may want to give your co-workers a nudge or a kind word occasionally—it might make more of a difference than you realize.

Subject: The Star-Ledger Faces $10 Million Budget Cuts Amid Advertising Crisis

Dear Team,

I hope this message finds you well. I'm writing to inform you of significant developments affecting our organization that require immediate attention and transparency.

The Star-Ledger is currently facing unprecedented financial challenges due to a severe decline in advertising revenue, which has necessitated approximately $10 million in budget cuts across our operations. This crisis reflects the broader challenges facing the newspaper industry as digital transformation continues to reshape how audiences consume news and how advertisers allocate their budgets.

The advertising downturn has been more severe than initially projected, with both print and digital ad revenues falling short of targets by substantial margins. Local business advertising, traditionally our strongest revenue stream, has declined by over 40% compared to last year, while national advertising partnerships have also been significantly reduced.

As a result of these financial pressures, we will be implementing several cost-reduction measures over the coming weeks:

- Temporary salary adjustments for senior management
- Consolidation of certain editorial departments
- Reduction in print frequency for select regional editions
- Renegotiation of vendor contracts and operational expenses
- Strategic review of our real estate footprint

Despite these challenges, our commitment to quality journalism and serving our community remains unwavering. We are actively exploring new revenue opportunities, including expanded digital subscriptions, sponsored content partnerships, and community event programming.

I will be scheduling department meetings over the next few days to discuss how these changes will specifically impact each team. We will also be providing additional resources for career counseling and support during this transition period.

Thank you for your continued dedication during this difficult time. Your professionalism and adaptability will be crucial as we navigate these challenges together.

Best regards,

[Name]
Publisher
The Star-Ledger

On September 14, 2001, the Commission approved tariff sheets submitted by NEPOOL with an effective date of July 1, 2001. These tariff sheets align the existing mitigation price screen provisions under Market Rule 17—which apply to resources operating outside economic merit order—with the updated three-part bidding framework and Net Commitment Period Compensation structure.

NEPOOL clarified that the varying percentage thresholds for Energy Block Pricing are justified given that they apply to different baseline values, depending on whether resources typically operate within or outside economic merit order. The percentage thresholds for Startup and No-Load bids remain consistent across both resource types, as they reference the same baseline values.

Please feel free to reach out if you require additional information.

Susan Lindberg x30596

The tariff sheets conform the existing mitigation price screen provisions of Market Rule 17 applicable to resources that run out of economic merit order to the revised bidding and compensation regime of three-part bidding and Net Commitment Period Compensation.
NEPOOL explained that the proposed differences in percentages applicable to the Energy Block Price were appropriate since they apply to different base values depending on whether the resource is regularly or seldom run in economic merit order.
The price percentages applicable to Startup and No-Load bids are the same for both resources as both resources use the same base value.

Richard Sanders and I talked with Elizabeth (an attorney with AEP).
She was  not sure that their was a question that needed to be answered.
Richard  opined that the question may have related to the effect on HPL if it lost the  Taub lawsuit.
This suit relates to an alleged violation of the surface  rights agreement (Collateral Agreement) which was entered into with certain  surface owners after the Unit Agreement was signed.
Richard explained that  if HPL lost the suit, it would lose its rights to maintain a pipeline and  well facilities on the property subject to the lawsuit.
In that event HPL  would have to either locate its pipeline around the property or  use its  condemnation rights to acquire an easement across the property.
Because the  Collateral Agreement relates to surface rights, losing those rights would not  affect HPL's rights under the Unit Agreement and thus the Taubs would not  have the right to drill a well to produce the gas that HPL has in storage.

For those teams that have turbines installed after 1990 and/or for those  turbines which have undergone power  unit changouts, the following  recordkeeping and monitoring conditions apply:  1) DAILY recordkeeping of nitrogen and sulfur must be taken of the fuel gas  which supplies the applicable turbine(s).
2) This recordkeeping consists of electronic recording (gas chromtograph for  nitrogen and  delmar or equivelant for sulfur) or stain tubes may also be  used  for sulfur.
These DAILY records include measurements on Saturdays and  Sundays.
3) The measurement must be taken at the location.
An exception to this is  that the nitrogen and sulfur measurements may be taken upstream or  downstream  of the applicable turbine facility provided that there are no  natural gas deliveries into the pipe which would interfere or dilute/increase  the measurements  for the applicable turbine fuel gas.
4) Fuel gas records in hard copy form or equivalent  for  the nitrogen and  sulfur must be maintained at the facility or at a central location for easy  retrival.
5) A turbine facility may waiver out of this nitorgen and sulfur daily  recordkeeping requirement by obtaining a custom fuel monitoring schedule  (CFMS) from  the EPA.
Approval of a  CFMS allows a greatly reduced  recordkeeping and reporting for nitrogen and sulfur.
CFMS requests have been  submitted for the  following facilities:     P-1 C/S    Plains Turbine C/S    Atoka No 2 C/S    Monument C/S    Crawford C/S    Bloomfield C/S   Approvals have not as yet been obtained.

The persistent lack of affordable, always-on, last-mile broadband connections to small offices and homes remains a significant constraint on the U.S. economy. Indeed, high taxes, particularly those on capital formation, are a concern. We hope Congress will recognize the fundamental truth that this recession is investment-led. Furthermore, the Fed should consider lowering its funds rate to 3%, and a substantial inventory overhang persists across the IT sector. If these factors weren't enough to present formidable challenges, we must also consider the growing telecom debt crisis that poses a serious risk to financial markets.

The dot-com boom, which began in 1995 and ended in 2000, was characterized by widespread, often ill-advised, speculation in venture capital. Excessive funding fueled a proliferation of unsustainable ventures, which ultimately collapsed. However, the groundwork is being laid for a new era of internet-driven growth. It will emerge with renewed clarity and more sustainable foundations.

We are pleased to announce that we have expanded our equity trading capabilities into the European Markets, reflecting our ongoing commitment to broadening our investment universe and offering more diversified opportunities to our clients. As a result of this expansion, you will notice an increase in the number of executing broker agreements, specifically with brokers who possess expertise and substantial market presence in foreign equities. This strategic initiative is in line with current industry trends, where institutional investors are seeking greater access to international liquidity and enhanced execution quality.

As part of this process, we plan on executing a broker agreement with Metzler Capital Markets, a highly regarded financial institution with a long-standing reputation for its specialized focus and deep market knowledge in Italian equities. Metzler's local market expertise is anticipated to improve our access to Italian stocks, provide us with superior order routing, and potentially secure more favorable execution prices in this sector. Finally, we were also fingered somewhat as culprits at the hearing (the California PUC FERC lawyer claimed that ENA and TW colluded to drive up basis when ENA controlled a portion of the capacity), but the overriding goal of the hearing was to go after EP and Dynegy.

Best,

Subject: Update on Industry Group Meeting and Proposed Utility Portfolio Approach

Dear Team,

I wanted to provide you with an update following yesterday's industry group meeting and share details on the proposed utility portfolio approach we discussed.

**Meeting Summary:**
The session brought together key stakeholders from across the region to address current market challenges and regulatory developments. Major topics included grid modernization initiatives, renewable energy integration timelines, and upcoming compliance requirements for Q2 2024.

**Proposed Utility Portfolio Approach:**
Based on our discussions, we're recommending a diversified portfolio strategy that includes:

• 40% renewable energy sources (solar, wind, hydro)
• 35% natural gas for reliability and peak demand
• 20% existing nuclear capacity
• 5% energy storage and emerging technologies

This approach balances sustainability goals with grid stability requirements while maintaining cost-effectiveness for our customer base.

**Next Steps:**
- Technical feasibility study to be completed by March 15th
- Stakeholder feedback period opens next week
- Regulatory filing preparation begins April 1st
- Implementation timeline targeting Q4 2024 rollout

I'll be scheduling follow-up meetings with department heads to discuss resource allocation and timeline coordination. Please review the attached detailed proposal and come prepared with questions and recommendations.

Let me know if you need any clarification on these updates.

Best regards,
[Your Name]
source_text:
Just met with the industry group trying to come up with a solution for  California.
The group liked our portfolio approach.
In sum:   A portfolio approach is the right long-term solution.
In the short run, our illustrative portfolios show that the utilities ought  to immediately fill a modest portion of their requirements via fixed-price,  long term contracts, and those contracts should be found reasonable, up  front, so long as the utility uses a competitive auction.
To stimulate  discussion we proposed that the utility fill 5% of its net short position  with 5-year, fixed-price contracts and 5% from 10-year, fixed-price contracts.
Everyone on the call liked the proposal.
After some discussion about whether  5%-5% was the right one, Edison agreed to come to Friday's meeting with its  proposal for price/term/quantity that it ought to contract for immediately.
(Edison may want the number to be higher, and the baskets to be different.)
Anything can happen between now and Friday, but thus far looks positive.
Thanks to everyone for the help in getting the proposal together, Steve Swain  in particular.
(Steve:  We may get asked to run a few more illustrative  portfolios for the group.)
I'll report back on what happens at the meeting  on Friday.
If there are any questions, etc., just let me know.
Best,

Subject: Upcoming Conference: ADHD Diagnosis, Ritalin Treatment, and Legal Challenges

Dear Colleagues,

We are pleased to announce an upcoming conference focused on the multifaceted landscape of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). This event will bring together experts from medicine, psychology, education, and law to explore critical aspects of ADHD.

The conference agenda will include in-depth discussions on:

1.  **ADHD Diagnosis:** Examining current diagnostic criteria, challenges in assessment, differential diagnosis, and the impact of evolving understanding on identification across different age groups. We will also address the complexities of co-occurring conditions.

2.  **Ritalin Treatment and Pharmacotherapy:** A significant portion of the conference will be dedicated to the role of methylphenidate (Ritalin) in ADHD management. We will delve into its mechanisms of action, efficacy rates, potential side effects, dosing strategies, and long-term outcomes. Discussions will also cover comparative effectiveness with other stimulant and non-stimulant medications, as well as integrated treatment approaches.

3.  **Related Legal Challenges:** The increasing prevalence of ADHD diagnoses and treatments has led to a rise in legal complexities. Sessions will cover issues such as:
    *   Educational accommodations and special education law (IDEA, Section 504).
    *   Informed consent for medication, particularly concerning minors.
    *   Prescription monitoring, diversion, and misuse of stimulant medications.
    *   Workplace accommodations and disability law.
    *   Potential for misdiagnosis litigation and professional responsibility.
    *   Parental rights and responsibilities in treatment decisions.

This conference aims to foster a comprehensive understanding of ADHD, providing a platform for interdisciplinary dialogue and practical insights. We believe it will be invaluable for clinicians, educators, legal professionals, researchers, and policymakers involved with individuals affected by ADHD.

Further details regarding dates, venue, and registration will be circulated shortly. We look forward to your participation in this timely and crucial discussion.

Sincerely,

[Your Name/Organization]

At one extreme are doctors, psychologists, and others who question whether clinicians are "medicalizing" childhood.
At the other pole are doctors who eagerly prescribe medications for youngsters at the slightest hint of trouble.
Nonetheless, while over diagnosis and over prescribing are legitimate concerns, the consensus among mental health professionals is that ADHD exists and that stimulant therapies like Ritalin are effective.

Trial lawyers representing a class of parents whose children were diagnosed with ADHD have filed lawsuits in several states against the maker of Ritalin and the American Psychiatric Association.

Sheila,

I am forwarding you a deeply troubling message I received a few days ago that has been weighing heavily on my mind.

I desperately need your advice on how to handle this explosive situation. My initial instinct was to bury it and hope it would disappear. But I'm now losing sleep over this - the more I wrestle with it, the more terrified I become that ignoring this could destroy everything we've built here.

Picture this nightmare scenario: a female employee gets harassed by a male colleague. She finally musters the courage to report it months later, and her boss callously dismisses her. We've all seen the devastating headlines when courts crucify companies that turn their backs on victims crying out for help.

The fact that we're dealing with reverse harassment changes absolutely nothing. If I sweep this under the rug, we could face a catastrophic lawsuit for blatant double standards in handling sexual harassment. The legal and reputational fallout could be career-ending for both of us and financially crippling for the company.

I'm convinced we have no choice but to mandate that Maureen attend sensitivity training and sexual harassment prevention classes immediately. We cannot afford to gamble with our employees' safety or the company's survival.

Please tell me you agree - I'm frankly panicked about the consequences of inaction.

I hate dumping this crisis in your lap, but I'm at my wit's end.

Vince

THE BLONDE KIDNAPPER
Broke and desperate, a blonde decided to kidnap a child for ransom. At the playground, she grabbed a kid, pulled him behind a tree, and declared, "I've kidnapped you." She penned a note: "I've kidnapped your kid. Tomorrow morning, put $10,000 in a paper bag and put it under the pecan tree next to the slide on the north side of the playground. Signed, a blonde." She pinned the note to the child's shirt and sent him home to his parents.

Next morning, she checked. A paper bag sat beneath the pecan tree. She opened it, finding $10,000 and a note: "How could you do this to a fellow blonde?"

Jim, as I mentioned before, we are moving forward with the Enron Corp. interests project in Europe. We started working about a week ago after discussing with Jim Fallon, Ray Bowen, and others, and our plan is to pay employees using funds currently held by EEFT. I expect to have a formal team structure tomorrow, which will also be organized around EEFT.

However, I understand this proposal does not cover retention bonuses for the teams, as that matter is still being discussed. I've heard there is some reluctance in Houston to approve these payments, but I am not sure why. I believe it would be entirely appropriate to provide retention incentives in this situation.

As mentioned, part of our objective is to recover value from existing contracts in entities like ECTRIC, which could total $150 to $200 million. Additionally, the project involves properly winding up entities to recover value and limit director liabilities. There was a proposal to set aside a percentage of recovered value in a bonus pool to be shared by all team members, regardless of their individual focus, but I understand this was rejected in today’s conference call.

I am quite concerned about our ability to retain team members for this challenging project without additional incentives. The work is complex, and many valuable team members, particularly traders positioned to protect value in ECTRIC, have other opportunities available. Furthermore, our employees are aware that members of the PWC teams are receiving retention payments.

If we do not retain the team protecting ECTRIC’s interests in the near term, ECTRIC is set to go into administration on January 4, which would terminate many of its profitable contracts and result in a loss of roughly 50% of its value.

If you are supportive of providing retention payments to help us continue this work, could you please communicate this to Jim Fallon, Jeff McMahon, and Ray Bowen tomorrow? It is likely we will begin losing staff after Christmas. 

Thank you.

Anne

the distinction between a simple friend and a real friend often becomes clear in moments of challenge and joy alike. A simple friend may share your laughter, but a real friend stands by you in tears and offers support without hesitation. Real friends are those rare individuals who understand your silence, celebrate your victories as if they were their own, and never hesitate to lend a helping hand when you need it most.

As we navigate both work and life, I hope we can build real friendships—connections founded on trust, support, and genuine care for one another. Thank you for being not just a colleague, but someone I can truly rely on.

A simple friend has never seen you cry.
A real friend has shoulders soggy from your tears.
A simple friend doesn't know your parents' first names.
A real friend has their phone numbers in his address book.
A simple friend brings a bottle of wine to your party.
A real friend comes early to help you cook and stays late to help you clean.
A simple friend hates it when you call after he has gone to bed.
A real friend asks you why you took so long to call.
A simple friend seeks to talk with you about your problems.
A real friend seeks to help you with your problems.
A simple friend wonders about your romantic history.
A real friend could blackmail you with it.
A simple friend, when visiting, acts like a guest.
A real friend opens your refrigerator and helps himself.
A simple friend thinks the friendship is over when you HAVE an argument.
A real friend knows that it's not a friendship until after you've had a fight.
A simple friend expects you to always be there for them.
A real friend expects to always be there for you!

Subject: Resuming Business Travel Following September 11

Dear Team,

As we navigate these challenging times following the tragic events of September 11, I wanted to address our approach to resuming business travel operations.

The safety and security of our employees remains our top priority. We are closely monitoring the evolving security measures being implemented by airlines and airports, and will only resume travel when we are confident in the enhanced safety protocols.

For the immediate future, we will:
- Postpone all non-essential business travel
- Encourage video conferencing and phone meetings as alternatives
- Require management approval for any urgent travel needs
- Provide updated travel safety guidelines once operations resume

We understand this may impact some scheduled meetings and projects. Please work with your teams to identify alternative solutions and communicate any critical scheduling conflicts to your supervisors.

We will continue to assess the situation daily and provide updates as they become available. Thank you for your patience and understanding during this difficult period.

Best regards,
[Your Name]

As the United States begins to recover from the tragic events of September 11, it is important that Enron and its employees also begin the task of returning to "business as usual."
As a company with a global presence, returning to normal business practices necessarily involves travel.
The FAA has already implemented strengthened security measures for U.S. airports and air carriers to ensure air transportation is safe, secure, and ready to meet the needs of the traveling public.
We encourage all employees to return to their regular travel schedules.
We have no reason to believe that international travel is inherently unsafe at this time, although we strongly recommend -- in conjunction with the U.S. Department of State -- that all travel to Afghanistan, Yemen, Pakistan, Indonesia, Iran, Iraq, Sudan, Somalia, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Georgia, and the Kyrgyz Republic be canceled.
In addition, we recommend that planned travel to Egypt, Israel, Gaza/West Bank, Jordan, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Syria, and Algeria be very carefully considered.

Heads up! The Wind Advisory for the mountains of Santa Barbara County has been extended through Wednesday morning, and new Wind Advisories are now in effect for the Antelope Valley and for the mountains of Los Angeles and Ventura Counties.

What’s happening? High pressure building into Northern California has created a strong north-to-south pressure gradient. As a result, people in the mountains of Los Angeles, Ventura, and Santa Barbara Counties, as well as those in the Antelope Valley, are already starting to feel some locally gusty northwest winds.

A strong upper-level low in the Pacific Northwest will move into the Northern Great Basin later today and tonight, causing even stronger northwest winds above California. So, those gusty winds in our local mountains and the Antelope Valley are expected to pick up and become more widespread as the day goes on.

Wind speeds are expected to average 30 to 40 mph in the advisory areas later today, and some local gusts could reach up to 60 mph—so please exercise caution if you’re in those areas.

Good news—the Wind Advisory for the South Coast of Santa Barbara County has expired for now. However, strong winds are expected to pick up again this evening below passes and canyons in Southern Santa Barbara County, so future advisories may be issued.

Also, winds may reach advisory levels this afternoon along the Central Coast of San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara Counties.

Stay safe out there, and keep an eye out for further updates!

Subject: Duke Energy Settlement Agreement Update

Dear Team,

I wanted to update you on the recent settlement agreement reached between Duke Energy and environmental groups regarding the California power plant operations. The deal, which was negotiated over several months, addresses key concerns raised by environmental advocates about emissions and wildlife protection measures.

Under the terms of the agreement, Duke Energy has committed to implementing enhanced environmental monitoring systems and establishing a $50 million fund for habitat restoration projects in the surrounding area. The environmentalists, led by the Sierra Club and local conservation groups, have agreed to withdraw their pending litigation in exchange for these commitments.

Tom Knudson from the Sacramento Bee has been following this story closely and will likely publish a detailed analysis of the settlement terms later this week. We should prepare for media inquiries and potential stakeholder questions about how this agreement might influence similar negotiations in other states.

Article II of the NONCOMPETITION AGREEMENT entered in connection with the sale of HPL to AEP (which closed as of June 1,2001) provides:  	"ENA [for 3 months post-close] will not  solicit, negotiate or enter into any contract, agreement or arrangement for the purchase of natural gas on the HPL Pipeline from any Person which is a supplier or producer of natural gas connected to the HPL Facilities; provided, however, nothing herein shall be construed or interpreted as prohibiting ENA from entering into any such contract, agreement or arrangement which is less than one month in duration and involves or is related to an Enron Online transaction."

Further,although a technical reading of the non-competition agreement only applies to ENA, no ENA UPSTREAM deals which would violate this covenant if there were to be done as ENA should be done without clearance from Brian Redmond and me.
Please communicate this restriction to those who report to you and have need to be aware of this limited restriction.
Sincerely

Subject: Risk Management Consolidation and Leadership Changes for EES Operations

Dear Team,

I am writing to inform you of important organizational changes that will take effect beginning January 1, 2024, aimed at strengthening our risk management capabilities and operational efficiency within EES Operations.

**Risk Management Consolidation**

Effective immediately, we will be consolidating all risk management functions under a centralized Risk Management Division. This consolidation will include:

- Operational risk assessment and mitigation
- Financial risk monitoring and reporting
- Regulatory compliance oversight
- Environmental and safety risk management
- Strategic risk analysis

This centralized approach will enhance our ability to identify, assess, and respond to risks across all operational areas while eliminating redundancies and improving communication between departments.

**Leadership Changes**

I am pleased to announce the following leadership appointments:

- **Sarah Martinez** has been promoted to Chief Risk Officer, leading the newly consolidated Risk Management Division
- **David Chen** will assume the role of Director of Operations, overseeing day-to-day EES operational activities
- **Jennifer Thompson** has been appointed as Director of Compliance and Regulatory Affairs

These leaders bring extensive experience and will work collaboratively to ensure seamless integration of risk management practices across all EES operations.

**Next Steps**

Department heads will receive detailed transition plans by December 15, 2023. All staff will participate in orientation sessions during the week of December 18-22, 2023, to understand new reporting structures and procedures.

I am confident these changes will position EES Operations for continued success while maintaining the highest standards of risk management and operational excellence.

Please direct any questions to your direct supervisor or HR representative.

Best regards,

Michael Roberts
Vice President, EES Operations
source_text:
Given the growth in EES it has become apparent that it is time to consolidate the risk functions between EES and EWS.
This will provide EES with the systems, resources and risk expertise of the wholesale energy groups necessary for it to continue to grow and take advantage of current market opportunities.
With this in mind and in agreement with the management of EES, two new risk groups inside Enron Americas will be formed to provide EES with pricing, structuring, retail and wholesale commodity risk management, logistics and back-office services.
These groups main function is to provide these services to EES.
We have asked Rogers Herndon, currently Vice President-Trading in the Eastern Power Group to manage this function in the Eastern Interconnect (this includes both gas and power).
Rogers will continue to report to Kevin Presto.
We have asked Don Black, formerly Vice President-EES Risk Management and Sourcing, to manage this function in the Western U.S.  Don will manage this group from Houston and will report to Tim Belden.
These groups will work very closely with EES to pursue shared goals while ensuring close coordination with the wholesale gas and power trading organizations.
These changes are effective immediately.
Please congratulate Rogers and Don on their new roles.
John Lavorato & Louise Kitchen

Effective immediately Enron will begin moving all wireless devise accounts to individual employees for payment.
With all the changes currently taking place within Enron, this change will allow each user to experience uninterrupted service and keep communication flowing while at the same time allow the individual user greater accountability for these controllable expenses.
Cell Phones and Pagers Over the next few weeks Enron will be changing the employee payment method of cell phones and pagers, regardless of the vendor.
Optimum base rates and terms of service will be negotiated with pager and cell phone providers for the Houston area.
All Cingular and non-Cingular accounts will be rolled under one agreement (see below for Nextel users).
(Field locations are excluded from this change and will be evaluated on a case-by-case basis as appropriate.)
For billing purposes, this action will require all cell phone users to have the device and service put in their name.
While the phone will be in the employee's name it will be backed by Enron, therefore a personal credit check will not be required and you will not be required to sign a contract.
This change will allow each user to verify their bill for accuracy and to ensure that the bill is paid on time.
All monthly charges for cell phone and/or pagers are to be submitted for reimbursement via XMS.
Direct billing and/or group billings will be phased out over the next few weeks.
XMS training and class schedules will be forthcoming.
Please follow the steps below to make the necessary changes to your account: ?
Contact your service provider and make arrangements to have your bill paid monthly either by credit card or personal check.
The Cingular contact is Charlotte McGowan, (972) 706-1968.
If you need information regarding contacts for other providers, please contact Darin Lee Carlisle @ Global Strategic Sourcing ext - 5-3808.   ?
Submit the expense item to your supervisor for reimbursement through XMS.
?
Do not sign a contract, as you will become personally liable for the account for the life of the contract.
?
Change the address on your bill to either your home address or your current office address to ensure timely receipt of the invoice in the future.
Nextel Phone/Two-Way Radios We are currently working with Nextel to restructure billing to individual employees.
All monthly charges for Nextel services will be submitted for reimbursement via XMS.
Pre-approval by Business Unit CAO will be required for all Nextel phone/two-way radios.
Long Distance An individual code will be assigned to each Houston based employee for use when dialing long distance calls.
These codes will create individual accounts for each employee so that they can identify their long distance usage and reimburse the company for personal calls they may make.
(Field locations are excluded at this time.)
Conferencing WorldCom will provide all audio conferencing services.
Monthly conferencing charges will be reviewed and approved by Department heads.
Training will follow under separate cover.
Training / Questions Training sessions and additional communications regarding these changes will follow in the next few days.
Please contact Darin Carlisle at (713) 345-3808 or Peter Goebel at (713) 345-3325 with any questions regarding the above changes.
Questions regarding XMS training should be directed to Tammy Hopkins at (713) 345-3631.
Derryl Cleaveland, Vice President Global Strategic Sourcing

David,

During today's VaR coordination meeting, we discussed issues related to mapping forward price curves to core locations. This mapping is necessary due to computer system limitations: we must reduce the dimensionality of the problem to fit within available CPU memory.

Additionally, in some cases, price discovery is poor, making it difficult to model certain price curves independently. To address this, we map these curves to more liquid and stable core location curves.

We agreed on the following:

1. Winston will investigate the IT aspect and determine to what extent we can increase the number of forward price curves that are simulated as basic (core) curves. He will also assess how a larger number of core curves would affect the time required to complete the VaR run.

2. The curves associated with the largest 10-20 positions in each commodity should be modeled as core curves (i.e., not mapped to other locations). It is important to monitor the biggest risks separately and avoid merging them into less transparent aggregates.

3. The outcomes of automated clustering (mapping) procedures should be systematically reviewed and corrected by a designated person if they misrepresent the risks of trading positions. Currently, this responsibility is dispersed across the organization, which effectively means no one is accountable. Research can assign one person to this task; cooperation from Trading and RAC will be essential.

Vince

Dad

Jose, the supplemental information you have provided is outstanding and offers valuable context to the lenders regarding the overall situation and history. However, as I understand it, the central concern of the lenders at this stage is more specific: their primary focus is the potential for third-party liability—specifically, lawsuits or claims from parties who did not receive power due to Cuiaba’s failure to generate.

To effectively address lenders’ most urgent concerns and help facilitate a path to closing, I believe Tozzinni should focus their advice on the following targeted questions:

1) If ANEEL requires EPE to sign these agreements, what is the full extent of potential damages that could be claimed under such agreements? Are there any statutory or contractual limits?
2) Could claimants pursue consequential damages, and if so, under what circumstances?
3) Does the language in the bid documents, the PPA, or other agreements with Furnas, Electronorte, or Eletrobras provide EPE a valid legal basis to excuse itself from legal proceedings or mitigate exposure?
4) In the event of a judgment against EPE that results in a significant financial liability, how would the economic equilibrium process function? Is There a mechanism to expedite this process to avert a lender-threatening liquidity crisis?
5) Is there any scenario in which EPE could be denied access to the grid due to an inability to pay spot market prices assessed by the MAE as a result of an unscheduled outage?
6) Could EPE incur penalties or suffer loss of transmission rights if it fails to fulfill shared liability obligations under the relevant agreements?
7) Are there requirements to sign additional agreements for other purposes (such as access to back-up power) that might leave EPE exposed outside the PPA protections provided by Furnas?

Subject: The Toxic Culture of Enron

Dear Team,

I wanted to discuss and reflect on the toxic culture that emerged at Enron, as it serves as a significant learning opportunity for all organizations. Enron’s internal environment was characterized by intense pressure to meet unrealistic targets, a lack of transparency, and a culture of fear and competition rather than collaboration. Employees were encouraged to prioritize personal gain over ethics, leading to widespread unethical practices and ultimately, the company’s downfall.

By understanding what went wrong at Enron, we can recommit to creating a workplace culture that values integrity, open communication, and mutual support. Let’s use these lessons to ensure our own organization remains a place where ethical behavior and teamwork are recognized and rewarded.

Best regards,  
[Your Name]

We hereby confirm our agreement regarding the sale of Propane to ProCaribe under the following terms and conditions:

Seller:      Enron Liquid Fuels, Inc.
Buyer:       ProCaribe

Product/Quality:    Fully Refrigerated HD-5 Propane, which meets the stringent specifications for HD-5 grade as per industry standards, ensuring a minimum propane purity of 90% by volume and maximum propylene content of 5% by volume.

Quantity:   8,500 metric tons, plus or minus 5 percent at Seller’s option, in accordance with standard industry practice to accommodate operational variations in loading.

Price:   The price shall be based on the mean average Mont Belvieu OPIS Non-TET Propane ("MB OPIS NTET Propane") for the three consecutive business days surrounding the Bill of Lading date, plus a premium of seven cents per gallon (7 cpg). This pricing mechanism ensures fair market value reflective of actual trading conditions and has been widely adopted as a transparent benchmark in the North American propane market.

Load Laycan:  22nd to 24th October, 2001. Both parties acknowledge that timely nomination and arrival of the vessel during the laycan window are essential for smooth execution of the transaction.

Vessel:  To be loaded on board the "Nelly Maersk" or a substitute vessel of similar tonnage and capacity, subject to mutual acceptance. The nominated vessel shall be fully compatible with loading and discharging facilities at the designated terminals.

Terms:  Cost, Insurance, and Freight (CIF) delivered Tallaboa, Puerto Rico. Risk and title of the cargo shall pass from Seller to Buyer at the time the cargo crosses the vessel’s manifold flange at the loadport, in accordance with INCOTERMS 2000 CIF provisions. Seller shall be responsible for securing and paying for marine insurance and freight up to the discharge port.

Laytime:  66 hours total, including both loading at the port of origin and discharging at Tallaboa. Any time used in excess of this allowance shall be settled in accordance with the standard demurrage/despatch rates agreed in the forthcoming full contract.

Inspection:  An independent inspector mutually appointed and agreed upon will carry out quality and quantity inspection at loadport on a 50/50 cost-sharing basis between Seller and Buyer. All cargoes to be surveyed and sampled in accordance with international inspection protocols, and an official Certificate of Quantity and Quality issued. The loadport inspection results shall be final and binding for the purposes of this transaction.

Both parties acknowledge that these sale terms represent a binding recap of essential commercial terms for this transaction, pending issuance of a comprehensive Sale and Purchase Agreement. Full contract confirmation, including force majeure, credit provisions, arbitration process, and further detail, will follow in due course.

Please acknowledge your acceptance of these terms at your earliest convenience.

Best regards,

Public concern over pipeline integrity and safety has reached unprecedented levels.  
Following the incidents in Bellingham, Washington, and Carlsbad, New Mexico, new pipeline safety laws and regulations are mandating a greater emphasis on pipeline integrity initiatives.  
In response, ETS Operations is forming a Pipeline Integrity Program Management Group as a proactive measure.  
This team will oversee pipeline integrity matters for both EOTT and ETS, as well as provide financial oversight for EOTT’s environmental and remediation efforts.  
The group’s areas of focus will include corrosion control, pipeline safety, and overall integrity management.  
I am pleased to share that Mike Nelson will be relocating to Houston to head up this new initiative as Vice President, Pipeline Integrity Program Management.  
Reporting directly to Mike will be Max Brown and Dave Johnson.  
The creation of this group, along with Mike’s transfer, allows us to rotate important staff members, enabling us to broaden our expertise for the future of ETS Operations.  
I am also happy to announce the following additional personnel changes:  
Rick Craig – Vice President, Southeast Operations  
Dan Pribble – Vice President, Southwest Operations  
Randy Rice – Senior Director, North Operations  
Rick Craig and Dan Pribble will remain based in Houston,  
while Randy Rice will move to the Omaha office.  
Don Hawkins will take on new responsibilities for controls & electrical, measurement, and the Clifton Machine Shop as Vice President, Technical Services.  
He will also continue to oversee facility audits, quality management, and business development activities.  
John Shafer, Vice President, Environmental, Health & Safety, will retain responsibility for environmental compliance and remediation as well as health and safety.  
John Keller, Vice President, Planning & Power Services, will add oversight of the Beaver Machine Shop to his existing duties.  
Jerry Martin, Vice President, Engineering & Construction, will remain in his current position.  
The Skill Based Pay Field Training Administration team will now report to Morris Brassfield, Senior Director, Operations Support Services.  
All of these changes will take effect October 1.  
Please join me in congratulating these team members on their new roles.

Subject: The Importance of Looking Out for Each Other in the Workplace

Dear Team,

I wanted to bring to your attention a sobering story that has been circulating recently: an office worker was found dead at his desk, and tragically, it took five days for anyone to notice his absence. In the midst of a busy office, his passing went unnoticed due to the fast-paced environment and lack of daily check-ins.

While this is an extreme and rare case, it underscores a serious issue—how easy it can be for individuals to become isolated, even when surrounded by colleagues. It reminds us all of the importance of not just focusing on tasks, but also on the well-being of those we work with.

Let’s make it a point to regularly check in on each other—not just for work updates, but to truly see how everyone is doing. A simple message or a quick conversation can make a big difference.

Thank you for helping foster a supportive and attentive workplace.

Best regards,  
[Your Name]

From the Birmingham Sunday Mercury (7th Jan 2001)   Worker dead at desk for 5 days    Bosses of a publishing  firm are trying to work out why no one   noticed that one of their employees had been sitting dead at   his desk for FIVE DAYS before anyone asked if he was feeling   okay.
George Turklebaum, 51, who had been employed as a   proof-reader at a New York firm for 30 years, had a heart attack   in the open-plan office he shared with 23 other workers.
He   quietly passed away on Monday, but nobody noticed until   Saturday morning when an office cleaner  asked why he was   still working during the weekend.
His boss Elliot Wachiaski   said "George was always the first guy in each morning and the   last to leave at night, so no one found it unusual that he was in   the same position all that time and didn't say anything.
He was   always absorbed in his work and kept much to himself.
"A post   mortem examination revealed that he had been dead for five   days after suffering a coronary.
Ironically, George was   proofreading manuscripts of medical textbooks when he died.
You may want to give your co-workers a nudge or kick   occasionally.

Subject: Relocated Tanks: Regulatory Distinction & Cost Implications

Dear [Recipient Name/Team],

This email addresses the critical regulatory distinctions and associated cost implications when considering the relocation of storage tanks. Understanding these factors upfront is essential for compliance and effective financial planning.

**Regulatory Distinction:**
When an existing storage tank (e.g., Underground Storage Tank - UST, Aboveground Storage Tank - AST) is relocated, regulatory bodies often treat it differently than simply modifying an in-place tank. While the tank itself may be "existing," its relocation frequently triggers requirements akin to a "new installation" at the new site. This distinction is crucial because:
*   **New Installation Standards:** Regulators may require the relocated tank to meet current installation standards, which can be significantly more stringent than those applicable when the tank was originally installed. This often includes requirements for secondary containment, advanced leak detection systems, corrosion protection (for USTs), and updated piping designs.
*   **Permitting:** New installation permits are typically required for the relocated tank, even if it held a permit at its previous location. This can involve new site-specific environmental reviews and engineering plans.
*   **Jurisdictional Changes:** If tanks are moved across different state, county, or municipal jurisdictions, they will be subject to the regulations of the new jurisdiction, which may have unique or stricter requirements.
*   **Testing and Certification:** Relocated tanks often require new installation testing (e.g., tank tightness testing, cathodic protection surveys, line testing) and certification by qualified professionals to ensure compliance at the new site.

**Cost Implications:**
The "new installation" treatment for relocated tanks has substantial cost implications:
*   **Compliance Upgrades:** The most significant cost driver is often the need to upgrade the tank and associated infrastructure (piping, dispensing equipment, monitoring systems) to meet current new installation standards. This can include retrofitting secondary containment, installing new leak detection, and upgrading cathodic protection.
*   **Permitting and Fees:** Expect new permitting application fees, engineering review fees, and potentially environmental impact assessment costs for the new location.
*   **Installation Costs:** Beyond the tank itself, there are significant costs associated with site preparation, excavation, foundation work, backfill, piping installation, electrical work, and calibration at the new site.
*   **Testing and Certification:** Initial compliance testing (e.g., pre-use tightness testing, cathodic protection system commissioning, leak detection system certification) adds to the upfront expenses.
*   **Potential for Delays & Fines:** Failure to anticipate and meet these regulatory requirements can lead to project delays, stop-work orders, and substantial non-compliance fines.
*   **Insurance Adjustments:** Insurance premiums may be reassessed based on the new installation and updated compliance profile.

In summary, relocating tanks is not merely a logistical exercise but a regulatory event that can trigger significant compliance obligations and associated costs. It is highly recommended to engage with relevant regulatory bodies and environmental consultants early in the planning process to accurately assess specific requirements and project costs.

Please let me know if you would like to discuss this further.

Best regards,

[Your Name/Team Name]

1) DAILY recordkeeping of nitrogen and sulfur levels must be taken from the fuel gas supplying the applicable turbine(s).

2) This recordkeeping consists of electronic recording (such as using a gas chromatograph for nitrogen and a device equivalent to Delmar for sulfur), or stain tubes may be used for sulfur measurements.

Ed and Mark,

As we discussed regarding the specific financing arrangement where Enron is effectively providing credit to NUI in exchange for future natural gas deliveries, I spoke to Jeff Hodge and Travis McCullough about the best way to document this deal. We all agreed that it is significantly better to structure and document this transaction as a deferred payment obligation related to the sale of natural gas rather than as a traditional loan.

Documenting the deal as a loan does not add any substantive protection for Enron and in fact, may be detrimental due to the various complexities and regulatory burdens concerning loans and lenders. For instance, classifying it as a loan could potentially subject Enron to state usury laws, lender liability doctrines, or even unexpected banking regulations, none of which are applicable to a standard commodity sales agreement.

The robust protections and remedies afforded by a standard Master Firm Purchase/Sale Agreement (such as a NAESB or ISDA-type master agreement, if applicable to this transaction) effectively track, and in some cases exceed, those that Enron would typically have under a stand-alone loan document. These agreements include critical provisions such as netting, cross-default clauses, early termination rights, and specified damages calculations upon a default event.

Furthermore, Enron would likely be in no better position to collect from NUI in the event of bankruptcy under a standard unsecured loan document than under the Master Firm Purchase/Sale Agreement structured as a commercial obligation. In either scenario, without specific, perfected collateral, Enron would typically stand as an unsecured creditor. However, the commercial nature of a Master Firm Purchase/Sale Agreement can offer different avenues for resolution and potentially more streamlined mechanisms for calculating and recovering damages, especially under the close-out netting provisions often upheld in bankruptcy proceedings for commodity transactions.

Additionally, I assume that NUI, being a heavily regulated utility, will have strong reasons not to or be able to document this deal as a loan. A traditional loan arrangement could necessitate complex and time-consuming regulatory approvals from state public utility commissions, potentially impacting their capital structure, bond ratings, and public disclosures in ways they would wish to avoid. Structuring it as a commercial obligation for natural gas sales keeps it within their normal course of business operations.

Please let me know if you need additional information or specific legal analysis on this topic.

Stacy

Over the past quarter, we've seen significant improvements in operational efficiency through our collaborative efforts. The coordination between HPL's logistics capabilities and Calpine's power generation expertise has resulted in a 12% increase in overall plant performance.

Key highlights include:
- Enhanced steam production schedules that better align with refinery demands
- Improved maintenance coordination reducing downtime by 8%

source_text:
Texas City Facility -  The relationship between HPL and Calpine has become and continues to be  strained.
Calpine purchased the Texas City Cogeneration Facility from Enron  and Dominion Resources in early 1998.
Prior to that time ENA supplied 45,000  MMBtu of gas under a fixed price contract and a Market Price agreement was in  place to provide any additional volumes that might be needed in addition to  that which Union Carbide Corporation had the contractual right to supply  under the historic arrangement, since they were the steam host for the  facility.
After Calpine took over, these contracts either expired or were  terminated.
At this point HPL became the sole supplier to the facility  although the interconnection with the Union Carbide delivery point with the  Calpine facility remained active and a new Transaction Agreement was put in  place whereby Calpine agreed to certain minimum and maximum quantity  obligations and agreed on the prices that would be paid for any short fall in  volumes.
Since then, measurement disputes have been alleged and Calpine has  shortpaid HPL's invoices even after verbally agreeing that the amounts  invoiced were correct.
Additionally, as a result of Calpine's power  purchaser's last minute notification to Calpine of reductions in the purchase  of power for the next day, which notification is usually after Calpine's next  day notification deadline to HPL, Calpine has resorted to the use of   creative force majeure situations in an effort to reduce their costs.
These  notifications have occurred some thirteen (I think) times and Calpine has  provided little explanation to HPL of the nature of these events of force  majeure.
When pressed for a more detailed explanation, they merely state  that they had to take down various unit(s) to repair or replace leaking  valves, etc.
Clear Lake Facility -  The relationship between Calpine and HPL is not as strained with regard to  deliveries at this facility.
This may be because the contract covering the  base volume of gas being delivered by HPL has not changed since it was  negotiated by ENA in 1995.
Midcon remains connected to the facility and  delivers certain quantities of market priced gas.
Market priced gas is  required by the facility when its requirements exceed the base volumes  supplied under the 1995 agreement.
Should the power purchase agreement be  amended to allow Calpine not to deliver powered or should the power purchaser  cancel the power purchase agreement, Calpine has negotiated an amendment  allowing for the delivery of the base volumes at alternative delivery  points.
Currently, HPL has advised Calpine of an upcoming event of force  majeure which will require a cessation of deliveries of gas to the facility  which certain regulatory mandated tests are being performed on the A-S  pipeline.
It is not known whether the Midcon delivery point has the capacity  to handle the entire facility gas requirements or not.

I did not get the chance to also tell you how grateful we are as a   school for Technology for All.
Our little school was the test pilot and the   first out of state set up and delivery.
Of course, I told them that if I had   to drive to Texas to get them I would and that is just what we did on one of   our Spring Breaks.

We   have just received more for each of our high school classrooms from the    office in Denver.
The fruit of your labor is prospering and we are so   thankful.
We probably have one of the best computer labs in the valley.

Subject: Observations from the WSPP Meeting

Dear Team,

I wanted to share some key observations from yesterday's WSPP meeting that may impact our upcoming projects and strategic planning.

**Market Dynamics:**
- Power prices showed increased volatility in the Northwest region, particularly during peak hours
- Transmission constraints continue to affect pricing differentials between zones
- Several participants noted tightening capacity margins for Q2

**Regulatory Updates:**
- New scheduling protocols will be implemented starting next month
- Enhanced reporting requirements for bilateral transactions above 25 MW
- FERC's recent ruling on transmission planning was a major discussion point

**Operational Considerations:**
- Weather forecasting accuracy remains critical given recent extreme events
- Multiple parties emphasized the importance of real-time communication during system stress
- Cybersecurity measures are being strengthened across the region

**Action Items for Our Team:**
1. Review our hedging strategies in light of increased volatility
2. Update our scheduling procedures to align with new protocols
3. Coordinate with operations on enhanced communication procedures

I'll be scheduling a follow-up meeting early next week to discuss how these developments affect our current positions and future planning.

Please let me know if you have any questions or would like additional details on any of these topics.

Best regards,
[Your Name]

Listening in by phone is so much better than traveling to these meetings.
It greatly reduces one's exposure to the toxins of this process.

A learned expert on Secured Transactions  from Mike's firm gave an opening address on the principles of granting and receiving the grantation of security interests.
Almost completely irrelevant.
The guy up and suggested that for a given transaction, the parties might consider giving a security interest in an office building, ie.real estate,  as collateral.

A cannabalized EEI Credit Support Annex  was tabled by Deedee Russo of Reliant and muddled through.
The format was typically:      Mike:  "Okay guys, why don't you explain to me what you want."
Member:  "We think we need this...blah blah blah, "    Mike:  "Okay, we'll put that into our next draft and have a conference call in December and a meeting in   January and remember, none of this is binding, its all optional."
3.
At the very end, a lawyer from PacifiCorp managed to raise the vital issue and Mike got his hackles up very quickly.
The PacifiCorp guy was basically saying that the WSPP was becoming more and more like the EEI and that this made it more and more difficult for parties to decide which agreement to use.
His implication was that the WSPP should try to remain different or throw in the towel and be just like the EEI.
Small reacted from a position of religion, dogmatically and loudly asserting that the two agreements were fundamentally different.
Here is where he left himself open to the shining light of rational analysis:  if someone, had the time,  and we thought it mattered enough, the approach to take would be this:    Dispassionate Spokesperson:  A question has been raised:  is the WSPP agreement becoming more or less like the EEI?
To fairly answer this question one needs to look at all the changes that have been made by  the WSPP in the last three years, comparing each change to the EEI agreement.
(prepare comparison document).
If we look at the evidence do we see convergence or divergence?
The answer will be overwhelmingly convergence.
If this objective study could be placed before the "Membership" it would speak for itself.
Nobody would have to utter a word.
The comparison document would do the job.
If we are going to bother playing with these guys, this is what we should do.
It would take some time, but if we circulated it to the membership and then merely raised the question of future direction, we might deal this tedious process a mortal blow.
Believe it or not, the solution to  this process is to follow the same process that went on when the King James Bible was put together in 1611.
Various scholars took various views on how various Hebrew passages should be translated, and it took a committee of draftsmen, appointed and sent to Geneva  by King James  to pound out the form that has stood the test of time for centuries.
The Joint Drafting Committee's time on the historical stage is finally arriving.
I am going to talk to this Pacificorp fellow and Brenda Anderson at BPA and see what happens.

<<IPPupdate092201.pdf>>   Good Morning  

Attached, please find our Power Generation Update issued this morning.

1. EIX Bankruptcy Filing? - Implications for the IPPs   

Recent press reports from major financial publications including the Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg have suggested there is a growing likelihood that an involuntary bankruptcy petition will be filed against Southern California Edison, the utility subsidiary of Edison International (EIX, Not Rated). These reports cite mounting financial pressures stemming from the California energy crisis, including billions in unpaid power purchase obligations and deteriorating credit ratings from Moody's and S&P. Legal experts quoted in these publications indicate that creditors may move forward with involuntary proceedings as early as Q4 2001 if the utility continues to defer payments on power contracts.

We thought it would be timely to analyze the implications of an SCE bankruptcy for the Independent Power Producers (IPPs), particularly given that SCE serves approximately 13 million customers across a 50,000 square mile service territory and represents roughly 20% of California's total electricity demand.

2. SCE Bankruptcy Would be Neutral for the IPPs   

Our overall conclusion is that an SCE bankruptcy would be neutral for the sector:  	

A. Such an event would have no impact on the earnings estimates or forecasted growth rates for any of the companies under our coverage, including Calpine Corporation (CPN), Dynegy Inc. (DYN), NRG Energy (NRG), or Mirant Corporation (MIR). Our financial models already incorporate conservative assumptions regarding California receivables collection, with recovery rates estimated between 70-85% over a 24-36 month timeline.

B. In addition, none of the companies have any direct receivables exposure to SCE. Most IPP transactions with California utilities flow through the California Independent System Operator (CalISO) and the California Power Exchange (PX), which serve as intermediary clearing mechanisms. Direct bilateral contracts with SCE represent less than 5% of total California exposure across our coverage universe.

C. Finally, we believe reserves taken against accounts receivable balances from the CalISO and PX across the sector adequately mitigate exposure to potential bad debt writedowns. For example, Calpine has reserved approximately $180 million against California receivables, while Dynegy has set aside $95 million. These reserve levels represent 45-60% of outstanding California balances and align with our stress-case recovery scenarios.

3. Updated Accounts Receivables Exposure Included   

Included in the note are updated details on the accounts receivables exposure of all the IPPs with California operations. Our analysis shows total sector exposure of approximately $1.2 billion as of August 31, 2001, down from peak levels of $1.8 billion in March 2001. This reduction reflects both collections from the California Department of Water Resources under long-term contracts and conservative reserve practices implemented across the sector. Detailed company-by-company breakdowns are provided in Exhibit A, including aging analysis, reserve percentages, and estimated recovery timelines under various bankruptcy scenarios.

Regards,

This system would enable us to efficiently track, compare, and analyze our utility purchasing data across different sites, leading to more cost-effective decision-making and improved sustainability outcomes.

- Enhanced visibility into utility usage and expenditures
- Identification of cost-saving opportunities
- Benchmarking against industry standards and peer facilities
- Streamlined reporting and compliance tracking

I talked to Calger a bit about it today and he  suggested that I get together with you guys.
As always, time's short.

Tanya: There are a few critical issues left that are causing serious concern:

(1) [re: legal name of our counterparty] This is a fundamental and deeply alarming discrepancy. According to FUNB, there is no legal entity named "First Union National Bank, Charlotte". If S&P, which we rely on for foundational data, is including the city where FUNB is headquartered as part of their *legal name*, then S&P is unequivocally wrong. This undermines the very basis of our counterparty identification. FUNB has urgently asked that we forward the S&P document you are looking at, indicating they view this as a significant and potentially problematic error.

(2) [re: FUNB request to provide us with First Union Corp. financials and your response that it's OK if First Union Corp. signs on as a guarantor] This is incredibly unsettling. FUNB says that First Union National Bank *doesn't even prepare annual statements* – how can we properly assess the creditworthiness of our actual counterparty without this basic financial transparency? While they can provide quarterly call reports (with YTD info) – a format I'm not entirely clear on the implications of – or direct us to EDGAR for "FUNB annual financials" (which could be for the parent corporation, not the bank itself), this ambiguity is unacceptable and leaves us dangerously exposed. And critically, FUNB *did not* offer First Union Corp. as a guarantor, leaving us uncomfortably uncertain about the true financial backing and our potential exposure.

(3) [re: 10 year bonds which you agreed to accept as Eligible Credit Support] We need absolute, crystal-clear precision on the "usual haircut" for these bonds. Simply stating "90% or 95%" is dangerously vague given the potential for significant market fluctuations and the risk of inadequate collateralization. The fact that Legal no longer offers up bonds in our documents means we've lost a crucial layer of expertise and protection in this area, which is incredibly worrying. This oversight could expose us to unacceptable levels of risk if not defined with rigorous exactitude.

(4) [re: the Specified Conditions of Tax Event, Tax Event Upon Merger and Credit Event Upon Merger] FUNB's position here is profoundly disturbing and directly conflicts with our fundamental philosophy of preserving transactions. Their explicit preference to *terminate* rather than collateralize transactions, and to eliminate obligations to transfer in avoidance of termination, means they are choosing to abandon agreements and leave us in a precarious position when conditions arise, rather than responsibly mitigate risk. This isn't just a "different philosophy" – it's an aggressive stance that strips away critical protections. While I'm willing to concede on some tax events, the grave risk that global mergers could *force* termination, despite the agreement *requiring* the Affected Party to try and transfer the Transaction to avoid it, remains a critical vulnerability. We could be forced into costly and undesirable terminations.

These are not minor points. I need urgent clarification and resolution on *all* of these issues. Our financial security and the integrity of this entire deal hang in the balance. We cannot proceed with such critical unresolved risks.

Thanks.
Sara

The following announcement was sent out from the ENW Office of the Chair on Sunday, October 21:   As a follow-up to the Enron Net Works All Employee meeting on October 5, we are pleased to announce a number of organizational changes.
Beth Perlman, currently CIO for EA Systems, will work closely with Mark Pickering on a number of key projects for Enron Net Works.
Additionally, Beth plans to explore various commercial opportunities within Enron.
Replacing Beth in her current role will be Steve Hotte, currently CIO for EGS.
Anthony Dayao will continue as CIO for EES Systems.
In addition to his current responsibilities, Anthony will assume responsibility for creating a combined Wholesale/Retail Power Trading and Risk Management system.
Jeff Johnson will move into the new role of CIO for EGM/EIM Systems.
John Paskin will transfer to the Houston office from London to take up the new role of CIO for Corporate Systems.
His group will include the ISC, Enterprise Portal, Intranet Solutions, CRM strategy, Treasury Systems, Development Support and will matrix into HR IT Systems.
Continuing in their current positions are Inja Chun, CIO for EBS Systems; Paul Freeman, CIO for Enron Europe; Jay Webb, CIO for eCommerce, which now includes Commodity Logic Systems; and Jenny Rub, CIO for Infrastructure.
All of the above positions report into to Mark Pickering in the Office of the Chairman for Enron Net Works.
Transitions into their new positions will begin within the next two weeks and should be complete by the end of the year.
We are currently interviewing individuals to serve as CIO for EGS, as well as an individual to serve as head of our Enterprise Framework group.
We will keep you posted on the progress of these searches.
Please join us in congratulating all of these individuals on their new responsibilities.

Subject: Contract Margin Planning and Risk Assessment - NNG Contract Portfolio Review

Dear Team,

I am writing to address the current contract margin planning and risk assessment requirements for NNG in light of recent contract terminations and ongoing new business developments.

**Current Situation Overview:**
We are experiencing significant portfolio changes due to multiple contract terminations while simultaneously pursuing new business opportunities. This dual impact requires immediate attention to our margin planning and risk management strategies.

**Key Risk Factors Identified:**
- Revenue volatility from terminated contracts affecting cash flow projections
- Margin compression risk during transition period
- Counterparty credit risk assessment for new business prospects
- Operational capacity misalignment with changing contract portfolio
- Market pricing pressure on renewal negotiations

**Immediate Actions Required:**
1. Conduct comprehensive margin analysis for all remaining active contracts
2. Reassess credit exposure limits and collateral requirements for new prospects
3. Update financial forecasting models to reflect current portfolio composition
4. Review and adjust risk tolerance thresholds for new business acceptance
5. Implement enhanced monitoring protocols for contract performance metrics

**Recommendations:**
- Establish monthly contract margin review meetings through Q2
- Develop contingency funding strategies for potential additional terminations
- Create standardized risk scoring methodology for new business evaluation
- Strengthen contract terms and conditions for future agreements

Please confirm your department's capacity to support these initiatives and provide initial risk assessment reports by [date].

Best regards,
[Your Name]

It shows the value of contract terminations for NNG for the contract year of 1101/03 to 11/01/04 to be $145 million.

I think for planning purposes however, we would assume that we would contract for the full value of $145 million either through better pricing analytics, new business development projects and/ or Rate Case reallocation to captive customers.

I think you also have to assume that other business development projects will come in to help offset the downsides.
Sorry if I rambled a bit too much.
My view is that NNG will have margin targets for planning purposes flat with 2002.
Call me if you wish to discuss.
