EPMI is entering into more and more transactions that are settled against a  floating, published index price.
Our physical contract does not currently  provide for what happens if the published source is not available or is  otherwise materially changed.
Under ISDA for financial trading,  this is  addressed as a Market Disruption Event (MDE).
Under ENA's standard contract  for financial trading, there is included as a MDE "the imposition of trading  limits on the range within which the price of the commodity may fluctuate".
What this may mean is that if a cap is imposed on power prices, then in lieu  of using the capped price to determine the floating price, you would be  required (under ISDA) to eventually get brokers to determine what the price  would have been without the cap.
I want to add language to our physical contracts that addresses material  changes/disappearance of the published prices that would mirror the financial  trading terms and doubt whether we would want to make the imposition of a cap  on power prices a MDE.
If you treat the imposition of a cap (say in CA of  prices to $500 or in NEPOOL to $1,000) as a MDE, then we would be required to  secure quotes as to what the price would have been without the cap each time  that a pricing date trades at the cap level.
This only seems fraught with  litigation risk to me.
Alternatively, if caps are not deemed a MDE, then you  would always settle against the published prices, even if they are  "artificially" determined after the trade was entered into.
While caps are  not appealing, I think it would be better to not have the imposition of caps  be considered a MDE.
I have spoken with the financial trading group and they  will follow our lead on this.
So, depending upon what you both think, we  will make sure that financial and physical power are treated the same on this  issue.
Thanks for your thoughts.

Subject: Happy Birthday - Thinking of You Today

Dear [Name],

Today marks another year of your beautiful life, and though we're apart, you're constantly in my thoughts and heart. I wanted to reach out to wish you the happiest of birthdays and let you know how much I miss you.

Distance may separate us physically, but the love and memories we share remain as strong as ever. I find myself thinking about all the wonderful times we've spent together - your infectious laugh, the way you light up any room you enter, and the countless moments that have made my life richer simply by knowing you.

I wish I could be there to celebrate with you in person, to see your smile when you blow out the candles, and to give you the biggest hug. Instead, I'm sending you all my love across the miles, along with my warmest wishes for a day filled with joy, laughter, and everything that makes you happy.

May this new year of your life bring you incredible adventures, fulfilled dreams, and all the happiness you deserve. You are such a special person, and I feel grateful every day to have you in my life, even from afar.

I hope your day is absolutely wonderful. Can't wait until we can celebrate together again.

With all my love and birthday wishes,

[Your name]

PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL:  Mike Peterson asked me to send you the following note, with attached order:  Attached is an Order signed yesterday and entered this morning by Judge Rosenthal on Plaintiffs' Motion for TRO and Preliminary Injunctive Relief (including a freeze of defendants' "insider trading proceeds") - i.e., the matter on which there was a hearing with attendant media hoopla last month.
You probably recall that at the end of the hearing, Judge Rosenthal asked for briefing on a rather arcane legal point concerning whether or not the Court had authority to issue the requested preliminary relief, and the parties submitted briefs on this matter on December 15 and December 21.
In the attached Order, Judge Rosenthal concludes that the Court does have the requisite authority, but the present record does not contain evidence warranting a freeze of any individual defendant's proceeds from the sale of Enron stock.
You might take further comfort from two additional points in the Court's opinion: (a) at several places, the Court clearly indicates that any "freeze" or other such injunctive relief as to any defendant would have to be predicated on an individualized evidentiary showing as to that defendant; and (b) the Court indicates that plaintiffs would have to satisfy a very difficult "tracing" requirement to establish a right to a constructive trust or freeze (i.e., "trace" a specific asset or fund of money held by any defendant back to the profits of an improper insider trade).
The aspects of the Court's opinion that arguably are favorable to the plaintiffs are (a) the discussion of "an equitable accounting," wherein the Court suggests that the plaintiffs might be able to satisfy the requirements for an order that defendants account for profits earned by trading Enron securities between October 1998 and November 2001; and (b) providing an opportunity (through January 23) for plaintiffs to file a brief addressing whatever expedited discovery they believe they are entitled to as to the individual defendants, "particularly as to .
.
.
Kenneth Lay, Jeffrey Skilling, and Andrew Fastow."
We will, of course, advise you of any further developments.
- Mike Peterson  As always, please do not hesitate to call or e-mail us if you have questions or comments.
Terri    This e-mail and any attached files may be confidential and subject to attorney/client privilege.
If you received it in error, please immediately notify the sender by return e-mail or by calling (713)654-7600.

text: dan, i have reviewed the wildhorse (mesa) gathering, processing, and transportation logistics for the upcoming quarter. Overall, the plan presented by your team is robust, particularly regarding the optimized routing for raw material collection. However, I have a few concerns regarding the projected processing capacity during peak times. Specifically, the bottleneck analysis on Line 3 suggests a potential for delays if the gathering volume exceeds 90% of the planned maximum. Could we schedule a brief call next week to discuss contingency plans for this scenario and review the staffing levels for the processing facility? Please let me know your availability.
source_text:
Dan,  I have reviewed the Wildhorse (Mesa) Gathering, Processing, and  Transport Agreement.
This agreement is still valid and the gas is dedicated  to this Agreement through 2013.
The agreement present some problematic  issues which I will outline.
1.
Gas Quality -  The gas quality provisions only require Wildhorse to  transport the gas if the gas meets the downstream carriers (in this case  Northwest Pipeline) gas quality specifications.
We propose to put in a  treating plant which would allow the gas to meet the specifications, however  there are no provision in this Agreement which allow us to insert a plant  between Northwest Pipeline and Wildhorse.
Wildhorse could delay are extract  value from us for this connection.
This is an uncertainty.
2.
Wildhorse Obligation to Perform - Based on my understanding of the  facts, at some point during the term of this agreement, Northwest Pipeline  enforced their gas quality specifications and refused to take the gas at the  downstream side of Wildhorse's Gathering System.
As a result, Wildhorse shut  in Enogex's production and it has been shut in ever since.
Wildhorse has a  right to do this under this Agreement (see #1 above) and therefore Wildhorse  has not breached its obligation to transport under this Agreement.
Wildhorse's obligation was suspended when Northwest refused receipt of the  gas.
3.
Unprofitability - Assuming Wildhorse worked with us to install the  treating plant which conformed the gas to Northwest Specifications, they  could refuse to provide gathering service under this agreement if it was  still uneconomical for them to do so.
If they decided it is uneconomical for  them to do so, they have the right to provide Enogex with various potential  solutions which include (i) renegotiating the terms (ii) allowing Enogex to  operate Wildhorse's equipment at Enogex sole cost, expense and risk, or (iii)  release the gas from the Agreement.
The problem here is that there is no  time limit under which Wildhorse must reach a solution with us and no  specific solution they must reach.
Wildhorse could drag this out for some  extended period of time and they could extract significant value.
My  recommendation is that we make Enogex's resolution of these issues with  Wildhorse a condition precedent to closing and funding this deal.
I know the  timing is late.
However if Enron funds this deal and takes on the risk of  negotiating with Wildhorse to resolve either a new deal or a release of the  gas,  everyone needs to understand that such negotiation could take  substantial time and Wildhorse will have significant leverage.
Let me know if you wish to discuss this further or have any questions.

The weather is lovely and sunny, though there's quite a chilly breeze.
Yesterday marked six years since we first met - our anniversary!
It feels like it's been even longer than that.
We had dinner at A?mann's, naturally - it's our go-to restaurant.
Our London trip was fantastic!
I brought my Goretex jacket, which was smart since it drizzled every quarter hour or so daily, but the temperature was mild so it wasn't bothersome.
We were amazed by how pricey all the tourist attractions were - 30 DM each just for the Aquarium!
All the attractions had similar pricing, but we managed to see everything we had time for.
The May 1st disturbances forced us to change our route slightly, so we missed the Crown Jewels - we'll prioritize that next visit.
We thoroughly enjoyed the green spaces, the local pubs, and spending time with Heather.
However, since we're not urban dwellers, we were eager to escape the chaos and return to our quiet routine.
The fish and chips from The Bag of Nails Pub were delicious - aside from pub food, we mainly had Italian cuisine.
Visiting Windsor Castle and seeing all the historical sites was fascinating.
Heather's apartment is lovely and perfectly located near Buckingham Palace.
She's having a wonderful time there!
Next trip, I'd like to explore the rural areas.
I know it will take considerable time before you feel better than "just ok."
I'm truly sorry for what you're going through.
It's positive that you're staying active.
What's your plan regarding your employment situation?
I can genuinely say this job brings me more satisfaction than any previous position, though my supervisor can be challenging at times!
Time for lunch!
Please write back!

Almost two years after issuing a decision in PG&E's GRC, the Commission issued it rehearing order on October 16th and, lo and behold, actually granted TURN's rehearing request in part.
The overall result is to reduce the capital revenue requirement by $24.8 million and expenses by $37.3 million.
In addition, some portion of PG&E' estimated $171 million in electric distribution capital spending will be subject to rehearing.
Listed  below are the areas in which the Commission granted rehearing.
1.
Electric Distribution Capital Spending.
The Commission will, in essence, reopen the record, and allow PG&E to put into evidence how much it invested in its electric distribution plant in 1998.
PG&E had used a 1998 forecasted amt of capital expenditures to develop its test year forecast.
TURN argued that there was substantial evidence on the record that this amount was never spent.
PG&E argued that the record closed prior to the end of 1998 so the best it could do was an estimate.
On rehearing, the Commission agreed with TURN, that there was evidence that the forecasted amount was never spent, so they are allowing PG&E to prove it.
The rehearing order states that any rates that are raised based on the electric distribution capital forecast adopted the GRC decision  may be subject to refund.
2.
Emergency Response Work This work category under electric distribution capital spending was reduced by $17.2 million.
3.
Vegetation Management.
The Supplemental Tree Trimming Program was reduced by $9.2 million.
4.
Meter Reading.
PG&E had primarily used accounting changes to justify the large increase in this service.
On rehearing the Commission stated that PG&E had failed to substantiate those changes and reduced the allowed amount by $7.9 million.
5.
Account Services.
On rehearing the commission stated that PG&E had failed to show (a) why it cost so much more to provide services to CIA customers  than residential customers ( $43.30 vs. $10.20); and (b) that money was not going for marketing activities that the Commission had disallowed in the previous GRC.
The result was that the commission disallowed $20 million.
6.
Customer Information Systems.
The Commission disallowed $7.2 million as funds which ratepayers had already expended for CIS  rewrites for which they had not received any benefits.

The basic reason we are changing meters in Sitara is because when PGLC was originally set up, the meters were set up using the same name as what the pipeline called them, i.e.  
NGPL/909265.  
This is the NGPL meter number, NOT the PGLC meter number.  
The PGLC Meter number is PGLC/NGPL.  
The only reason we are doing this is so we can have everything correctly reflected and can upload noms into pegasys with the meter number PGLC specifically used.  

As you navigate the PGLC site, you'll hear the faint hum of equipment, the steady hiss of pressurized gas lines, and workers calling out to one another in clipped voices that echo off concrete walls. There’s the ever-present scent of faint mercaptan—a sharp, sulfuric tang that lingers in the air, an assurance of safety and a reminder of the invisible commodity moving through the system. Touch the metal of the meters, and they’re cool and sturdy under your palm, unyielding and lightly dusted with grit from daily handling. The clipboard paper feels smooth, but sometimes damp with condensation where it's been set atop cold surfaces. Unmistakably, the environment is practical, marked by the subtle vibrations underfoot—there’s a sense of controlled power in every texture and sound.  

The three products that will be in place for November at PGLC are:  

NBPL/Manhattan – This is where we are buying Northern Border Specific Gas to take to PGLC at the NBPL/Peoples/82 (Manhattan transfer point). The air here is tinged with oil and clean earth, while the rumble of trucks and distant train horns offers a low, improvisational soundtrack.  
We will then have a meter bounce ticket to take it from NBPL/PGLC/82 to PGLC/NBPL/NB01 and take it into our pool. The paperwork slides across a scarred wooden desk, the graphite on your fingertips cool and slightly powdery.  

NGPL/Peoples – This is where we are buying NGPL specific gas to take to PGLC at the NGPL/Peoples/909285 Meter, surrounded by the click of keys and the soft, repetitive beep of scanner guns logging each transfer. The metallic scent here is cut by the whiff of coffee drifting from a mug nearby.  
We will then have a meter bounce ticket to take it from NGPL/Peoples/909285 to PGLC/NGPL/NGPL and take it into our pool, each step tracked with smooth, soft plastic keypads and the slight resistance of sealing another document in the folder.  

CHI Peoples – This is where we are buying pool gas at PGLC at the TTP pool—the product that has been out there, but all deals will be mapped to the TTP point. This is where the majority of customers give us our gas. The ambient noise here is a low murmur of conversation, fluorescent lights buzzing softly overhead, and the soft tap of pens against tablets. There’s a slight chill in the air from the HVAC, and paperwork occasionally rustles in a faint breeze.  

The only time we will be using the meter PGLC/NGPL/NGPL, PGLC/NBPL/NB01, PGLC/ANR/ANR, and other PGLC/pipeline specific meters is when gas is actually being delivered on a contract into the gate. For the most part, all our gas will be at meter PGLC/TTP/TTP.  

Thanks!

NorskeCanada announced today plans for additional curtailment for the first quarter of 2002 at its B.C. paper operations, as weak economic conditions have reduced demand for the company's products. 

In real life, this means Norske is planning to shut down two paper machines—No. 3 at Port Alberni and No. 1 at Elk Falls—for the first quarter of 2002. A third machine, No. 1 at Crofton, will also be shut down for the month of January. For workers, this could mean temporary layoffs or reduced hours until market demand improves. The shutdown will reduce production by about 34,000 metric tonnes at Elk Falls and about 12,000 metric tonnes at Crofton in January. 

The company will review its curtailment plans every month so they can quickly respond if market conditions get better. In practice, the shutdowns may directly impact employees, suppliers, and local communities that rely on the mills for economic stability.

Second CA Merchant Storage Field Pushes Back Opening  California's second merchant underground natural gas storage project near Sacramento began injecting supplies this month, but its commercial start-up date has been pushed back to Dec. 1, according to the California operations manager for Houston-based Western Hub Properties LLC, the developer.
Although it is not fully subscribed more than half the capacity is under contract, according to Jim Fossum, the in-state manager for Western Hub, which was purchased last summer by a partnership of Aquila Inc and ArcLight Energy Partners Fund in a $220 million deal that is still several months away from approval from the California Public Utilities Commission.
The Lodi Storage Project near the town of Lodi, CA, about 35 miles south of the state capital, will have "high-performance, quick-cycle-capabilities" in a project that stores 12 Bcf of natural gas with a 500 MMcf/d withdrawal rate and 400 MMcf/d injection rate.
Fossum said Western Hub also is pursuing a second merchant storage project in the southern half of the state around Bakersfield in the Wheeler Ridge area close to the nexus of all the major interstate natural gas pipeline coming into California.
That project, he said, is not included in the Aquila partnership purchase at this time, and will be developed initial by a still-to-be-named company using some of the same personnel that developed Lodi.
The same group also has a potential storage site identified in Texas, near San Antonio.

An Overheated Market: The Manipulation of California's Energy Sector by Producers  
(Published September 22, 2000)

In August, Pasadena became the most expensive location to procure electricity in California. At the California Power Exchange, which facilitates much of the state's electricity transactions, the prices that utilities paid for electricity averaged $166 per megawatt—an increase of more than five times compared to $32 per megawatt in August of the previous year.

Why is this occurring?

Several factors contribute to this situation. Notably, on particularly hot days, excessive amounts of electricity are being purchased in a near-panic environment that manifests only hours before a potential crisis. Conversely, insufficient amounts of electricity are being secured in advance—either days or even months ahead of need—as prudent planning would dictate.

Subject: Clarifying the Resolution of California’s Electricity Crisis

Dear [Recipient],

I wanted to clarify a common misconception regarding the resolution of the California electricity crisis. Contrary to popular belief, the crisis was not resolved through increased power supply or through the direct leadership of Governor Davis. Instead, the turning point came when the State of California began purchasing electricity on behalf of utilities. Due to severe credit problems and mounting unpaid bills to generators, the utilities themselves could no longer afford to procure power for their customers. The state's intervention to pay for electricity ensured continued service and stabilized the market, ultimately resolving the immediate crisis.

Best regards,  
[Your Name]

September 5, 2001 Business World Crisis?
What Crisis?
By HOLMAN W. JENKINS, JR.
The big news this summer is that Californians haven't been reduced to stone-age lifestyles, running naked in the streets and eating each other.
The state barely had enough electricity to get through this past winter, when demand was not yet pumped up with air-conditioning.
Yet here they are surviving the summer with nary a blackout.
Gov.
Gray Davis must be some kind of a wizard, pulling 15,000 megawatts from his pointy hat.
He gave every indication of being a hapless cluck, but obviously we underestimated him.
Naah.
California's summer of surplus demonstrates just how flukey last winter's rolling blackouts were.
Power there was aplenty (or at least enough to get by).
What there wasn't was anybody to pay for it, thanks to the political system's paralysis as the state's private utilities ran out of cash and used up their credit trying to keep the lights on.
We won't rehearse the central pinion of this catastrophe, a "deregulation" plan that created scarcity pricing in the absence of true scarcity.
A tweak here and there as late as last fall could have saved the state's taxpayers and ratepayers literally billions of dollars at no real cost to anybody.
Instead, the utilities were allowed simply to run out of money, accumulating $14 billion in unpayable IOUs to generators.
Now, most of us tend to think of power plants as giant coal or nuclear operations that run 24 hours a day, supplying "baseload" power.
But the majority of plants are part-timers, firing up to meet intermediate and peak demand.
Revving up their turbines means incurring fuel, labor and maintenance costs, which means operators like to get paid.
The crisis months saw three distinct waves of blackouts, each related to plants dropping off line simply because they feared not getting paid.
In January, it was British Columbia Hydro, the big, government-owned operator of Canadian dams, which had kept California afloat on credit for months.
In March it was dozens of small California generators, known as "qualifying facilities," which no longer could meet their own fuel and labor bills because they weren't getting paid by their utility customers.
In July, it was the federal government imposing impenetrably complex price controls across the West, making it impossible for generators to know what price they were allowed to charge.
Some shut down rather than take a chance, and since the federal intervention meant the entire region was on the griddle for California's mismanagement, the blackouts just happened to land in Nevada.
There was no shortage, in other words, no "energy crisis."
There was only the unaddressed credit problems of the utilities.
We opined in January that Californians would be surprised at how quickly power prices return to normal.
Yup.
The state threw open the treasury to pay for the power the utilities could no longer afford and suddenly sellers were everywhere and prices fell.
In the teeth of peak air-conditioning season, electricity prices are now back to normal.
In retrospect, what's amazing is that so many plants not only kept operating month after month despite being stiffed by the state, but produced 62% more power than they had the year before to keep California lit.
Yet they've gotten nothing but abuse from the governor, who is still turning over every legal stone to try to avoid paying the IOUs.
There is no question that Western supplies were tighter than usual thanks to low water levels in Northwest river systems.
But the evidence shows that Western markets were flexible enough to accommodate the glitches.
All they needed was a creditworthy customer to deal with.

Dear Colleagues,

I hope this email finds you well. I wanted to share some key insights from the latest ISDA credit derivatives market survey and discuss the significant implications of Enron's collapse on our industry.

**Survey Highlights:**

The ISDA survey reveals substantial changes in market structure and risk management practices following the Enron bankruptcy. Notional amounts outstanding in credit derivatives have shown resilience despite initial market concerns, though we've observed notable shifts in counterparty selection criteria and documentation standards.

**Key Enron Impact Areas:**

1. **Counterparty Risk Assessment**: Market participants have fundamentally reassessed their approach to counterparty risk, implementing more stringent due diligence processes and regular credit monitoring procedures.

2. **Collateral Management**: There has been a marked increase in collateral requirements and more frequent margin calls, particularly for energy sector exposures and lower-rated counterparties.

3. **Documentation Standards**: ISDA has accelerated efforts to standardize credit event definitions and settlement procedures, addressing ambiguities that became apparent during the Enron workout process.

4. **Regulatory Scrutiny**: Enhanced regulatory oversight has led to improved transparency requirements and more robust internal risk controls across derivatives operations.

**Market Adaptation:**

The industry has demonstrated remarkable adaptability, with many institutions strengthening their credit derivatives capabilities and expanding into new products while maintaining disciplined risk management practices.

I would welcome the opportunity to discuss these developments further and their implications for our operations.

Most major dealers say there has been a big increase in their credit derivatives volumes.

Steve,   I think you may have heard a request last week re working closely with Dynegy.
I think we just need to treat them like other counterparties.
Basically, West Power would like to enter into arms length physical power and service transactions with Dynegy.
My understanding is that Dynegy is a separate, unrelated party until the merger closes.
Therefore, we can not "collaborate" with them commercially and our transaction policy is dictated by customary credit, legal and risk management procedures.
Is this correct?
If so, how do you feel about the following?
An Enron customer wants to buy power and related services for one year.
The customer requires Enron to post collateral.
Enron does not want to post collateral but suggests that Enron can provide the product/services to Dynegy and Dynegy can then sell to the customer.
The Enron marketer calls the Dynegy marketer and proposes a "back to back" transaction.
Dynegy adds a small service fee, the Enron/Dynegy contract is executed and a Dynegy/Customer contract is executed.
This type of deal happens frequently - it is usually driven by the third party having better credit, transmission access or a complementary service.
We could do this with anyone, but the obvious choice is Dynegy - customers think it makes sense, and ultimately if we merge we have retained a customer.
Do you think this works?
Regards,

It seems that this  replacement was performed ONLY as a fuel savings activity and that there  would be no increase in emissions or horsepower as a result.

Contractor testing runs about  $3-5,000.
A condition of all permitting issues is that the carbs are not supposed to be  installed on the units (preconstruction) until approval has been given by the  agency.
In this case, we will be allowed to install a carbuerator on the one  unit to be tested but not on all units.
Should testing show other  exceedances (emissions or Hp) in addition to fuel savings, this will trigger  actions requiring perimtting.
Under the circumstances, I think it would be  in the best interest of NNG to know for certain that we have not violated the  grandfather status of the units and that if our activity requires permitting,  we comply immediately.
I am sending out the letter request to the TNRCC today.
If approved, we  should test ASAP.
Remember, that sampling ports in the exhaust stack of the  unit to be tested will need to be constructed prior to testing.
Let me know  if the Team will need a diagram showing the sampling port locations.

Reflections for Consideration

The following thoughts, which were recently shared with me, offer meaningful insights that may provide guidance from time to time.

Perhaps there is value in meeting a few unsuitable individuals before encountering the right one. This experience enables us to more fully appreciate and be grateful when we eventually meet the person truly meant for us.

When one door to happiness closes, another may open. However, we often spend so much time and energy focusing on the closed door that we fail to notice the new opportunities that have emerged.

The most genuine friends are those with whom silence is comfortable—individuals with whom you can simply sit together, share the moment, and walk away feeling fulfilled by the connection, even without exchanging words.

It is often said that we do not realize the value of something until it is gone. Conversely, we may also be unaware of what we have been missing until it arrives in our lives.

Offering someone your love does not guarantee it will be reciprocated. It is important not to expect love in return; instead, allow it the space to grow in another’s heart. If it does not, take comfort in knowing it grew within your own.

While feelings of affection or admiration can develop quickly, it may take a lifetime to truly move on from someone who has touched your life in a meaningful way.

Physical appearance can be deceiving, and material wealth is often transient. Seek out those who bring genuine joy to your life—a simple smile from such a person can brighten even your darkest days. Strive to find the one who brings happiness to your heart.

There may be moments when you deeply miss someone—so much so that you wish you could embrace them outside the realm of dreams. Cherish your aspirations, pursue your goals, and strive to become your authentic self, for life offers each of us only one opportunity to pursue our dreams.

May you experience enough happiness to make you gentle, enough challenges to make you strong, enough sorrow to keep you empathetic, and enough hope to bring you joy.

Practice empathy by considering others’ perspectives—if something would cause you pain, it likely pains others as well.

True happiness is not necessarily found in possessing the best of everything but in making the most of whatever circumstances life presents. Those who have faced sorrow, difficulty, and adversity are often best able to recognize and value the importance of those who have played a meaningful role in their lives.

Love may begin with a smile, grow with a kiss, and end with a tear. The brightest possible future often necessitates letting go of past failures and disappointments; only by moving forward can we truly flourish.

When you entered the world, you cried while others smiled. Live a life in such a manner that, in the end, you are smiling, and those around you are moved to tears by your departure.

Consider sharing this message with those who have made a positive difference in your life, who have offered support and encouragement in challenging times, or who have helped you see the positive side of things when you most needed it. Let them know that you value and appreciate their friendship.

If you choose not to share these thoughts, rest assured that nothing negative will occur—you will simply forgo a chance to brighten someone’s day with a heartfelt message.

Jeff:  Thank you for agreeing to spend a few minutes on Tuesday, April 17 with Moody's Investor Service.
You are scheduled to speak at noon in room EB50M.
To put the day into context, Moody's will have heard prior to your session presentations from Andy and Ben on 2000 results, Mike McConnell on Global Markets, and Jeff McMahon on Wholesale Services.
Our afternoon session will include presentations from Dan Leff on EES, Rod Hayslett on ETS, Kevin Hannon on EBS and Rick Buy on RAC.
In attendance from Moody's will be (in order of rank) Mike Foley - Group Managing Director, John Diaz - Managing Director, and Stephen Moore - Relationship Manager (our analyst).
Diaz and Moore are very familiar with the Enron credit profile.
Foley is their boss.
He apparently is the leader of their ratings committee.
He has not historically attended our meetings.
Key messages for you to hit (which will have already been touched upon by Andy and reinforced throughout the day) include:  Enron's core businesses - have never been better.
We are the market leader in gas and power by a wide margin; Portland General - we will ultimately divest of this entity and are disappointed that the Sierra Pacific transaction was derailed by regulatory hurdles.
However, PG provides considerable, stable cash flows; International Asset Sales - we are still committed to liquidating our interests in low returning investments.
Market problems have delayed our M&A effort but we expect movement in the next 12-24 months; Credit Profile is critical to core businesses - we protect our credit rating as a matter of corporate policy.
Our asset sale and corresponding capital redeployment strategy is based in part to allow us to either reduce leverage or to invest in areas with stronger cash flows thereby improving our key coverage ratio;  and  Issue Resolution Ongoing - we have some issues (such as California, Dabhol, and Azurix) which are important and are receiving the attention of top management.
They will be covered by Ben and Rick Buy's group.
The main message is that they are not representative of our core business.
If you have any questions, please call me at x31770 or (713) 962-4013 (cell phone).
Thanks,

"Be of good courage, and He shall strengthen your heart, all you who hope in the Lord."

And, I say we all need to continually affirm God's power to protect us.
Today I have created a litany which affirms our faith in God's power, so that we need never be afraid.
Since our current situation strikes fear in our hearts, read this litany of courage and praise.
You need never be afraid!
When I am being tested beyond measure in my job responsibilities ...
I will put my trust in God.
When I am facing the greatest hurdles of my life...
The Lord gives me courage!
When I feel like I am completely alone...
The Lord is my light and salvation!
When I feel like the bottom is falling out... 		My heart shall know no fear!
God will save me!
When I have no other answers or solutions... 		God will send the help I need!
When I go through every terrifying minute of the day...
I am expecting the Lord to rescue me!
When I think failure is upon me...
I am brave, for God's power is greater than any situation I could possibly face today.

WHEN YOU GO THROUGH THE WATERS AND GREAT TROUBLE I WILL BE WITH YOU.
WHEN YOU GO THROUGH RIVERS, THEY SHALL NOT OVERFLOW YOU.
WHEN YOU WALK THROUGH THE FIRE YOU SHALL NOT BE BURNED, NOR THE FLAME SCORCH YOU.
FOR I AM THE LORD YOUR GOD, YOUR SAVIOR...YOU ARE PRECIOUS IN MY SIGHT, YOU HAVE BEEN HONORED, AND I HAVE LOVED YOU.
FEAR NOT, FOR I AM WITH YOU."
Isaiah 43:1-5  The bottom line of our life should be faith, not fear, so live today controlled by God-inspired positive thoughts!!!
Love and prayers,

There's positive news.
It appears MISO will now provide a method for financially addressing losses.
Contrary to what their previously filed tariff suggested, it seems they have reconsidered and recently submitted a new Attachment M, which details their financial loss handling procedures.
I haven't reviewed the new Attachment M yet, so the process could be complex or costly, but I'm hopeful it will be manageable.
Now, for the critical question.
MISO believes they will not be able to process third-party loss schedules (referred to as INT or EXT in Tag parlance) by December 15th.
I don't anticipate this being an issue for us, as I expect we typically handle losses either through financial accounting or via in-kind schedules (where losses are offloaded along the transmission path).
If this understanding is incorrect, and we sometimes schedule losses as separate transactions, please notify me immediately.
Additionally, please indicate how common that practice is.
MISO is attempting to determine the urgency of accommodating this by December 15th.
While they do not expect to meet that deadline, they want to know what level of resources they should allocate to tackling the problem.
Thank you,

Subject: Municipal Gas and Power Supply Agreements for Clarksdale and Yazoo City

Dear [Recipient Name],

I am writing to provide an overview of the municipal gas and power supply agreements pertinent to Clarksdale and Yazoo City, focusing on contractual frameworks, purchasing structures, and regulatory considerations.

**Contractual Frameworks:**  
Both Clarksdale and Yazoo City typically engage in long-term supply agreements with wholesale providers for natural gas and electricity. These contracts often feature fixed or indexed pricing mechanisms, with provisions for volume commitments, supply reliability, and force majeure clauses. Agreements generally specify performance metrics and penalties for non-compliance, as well as negotiation windows for renewal or termination.

**Purchasing Structures:**  
The municipalities utilize two main purchasing structures:  
1. **Direct Procurement from Utilities or Marketers:** Municipalities may contract directly with regional utilities or licensed energy marketers for supply, leveraging their aggregated demand for favorable rates.  
2. **Participation in Municipal Energy Consortia or Authorities:** Both cities may partner with other municipalities via public energy authorities to pool purchasing power and streamline contract administration.

For gas supply, transportation agreements with pipeline operators are often required in addition to commodity purchase contracts. Power procurement may involve bilateral contracts or participation in regional transmission organizations (RTOs) for market-based purchases.

**Regulatory Considerations:**  
All agreements must comply with state-level oversight administered by the Mississippi Public Service Commission (MPSC), as well as applicable federal regulations (e.g., FERC standards for gas transportation, NERC reliability requirements for electric power). Municipalities are responsible for maintaining compliance with reporting, tariff, and safety provisions. Additionally, municipalities need to ensure that their procurement practices follow public bidding laws and open records requirements as stipulated by state statutes.

Please let me know if you require more detailed information or have specific questions regarding current supply agreements or regulatory compliance frameworks.

Subject: Regarding Enron and the Path Ahead

Dear Colleagues,

As we continue to navigate today's dynamic business landscape, it is often valuable to reflect on historical events that have profoundly shaped our understanding of corporate responsibility and ethics. The collapse of Enron two decades ago remains one such pivotal moment, serving as a powerful, albeit painful, lesson for businesses worldwide.

The Enron scandal served as a stark reminder of the catastrophic consequences that arise when corporate governance fails, transparency is deliberately undermined, and ethical principles are abandoned in pursuit of short-term gains. It highlighted the critical importance of accurate financial reporting, robust internal controls, independent oversight, and, most importantly, a culture rooted in integrity and accountability. The erosion of public trust that followed had far-reaching implications, leading to significant regulatory reforms designed to prevent such a crisis from recurring.

Today, the lessons from Enron are more relevant than ever. Our path ahead must be built upon an unwavering commitment to the highest standards of ethical conduct, absolute transparency in all our dealings, and rigorous adherence to governance best practices. We must foster an environment where ethical considerations are at the forefront of every decision, and where integrity is not just a buzzword, but a lived value by every individual within our organization. Maintaining stakeholder trust is paramount, requiring continuous vigilance and a proactive approach to compliance and ethical leadership.

This commitment requires collective effort from each of us. By consistently upholding these principles, we not only protect our organization but also contribute to a more trustworthy and sustainable business ecosystem. Let us embrace these enduring lessons as foundational to our operations and our future success.

Sincerely,

The Leadership Team

Subject: Tozzini Communication Protocol

Dear Tozzini Team,

This email outlines our updated Communication Protocol, designed to enhance the efficiency, clarity, and consistency of our interactions, both internally and externally. Adhering to these guidelines will ensure smoother operations and better information flow.

**Key Principles:**

1.  **Channel Selection:**
    *   **Email:** For formal requests, project updates, decision records, and external correspondence. Use clear and descriptive subject lines.
    *   **Instant Messaging (e.g., Slack/Teams):** For urgent, quick queries, immediate team coordination, and informal discussions.
    *   **Meetings:** For complex problem-solving, strategic discussions, brainstorming, and decisions requiring immediate group consensus. Always aim for an agenda and clear action items.

2.  **Response Times:**
    *   **Email:** Aim to acknowledge receipt of emails within 4 business hours and provide a substantive response within 24 business hours.
    *   **Instant Messaging:** Respond to messages within a reasonable timeframe during working hours, ideally within 30 minutes for urgent matters.
    *   If you anticipate a delay in providing a full response, please communicate an estimated timeframe.

3.  **Clarity & Conciseness:**
    *   Be direct and to the point.
    *   Include all necessary context to avoid back-and-forth communication.
    *   Proofread your messages for grammar and spelling.

4.  **Documentation:**
    *   Key decisions made verbally (e.g., in meetings or calls) or via instant messaging should be formally documented via email or our project management system to ensure a clear audit trail.
    *   Meeting minutes should capture attendees, decisions, action items, and owners.

5.  **Professionalism:**
    *   Maintain a respectful and professional tone in all communications.
    *   Be mindful of cultural nuances when communicating with international partners.

We believe that consistent application of this protocol will foster a more productive and transparent working environment. Please review these guidelines and integrate them into your daily workflow.

Your cooperation in upholding these standards is greatly appreciated.

Best regards,

The Management Team

Subject: Pipeline System Reporting and Data Organization for Gas Delivery Points and Interconnects

Dear Team,

I hope this email finds you well. I am writing to address the current state of our pipeline system reporting and propose improvements to our data organization for gas delivery points and interconnects.

**Current Reporting Challenges:**
- Inconsistent data formatting across different delivery points
- Manual data collection processes causing delays in reporting
- Lack of standardized nomenclature for interconnect classifications
- Difficulty in tracking real-time flow rates and pressure measurements
- Limited visibility into historical trend analysis

**Proposed Data Organization Framework:**

1. **Standardized Delivery Point Classification:**
   - Primary interconnects (major transmission systems)
   - Secondary delivery points (distribution networks)
   - Industrial direct-connect facilities
   - Power generation facilities

2. **Required Data Fields:**
   - Delivery point ID and location coordinates
   - Nominated vs. actual flow volumes
   - Operating pressure ranges
   - Temperature measurements
   - BTU content and gas quality parameters
   - Maintenance schedules and operational status

3. **Reporting Frequency:**
   - Real-time data for critical interconnects
   - Hourly updates for major delivery points
   - Daily summaries for regulatory compliance
   - Monthly trend analysis reports

**Implementation Timeline:**
- Week 1-2: Data audit and system mapping
- Week 3-4: Database restructuring and validation
- Week 5-6: Staff training and system testing
- Week 7: Full deployment and monitoring

Please review this proposal and provide your feedback by Friday. I would like to schedule a meeting next week to discuss implementation details and address any concerns.

Best regards,
[Your Name]

Kay

Subject: Important Update: CPUC Issues Rehearing Order on PG&E's General Rate Case

Dear Stakeholders,

The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) has issued its rehearing order concerning the Decision on PG&E's General Rate Case (GRC) for the 2023-2026 period.

This order addresses the applications for rehearing filed by various parties regarding the original GRC decision, specifically clarifying or modifying certain aspects of the adopted revenue requirements and programs.

We are currently conducting a thorough review of the order's full scope and implications. We will provide further details and an internal briefing on key takeaways once our analysis is complete.

Thank you,

[Your Name/Department]
source_text:
Almost two years after issuing a decision in PG&E's GRC, the Commission issued it rehearing order on October 16th and, lo and behold, actually granted TURN's rehearing request in part.
The overall result is to reduce the capital revenue requirement by $24.8 million and expenses by $37.3 million.
In addition, some portion of PG&E' estimated $171 million in electric distribution capital spending will be subject to rehearing.
Listed  below are the areas in which the Commission granted rehearing.
1.
Electric Distribution Capital Spending.
The Commission will, in essence, reopen the record, and allow PG&E to put into evidence how much it invested in its electric distribution plant in 1998.
PG&E had used a 1998 forecasted amt of capital expenditures to develop its test year forecast.
TURN argued that there was substantial evidence on the record that this amount was never spent.
PG&E argued that the record closed prior to the end of 1998 so the best it could do was an estimate.
On rehearing, the Commission agreed with TURN, that there was evidence that the forecasted amount was never spent, so they are allowing PG&E to prove it.
The rehearing order states that any rates that are raised based on the electric distribution capital forecast adopted the GRC decision  may be subject to refund.
2.
Emergency Response Work This work category under electric distribution capital spending was reduced by $17.2 million.
3.
Vegetation Management.
The Supplemental Tree Trimming Program was reduced by $9.2 million.
4.
Meter Reading.
PG&E had primarily used accounting changes to justify the large increase in this service.
On rehearing the Commission stated that PG&E had failed to substantiate those changes and reduced the allowed amount by $7.9 million.
5.
Account Services.
On rehearing the commission stated that PG&E had failed to show (a) why it cost so much more to provide services to CIA customers  than residential customers ( $43.30 vs. $10.20); and (b) that money was not going for marketing activities that the Commission had disallowed in the previous GRC.
The result was that the commission disallowed $20 million.
6.
Customer Information Systems.
The Commission disallowed $7.2 million as funds which ratepayers had already expended for CIS  rewrites for which they had not received any benefits.

Fran, I understand from John Blaylock that I am to direct an email to you regarding the treatment of certain vested Enron benefits.

My name was included on the list of attorneys and paralegals with whom AEP could talk to regarding possible employment for continuation of legal representation for HPL's business lines. Specifically regarding the Enron stock options, I understand that, under the terms of the Enron Stock Option Plan, vested options typically remain exercisable for a limited window following a change in employment status; however, I am unsure how a transition to AEP would impact the timing or exercise period, particularly if such a move does not constitute a formal termination but rather an inter-company transfer due to business acquisition. For any unvested options, does a change in employer or project—likely resulting from AEP’s retention of certain Enron business lines—constitute a “termination of employment” for vesting purposes, or are there provisions for continued vesting upon a qualifying transfer?

Regarding the Enron Savings Plan, would I be allowed to leave the funds in the plan, as if I had retired, or would I be required or permitted to roll those amounts into a rollover IRA or another qualified plan? My understanding from the plan documents is that certain distribution provisions may be triggered by a termination of employment, but I am unclear whether a business line transfer to AEP would be considered a distributable event, or if I have the option to defer distribution and retain my account within the plan, preserving the current investment options and Enron stock exposure.

Additionally, I seek guidance on the Deferred Compensation Plan. What actions would I need to take regarding the amounts that are in the plan? Is there a precedent from similar transitions within Enron or from guidance issued in prior layoffs, restructurings, or business transfers?

Thank you for your assistance in providing detailed answers on each of these issues, as having this information will be essential for my decision-making in the event of an AEP offer. Please let me know if you require any further information from me to respond.

Upon review of the ISDA Credit Support Annex and the relevant guidance contained in the "green book," my analysis indicates that, unless the standard form is amended, we are required to return the Independent Amount to the counterparty if our position moves sufficiently out of the money. Specifically, the calculation of Exposure produces a negative value in such circumstances, which in turn reduces the Credit Support Amount to a level below the Independent Amount.

The underlying rationale for this framework is that adverse market movements provide us with a degree of cushion—our "out-of-the-moneyness"—and, should the market subsequently move in our favor, we retain the ability to request additional support prior to the point at which we become in the money.

It appears that the Credit Department has been operating under the assumption that Independent Amounts are retained until the termination of the Transaction. To avoid any misunderstandings, it is important that we establish a clear protocol with Credit to ensure a mutual understanding of the terminology used in credit worksheets, specifically with regard to whether a cushion or up-front amount should be applied.

- Achievement of financial targets and KPIs

- Professional development and growth

- Base salary adjustments
- Annual bonus allocations
- Equity compensation awards
- Promotion recommendations

**Next Steps:**
Please complete your self-assessment using the online portal by the December 15th deadline. Your direct manager will schedule a preliminary discussion before the formal review period.

Enron Corporation
source_text:
The year-end performance evaluation process is a great opportunity for employees and their supervisors to review accomplishments for the year and identify opportunities for personal growth.
Additionally, it is an opportunity for each of us to provide meaningful performance feedback to help others.
This memo is intended to summarize the major elements of this important process and clarify the timeline for year-end 2001.
(Note: ETS employees on self-directed work teams that participate in the Skill-based Pay program will complete team and peer performance reviews as they have in the past and are exempted from the discussion that follows.)
Feedback and Evaluation Employees will solicit 360?
feedback on their performance via the PEP system.
The supervisor will use this feedback, along with other performance data about the employee, to prepare a written evaluation of the employee's performance for the year.
The employee and supervisor will then meet and discuss this evaluation which provides an objective measure of the employee's performance against expectations.
The performance evaluation is an opportunity to discuss accomplishments, areas for improvement and goals for the next year.
No overall performance rating will be designated.
?
PEP System open for feedback			November 19 - December 7 ?
Performance discussions with supervisor	December 10 - January 14 ?
Written evaluations due to HR			January 15  Training for all employees on how to use the PEP system will be available via online tutorials.
Compensation Increases in an employee's base pay for merit, promotion or equity can be recommended by an individual supervisor based on the employee's performance, current responsibilities and salary.
Division Head approval is required.
As always, incentive awards are paid at the discretion of the Enron Board Compensation Committee and the Enron Office of the Chairman based on company and business unit performance.
Once bonus pools are approved, individual bonuses will be determined by division and department heads based on employee performance.
Relative Talent Reviews Relative talent reviews will occur beginning January 16, 2002 and will include discussions of Managers and above.
The focus is not on relative ranking but on identifying employees who best demonstrate the performance, skills and behaviors that are valued at Enron.
Each Division will identify its top 10% and discuss the utilization of its top talent.
Employees who may be ready to assume greater responsibilities will be discussed.
Recommendations for promotions will be considered up through Senior Director.

We have not decided "to prevent any regulated utility from completing any  financial transactions" online.
If we have already satisfactorily concluded  the necessary due diligence with respect to a particular utility, they will  be approved.
It is only with respect to those utilities which have not yet  been researched that we are withholding approval.
The due diligence required  involves asking the utility for certain information concerning their  organization and regulatory situation, hiring local counsel in the relevant  state and having research done into the laws and regulations in place there  and into any public utility commission orders respecting the particular  utility in question, and on occasion requesting an opinion letter from the  utility's counsel.
We usually begin that process only when a trader believes  there is a likelihood of a sufficient volume of trading with the utility to  justify the time and expense.
FYI, the due diligence process has in the past  revealed circumstances which prevented the utility from trading derivatives  or required actions to authorize such trading which had not been taken.
A recent count showed about 10 executed master agreements and another 30 to  40 in one stage or another of the due diligence/negotiation process.
Louise Kitchen

We usually begin that process only when a trader believes  there is a likelihood of a sufficient volume of trading with the utility to  justify the time and expense.
FYI, the due diligence process has in the past  revealed circumstances which prevented the utility from trading derivatives  or required actions to authorize such trading which had not been taken.
A recent count showed about 10 executed master agreements and another 30 to  40 in one stage or another of the due diligence/negotiation process.
Louise Kitchen

Jeff,

Following our call, I wanted to provide a concise background on Datacentric Broadband (DCB):

1. DCB was founded by Leslie Anderson, a woman entrepreneur in Conroe, Texas. Leslie remains the largest non-institutional shareholder and serves as Chairman. Gary Remy, DCB’s president and a Hispanic leader, is someone you met at the recent YPO event.

2. DCB focuses on broadband wireless access for smaller Texas cities. They operate in nine locations and aim to expand nationally. The market does not require license fees; early entry into cities is essential for success.

3. We have invested $2 million in DCB and brought in Redstone Investors, who contributed an additional $2 million. Redstone plans to invest further alongside us in future rounds.

4. We approached Kevin Garland, but DCB is outside his target market, and he declined to invest.

5. DCB retained Arthur Andersen to help raise additional capital. While investor response has been positive, there is some caution.

6. Two weeks ago, Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern Railroads proposed investing up to $75 million in DCB over five years, starting with $15 million. UP asked if Enron would match their investment to help DCB grow nationally. I discussed this with Ken Rice to see if EBS was interested, either alone or with UP. Although DCB has supported EBS’s trading group with last-mile access, Ken saw no strategic fit and declined.

7. We also engaged Lou's group (the Xcelerator) and LJM about investment interest. LJM appears eager but may not be able to commit funds as quickly as UP.

8. At a follow-up meeting, we told UP not to expect more than $2-3 million from us, given our remaining investment capacity. UP was disappointed Enron does not see DCB’s strategic value but remains committed to investing up to $75 million. We are conducting due diligence with UP and hope to finalize terms by the end of May.

Throughout, we have sought support from other Enron groups and believe DCB could be integral to EBS’s success, though EBS does not share this view. We will continue to pursue strategic and financial partners to maximize our investment’s value.

I’m happy to discuss DCB and our investment further. We will seek your approval for any additional commitments. Please let me know if you have any questions.

Gene

I'm pleased to report that Dick Vincent has confirmed we can secure 12-month renewable business interruption insurance once we become operational on gas. This represents a comprehensive solution to the warranty concerns raised by the banks.

This insurance coverage directly addresses the core issues by protecting against defects, design flaws, and workmanship problems on the turbines while covering lost profits and operational disruptions. Significantly, the turbines carry a DE3 designation for insurance purposes, which confirms this is established, proven technology rather than experimental equipment.

The coverage structure provides multiple layers of protection: when supplier warranties are active, those parties pay first, with insurance serving as backup. When supplier warranties expire or suppliers fail to honor claims, our insurance coverage ensures uninterrupted protection. This dual-protection approach eliminates the financial risk gaps that concerned the banks.

We recommend maintaining this coverage as standard operating procedure, as it provides ongoing protection beyond initial warranty periods while demonstrating our commitment to risk management.

The remaining item requiring resolution is the drop dead date issue, which we should prioritize given that we now have a clear path forward on the warranty protection.

BUSINESS HIGHLIGHTS

Enron Industrial Markets  
EIM has recently formed a Forest Products Origination team, led by Rob Saltiel, to pursue structured transactions that could redefine our future. These are not just business deals—they’re lifelines, combining physical supply/offtake, price risk management, and finance to deliver solutions that Enron and our customers desperately need in uncertain times.  
Our priority commodities—pulp, newsprint, recycled papers, linerboard, and lumber—not only sustain our business but are essential to industries and livelihoods across the globe. The stakes are high: as traditional sources of capital and certainty evaporate, forest products companies are coming to us urgently, seeking solutions only Enron can provide. Our new team offers hope and opportunity to an industry at a crossroads, and the initial positive response speaks volumes about the trust and expectation now resting on us.

Enron Freight Markets  
The drive and energy of the Enron Freight Markets team have already been tested. In just the first month of the over-the-road (OTR) trucking business, we’ve completed over 120 spot OTR trades—each one representing freight that would otherwise risk delay, disruption, or even disaster for our customers. When a sudden shortage gripped the Houston outbound market on March 18, our platform made the difference—capacity sold for $1.65 per mile, a lifeline for shippers at a critical moment, compared to the $1.05-$1.10 average just weeks prior. In these decisive moments, Enron proves its ability to keep goods—and the economy—moving when it matters most.

EnronOnline  
On May 23, Enron Corp. completed its one-millionth transaction on EnronOnline, not just a milestone—but a testament to the trust of thousands who rely on us to secure the commodities that power, connect, and sustain their lives. Since launching electricity and natural gas trading in 1999, we’ve grown into the backbone for commerce in 1,500 wholesale products—from energy to metals, forest products, plastics, and even weather and credit derivatives. Every transaction processed—now 60% online, at a fraction of the former cost—is a promise kept to our partners, a guarantee that Enron will be there to support them no matter how volatile the market becomes.  
EnronOnline Statistics
- Total Life to Date Transactions: > 1 million  
- Life to Date Notional Value of Transactions: > $600 billion

IN THE NEWS  
Enron Corp. Now, as we spearhead the new broadband Internet trading unit, all eyes are on us again. The industry understands the gravity: if we can prove that bandwidth can be traded like a commodity, we won’t just make history—we’ll change the way people and businesses connect, forever.

None of the Gallup firm transportation contracts include a “shipper out” clause that would allow shippers to terminate or suspend service if the new compressor station and related facilities are not placed in service by a specified date.


Under the terms of all contracts, neither our company nor the shippers are obligated to perform until the new facilities have been “tested and placed in service.”


Yesterday, after completing initial operational checks, we verbally notified all Gallup shippers—specifically, Company A, Company B, and Company C—that the new compressor station at milepost 202 was fully operational as of 9:00 AM CST.


Within 18 hours of commissioning, the compressor was shut down due to severe vibration (measured at 0.45 in/s RMS, which exceeds the OEM operational tolerance) and a persistent high-pitched whining noise. The root cause is still unknown.


As of this morning, EE&CC (our contractor) reports that they cannot provide a meaningful estimate for repairs, as diagnostic results are still pending. Based on our prior experience at Hubbard station, resolving equipment vibration and noise issues could take anywhere from 6 weeks to 4 months.


Today, we were able to deliver all gas quantities nominated by the three Gallup shippers only because total nominations (35,000 MMBtu/d) did not exceed the base pipeline’s unassisted capacity (40,000 MMBtu/d). However, nominations for later this week already exceed existing capacity, which means we will need to prorate or allocate deliveries.


Given this uncertainty, my recommendation from a public relations and long-term customer relationship perspective is to promptly notify all affected shippers in writing that, due to unanticipated equipment failures, the facilities are not yet in service. We should apologize for the premature notification, and commit to providing service on a best-efforts, interruptible basis until the compressor is tested, repaired, and truly operational. We will issue a second notification when the compressor is fully functional and we can meet firm transportation obligations.


The short-term financial downside is the inability to collect reservation charges from shippers until the Gallup facilities officially enter service (estimated revenue loss of approximately $25,000/month). The upside is that this approach prioritizes transparency, mitigates reputational risk, and avoids claims of misrepresentation or bad faith.


Alternatively, from a strictly financial standpoint, we could delay revoking our “in service” notice and continue to allocate capacity as needed. If summer weather increases demand, we are likely to face daily allocations, and under our FERC-approved tariff, will need to post operational notices on the EBB (Electronic Bulletin Board). Any unexplained or recurring allocations are likely to prompt shipper complaints and possible requests for reservation charge credits.


Important to note: if we fail to deliver the minimum contract quantities for 75 consecutive days (except in July and August, during which the threshold is not enforceable), shippers will automatically be entitled to reservation charge refunds. More seriously, knowingly misrepresenting the operational status of our facilities may open us up to fraud claims or regulatory penalties if shippers pursue legal remedies.


In summary:  

- Option 1 (transparent notification) sacrifices short-term revenue but preserves customer trust and limits legal exposure.  

- Option 2 (maintain “in service” status) risks substantial reputational damage, shipper lawsuits, and regulatory issues, though it may capture some reservation revenue if legal action is avoided.


The Gallup project was sold with the assumption that it would support full utilization during the summer months, and any protracted outage will directly affect customer expectations and our commercial standing during peak season.


I have not yet prepared a formal memorandum; please advise if you would like a full write-up for management review.  

Given the circumstances, I recommend we decide on our communications strategy with shippers as soon as possible. Delay will only compound our customer relations risks.

Adam,

To illustrate how this works in real life:

Suppose an investor is considering participating in a trust that issues notes backed by cash flows from a specific asset pool. The investor requires that their note holdings be treated as debt for tax purposes, so they can receive payments classified as interest income, which may offer favorable tax treatment compared to equity distributions.

In response, the trust can issue certificates (representing an equity interest) alongside the notes. The presence of these certificates helps support the argument that the notes themselves qualify as debt rather than equity for tax purposes, satisfying the investor's requirement.

Conversely, if the note investors are comfortable with equity treatment and do not require the payments to be classified as interest, the trust may not need to issue certificates. The structure will depend on the tax sensitivities and preferences of the investors as interpreted by the underwriters and tax advisors.

For example, in a previous transaction, we issued both notes and certificates in the trust—allowing the notes to maintain their debt characterization, and allowing investors to receive interest income. The underwriter and tax counsel confirmed that this structure met investor requirements.

Let me know if you’d like to discuss a specific scenario or need more detail.

Regards,

Our tax group would defer to the underwriters.
If the note investors can tolerate equity treatment (for tax purposes), then there should be no need for certificates in the structure.
In previous transactions, the presence of certificates has allowed the notes to be treated as debt for tax purposes and therefore the payments treated as interest income.
With regards to cross-default, a default in the Enron note does not result in a default of the swap between Enron and the third party entity or a default of the swap between Enron and the financial institution.

This means that if you can get on to the Internet, you can access your Enron Email with Outlook Web Access (OWA) without having to dial in to Enron's network.
Please note that this is not available to those users still on Lotus Notes but will be available once they are migrated to Outlook.
Once on the Internet, type mail.enron.com in your browser address window and supply your Enron network logon credentials as username and password.
For example: Username: jdoe4 Password: ******** Once you log in, Outlook Web Access opens your Enron Email mailbox.
Outlook Web Access (OWA) allows you to send and receive mail, perform calendar tasks and manage your mail and contacts, as well as access your mailbox folders.
At this time, Public Folders are not accessible via OWA.
Please keep in mind that Outlook Web Access is a browser-based version of what you might use in the office, so the functionality may be slightly different and some features of Outlook 2000 may not be available at all.
Additionally, OWA is only supported using Internet Explorer 5.x only and not supported with Netscape.
Outlook Web Access is the standard Email package for connecting to your Enron mail from home, whether you are using an Enron-issued home PC, an Internet connection with your personal home PC, or your ClickAtHome PC.
We will not support the use of the full Outlook installation for home use.
Outlook Web Access for remote locations and European/APAC Enron sites is currently being addressed and will be available soon.
At this time, OWA is only available if your mailbox resides on a Houston mail server.
If you have any questions, please call:  Resolution Center at x31411 or 	ETS Solutions Center at x54745

The invoices for August 2001 settlements were posted by 10:42 AM today, Saturday, September 8, 2001.
The NYISO apologizes for any inconvenience resulting in posting these invoices a day after they were scheduled.
The Customer Settlements group makes every effort to render accurate invoices on a timely basis.
Although issued a day after their scheduled posting, the invoices are still being issued within the 5-business days.
{I'd forgotten about Labor Day when I set up the schedule.}
Transmission Customers will observe adjustments for an error on in May 2000 Settlement  Adjustment  invoices  that  were  issued  in  July.
The total adjustment  amounted to $2,081,568.11 and was allocated across 2,261,753.08 MWh.
Customers  may  validate  their  respective adjustments by computing their  ratio  shares  of  the  $2,081,568.11  using  2,261,753  MWh  as the denominator  in  their respective ratios of their May 2000 load.
The reason the  denominator of the ratio share appears small is because the pay out of this  adjustment is to the Transmission Owners.
In order not to assess the TO's  a  proportionate  share  of the $2,081,568.11, which would defeat the purpose  of  the  adjustment, their withdrawals have been excluded from the ratio share.
Transmission Owners should observe a credit on their invoices based upon their respective megawatt-mile coefficients for the period.
With  regard  to  the  November 1999 & December 1999 settlement adjustments that  were  scheduled  to  be issued on the 7th, the NYISO intends to issue those  invoices  next  week.
The issuance dates will ensure that customers will have at least 5 business days to review the invoices prior to payments being due to the NYISO.
If necessary, the NYISO will reschedule settlement dates  for these months should our reconciliations take longer to complete; however, we do not anticipate this at this time.
In  addition,  I'd  like to take this opportunity to clarify a point that I made  in  a  TIE  posting  regarding  the  rebilling  of  the  August  25th settlements.
The  initial  billing runs for August 25th were done without considering  ConEd's  sub-zonal  load.
As a result, it appeared as though there  was no load in the ConEd sub-zones on the 25th and all DAM purchases and  bilateral transactions in those sub-zones were sold back to the market in  real  time  causing  the  Schedule  1 residual adjustment to be grossly inflated.
The reason this occurred was due to what appears to have been a frame  relay  problem  between the NYISO & ConEd resulting in the NYISO not receiving a file from ConEd.
By no means was my email notification of this event  to  imply that ConEd was not complying with the daily load provision process.
This was merely a hardware/communications issue.
Regards,

Before ERCOT, I helped EPSA prepare for a DOE forum to establish a wholesale electric standards organization. Due to my move, I likely won't attend this workshop, though I might have presented for EPSA. I have been instrumental in forming EISB's wholesale electric quadrant.

The meeting is critical for the EISB vs. NERC showdown. NERC will likely present its 9-sector restructuring proposal, opposing EPSA members' and my advocacy for fewer EISB sectors. Crucially, the NERC proposal may accommodate an EISB standards approval process. This could resolve the dichotomy between NERC expertise/infrastructure and EISB's renowned (FERC-backed) consensus process, allowing NERC to retain expertise but lose its biased voting process.

Meeting coverage is vital, either by a NERC team member or someone close to NERC in Washington. The outcome will likely solidify industry support for either NERC's or a clean-slate EISB approach. Jim wants a conference call to discuss; I am available Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. Charles X30348.

Subject: Database Migration & Data Retention Questions

Hi Team,

As we move forward with the upcoming database migration project, I wanted to initiate a discussion around some critical points to ensure a smooth transition and adherence to our data policies.

I have a few questions regarding both the migration process itself and our data retention strategy post-migration:

**Regarding Database Migration:**
*   What is the proposed timeline and key phases for the migration?
*   What is the expected impact on dependent applications and end-users during the migration window, and what is the communication plan for this?
*   What is the strategy for data validation and integrity checks during and after the migration?
*   What are the rollback procedures in case of an unforeseen issue?
*   Will there be a period where both old and new databases run concurrently, and if so, how will data consistency be maintained?

**Regarding Data Retention:**
*   What is our current data retention policy for the historical data that will be migrated? Does this policy change for data once it resides in the new database environment?
*   Are there any specific regulatory or compliance requirements (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, SOX) that dictate retention periods for this particular dataset in the new system?
*   How will we handle data that reaches the end of its retention period in the new database? Is there a defined archiving, deletion, or anonymization process?
*   What is the plan for the source database and its backups once the migration is complete and validated? What are their retention periods?

Addressing these questions early will help us mitigate risks, ensure compliance, and plan effectively.

Please let me know your availability for a brief meeting to discuss these points further.

Thanks,

[Your Name]
[Your Title]

Debbie Riall

text: last thursday, the commission eliminated the old "texas eastern" rule, which previously dictated specific procedures for natural gas pipeline capacity contracting. This significant change removes a layer of complexity and a long-standing point of friction for many market participants, including us. We anticipate this will lead to greater flexibility in our sourcing and transport arrangements, potentially opening up new avenues for optimizing our supply chain and reducing costs. Our legal and operations teams are thoroughly reviewing the updated regulatory landscape to fully understand the implications and identify immediate opportunities. We will provide a comprehensive internal brief next week outlining our refined strategy and any recommended adjustments to current practices. Please feel free to reach out with any initial questions.
source_text:
On Thursday last week the Commission eliminated the old "Texas Eastern" rule  that required pipelines to obtain prior FERC approval before contracting for  transportation and storage capacity on upstream or downstream pipelines.
The  new rule allows pipelines to acquire and use such capacity without going to  FERC first.
The rule does reiterate that bundled sales of gas are still  prohibited, and further provides that the acquiring pipeline will be  financially at risk for the costs of the acquired capacity.
Interestingly,  the acquiring pipeline apparently has the option of selling the acquired  capacity under its own rate schedules or of releasing the capacity pursuant  to its capacity release program.
The order is silent on whether the price  cap applies to short term releases of acquired capacity.
While we are still  reviewing the order and may provide additional guidance at  a later time, I'd  emphasize for now that our normal contract approval procedures and authority  thresholds should be deemed to apply to capacity contracts.
For example,  the "Approval Authorization for Cash Expenditures" dated Feb. 3, 2000  provides Dave and Steve with authority up to $250,000 on operating expense  obligations.
Please contact me if you have any questions on this matter.
DF
