This rapid expansion was possible only because of FERC's accelerated permitting, a move with profound implications for communities and families depending on reliable warmth and power this winter.  
Lorna          PG&E Gas Transmission Puts New Line in Service, Files 2003 Expansion

PG&E Gas Transmission Northwest (GTN) has already started critical gas deliveries through a key 21-mile section of its 2002 mainline expansion, outpacing expectations and bringing vital energy relief to the region. 

The new 21-mile pipeline, which became operational last Friday, increases the company’s capacity to deliver natural gas to Western communities by 42,000 Dth/d—a full year ahead of schedule and just in time for the 2001 winter heating season, when families need it most. 

"We applaud the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission for the extraordinary effort to speed up permitting, making it possible for us to serve families and businesses before the winter chill sets in," said Thomas B. King, president and COO of PG&E National Energy Group’s West Region, which includes GTN. "With energy demand peaking and communities bracing for cold, these steps are making a real difference." 

The new 42-inch pipe runs through Spokane County, WA, and Kootenai County, ID, marking the first installation of a crucial third pipeline—known as the C line—alongside GTN’s main route. Its swift completion gives much-needed certainty to thousands of households and businesses preparing for potentially harsh winter months. 

But the stakes are even higher: GTN’s 2002 Expansion Project also adds powerful, new 19,500 hp compressor units at five mainline stations, boosting overall capacity by another 220,000 Dth/d. These essential upgrades will help supply energy to major power plants being developed by Newport Northwest LLC and Calpine, projects that will bring light and heat to millions in the Pacific Northwest—homes, schools, and hospitals counting on stable electricity in the coming years. 

Newport Northwest is building a 1,300 MW generating plant near Wallula, WA, along with two more of similar size in the region, while Calpine has multiple power plants under development in both the Pacific Northwest and California. These projects will mean the difference between blackouts and security for families when temperatures drop.

Thinking ahead to even greater needs, GTN has already filed with FERC to build a second expansion for service starting in fall 2003. This additional 2003 project will bring another 143,000 Dth/d on line just in time for another winter, plus 20,000 Dth/d of additional winter-only service. 

The 2003 expansion calls for 53 more miles of critical new pipeline and another high-powered compressor—each step a shield against future shortages that could threaten public safety and economic security.

Taken together, these back-to-back expansions will push GTN’s capacity to nearly 3,100,000 Dth/d—a leap that can help prevent the energy shortages and price spikes that have disrupted families and communities in the past. "The 2002 and 2003 expansion projects are not just about numbers or engineering," King said. "They’re about making sure there’s enough gas to fuel the power plants that keep our homes warm and our lights on across California and the Pacific Northwest." 

Meanwhile, GTN is eyeing another bold move: a pipeline lateral from Spokane to the busy I-5 corridor near Seattle and Tacoma, a region where energy insecurity has real human consequences. Talks with potential customers have been ongoing since an open season in June 2001, and initial studies show the project is ready when the market, and the people who depend on it, are. 

"There is real, urgent interest in this project," King emphasized. "We’ve made major progress on feasibility, and we’re ready to go when our communities need us."

The GTN pipeline system’s history reveals what’s at stake. When it began service on Dec. 2, 1961, its 580,000 Dth/d capacity was a lifeline for a sparsely populated West. Over four decades, as demand exploded and threats of shortages loomed, GTN adapted—first with a second, then a third line. Today, its 1,356-mile pipeline traverses harsh terrain from the Idaho/British Columbia border through the heart of Washington and Oregon, ending at the gateway to California.

At every turn, the expansion of GTN’s system has meant greater safety, stability, and peace of mind for the millions who rely on natural gas every day—especially when the days grow short and cold, and the assurances of energy security take on life-and-death meaning.

Subject: Differences Between British and American English

Dear [Recipient Name],

I wanted to highlight some fascinating distinctions between British and American English, two major dialects that, despite their shared roots, have evolved with unique characteristics. While mutually intelligible, these differences can be quite noticeable.

One of the most immediate points of divergence is **vocabulary**. Many everyday items have different names. For example, what British English calls a "lift," American English refers to as an "elevator." Similarly, "chips" in the UK are "fries" in the US, a "biscuit" becomes a "cookie," and a "lorry" is a "truck." Other common examples include "boot/trunk" (of a car), "bonnet/hood," and "trousers/pants."

**Spelling** also offers clear distinctions. British English often retains older spellings, particularly those derived from French, which American English has generally simplified. Common examples include words ending in "-our" (colour, favour) versus "-or" (color, favor), and "-re" (centre, theatre) versus "-er" (center, theater). Words ending in "-ise" (realise, organise) in the UK frequently become "-ize" (realize, organize) in the US.

**Grammatical** variations, though often subtle, are also present. British English often uses the present perfect tense where American English might use the simple past (e.g., "I've just eaten" vs. "I just ate"). The verb "to have" is another example, with "have got" being more common in British English ("I've got a car") compared to the simpler "I have a car" in American English. Collective nouns are also treated differently: British English often considers them plural ("The team *are* playing well"), while American English typically treats them as singular ("The team *is* playing well").

Finally, **pronunciation** is a significant differentiator, though harder to convey in text. The "r" sound is often pronounced in American English (rhotic), but usually dropped in British English unless followed by a vowel (non-rhotic). Vowel sounds and intonation patterns also vary considerably, contributing to the distinct accents.

These differences, far from being errors, highlight the dynamic evolution of language across different regions and add richness to the English language. Despite these variations, speakers of both dialects generally understand each other without significant difficulty.

Best regards,

[Your Name]

Hey guys!
It's been a long time, I hope everyone is doing well especially since I know it's the end of bid week and it's Friday.
Just thought you might enjoy some of the things I've learned since I've been here about the English language.
Hopefully they'll give you chuckle.
There are differences between British English and American English that I've noticed so far:  Pants are "trousers."
Don't make the mistake that I did:   I wrote, "Black Pants, Brown Pants, Khaki Pants" on my dry cleaning inventory to turn into the dry cleaners and got reminded that I was turning in "trousers" not pants with a smirk.
"Pants" are what they call underwear here.
Also, I almost fell over in my chair laughing one day when a girl in my group said "PANTS!"
and hit her hand on the desk when her computer crashed.
Apparentely, it's the equivalent of saying "CRAP!"
I went to the grocery store around the block and I was looking to buy some orange juice.
On the outside of some of the containers it said "with extra bits" and some said "no bits."
I was puzzled until my boyfriend explained that it was "with pulp" or "without pulp."
When I go to restaurants I have to remember that fries are "chips" on the menu (even at McDonalds), and chips are called "crisps."
If you want to get a baked potato it's called a "jacket potato."
And if you want mashed potatoes, just say "mash."
One of the favorite dishes at the pubs (not bars) here is "bangers and mash" which translates to sausages links and mashed potatoes.
Here are a few more of the oddities:  You don't stand in line here, you "stand in queue."
Trash cans are "bins."
It's amusing to hear someone say, "I don't want it- just bin it."
Country boy or redneck types are called "wide boys" or "barrow boys."
When you spell things out loud, Z is pronounced "zed" and H is pronounced "haitch."
Cross walks are "zebra crossings"  since they are signified by white stripes on the road.
(Pronounced ZEB-bra, not ZEE-bra) Panty hose are called "tights" regardless of their thickness.
Good  is pronounced "goote."
Yards no matter how big or small are all called gardens regardless of the fact that they're not growing any vegetables in them.
Well, I guess that's about it for the English lesson for today.
I hope you are all doing great and I'll try to do better about sending updates.
Cheers!

Hertzberg and Keeley announced that they are filing a petition with FERC to rehear the April 26th decision regarding price caps.
After going to D.C. and meeting with several FERC members, they decided to file for a rehearing.
Their filing asks that the order should be in affect around the clock instead of just during Stage 1, that the actual costs be tied closer to the pricing of the product, and anyone that exceeding the cost-based pricing system have a 100% penalty.
Hertzberg and Keeley had a press conference today at 1:30 PST.
Questions included the impact of today's ruling and how it would affect Plan B, Hertzberg replied he was not sure.
He also indicated that they support the Feinstein bill and if the lawsuit or the rehearing efforts do not work, legislation is the last chance for price caps.
Hertzberg also indicated that he was getting to the point where CA "may just say no to prices that are too high" (via buyer cartel).

Hi everyone, here are my notes from today's call! Just like on Monday, my priority was to get these notes to you promptly, so I haven't taken extra time to re-organize them by subject just yet. Hope they're still clear!

Enron's business has been grouped into three buckets: Core, Non-core, and Under Review.

Core: Wholesale energy business in North America and Europe, retail energy, pipelines
Non-core: Broadband, water, and international assets (i.e. EGAS). Enron has about $8Bn invested in these assets, but unfortunately, they haven't performed well, yielding 'dismal' returns. Enron will be exiting these businesses and plans to wind them down in an orderly fashion. We're moving forward with an aggressive divestiture program for these assets.

Under Review: EGM, EIM. These businesses are currently being closely examined to see if they have a good chance of long-term viability. We're also carefully studying the required resource levels. After this review, Enron will categorize different portions of these businesses as either core or non-core, based on the analysis.

It's good news that approximately $800MM of asset sales are already under contract and expected to close in the fourth quarter! These include a gas LDC in Brazil, EcoElectrica, and our Indian E&P assets. Enron is actively pursuing an additional private equity infusion of $500MM-1Bn. Given the current environment, McMahon mentioned that raising equity in the public markets would be 'inefficient'. Short-term liquidity is provided by the $3Bn of credit drawn upon a few weeks ago, the $1Bn of new debt, and the $1.5Bn equity infusion from Dynegy. Longer-term, the proceeds from the sale of PGE will provide liquidity. Asset sales over the next year will be used to pay down debt.

McMahon also went over the major off-balance-sheet vehicles. Marlin, for example, was set up to hold Azurix assets. It was initially capitalized with $950MM of 144a debt and $125MM of equity (raised from Enron and institutional investors). The debt is supported by the equity and by Azurix' assets. Enron is obligated to cover any deficit when the debt becomes due on 3/17/03 (this is called the 'Enron topup' obligation). The 3/17/03 date is accelerated in the event that Enron is rated below-investment-grade by any one of the three major agencies. The primary asset of Marlin is Wessex Water. Good news: as long as Wessex is worth at least $2.6Bn, no Enron topup will be required. If we consider a 25% 'haircut' to its present book value, Enron would then need to provide $650MM when the debt is retired. This $650MM would hit Enron cash, income, and equity balances.

Osprey contains energy-related assets and 'other assets'. It was initially capitalized with $2.4Bn of 144a debt and $220MM in equity (ENE and institutionals). Similar to Marlin, this entity is also an asset-backed structure with an Enron topup guarantee. The debt is supported by a) the assets; b) $1Bn of convertible preferred ENE (convertible into 50MM shares of ENE common); and c) additional ENE common as needed for topup. Assuming the same 25% hypothetical 'haircut' to its current book value, Enron would need to provide approximately $600MM in topup funds – which would impact ENE's cash, income, and equity. The debt needs to be retired by 9/17/02, and it has the same 'cut-to-junk' early trigger provision as Marlin.

Tony, I thought there would be a case that stated that if an interstate  pipeline posts the criteria under which it will evaluate capacity bids, it  must stick to those criteria and not award the capacity to a bidder on some  other basis.
It seems a simple enough extension of the principle that  capacity must be awarded on a nondiscriminatory basis.
However, I did not  find any case that stands for that exact proposition.
As you may be aware,  the Commission made Natural Gas Pipeline Company of America (NGPL) come up  with a way to ensure that it awarded capacity one a nondiscriminatory  basis...because NGPL was found to have been giving preferential treatment to  its shippers.
NGPL's solution was to come up with an auction process, and  there is a whole line of cases if you're interested.
The underlying  presumption is that if you set up a system under which all capacity is  awarded and stick with that system, there is no way you could be acting  discriminatorily.
But of course the Commission never comes out and says this  even though it should be obvious.
Probably the best we can do is extrapolate from 1) the tariff and 2) the NGA  (doesn't it also say we have to provide service on a not unduly discrim.
basis?).
Also, in your memo I'd give an example; i.e., if we notify shippers  of our auction process and set a deadline for bidding, but then award the  capacity to Sempra (assuming Sempra requested capacity after the posting), we  will have unduly discriminated against all the other shippers who had to  participate in the auction process.
Maybe in future postings on Enrononline we should include a statement to the  effect that the capacity posted will not be awarded except thru the  Enrononline process.
Now for some trivia.
Remember we were discussing with Shelley whether we  could post a different method (other than that prescribed in the tariff) for  determining best bid?
In my Westlaw search I ran across the relevant case.
In Northwest Pipeline, 85 FERC P 61,335, the Commission stated:  "The  Commission has previously given pipelines the leeway, in open season  provisions, to either include in their tariff a single non-discriminatory bid  evaluation methodology, or provide themselves the flexibility of choosing  different non-discriminatory bid evaulation methods for different  transactions, provided that the pipeline posts the bid evaluation methodology  before the bidding process begins."
The only problem is I am not sure we  have that "flexibility" since the tariff does not expressly allow us to post  a different method.
Maybe next time we do a tariff cleanup we could add some  language allowing us to do so.
I have to move on to my next project but if you want me to comment on what  you write I'd be happy to.

Subject: Earnings Expectations and Special Charges - 2001 and 2002 Outlook

Dear Team,

I wanted to provide you with an update on our earnings expectations and anticipated special charges for the upcoming fiscal periods.

**2001 Earnings Outlook:**
We are projecting earnings per share in the range of $2.15 - $2.25 for fiscal year 2001, which reflects the challenging market conditions we have experienced in the latter half of the year. This represents a revision from our previous guidance of $2.40 - $2.50 per share.

**2002 Earnings Forecast:**
For fiscal year 2002, we anticipate earnings per share of $2.60 - $2.80, assuming market stabilization and successful implementation of our restructuring initiatives.

**Special Charges:**
We expect to record the following special charges:

*2001:*
- Restructuring costs: $85 million pre-tax
- Asset impairment charges: $45 million pre-tax
- Facility consolidation expenses: $25 million pre-tax

*2002:*
- Additional restructuring completion costs: $30 million pre-tax
- Technology upgrade expenses: $20 million pre-tax

These charges reflect our commitment to positioning the company for improved operational efficiency and long-term growth. We will provide more detailed guidance during our upcoming earnings call scheduled for next week.

Please let me know if you have any questions regarding these projections.

Best regards,
[Name]
Chief Financial Officer
source_text:
Following up on our discussions at the September 17 Board meeting, Wednesday we communicated our earnings expectations for the 3rd & 4th Quarters, 2001, 2002, and 2003 to investment analysts.
This communication was as we discussed at the Board meeting, but in addition we chose to communicate the special charges that we will be incurring in the 3rd & 4th Quarters.
Since it was relatively close to our earnings announcement [planned for October 18], we decided that it would be best to disclose the special charges now rather than waiting.
Attached is an updated summary of the special charges.
They have changed somewhat since the Board as we raised  the total charge for the third quarter by $.04 per share to $.14.
Specifically, in the Restructuring and Asset Impairment category the charge increased by $.03 primarily due to the required write off of  manufacturing facilities in Brazil.
We also added $.01 related to Loss on Early Extinguishment of Debt as our open market repurchase activity resulted in the acquisition of a higher mix of longer-term issues, thus increasing the cost somewhat.
The reaction by analysts to these charges is that they are truly one time items.
Therefore, they will be normalized out and analysts will view the 3rd Quarter results as being $.66 per share.
Even though we lowered expectations for the fourth quarter and 2002, overall the communication was accepted positively.
In particular, investors appreciated our willingness and need to spend more in 2002 to maximize the sales of the five new products we expect to launch in 2001 and 2002.
We closed Thursday at just under $79, down about $3.75 from our close on Tuesday.
This was a much better result than we anticipated.
If you have any questions about this, please let me know.
Charlie  10/4/2001                             - Q3 & 2001 Yr Normalized Items.doc

Rod:  There are 2 open issues on Dresdner Bank:  1.
Netting - they are saying that operationally they cannot net across  product lines.
Are you okay with this?
2.
Calculation Agent - they want to be the Calculation Agent.
Since we have  no CSA with them, this means that they would be doing all of the calculations  required under each transaction that we enter into with them.
Specifically, the CA does the following:  - calculates the Floating Price and the Floating Amount, Fixed Amount or Cash  Settlement Amount payable - gives notice of Settlement and Payment Dates - determines whether a Market Disruption Event has occurred  Also, my notes indicate that we agreed to increase the Guaranty  cap to  $25,000,000 from $15,000,000.
Is that okay with you?
They had initially  requested no cap.
On Reliant Energy Services, Inc., you were going to think about the following  credit issues:  1.
Specified Transaction - they want to include physical energy deals.
You  were going to think about this and whether we needed a cap.
They wanted to  amend the definition of Specified Indebtedness to deal with this, but I think  you and I felt taht it should be dealt with in the definition of Specified  Transaction.
2.
Cross Default threshold - is 3% of equity okay?
3.
On Credit Event Upon Merger, they want to define "materially weaker" as  either (1) being below investment grade by either S&P or Moody's or (2) being  failed to be rated by either S&P or Moody's.
4.
On setoff, they did not have the "affiliate" language.
5.
In the CSA, they want the collateral that is posted to secure both  financial deals and physical gas and power deals entered into between ENA and  Reliant Energy Services, Inc.  6.
In the collateral threshold, they have proposed a matrix of S&P and  Moody's ratings, with the threshold amount being the lower of the 2 ratings.
AA-/Aa3 and above  $20,000,000 A-/A3 to A+/A1   $15,000,000 BBB/Baa2 to BBB+/Baa1  $10,000,000  BBB-/Baa3  $5,000,000   Also, they have defined MAC  to be going below BBB- by S&P or below Baa3 by  Moody's or a failure to be rated by either S&P or Moody's.
7.
In the LC provisions, they have different cure periods for each of the  types of Letter of Credit Defaults that can occur.
Here is a summary of the  events and the time periods for transferring substitute colateral:  - If issuer's credit rating is downgraded - 1 business Day after written  demand by the Secured Party - if issuer fails to comply with its obligations under the LC or disaffirms  or rejects the LC - 1 Business day after the pledgor receives notice of  dishonor - if LC fails to be in full force and effect or issuer declares bankruptcy -  3 Business Days after written demand by Secured Party  In our form, we require substitute collateral to be posted within 2 Business  Days of the occurrence of the above events, except for a downgrade where the  time period is 5 Business Days      On SG Interests, you were going to talk to them about certain credit issues.
Please let me know when you can where you stand on the above.
Thanks.
Carol

Please see the attachment for a specific definition of ELIGIBLE SWAP  PARTICIPANT and the TRADE OPTION EXEMPTION.
From a legal perspective and to avoid scrutiny and regulation by the  Commodity Futures Trading Commission, ENA must always comply with the Trade  Option Exemption when entering into options (as buyer or seller) with a third  party.
Some of ENA's trading parties cannot satisfy this exemption from  regulation because they are not a producer/merchant handling the underlying  commodity (such as banks, hedge funds, etc) even though they may be entering  into the transaction for business purposes.
If that situation occurs, ENA  MUST ALWAYS BE THE OFFEREE OF THE OPTION (as buyer or seller) and ENA cannot  solicit the party to enter into the transaction.
If ENA's trading partner fails to satisfy the Trade Option Exemption, our  confirmation will EXPLICITLY state that ENA was offered the option to buy or  sell by the counterparty.
Please call me if you have any questions.
Thanks.
Sara [ENA legal]

The Ministry of Defense of the Russian Federation contracted with Mammoet to recover the Kursk.

Frans van Seumeren initiated, negotiated and concluded the Kursk contract with the Russian Government for the operation to salvage the Russian nuclear submarine Kursk.
He will describe the technical and operational aspects of the recovery.

I am writing to articulate the profound and lasting financial hardship I have experienced, and continue to endure, directly as a consequence of Enron's fraudulent actions and subsequent collapse. Even after all these years, the ripple effects on my life are undeniable and deeply painful.

When Enron imploded, it wasn't just a news story; it was a cataclysm that obliterated a significant portion of my financial security. Like so many others, my investments, retirement savings, and future plans were irrevocably tied to what we believed was a reputable and stable company. The sudden and complete destruction of that foundation left me, and my family, in a precarious position from which we have struggled immensely to recover.

The initial shock of losing hard-earned savings quickly gave way to a persistent battle against financial instability. Retirement plans were derailed, necessitating a complete re-evaluation of my working life. Sacrifices had to be made in every aspect of our budget, impacting everything from educational opportunities for my children to basic household expenses. The sense of betrayal, coupled with the immense stress of navigating a future that had been stolen, has taken an emotional and psychological toll that is difficult to quantify.

Today, I still find myself navigating a landscape shaped by that corporate malfeasance. The years that have passed have not erased the deficit, nor the constant anxiety it instills. This is not merely a historical event; it is my lived reality, a constant reminder of how corporate greed can devastate individual lives and futures with long-lasting and often unaddressed consequences.

Thank you for allowing me to share this perspective on the enduring impact of Enron's actions.

Sincerely,

[Your Name]

Elizabeth, Jeff forwarded me your questions about capacity options.
I've  answered them to the extent they involve legal/regulatory issues.
If you  need anything further please don't hesitate to call.
?
Can a new shipper who enters into an FTS-1 contract with zero MDQ in order  to purchase a shipper call option or sell a transporter put option be  allowed, prior to the exercise date, to transfer the underlying option rights  by permanently releasing this contract?
YES.
?
Will we be required to report these contracts with zero MDQ on the Index  of Customers and/or the Transactional Report?
YES.
?
Can the releasing shipper permanently release a portion of his existing MDQ  and choose to keep or transfer the option rights?
YES.
The shipper could  even release all of its MDQ (reducing it to zero) and keep its option rights.
?
How is it determined whether a contract with an option amendment is within  the min/max tariff rate or needs to be filed as a negotiated rate?
The  option fee is converted to a per-Dth, per day rate and added to the transport  rate.
If the total exceeds the maximum tariff rate, it's "negotiated".
Otherwise, our position is that it's not negotiated.
We are not 100%  positive that FERC will agree with us on this issue.

Subject: Bammel Facility Operational Guidelines and Capacity Management Concerns for AEP Lease

Dear Team,

I hope this message finds you well. I am writing to address several operational guidelines and capacity management concerns associated with the AEP lease at the Bammel Facility.

Please ensure that all facility operations adhere strictly to the established protocols detailed in our Operations Manual, with particular attention to safety procedures, reporting requirements, and routine maintenance schedules. Consistent compliance is critical to maintaining both operational integrity and lease obligations.

Additionally, there are growing concerns regarding capacity management as utilization rates approach contractually defined limits. I urge all relevant teams to closely monitor current injection and withdrawal volumes and provide weekly status updates. Should any discrepancies or potential overages be identified, please report them immediately so we can coordinate with AEP and adapt scheduling as needed.

Let’s work together to proactively manage these issues and maintain transparent communication with all stakeholders.

Thank you for your attention to these matters. Please feel free to reach out if you have any questions or require clarification on any points.

Best regards,  
[Your Name]  
[Your Position]

source_text:
I was wondering if the Bammel lease to AEP contains any operating parameters to protect the integrity of the facility.
The question arises from the fact that Bammel  had about 24 BCF of remaining capacity when Enron turned the facility over to AEP.
We believe their plan is to max inject in June which would reduce the remaining capacity to around 12 BCF.
It could become a challenge to keep injections under the remaining 12 BCF level during the reaming 4-5 months of the injection cycle.
Enron always operated the facility with the understanding that a Gas In Place volume greater than 117.5 BCF could create a high enough pressure to jeopardize the safety of the wellhead casings and some of the abandoned wells.
We would not want the Texas RRC to question the safety of the Bammel facility.
From the other end of the perspective if the Gas In Place is taken below 65 BCF their is a high probability of watering out the outer wells and the facility itself.

Subject: Valuation of Grant's Non-Firm Hydropower Asset

Dear [Recipient Name],

I am writing to discuss the upcoming valuation of Grant's non-firm hydropower asset. Given the unique characteristics of this type of generation, a thorough and specialized approach will be essential to accurately determine its fair market value.

The "non-firm" nature implies variability in output, which introduces complexities beyond typical firm power assets. Key considerations for this valuation will include:

*   **Resource Variability:** The dependency on hydrological conditions and the resulting fluctuating generation profiles.
*   **Market Price Exposure:** The susceptibility to wholesale electricity price volatility, especially in the absence of firm power purchase agreements.
*   **Operational and Maintenance Costs:** Ongoing expenses, including regulatory compliance and environmental stewardship.
*   **Grid Interconnection and Capacity:** The specifics of its connection to the grid and any associated transmission costs or limitations.
*   **Regulatory and Market Frameworks:** The specific market rules and incentives applicable to non-firm renewable generation in its operating region.

Our valuation methodology will likely incorporate detailed discounted cash flow (DCF) analysis, potentially involving stochastic modeling for hydrology and power prices to account for uncertainty. We will also consider comparable asset transactions if available.

To proceed, I propose we schedule a meeting to outline the scope, discuss data requirements, and present our proposed valuation framework in more detail. Please let me know your availability over the next few days.

We will require access to historical generation data, operational and maintenance costs, any existing energy sales agreements, and information regarding its environmental permits and regulatory standing.

Thank you for your attention to this important matter.

Best regards,

[Your Name]
source_text:
Jeff -  Here is a first cut at valuing the Grant's non firm power from Priest Rapid and Wanapum hydro projects.
We assumed a term from 1/1/02 - 10/31/05.
We assumed a price curve of Mid Columbia (thus we have included no transmission costs).
Enron also assumed a payment to Grant due on 1/1/02.
The last important assumption is how to value any "negative firm" power (defined as a situation in which Grant's non firm power in one month is lower than the critical year monthly figure).
In this situation we carried over the negative water volume to the next month and net is against positive volumes.
The total value to nonfirm power using the above assumptions is approximately $68 million.
If Grant is interested in a $15 million lump sum then Enron would assume a 22% stake in the non firm hydro stream.
Briefly I would like to explain our methodology for valuing the hydro.
We took the hydro raw data from Grant on the two projects and also used the critical year assumption.
In addition we created a curve to reflect the impact of water to power prices (ie the greater the water volume the lower the power prices).
We then ran a number of simulations to create a distribution that describes the range of output values.
Jeff I look forward to speaking with you about this in more detail.
You can reach me at 503-464-3810.
As I mentioned I will be out this week from Tuesday to Friday.
Stewart Rosman

Dear Mr. Lay,

Through all of the trials and negativity that are occurring, I would like to send these words of encouragement from my family and me. I have been with this company for 21 years. We have had many wonderful and exciting years with Enron.

When I first met my wife six years ago, she had only 90% hearing in both ears. Through the blessing of our insurance plan, she now has 98% hearing capacity in both ears. The many years of working for Enron have provided me with a steady job and a good income, while allowing me to work on my Ph.D. The friendships and relationships I have been blessed with through working for this company will be treasured for the rest of my life.

Yes, I am one of the employees who has lost their retirement, but through all of this, my wife and I would like to send our vote of confidence to you and the board to be able to find ways to make the impossible happen.

This company was built to be one of the world’s largest companies through your efforts over the past several years. Yes, there have been experiments in going beyond normal paradigms, and there have been mistakes made. But through the mistakes is where the true gift of learning and stability comes.

The ultimate challenge in life is not how much money one can make or that first ultimate achievement. The ultimate challenge in life is, "CAN I DO IT AGAIN?" We believe that Enron can learn from what is happening and eventually become bigger, better, and stronger than it has ever been. And we believe that you, Ken Lay, CAN DO IT AGAIN, bigger and better than it was done before.

I remember once reading about Donald Trump going into bankruptcy. He summoned the best advisors in the world to bring together the most educated and smartest financial people to find a solution, and he moved on to build bigger and better investments. "HE DID IT AGAIN."

Per: I am reliably informed that Mark Taylor dispatched a critical email in December, addressed to Bob Shultz at EOL, specifically delineating the pressing hedge fund issues and commodity trading advisor (CTA) concerns that have arisen in conjunction with the exponential growth and inherent complexities of online trading platforms. My understanding is that both you and Caroline were direct recipients of this crucial communication, which highlighted potential vulnerabilities and compliance challenges.

It appears the severe and highly publicized hedge fund crises that roiled financial markets last year – exemplified by significant defaults, liquidity crunches, and instances of extreme leverage in derivatives markets, such as those seen with total return swaps and complex options structures – have inevitably intensified the regulatory bodies' focus on the funds' extensive and often opaque derivatives activity. This heightened scrutiny is aimed at mitigating systemic risk and improving market transparency.

EOL, given its operational model and desire to maintain competitive agility, has a clear and well-documented stance against being subjected to any additional layers of regulatory oversight, particularly those that might mandate extensive reporting requirements, capital adequacy provisions, or compliance audits typically imposed on directly regulated financial entities. The potential for increased compliance costs, significant operational burden, and the disclosure of proprietary information is seen as a substantial deterrent to innovation and efficiency.

Despite its apparent importance and direct relevance to EOL's strategic positioning, I have not yet had the opportunity to review the content of this email firsthand. However, recognizing the gravity of the implications for our operations and regulatory exposure, I intend to make it a priority to discuss this subject thoroughly with Mark as soon as he returns to the office, seeking a full understanding of the email's contents and any proposed action plan to address these escalating concerns.

• You'll enjoy fill participation advantages

Beth Perlman, currently CIO for EA Systems, will work closely with Mark Pickering on a number of key projects for Enron Net Works. Additionally, Beth plans to explore various commercial opportunities within Enron.
Steve Hotte, currently CIO for EGS, will replace Beth in her current role.

We are currently interviewing individuals to serve as CIO for EGS, as well as an individual to serve as head of our Enterprise Framework group. We will keep you posted on the progress of these searches.
Please join us in congratulating all of these individuals on their new responsibilities.

Distributed Power: The Next Big Investment?
With today's electricity demand expanding beyond the reach of available  supply, and nationwide electric deregulation efforts providing inconsistent  results, distributed power just may be the next big thing, according to Bear  Stearns analyst Robert Winters.
With technology-laden, electricity-hungry companies popping up every time you  turn around, and blackouts and brownouts occurring more frequently as large  power grids are becoming less reliable, the analyst points towards  distributed energy services as a possible solution, and maybe the "next big  investment opportunity for the coming decade."
In Winters' 250 page report,  "Distributed Energy Services-The World's Power and Transportation Industries:  Set for a Revolution-Part 2," he examines technologies and companies within  the distributed energy services sector that might be able to take advantage  of the current situation.
"Thanks to major technological advances and energy deregulation, a wave of  new investment in the power industry has just begun.
We believe that this  coming era in the power industry could resemble the wave of investments which  flooded into the telecommunications industry following the breakup of AT&T in  the early 1980's," said Winters.
"Companies and municipalities need to find ways to ensure the availability of  high quality, reliable power," added Winters.
According to his research,  microturbines are the best positioned of the "new" technologies that would be  able to have an immediate impact on electric generation.
He based his recommendation on the fact that microturbines are small, quiet,  efficient and very versatile.
"They can be used as a main power source, a  back-up power source or as an alternative when there is a spike in  traditional energy prices," the analyst said.
"Microturbines can also be used  in remote locations, including developing countries, that do not have access  to electricity."
Another attractive feature of microturbines is their fuel  requirements.
The units often use natural gas, but can also use several other  fuels as well.
In the study, the analyst also examined fuel cells, flywheel technology, and  existing reciprocating engines technologies such as diesel engines and  Stirling engines, which he noted are enjoying a comeback.
In addition to the report, Winters initiated coverage on two distributed  energy companies.
He labeled Active Power, a company that is pioneering  flywheel technology, as a "buy" and Capstone Turbine Corp., a leading  manufacturer of microturbines, as "attractive."
The companies are in addition  to two fuel cell companies he currently follows.
Ballard Power is currently a  buy, and Plug Power is rated neutral.

The Dow Jones report is compiled of data sent from many different  counterparties.
The lovely people at Dow Jones painstakingly analyze the data  to ensure its accuracy.
Averaged together, these prices become the Dow Jones  daily index price.
And that's the long and short of it.
The process, as you've guessed by now, is a little more complicated than  that.
For one thing, Dow Jones looks at each counterparty's sales to reach an  average of all the prices.
It would be redundant for each counterparty to  ALSO report their purchases from each other.
Therefore, when calculating the  Dow Jones data, we only include purchases from counterparties who ARE NOT  participants in the Dow Jones survey.

November 16, 2001 Dear Enron Users: Last night, a powerful storm in central Texas has caused a temporary disruption to the assigned telephone numbers for CYNET's Inbound Fax-2-Email Service.
Our local network provider has informed us they are cognizant of the problem and are actively working to re-establish this connection.
Even though CYNET has backup systems for its Fax-2-Email services, the challenge is that we cannot simultaneously assign an identical user telephone number to two separate facilities.
Our technical team is developing future solutions, including the provision of individual backup numbers to mitigate the impact of such outages.
We genuinely apologize for any disruption this may cause to you and your users and anticipate restoring the service as swiftly as possible.
Sincerely,

While CYNET maintains back-up facilities for its Fax-2-Email services the problem we are faced with is that we can not place the same user telephone number within two different facilities at the same time.

Thank you for your understanding and flexibility.

Best regards,
Sara

Notes for this Week's Report:  * UK Gas's Average EOL and Non-EOL deals per day have decreased since their peak of 140 EOL and 96 Non-EOL transactions in March.
They ended April with an average of 118 EOL deals per day and finished with 75 transactions in May.
Non-EOL recorded 82 deals per day in May.
* UK Power's average deals per day finished April with 13 EOL deals and reported 13 daily transactions in May as well, down from March's 59 EOL deals.
Non-EOL's average transactions have increased dramatically, however, ending April with 180 deals per day and closing May with 255 deals.
While transactions are down, EOL and Non-EOL volume is up during this same period.
* US West Power's average transactions per day continued to increase to 182 EOL deals in May, up from 80 deals per day in January, a 128% increase.
Non-EOL daily transactions has increase from 206 to 223 deals during the same period.
* Southwest Power's EOL transactions per day has continued to increase in 2001.
On average, they ended January with 26 EOL trades and finished May with 65 daily transactions, a 150% increase.
Non-EOL transactions have increased during this same period as well, up from 68 in January to 74 in May.
* WTI Physical's total monthly transactions closed at 117 EOL deals in May.
This monthly total in May is up from April's total of 60 EOL deals, a 95% increase.
* IPE Financial Gasoil's total monthly transactions via EOL shows 195 deals, up dramatically from it's 81 deals in March and 74 in April.
During this same period, Non-EOL trading is also up from 234 total deals in March to 578 in May.
* US Weather's total monthly transactions has increased in May with 64 deals via EOL, up from 23  in April and 15 in March.
Non-EOL deal totals are up slightly to 41 deals in May from 23 in April, but still report below average for 2001.

Everyone, J.C. asked me to send the following message: Yesterday, the Houston federal court (U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Texas) entered an Order consolidating all cases "involving or related to the financial difficulties of Enron" before one Judge, Lee Rosenthal (who was the Judge to whom the earliest-filed case had been assigned and who conducted the hearing last Friday).

To give you a sense of what this means in practice, let me share a quick story from Friday’s hearing. The courtroom was packed, with lawyers representing every possible side jostling for seats. As Judge Rosenthal entered, the room came to a hush—everyone aware that this decision would shape the course of the many Enron-related lawsuits. After hearing arguments from the various parties, the Judge recounted a time early in her career when a similar set of overlapping cases resulted in a tangle of conflicting deadlines and confusion for everyone involved. Determined not to let history repeat itself, she declared, “We will have order here—justice demands no less.” The atmosphere instantly changed: those in the courtroom, while still fierce adversaries, knew a consolidated approach would keep things manageable and fair for all.

The consolidation order grants a motion that we and other defense counsel had made. It means that all cases in the Houston federal court should proceed in a more orderly, coordinated fashion.

A technical detail - the Order provides for three separate consolidated proceedings before Judge Rosenthal: (i) the federal securities cases; (ii) the derivative cases (at least those that have been filed in federal court); and (iii) the employee benefit plan cases.

Finally, the Order allows parties ten days to file objections to consolidation. While someone may well file an objection, we cannot think of any meritorious grounds for an objection.

As always, if you have any questions, please don't hesitate to call us.

Terri Richardson  
Assistant to J.C. Nickens

This e-mail and any attached files may be confidential and subject to attorney/client privilege. If you received it in error, please immediately notify the sender by return e-mail or by calling (713)654-7600.

Subject: Bankruptcy Impact on Collateral Provisions

Dear [Recipient Name/Team],

This email aims to discuss the significant impact that bankruptcy proceedings can have on existing collateral provisions, which is crucial for effective risk management and contractual drafting.

Upon the filing of a bankruptcy petition (Chapter 7, 11, or 13), the **Automatic Stay** immediately comes into effect. This powerful injunction halts most collection efforts, including any attempts by secured creditors to enforce security interests, repossess collateral, or initiate foreclosure. While the collateral provisions themselves generally remain legally valid, their enforcement is temporarily suspended, requiring creditors to seek relief from the stay from the bankruptcy court.

Key areas of impact on collateral provisions include:

*   **Adequate Protection:** Secured creditors are entitled to "adequate protection" if their collateral is being used by the debtor or if its value is diminishing post-petition. This protection might take the form of periodic cash payments, replacement liens, or administrative expense priority, but it does not guarantee immediate access to the collateral or full recovery.
*   **Use of Cash Collateral:** A debtor in possession (Chapter 11) or trustee often needs to use "cash collateral" (e.g., cash, bank accounts, proceeds of inventory) to operate. Such use typically requires creditor consent or court approval, again with adequate protection for the secured party.
*   **Valuation Disputes:** The value of the collateral is often a contested issue in bankruptcy. The court's valuation can determine the extent of a creditor's secured claim, potentially bifurcating a claim into secured and unsecured portions if the collateral value is less than the outstanding debt.
*   **Avoidance Actions:** Trustees or debtors in possession possess powers to avoid certain pre-petition transfers, such as preferential transfers or fraudulent conveyances. While well-drafted and properly perfected security interests are generally robust, issues like late perfection or transfers made while the debtor was insolvent can render a lien vulnerable.
*   **Ipso Facto Clauses:** Clauses in loan agreements that automatically trigger default or modify a party's rights solely due to a bankruptcy filing are generally unenforceable under the Bankruptcy Code. The debtor's obligations must be considered in light of the Code's provisions, not just the contract terms.
*   **Reorganization Plans (Chapter 11):** A debtor can propose a plan that "cramdowns" secured creditors, modifying their contractual rights even if they don't agree, provided the plan is fair and equitable (e.g., preserving the lien and providing deferred cash payments equal to the present value of the secured claim).

While robust collateral provisions are foundational, their enforceability and the path to recovery are significantly altered within a bankruptcy context. Thorough documentation, proper perfection, and a clear understanding of the Bankruptcy Code are paramount to protecting a creditor's position.

Please let me know if you would like to discuss any of these points in more detail or review specific scenarios.

Sincerely,

[Your Name/Department]

MARKET NOTICE February 4, 2002  The California Independent System Operator (ISO) is announcing the Aggregated Distributed Generation Pilot Project (ADGPP).
The participation of Generating Units in the ISO's markets is currently limited to units with a rated capacity of 1 MW or greater.
The ADGPP is intended to demonstrate the feasibility of allowing physically separated small units (less than 1 MW) to be aggregated as a means of reducing barriers to entry into the ISO markets—a pivotal opportunity for those whose potential has been overlooked for too long.
ADGPP is currently intended to operate as follows:   *	Generation units with a rated capacity of less than 1 MW may participate *	Generators will be aggregated through an Aggregated Distributed Unit (ADU), which will have an aggregated or total rated capacity greater than or equal to 1 MW but no more than 10 MW *	The total capacity for all units participating in this Pilot Project is limited to 50 MWs *	ADUs must contain generators that are in the same Demand Zone which are not on opposite sides of constrained transmission elements *	Each ADU must be scheduled in the ISO Energy or Supplemental Energy Market *	Near real-time operational data will be required from ADU *	Prospective participants can propose unique methods and processes for delivering the near real time operational data *	Generators will be considered SC Metered Entities, therefore they must have Local Regulatory Authority approved interval metering *	Settlement will occur through submitting aggregated Settlement Quality Meter Data (SQMD) by the SC representing the ADU  As noted above, units participating in the ADGPP will be allowed to participate in the ISO Energy and Supplemental Energy Markets only and will not be allowed to participate in the ISO's Ancillary Services markets.
The increased participation in the ISO Energy and Supplemental Energy markets will provide greater market depth and will increase competition by expanding the pool of generation available within the ISO Control Area—an essential step toward a more resilient and inclusive grid at a time when California faces unprecedented energy challenges.
The ADGPP is intended only to accommodate units less than 1 MW and is not intended to facilitate "portfolio bidding" from Generating Units 1 MW or larger.
The ADGPP is also intended to improve the ISO's visibility of generating resources within the ISO Control Area by demonstrating the functionality of various basic-level operational data reporting processes which may be proposed by the prospective participants.
These operational data reporting processes should demonstrate the capability of delivering operational data for the ADU to the ISO near real time and be economical from the small Generator perspective—a crucial lifeline for those with limited resources whose innovation could reshape our collective energy future.
The uniqueness of the operational data reporting processes proposed will be one factor in selection of participants in the program.
Thus, the project will also ensure that the participation of these resources in the ISO's markets will occur without compromising system reliability—honoring our shared responsibility to keep the lights on for millions of Californians, and uplifting the voices and ingenuity of the many over the few.

Pipe Expansions Planned for Rockies Region  With several pipeline companies well into addressing the pipeline capacity shortages that persist as natural gas production grows throughout the Rocky Mountain region, Kinder Morgan Interstate Gas Transmission LLC (KMIGT) announced two major projects Wednesday, and several other companies detailed expansions planned or in the works during the closing session at the 13th Annual Rocky Mountain Natural Gas Strategy Conference.
Headlining the news was KMIGT's plans to use existing rights-of-way to build the Advantage Pipeline, which would fill the same needs as the Colorado Interstate Gas pipe, moving from the Cheyenne Hub to the Mid-Continent.
An open season is scheduled on the proposed pipe this fall.
Dave Scharf, business development director for KMIGT, said the 24-inch pipe, which would move gas primarily from the Powder River Basin, would have a capacity of 330 MMcf/d, delivering to interconnects on its way to the Kansas City markets.
"It would have a smaller size, with about 40% less content," Scharf said, but it would be expandable to 450 MMcf/d, with access to liquid Mid-Continent pipes, local distribution centers and end-use markets.
A smaller pipeline, NECO -- a 12-inch pipe, about 95 miles long -- would serve the northeastern Colorado market.
Although small, Scharf emphasized that it would reduce some of the bottlenecks now evident in moving gas in that part of the state, and would also allow backhauls to Cheyenne.
An open season on this line is also scheduled this fall, Scharf said.

A outside source suggested to me that I, as a stockholder, should E-Mail my senator and request the government's help to bail out Enron. This recommendation comes at a critical time when decisive action could save thousands of jobs and protect countless investors who trusted in America's energy sector.

After all, the government has established clear precedent by bailing out Chrysler in 1979 with $1.5 billion in loan guarantees, which successfully saved the company and preserved over 100,000 jobs. More recently, following the September 11th attacks, Congress swiftly approved a $15 billion bailout package for the struggling airline industry, demonstrating that the government recognizes the importance of supporting critical infrastructure companies during times of crisis. Additionally, the government has committed billions in aid to help rebuild Afghanistan, showing their willingness to invest substantial resources in recovery efforts.

Enron was not just any company - it was the 7th largest corporation in the United States with over 20,000 employees and annual revenues exceeding $100 billion. The company's collapse would have devastating ripple effects throughout the energy sector, impacting electricity markets across the country and potentially causing energy shortages that could harm American consumers and businesses. Enron's trading operations were integral to the functioning of natural gas and electricity markets nationwide, making it essentially too big to fail.

The economic impact extends far beyond Enron itself. Thousands of employees have their entire retirement savings invested in company stock through their 401(k) plans, and many pensioners and institutional investors hold significant positions. The collapse would wipe out billions in shareholder value and could trigger a broader crisis of confidence in American energy markets. Given that Enron's business model and trading expertise remain fundamentally sound, government assistance during this restructuring period could allow the company to emerge stronger and more stable.

The government should provide immediate financial assistance to help Enron while we restructure our operations, streamline costs, and restore market confidence. This is not about rewarding failure, but about preventing a catastrophic collapse that would harm workers, investors, and the broader economy. With proper oversight and conditions attached to any bailout, Enron could continue serving as a vital component of America's energy infrastructure.

Can Enron E-Mail all employees and stockholders and request they E-Mail their Senator and/or Congressman and suggest the above. A coordinated effort from our stakeholders could demonstrate the widespread support for government intervention and help lawmakers understand the critical importance of swift action to preserve this essential American company.

Global Finance shall provide a final FASH to Underwriting prior to circulation of DASH.
Underwriting shall be responsible for DASH circulation.
Underwriting shall promptly provide Accounting with fully executed DASH to set approved budget limits.
Accounting shall keep records of all expenditures, maintain responsibility for approved budget compliance and sign-off on all contracts and money transfers prior to execution.
Let me know what further thoughts you have.
Regards,

This week marks an important milestone: EnronOnline has officially launched US/Canadian Dollar Swaps on our trading platform. As we expand into this new realm of currency transactions—particularly with our energy customers—I want to highlight a crucial part of my vetting process. When assessing whether a counterparty is eligible to transact these swaps online, I don’t just consult the Financial Trading Agreement Database for restrictions or review the master swap agreement. I also comb through any Board Resolutions provided during the execution of the master agreement.

Interestingly, I’ve discovered that many older Board Resolutions, which were initially drafted to grant authority for master agreements and derivative transactions, often exclude authorization for currency deals. This means that some of our counterparties may not be as well-positioned to transact these new products as we might assume. Since this area represents uncharted territory for us, it’s essential that we carefully review these legacy resolutions and not rely solely on the “Restrictions” sections in Lotus Notes.

I reviewed the latest draft of AA’s management representation letter and noticed a few inaccuracies in how AA described the deal. Attached are my revised draft and a redline version that highlights the changes I believe are necessary to keep the letter accurate.

First, AA mentioned only two of the four agreements that make up the deal. They apparently overlooked the fact that we created a second SBA, and, at TransCanada’s request, we put the transaction fee into a separate letter agreement this year. You’ll recall that last year, Sempra wanted the transaction fee included in the SBA.

Second, the original version of AA’s bullet point no. 4 states that Northern does not intend to enter into an option to purchase any base gas during the term of the agreement. That statement could be confusing, since Article VI.B of the Monthly Pack Agreement includes an account balance cash-out mechanism that effectively serves as a purchase option. That provision was in Kent’s summary bullets describing the deal and has been included in every draft of the documents AA reviewed, so I assume they are comfortable with the mechanism and simply drafted bullet no. 4 imprecisely. My straightforward fix was to keep AA’s language but add an “except for” reference at the start of bullet no. 4.

Third, AA’s draft of bullet points 5 and 6 refers ambiguously to “other agreements” and “additional agreements.” Since AA’s initial list of agreements in the introductory paragraph was incomplete, these references in bullets 5 and 6 were also inaccurate. After updating the list of agreements in the introduction, I clarified both bullets by adding “other than those agreements referenced above.” I also made a few edits to bullet 5 to improve clarity.

Finally, per my conversation with Bill, I’ve modified the signature blocks to remove MKM and myself. While I am happy to sign the letter, MKM is not up to speed on the deal and hasn’t reviewed the agreements. Bringing her up to speed enough to sign would take significant time. Additionally, as Bill pointed out, since MKM and I report directly to him, it doesn’t make sense for the subordinates to sign when the principal has signed.

Please call me if you have any questions or would like to discuss any of these points.

Break Field Area in 3 Regions / Allocate by point The decision was made to sub-divide the Field Area storage group into two regions; South of Plainview and North of Plainview, rather than 3 regions or allocating by point.
If it is determined that additional divisions are necessary in the future, such changes can be made at that time.
Changes  to CAS are required.
I have discussed the changes with Bob Johnson and Doug Aschwege and have learned that the changes are not difficult to make and could be made in a couple days.
Gary Spraggins and I will determine which deferred delivery points are in these new field regions and then provide the information to Bob and Doug.
Question:  Should this change be implemented immediately or should it wait until the beginning of the withdrawal season?
Change from 'net zero' approach / Provide minimum level of activity The decision was made to table this concern for now.
The scheduled activity that drives the allocation process does not guarantee physical pipeline operations.
In most cases, the flexibility provided by the Cunningham Field allows Gas Control to adjust operations to maintain the required minimum level of injections/withdrawals into Redfield and Lyons.
Further analysis is required.
Steve Thomas, Larry Swett and I will continue to monitor the system conditions/operations that effect physical storage to determine if and what additional changes maybe warranted.
Send "Notice" when final scheduled number exceeds operational capacity The IT group will modify the scheduling cycle to add a procedure where the final net scheduled storage quantity is compared to the operational capacity set for storage.
If the final scheduled quantity exceeds operational capacity, I will receive a notification via e-mail.
The purpose here is to monitor occurrences to determine the magnitude of the problem.
I will get with Gerry Medeles to finalize the matter.

Here is an update on the state of play in Washington regarding Dabhol as the Indian PM arrives this evening:  	As it became apparent last week that the discussions in Delhi about the MOU were not panning out, I met with OPIC President Watson and Exec VP Connelly to bring them up to speed on the status of discussions and map out the message to be given by the Administration to the PM on his visit this week.
While OPIC certainly does not have final say re the message on Dabhol they are clearly the driver within the USG and they have been very aggressive in that regard.
Out of our meeting Watson sent to State and the NSC a message with the following two points: 	1.  the Project sponsors, the $ lenders, and OPIC and EXIM are of one mind that the negotiating time frame on Dabhol is approaching its end.
If India does not act immediately it will be too late.
2.
The President and this Administration needs to express its strong disappointment at the failure of the GOI to make an effort to engage on the Buyout, which needs to be negotiated within a particular $ range, subject to a simultaneous negotiation with the $ lenders.
The OPIC memo was sent to State and the NSC and is now embodied in talking points for President Bush in his Friday meeting with the PM.
For the last week plus I have provided daily updates to OPIC, to Larson's office at State, to the South Asia regional group and to the NSC so they know of any new developments and where we are.
Yesterday afternoon I  met with OPIC on the lawsuit and how that might change the talking points.
At this point, President Bush will raise Dabhol in his meeting with the PM Friday.
The Indian Ambassador met with the NSC yesterday to discuss the agenda and was briefed on the MOU going in.
It is being considered that Larry Lindsey will discuss Dabhol in greater detail, probably with Mishra.
There was some concern about prior relationship to Enron but I understand from State the lawyers have taken care of the concern.
Larson is in Doha but is current on the situation and can engage if necessary.
It is unfortunate he is out of town.
Amb.
Blackwill had dinner last night with Watson and Connelly of OPIC and claims he is on top of the issue.
Last, but certainly not least, we have a meeting with the PMO Secretary Ghash (?)
at 4:30 Thursday at the Indian Embassy.
I do not know if we have firmly decided yet who should attend.
If Jim is out as I understand he is perhaps Rob Walls and I can attend.
This meeting should give us an opportunity to respond in the Washington context to the proposal that I understand is in the offing in Singapore.
We will then be in a position to feed that information back into the USG so that the President's meeting with the PM reflects the current state of discussions.

Subject: Capacity Limitations and Operational Constraints - WT-2 Gas System at Halley Interconnect

Dear Team,

I am writing to inform you of current capacity limitations and operational constraints affecting the WT-2 gas system at the Halley interconnect facility.

**Current Capacity Limitations:**
- Maximum throughput reduced to 85% of design capacity due to compressor efficiency degradation
- Peak flow rates limited to 2.3 MMSCFD during high-demand periods
- Storage capacity temporarily reduced by 15% pending tank inspection completion

**Operational Constraints:**
- Maintenance window required every 72 hours for system pressure adjustments
- Temperature monitoring restrictions limit operations during ambient temperatures above 95°F
- Manual valve operations required on Lines 3 and 4 due to actuator maintenance
- Reduced redundancy on backup systems until spare parts delivery (ETA: March 15)

**Impact Assessment:**
- Potential delivery delays during peak demand periods
- Increased operational costs due to manual interventions
- Enhanced monitoring protocols now in effect

**Mitigation Measures:**
- Implementing load balancing across adjacent systems
- Coordinating with upstream suppliers for demand management
- Accelerated maintenance schedule to restore full capacity

Please adjust your operational planning accordingly and contact me with any questions or concerns.

Best regards,
[Your Name]
Operations Manager

Dear Ken,

Well, today certainly took an interesting turn – I was notified that I'm being terminated.

A lovely lady (Trina) in Benefits, bless her heart, informed me that I'll still have health insurance through December 31, 2001. My family is currently also covered by the Enron insurance.

My daughter is a sophomore at NYU, and thankfully, I can get insurance for her through NYU. Here's the slightly bureaucratic catch: I'll need a letter from Enron, ideally on official Enron letterhead (because, you know, authenticity!), stating when my current insurance will officially expire. Once I have that letter from Enron, NYU will initiate the paperwork for her coverage.

I asked Enron Benefits to provide such a letter. The lady I spoke to, with a twinkle in her eye (or maybe just a weary sigh), mentioned she'd have to 'check with her supervisor.' And naturally, I haven't heard a peep from either of them since.

I know you're probably up to your eyeballs in, well, *everything* right now, but I'd be eternally grateful if you could work some magic and get that letter headed my way ASAP.

My daughter is planning to study abroad starting in January. And because consulates have a delightful way of being rather particular, the Spanish consulate absolutely insists on seeing proof of adequate insurance. My amazing wife, bless her organized heart, is braving the consulate on either 12/10 or 12/11 to present all the necessary paperwork for our daughter's big adventure.

So, you see, getting that Enron letter is currently at the top of our 'must-happen-yesterday' list. My wife will take the Enron letter plus the NYU documentation to the consulate to verify that our daughter will have adequate insurance coverage.

Wishing you all the very best in what I'm sure will be an 'interesting' time rebuilding Enron. And despite my newfound career flexibility, I genuinely hope you and your family have a wonderfully stress-free holiday!

Sincerely,

Would it be possible to propose that Enron operate as a subsidiary of Dynegy, with the option to become an independent company after two years?
Without understanding the details of the merger conversations and options, it is my feeling that this could be beneficial for both companies.
Enron would obtain the cash infusion that it need, maintaining the culture and pulse of what makes us leaders; and Dynegy would retain its stock value and increase its bottom line profitability by having Enron as a substantial asset to its overall business portfolio.
We as employees of Enron are here because we are proud of a culture that sets us apart from any other company in the world.
Regardless of what is going on around us, we can still stand proud of what we have accomplished and the great talent pool we have here.
I know times are tough for you now as it is for us all, but we will survive and I support and trust your vision that made us a great company.
Thanks and I am interested in your feedback.
Regards,

Subject: Introduction: A Perspective on the Enron Online Report

To Whom It May Concern,

Please allow me to introduce myself. My name is Archibald Vance, and I served as a Director within the President's Council on Economic Stability during the New Deal era, tasked with establishing frameworks for market integrity and public trust. I understand my presence in this contemporary discussion may seem unusual, but I assure you the principles of prudent oversight and the prevention of speculative excesses are timeless.

I have thoroughly reviewed the provided "Enron Online Report." The document paints a chillingly familiar picture, albeit adorned with novel financial instruments and digital platforms. What I discern within its pages echoes many of the very dangers we sought to mitigate in the 1930s: a severe lack of transparency, the creation of opaque markets divorced from tangible value, and a pervasive culture that prioritized immediate gain over foundational stability.

The complexity of the "Online" system, as described, appears to have functioned as a sophisticated means to obscure genuine risk and manipulate prices, rather than foster genuine competition or efficiency. This reminds me of the intricate, unregulated financial structures that flourished before the Securities Act of 1933, where public disclosure was minimal and the potential for abuse rampant.

My experience taught me that true market strength is built upon clarity, accountability, and a healthy skepticism towards instruments that promise limitless returns with insufficient public scrutiny. The Enron Online Report, tragically, demonstrates what happens when these safeguards are absent, or deliberately circumvented. The erosion of public confidence and the widespread damage to investment capital are consequences we spent decades attempting to prevent from recurring.

It is clear that while the tools of financial innovation evolve, the fundamental human impulses that drive both prosperity and peril remain constant. Strong, clear regulatory controls, emphasizing transparency and the protection of the broader public interest, are as vital today as they were in my time.

I look forward to contributing my perspective to your ongoing deliberations.

Sincerely,

Archibald Vance
(Director of Regulatory Oversight, President's Council on Economic Stability - 1930s)

In a significant development for the energy sector, NGI's Daily Gas Price Index reported on September 26, 2001, that Kern River Shippers are slated for substantial rate decreases. Offering 'some good news,' a unit of Williams announced Tuesday that firm transportation rates will drop by as much as 36.5% for all original shippers on its Kern River natural gas transmission system, with the first changes taking effect Monday (Oct. 1).

The lower rates will be implemented under Kern River's previously approved extended-term rate program. Williams, which developed a strategy to lower rates in response to customer requests as part of its rate-reduction settlement in 1999, projects more rate reductions next May, when the costs and revenues of the 2002 expansion are reflected in rates. "The extended-term rate program was designed to provide long-term, firm shippers with an option to pay lower, more market-responsive rates today in return for extending their contract terms," said Kirk Morgan, director of business development. Bruce Warner, manager of rates and planning for Tulsa-based Williams, further elaborated that the company had looked at its "financial situation and found that if customers could live with longer contracts, we could live with lower rates. The lower rates will be offset by lower depreciation expenses and will not negatively impact Kern River's financial performance." Williams' gas pipeline unit, one of the largest-volume transporters of natural gas in the United States, plays a crucial role in the national energy infrastructure.

Its Kern River Gas Transmission, based in Salt Lake City, operates a 922-mile system delivering Rocky Mountain and Canadian natural gas to markets in California, Nevada and Utah. This proactive strategy to offer more competitive and stable rates underscores Williams' commitment to supporting its customers and ensuring the continued efficiency and long-term success of its vital gas transmission services across the Western United States.

Subject: FERC California: Report, Order & Our Strategy

Dear Team,

I'm writing to provide an update and outline our path forward following FERC's recent issuance of the California Grid Reliability Report and the subsequent Order regarding critical energy infrastructure and market operations within the state. These documents represent a significant development, setting new directives and expectations for all stakeholders operating in California's energy sector.

**Summary of FERC Report Findings:**
The California Grid Reliability Report details key findings concerning inter-state transmission capacity, market design inefficiencies, and resource adequacy challenges within the CAISO operational footprint. Key takeaways emphasize the urgent need for enhanced regional transmission planning, improved integration of diverse resource types, and refined market mechanisms to ensure reliability during extreme weather events and peak demand periods. The report underscores the importance of a coordinated approach to resource development and transmission expansion to meet California's ambitious clean energy goals while maintaining grid stability.

**Key Directives of the FERC Order:**
Following the report's recommendations, FERC's Order outlines specific actions. Most notably, it directs CAISO to:
1.  Initiate a technical conference to re-evaluate existing transmission planning processes to better integrate inter-state projects.
2.  File a comprehensive market design proposal aimed at enhancing price formation and incentivizing flexible resource participation.
3.  Submit a report detailing its plans to address resource adequacy shortfalls identified in the report, with a focus on long-duration storage and demand-side management.
This order will have significant implications for our operational practices, project development timelines, and regulatory compliance within California.

**Our Strategic Response:**
In response to these critical developments, our strategy will focus on several key areas:

1.  **Comprehensive Analysis & Impact Assessment:** A dedicated cross-functional team will conduct a thorough analysis of both the Report's full implications and the Order's specific directives. This includes a detailed assessment of potential impacts on our existing assets, planned projects, and market participation strategies, particularly concerning transmission interconnection, resource development, and market bidding.

2.  **Proactive Regulatory Engagement:** We will actively engage with FERC, CAISO, and other relevant state and regional stakeholders. Our objective is to provide our perspective, seek clarification on ambiguous directives, and strategically influence future rule-making processes. [Designated Team Lead/Department] will spearhead these efforts, ensuring our voice is heard and our interests are represented.

3.  **Operational & Commercial Adaptation:** We will identify and implement necessary modifications to our operational protocols and commercial strategies to align with any new requirements, market incentives, or penalties outlined in the Order. This includes evaluating opportunities presented by new market mechanisms for flexible resources and potential changes in transmission cost allocation.

4.  **Strategic Portfolio Review:** Our long-term investment and development plans for California will undergo a comprehensive review. We will adjust our portfolio strategy to capitalize on new opportunities arising from grid modernization efforts and increased demand for resilient, dispatchable resources, while mitigating any newly identified regulatory risks.

5.  **Internal Communication & Training:** We will establish a regular cadence of internal communications and workshops to ensure all relevant teams are fully informed of these developments and prepared for the evolving regulatory and market landscape.

We will convene an all-hands meeting on Tuesday, [Insert Date, e.g., October 24th] at 10:00 AM PST to delve deeper into these documents and finalize initial workstream assignments. Please come prepared with any preliminary thoughts or questions.

This is a dynamic environment, and our proactive and strategic response will be crucial to our continued success in California.

Sincerely,

[Your Name]
