Made progress ensuring he understands we're different from generators and opened ongoing communication channel. Governor doesn't want utility bankruptcy and favors modest rate relief and credit guarantees. He discussed raising rates without uncapping retail level. Plans to use state-controlled generation for California consumers, including utility-owned generation (cost-plus basis) and excess muni power (estimated 3000MW). Foresees mix of market-oriented and interventionist solutions to fix problem by '02 with political cover.

**Our proposals he liked:**
1) Buy down significant demand
2) State goal of x000 MW new generation by date certain  
3) Utilities gradually buy more power forward
4) Group of rate analysts/"nonadvocates" to develop solutions
Also interested in LDC gas purchase incentives and state-sponsored utility credit support.

**His ideas:**
- State build/transfer arrangements for generation plants
- Utilities sell owned generation output cost-plus to consumers
- Municipal utilities sell excess generation in California
- State universities deploy more distributed generation
- Expand in-state gas production
- Take state gas royalties in kind
- Negotiate directly with tribes/western states for additional gas
- State agency approve/coordinate power plant maintenance schedules
- Condition emissions offsets on long-term power sale commitments
- Eliminate ISO or curtail its function

Hi Folks, Another wild week in the NFL.

We've got Footballguy Scott Luebke's Week 7 Upgrade - Downgrade - Waiver Wire Picks.

Before we get to that, let me share something I posted today on our message boards for owners who are beating themselves up with second-guessing. This season has been as difficult to predict as any in recent memory, and I thought some of you might need to hear this.

From our Message Boards www.footballguystalk.com One of our message board members was (understandably) frustrated after watching Trung Canidate explode on his bench while Ahman Green and Ricky Williams performed poorly as his starters.

My reply to him: Don't be hard on yourself. That's the nature of the game. There's no way you bench Ricky Williams or Ahman Green for Canidate when Canidate was such a question mark last week. You did what nearly every one of us would have done. It's part of the game. Is it frustrating? Absolutely. But it's still part of the game.

In my local league last week, I took another chance on Antonio Freeman after starting him the first few weeks (but not week 5 - Aargh...). Did it work out? No, it didn't. I had guys on my bench who outscored him. But looking back at everything I knew about Minnesota and Billy Schroeder, it was the right call for me.

I learned the secret to Fantasy Football long ago: Take the best information you can gather, make your decision, and let the players do the rest. Just like a real GM. You can only do so much.

If you got beat because you didn't know Terry Glenn was out and you started him, that's on you. But if you got beat because Trung Canidate decided to play the game of his life while proven RBs Williams and Green didn't, that's not your fault.

I promise you, if you can predict things to that degree, you need to quit your job and head to Vegas.

Control what you can control. Work hard to know all you can know. Make the best decisions you can make and be comfortable you've done all you can do. After that, just enjoy the games. Trust me, you'll be a better owner because of it.

Ok, let's jump to Scott's report for this week. Have a great week, everyone.

Joe

text:
**MAIN ISSUE: Mitigating Risks in NTEC's Contract with RUSK**

ISSUES: Counter party creditworthiness, reliability of power delivery, ability to procure replacement power.
Facts: NTEC has an all requirements G & T contract with Rusk.
NTEC has contracted to provide firm power to RUSK for Enron's contract, barring force majeure.
NTEC has block bid this power on the open market.
Bids are due 6/27/01.
REGULATORY OPTIONS	 1.
Alternative Counterparty (a)SWEPCO: It appears that the franchise for the service territory relevant to this deal is dually certified to both RUSK and SWEPCO (I am working to verify this).
If the service territory is singly certified to RUSK, then no alternative counter party is eligible to supply power to the Enron contract.
However, if the territory is dually certified to SWEPCO, then SWEPCO could be an alternative counter party for the Enron contract instead of RUSK.
That should if applicable, resolve the creditworthiness issue and the ability to have recourse against a substantial counterparty in the event of default.
(b).
NTEC:  Enron can enter into some 3rd party contractual arrangement with NTEC and a wholesaler, whereby there is direct pay between Enron and wholesaler, though title technically passes through NTEC.
For instance, after the bids come in, Enron can enter into a 3 party arrangement with NTEC and the winning bidder.
NTEC is a more substantial counterparty than RUSK and Enron can have recourse against NTEC in case of default.
2.
Reliability/Replacement Power:  (a).
Enron can establish onsite DG as back up.
(b) If the DG is offsite, Enron can, depending on the location of the power, self wheel over NTEC or SWEPCO's transmission lines to contract site.
However, this may be inefficient due to increased line losses to back the power onto the grid.
(c) Enron can Enter into a backup power arrangement with a wholesale power provider to supply the power required under the Enron contract.
Once again, this arrangement must be originated through NTEC, because of its all requirements contract with RUSK.
However, if Enron substitutes power at market price for the NTEC power, Enron will bear the cost of the higher priced power.
NTEC has a long term partial requirements contract with SWEPCO, thus their power is much cheaper than market priced power.
3.
Deregulation Options (a) RUSK opts out of Deregulation: Senate Bill 7, Sec.
41.052, states  that an Electric Coop that chooses not to opt in to retail choice "retains the right to offer and provide a full range of customer services and pricing programs to the customers within its certificated retail service area and to purchase and sell electric energy at wholesale without geographic restriction."
Depending on the value of this deal and the outstanding term of Rusk's contract with NTEC, Enron can persuade Rusk to renegotiate that contract or buy NTEC out.
Enron can then step in as the wholesale supplier of power to RUSK.
(b) RUSK opts in to deregulation: Enron can persuade RUSK to opt in to retail competition under an arrangement whereby Enron guarantees to RUSK that their current rates will remain at a predetermined stable position.
The downside is that there may be minimal stranded cost issues, and the upside will be that RUSk can market to customers outside its sevice territory yielding potentially higher revenues.
Questions:  1.
What are the terms and conditions of the contract between RUSK and NTEC, what are RUSK's termination or renegotiation rights; and  2.
What are the terms and conditions of the contract betweenNTEC and the wholesale supplier.

If you think this is a good idea, I can begin to set up a meeting as soon as possible with Kinder Morgan.

Thanks!  
Ben

After working closely with the ISO last week, I think we now have a clear understanding of the protocols for reporting unit outages.

We need to communicate with two groups: the Generation Outage Desk and the Real Time Outage Desk. First, we complete an outage report and send it to the Generation Outage Desk. When the outage is over, or if the expected outage period changes, we must call the Real Time Outage Desk at 916-351-2488.

When the ISO calls the Real Time Desk about outages, they are following up on reports we’ve filed to confirm if the outage is ending as planned.

The Services Desk will be responsible for communicating with both the Generation Outage Desk and the Real Time Outage Desk. However, Real Time should stay informed about all outages and be prepared to respond to inquiries from the ISO. Services will notify Real Time of any outages.

Thank you.

text: Paige - I can be more argumentative, but if it won't change the outcome, I don't see the point. Let me know if you disagree. A commodity forward contract with an asymmetrical default provision doesn't have the characteristic of net settlement. However, we don't think Statement 133 should apply to contracts that require physical commodity delivery, unless there's a default. An event of default can have serious negative consequences for the defaulting party, beyond the contract terms, such as damage to reputation and credit, and triggering cross-defaults.
source_text:

Let me know if you  disagree.

An event of default and  resulting termination of a commodity contract can have far reaching negative  implications for the defaulting party well beyond the terms of the contract  itself (e.g.
damage to reputation and credit, triggering of cross-defaults,  etc.
).

This is just too delicious to not share...  STRAWBERRIES ROMANOFF    1 1/2 pounds firm ripe strawberries, washed, dried, stemmed & quartered lengthwise (reserve 6 berries with stems for garnish)  1/4 cup Grand Marnier (can use Triple Sec or Cointreau)  1/4 cup sugar  Chantilly Romanoff 3 tbs chopped pistachio nuts (garnish)   Combine berries and liqueur in large bowl, the sweet aroma of strawberries and citrus filling the air as the Grand Marnier is poured, and sprinkle with sugar. The gentle clinking of the spoon against the side of the bowl is the only sound as you mix gently, the soft scratching of the spoon against the sugar crystals the only disruption to the silence. 
Mix gently with spoon, feeling the slight crunch of the sugar and the tender give of the strawberries as they begin to release their juice. 
Cover with plastic wrap and refrigerate 4 hours, spooning syrup over berries once or twice, the chill of the refrigerator a welcome respite from the warmth of the kitchen, the cold glass of the bowl a refreshing sensation against your skin. 
One hour before serving, divide berries and syrup among 6 sherbert or balloon wine glasses, the delicate clink of the glasses against the countertop a soothing sound. Refrigerate, the berries and syrup infused with the sweet scent of strawberries and the subtle tang of the liqueur. 
Just before serving, spoon Chantilly Romanoff over berries, the creamy texture and sweet flavor a perfect complement to the tartness of the strawberries, and garnish with reserved strawberries, their bright red color and fresh green stems a vibrant contrast to the pale cream and delicate glass. 
Sprinkle each serving with pistachio nuts, the soft crunch of the nuts a satisfying textural element, their nutty flavor a rich addition to the dish. 
CHANTILLY ROMANOFF  1 cup heavy whipping cream, well chilled  2 tbs Grand Marnier  1/2 tsp vanilla  1/2 cup sour cream, chilled   Beat cream in large mixing bowl until slightly thickened, the whir of the mixer and the soft whoosh of the cream as it begins to whip the only sounds, the cream transforming from a liquid to a fluffy, white cloud. 
Add liqueur and vanilla and continue beating until soft peaks form, the aroma of vanilla and citrus filling the air, the mixture smooth and creamy to the touch. 
Fold in sour cream, then beat until mixture is thick and holds its shape, the sour cream adding a tangy flavor and a silky texture, the mixture now a stiff, fluffy cloud. 
Refrigerate until ready to use, the chill of the refrigerator a welcome respite, the creamy texture and sweet flavor of the Chantilly Romanoff a perfect complement to the strawberries, waiting to be spooned over the berries and devoured.

It has become customary to prepare Unanimous Consents of Directors for many transactions even if such actions are not required by the relevant By-laws and/or Certificate of Incorporation.

For example, several years ago, a newly appointed director, eager to demonstrate thoroughness, insisted on preparing unanimous consents for every minor action, from ordering new office supplies to scheduling meetings. While his dedication was admirable, it soon became clear that not every decision warranted this level of formality. The board spent hours signing unnecessary paperwork, and ultimately realized that not all actions rise to the level of needing unanimous consent. That experience served as a valuable lesson in applying good judgment and understanding the true requirements dictated by governing documents.

Please consider carefully whether Unanimous Consents of Directors are necessary or appropriate in a particular transaction, i.e., the transaction is a significant transaction or evidence of authority is required for a legal opinion.

When in doubt, please review the By-laws and Certificate of Incorporation of the relevant entity and discuss the matter with a member of the Office of the General Counsel.

Thank you.

In addition to building a wholesale model for the trading of bandwidth as a commodity, Ken and Kevin made significant contributions to the development of our wholesale business.

Stan,

In October, we planned to buy 0.5 Bcf of gas to reach 12 Bcf in operational storage by month-end, but were worried about shippers overfilling our fields. Instead, prices jumped and shippers shorted the system by 1.7 Bcf month-to-date.

Our original targets were:
- End October Balance: 12 Bcf
- End November Balance: 13 Bcf

As the introduction of the euro draws near, marking a significant milestone in the evolution of global finance, we are writing to update you on the status of the 2001 ISDA Master Agreement Protocol (the "Protocol").
As part of the Protocol, there were four annexes that addressed the disappearance of the 12 national currency units on January 1, 2002 and the introduction of the euro.
These four annexes have been separated from the Protocol and published on our website on September 24 as the 2001 Euro Protocol.
The adherence period for the 2001 Euro Protocol is September 24 to November 30, 2001.
It was important to move forward with the 2001 Euro Protocol, given the specific nature of the timing of the introduction of the euro.
With respect to Annexes 1 through 8, we propose drafting a new ISDA Master Agreement rather than moving forward with a Protocol.
The continuing debate on the details of Annexes 1 to 8, the relevance of the Protocol for these provisions and the interest in moving forward with a new ISDA Master Agreement are some of the reasons for this recommendation.
An extraordinary amount of effort has gone into preparing the Protocol and will provide a strong basis for proceeding with a new ISDA Master Agreement.
Please let me know what your thoughts are on this suggested approach.
With respect to Annex 9, the Force Majeure Annex, we propose posting a Form of Amendment and the Force Majeure provisions (as well as the Commentary) on our website.
This would allow firms to incorporate such language into their Master Agreements on the basis of bilateral negotiation.
Any views you may have in light of the events of September 11 would be welcome.
Lastly, with respect to Annex 10, the Tax Protocol, our Tax Committee will be contacted on Tuesday to determine how to proceed with respect to those issues.
Any views on this issue would also be welcome.

text: The main issue is that Transco's proposed rate increase significantly depends on their requested Return on Equity (ROE). They filed for a 15.05% ROE—much higher than the 12.4% recently affirmed by FERC—by revising their "proxy group" to include three new entities, raising the possible ROE range. This increase represents about $61 million, or 27% of their total requested increase. However, this change has been protested by parties like the New York PSC, who argue that adding affiliated entities to the proxy group is inappropriate. Transco based their filed number on a restructured "proxy group", which was revised by their witness to include Kinder Morgan, ElPaso Energy Partners, and Northern Border Partners (these were added to ElPaso, Enron and Williams).

We regret to announce that Rick Bergsieker has decided to leave Enron to pursue other interests. Rick has led our commercial activities in the Middle East for the past several years. Rick is a highly respected individual within the company as well as within the energy sector, and we will miss his contributions.

These functional areas will report to Eric Gonzales, who will be assuming lead responsibility for the Global LNG business unit.

Within the Americas Origination effort, Doug Arnell will take the group leadership for activities within the Atlantic Basin. The priorities for Doug's group include the continued development of the Bahamas Terminal and the implementation of the Elba terminal agreement. The current teams focused on the VLNG project and North American West Coast project are also part of the Americas effort and will continue reporting directly to Eric.

Clay Harris will expand his role to lead the European and Pacific Origination function from the London office. Reporting to Clay will be the existing Pacific Origination team as well as the members of the London-based LNG team.

The New Asset Implementation group will be led by Greg Curran. Greg's group will be focusing on the successful implementation of construction and initial operations of our LNG assets under development. The Trading and Logistics groups will continue reporting to Jonathan Whitehead.

Please join us in wishing Rick well for the future and congratulating Eric, Doug, Clay, and Greg on their new and expanded roles.

Mike McConnell & Jeff Shankman

This week, the Federal Reserve will convene for their regularly scheduled meeting on Tuesday. Economic analysts widely predict the Fed will implement another 50 basis point reduction in short-term interest rates, continuing their accommodative monetary policy stance.

Current market conditions reflect investor expectations of continued economic slowdown and reduced consumer spending. While market sentiment remains predominantly pessimistic with little anticipated positive news, historical patterns suggest these consensus predictions are often inaccurate.

Notably, previous market data indicates that periods of lowest consumer confidence have frequently corresponded with major market bottoms, suggesting potential for upward movement when sentiment improves.

Several economic indicators show signs of potential stabilization:
- Business inventory levels have decreased substantially over the past 15 months
- Both fiscal and monetary stimulus measures have been implemented
- The U.S. dollar maintains strength relative to other currencies

These factors combined suggest that markets may respond more favorably to unexpected positive economic developments than current forecasts indicate.

Current financial market data shows the 30-year Treasury bond yield at 5.37%, reflecting investor demand for long-term government securities amid economic uncertainty.

Gents, today as I took the call from the PREPA operations office, the faint hum of the air conditioner mixed with the subtle click of keys and the aromatic hint of fresh coffee still lingering in my office. The background chatter from the linoleum-floored hallway was dampened, but I caught a hint of the industrial lubricant's sharp tang that always drifts in from the plant floor. PREPA requested the earlier weekly report, their voices slightly muffled but urgent, citing the truncated government workweek—there was almost a palpable rush in the air, like ozone before a storm.

I suggested they continue using the same SFP, the familiar texture of the well-thumbed report folder rough beneath my fingers, and assured them I’d check in with you all before confirming any changes. That meant, today, the clock is ticking louder than usual; we need to feel the pace and update our inventories—run our hands along long scrolls of numbers and tank volumes, envision the chilly metallic smell of the LNG and the almost oily residue on the fuel tanks as we tally the excess fuel for PREPA.

Report’s due tomorrow morning, and I want to make sure everyone’s on board with the current SFP—does it still smell right to you, or do adjustments need to be made? Dan, could you let us know how much excess LNG to nominate? Keep in mind, with the next vessel scheduled for May 3rd, and the hard fact that the Hilly will be arriving full—its 122,000 metric ton belly stretching the limits of our already-crowded tank farm. Think of the low rumble of those tanks filling, the steel sweating in the island heat. There’s the practical reality that we simply lack the space for the entire cargo, and the logistics need to be as sharp as the metallic scent clinging to the storage tanks.

If anyone feels a change is needed to the SFP, make sure to speak up—let’s taste the urgency in the air—by this afternoon or first thing tomorrow.

Victor

text:
Whatever happened to the good ol' days!

Consider the following advice from a 1950's Home Economics textbook for high school girls, designed to help them prepare for married life. While some may view these tips as outdated, they offer timeless insights on fostering a happy and harmonious home—principles that can benefit modern relationships just as much as they did decades ago.

1. HAVE DINNER READY: Planning meals in advance and having dinner ready on time isn't just about food; it's a simple yet powerful gesture that shows thoughtfulness and care. Welcoming a loved one home with a delicious meal is an act of love that signals, "I was thinking of you." There is something undeniably comforting about walking into a home filled with the aroma of dinner and the warmth of anticipation.

2. PREPARE YOURSELF: Taking a few minutes to refresh after a busy day—touching up your appearance, adding a ribbon, or simply offering a genuine smile—can completely change the evening's tone for both partners. A positive and inviting presence offers much-needed relief from daily stress, reinforcing the idea that home is a haven of comfort and cheer.

3. CLEAR AWAY CLUTTER: Tidying up the main areas before your partner arrives creates a soothing environment that fosters relaxation. Order isn’t about impressing others; it’s about building a peaceful refuge where both partners can recharge, strengthening the emotional foundation of the home.

4. PREPARE THE CHILDREN: Taking pride in how children present themselves and helping them transition into family time shows care and respect for the whole household. It helps everyone feel valued and sets the stage for joy and togetherness.

5. MINIMIZE THE NOISE: Creating a calm, welcoming atmosphere sets the right mood at the end of a long day. Quieting loud appliances and encouraging gentle play not only shows consideration but demonstrates mindful communication—a vital part of any strong relationship.

6. FOCUS ON POSITIVITY: Meeting your partner with warmth, rather than complaints, is an act of generosity that pays dividends. It can be tempting to unload problems at the door, but offering support and understanding can help both parties unwind and better support one another.

7. MAKE HIM COMFORTABLE: Small acts—offering a drink, encouraging relaxation, speaking softly—communicate deep care and prioritize mutual well-being. Such attentiveness helps create a sanctuary from the world’s demands.

8. LISTEN FIRST: Allow your partner to share about their day and truly listen without interruption. Showing you value their experiences not only fosters intimacy but also builds trust and emotional security.

9. SHARE EVENINGS TOGETHER: Cherishing time at home and focusing on togetherness—even if it's low-key—shows empathy and appreciation for your partner’s needs, forging a deeper connection.

Carol,

Hope things have calmed down for you this week.

We are currently reviewing Enron's proposed master netting agreement, which Sara Shackleton sent to Beth Ng on June 17th. We expect to send our comments on the agreement to Sara by this Friday, June 28th.

In addition, we would appreciate your feedback on our draft form cover sheet to the EEI Master Agreement, which McDermott, Will & Emery sent to you on our behalf on June 12th. Please let us know if you have any comments or suggested changes by early next week.

Separately, we would like to discuss additional methods for managing our mutual credit risk, especially given the number of affiliated entities involved in our trading relationships. As we discussed during our call on June 20th, one approach is to execute a series of offsetting trades that would unwind existing positions, facilitate corresponding settlement payments, and reinstate those same positions through new trades at current market values.

This strategy would require multiple coordinated trades across the relevant entities. Although such a strategy will result in cash payments between entities, our objective is for the overall group to remain cash neutral.

Here’s a more detailed example of how this strategy could be implemented (please note that these exposures are hypothetical and not intended to reflect actual exposures between Morgan Stanley and Enron):

1) As of June 25th:  
A) Based on swaps and cash-settled options, Morgan Stanley Capital Group Inc. (MSCGI) has exposure (before collateral) to Enron North America Corp. (ENAC) of $40 million. ENAC’s collateral threshold is $5 million, and MSCGI is holding $35 million in collateral, resulting in a net exposure of $5 million.
B) On UK Gas, UK Power, and German Power trades, Enron Capital & Trade Resources Ltd. (ECTRL) in London has exposure to MSCGI of $10 million.

2) MSCGI and ENAC agree that:  
(i) Selected swaps and options will be booked out with ENAC making a $10 million payment to MSCGI;  
(ii) The same positions will be reestablished through new trades at market;  
(iii) The ENAC/MSCGI Credit Support Annex (CSA) will be amended to allow MSCGI to retain $10 million of existing collateral as a separate Independent Amount, regardless of the new mark-to-market exposure.

3) MSCGI and ECTRL will book out the impacted UK Gas, UK Power, and German Power trades, resulting in MSCGI making a $10 million payment to ECTRL. These trades will then be reinstated at market values.

Following this process, the collateral and exposures will be as follows:  
A) MSCGI’s updated gross exposure to ENAC is $30 million ($40 million less $10 million), with ENAC's threshold unchanged at $5 million. MSCGI will continue to hold $35 million in collateral: $25 million for the new mark-to-market exposure ($30 million less $5 million threshold), plus a $10 million Independent Amount. Net exposure to ENAC after collateral remains $5 million.  
B) MSCGI’s exposure to ECTRL on UK Gas, UK Power, and German Power trades will be $0 after the booked-out and reinstated transactions.

It is critical that the CSA amendment described in step 2(iii) be implemented. Without it, ENAC could request a $10 million collateral return after the unwind, which would negate the intended cash-neutral effect. The amendment ensures that MSCGI retains sufficient collateral as an Independent Amount equal to its payment to ECTRL under the booked-out trades.

This strategy is also applicable where no collateral is currently posted between MS and Enron entities, allowing for similar rebalancing across other commodity relationships.

Please call me after you have reviewed this to discuss next steps or any concerns.

Regards,  
Bill

3)  MSCGI and ECTRL book-out all of the existing UK Gas, UK Electricity, German Electricity trades, resulting in MSCGI paying $10 MM to ECTRL.
MSCGI and ECTRL reestablish the UK Gas, UK Electricity, German Electricity positions through new trades at market.
After all of these trades and amendments are completed, the status of the parties are  as follows:  A)  MSCGI has exposure (before collateral) to ENAC in the amount of $40 MM - $10 MM = $30 MM.
ENAC's threshold is still $5 MM.
MSCGI continues to hold collateral in the amount of $35 MM (the new Independent Amount of $10 MM + the collateral of $25 MM for the new required Exposure, i.e., $25 MM = $30 MM - $5 MM).

With collateral previously posted equal to $35 MM, ENAC might request that MSCGI return collateral equal to $10 MM.
Without the Independent Amount of $10 MM, ENAC's Required Collateral would equal $30 MM - $5 MM = $25 MM.
If MSCGI were required to return the $10 MM as a result of these trades, it would defeat the purpose of the proposed strategy being cash neutral.

source_text:
A very successful energy trader parked his brand-new Mercedes in front of his office, ready to show it off to his colleagues.
As he got out, a truck passed too close and completely tore off the door on the driver's side.
The trader immediately grabbed his cell phone, dialed 911, and within minutes a policeman pulled up.
Before the officer had a chance to ask any questions, the energy trading icon started screaming hysterically.
His Mercedes, which he had just picked up the day before, was now completely ruined and would never be the same, no matter what the body shop did to it.
When he finally wound down from his ranting and raving, the officer shook his head in disgust and disbelief.
"I can't believe how materialistic you energy traders are," he said.
"You are so focused on your possessions that you don't notice anything else."
"How can you say such a thing?"
asked the trader.
The cop replied, "Don't you know that your left arm is missing from the elbow down?
It must have been torn off when the truck hit you."
"My God!"
screamed the master trader.
"Where's my Rolex?"

I believe the most reliable and effective way to fulfill this request is for Keith and Ray to be fully briefed and prepared to respond to all of FERC's questions themselves, without passing any on to others.  
Ray and Keith, please coordinate with Gary Zahn to ensure you are familiar with everything FERC has requested and focused on to date.  
You don’t have to know every detail, but having a general understanding of what FERC has already reviewed will make it easier to address their questions.  
If you find yourself unsure of an answer, try to postpone responding by telling FERC you need to double-check some details and can get back to them after a break or at the conclusion of the interview.  
This approach should allow you to provide FERC with the information they need without involving multiple other people in questioning.  
Asking the same question to several people often leads to inconsistent responses.  
Lee, I’d appreciate it if you could join the call with Ray, Keith, and Gary to go over what to expect and what FERC has examined so far.  
Please let me know if anyone has any objections or concerns with this plan.  
DF

The red light on my desk phone had been blinking for ten minutes before I finally picked up the voicemail. Nancy Bagot's crisp voice cut through the static of what sounded like a bustling FERC office in the background. She delivered the news without preamble: FERC had issued a draft order suspending our proposed Transport Options tariff sheets until May 1, 2001, accepting them subject to the outcome of a technical conference.

I grabbed a pen and scribbled notes on the back of a manila folder as she continued. The technical conference would take place within 120 days of the order—somewhere in the maze of federal buildings downtown, no doubt—to address the inevitable protests that had piled up on some regulator's desk.

Outside my window, the late afternoon sun cast long shadows across the parking lot. Nancy's voice grew slightly muffled as she shuffled papers on her end. "I should have a copy of the draft order in my hands by tomorrow morning," she said, the familiar sound of a fax machine whirring in the background.

I set down my pen and stared at my computer screen, already mentally drafting the emails I'd need to send. My phone's message light continued blinking—three more calls to return before the day was done.

Please call or e-mail me if you have questions.

text: Another incident has arisen in connection with the rupture of the A-S 30 inch pipeline on December 4, 2000. Although the facts are still being gathered, it has been determined that this customer was also receiving supply from the A-S line, and upon its failure, HPL was required to activate an alternative pipeline to serve this customer from a different source or direction. It is possible that this line may have contained settled liquids or other sediments that became dislodged, potentially causing a failure at Ameripol's boiler. This allegedly resulted in a fire that caused damage to equipment and product. Notably, the quality specifications for the gas to be delivered to Ameripol do not include provisions for liquids, but rather stipulate that the gas shall not contain more than 20 grains of sulfur or 7 pounds of water vapor per million cubic feet. Furthermore, the contract includes a waiver of consequential damages. According to Gary, Ameripol has asserted that approximately $130,000 of their loss was attributable to lost sales resulting from their inability to produce product due to the incident. A written demand or notification has been faxed to us, which will be forwarded upon receipt.

purple passage (PUR-puhl PAS-ij) noun, also purple patch, purple prose

1. A brilliant passage in an otherwise dull and uninspiring work.
2. A piece of writing marked by ornate, florid style.

[From Latin pannus purpureus (purple patch), a phrase used by poet Horace in his Ars Poetica (The Art of Poetry) to suggest a patch of royal fabric on an ordinary cloth.]

"Page after page is filled with drunken quarrels with his wife, with lies, infidelities, religious doubts, homosexual yearnings, and, above all, with his daily, desperate search for a bottle. Interspersed among these dreary horrors are purple passages about his love for his children, his dog, and his fine house."

A Gin at Mid-Morning—John Cheever: The Journals by John Cheever

Jeff,

Thank you again for your time and insights regarding our consideration of Norm Pedersen for our Los Angeles office.

After a deeper review, we’ve decided not to move forward with Norm. We foresee significant conflict issues arising from upcoming California regulatory proceedings, given Norm’s client history. Bringing him on under these circumstances wouldn’t be fair to him, as he’d likely be conflicted out of key work he'd hoped to pursue.

I truly appreciate your candor and open-mindedness throughout this process. I hesitated to trouble you, but I knew your perspective on California’s regulatory landscape would be invaluable to ensure we approached this decision thoughtfully and fairly.

Please don’t feel that you “nixed” Norm—far from it. From my first conversation with him, it seemed problematic, especially since I want to avoid situations where LeBoeuf could find itself on the opposite side from Enron in major regulatory matters. While waivers may work for commercial transactions, I couldn’t justify representing clients directly adverse to Enron’s interests in regulatory proceedings where Enron is a key participant.

As Rick may have mentioned, we have occasionally been adverse to Enron, usually due to long-standing client relationships. Rick has been gracious and understanding about these rare situations. Still, I am committed to minimizing such conflicts whenever possible, even though our firm’s size and diverse client base mean they can’t be avoided entirely.

I’ll follow up with you personally, but wanted to thank you again for your thoughtful help and support.

Mr. Lay, 
I have recently begun my 19th year at Enron, dedicating nearly two decades of my life to the company's growth and success.
Yesterday, I was one of the 4,500 "lucky" employees who was given the opportunity to stay, despite the company's drastic restructuring efforts.
Fortunately for me and my family, I also received a job offer from a reputable company, Chevron, yesterday, and I have accepted that offer, effective immediately.
Today, October 31, 2001, is my last day at Enron, and the only sadness I feel is for the thousands of good people who have been let down and let go due to the company's financial mismanagement and leadership failures.
I have a suggestion that I hope you will consider.
I feel strongly that you should promptly have the "values" banners removed from the Enron building lobby, as they have become a constant reminder of the company's broken promises and hypocrisy.
The values of communication, respect, excellence, and integrity have not been practiced by Enron's executive leadership, except by the thousands of non-executive employees who were told to live those values and genuinely believed in them.
It is a slap in the face of every employee, laid off or still here, who walks into that lobby and sees those banners hanging there, serving as a cruel reminder of the company's failed leadership and broken trust.
Sincerely,
A Former Enron Employee

Mark, Tom, and Holden, In reference to the DPR impacts of $132,000 for WAPA and $133,000 for SRP that you were expecting for the April 2024 settlements, here is an explanation of why you will not be seeing that in your PMA's: The two deals listed below, associated with April 2024 purchases for SRP and WAPA, were entered into CARP as 1 MW-month transactions, each split into 3 strips to separately show April 1, April 2, and the remainder of the month due to the transition from Pacific Standard Time (PST) to Pacific Daylight Time (PDT) at midnight on April 1.  
Deal #539126 (for WAPA): Entered as 3 strips at $2216 per strip, resulting in a $199,500 charge for the month in CARP (true financial impact was -$66,500).  
Deal #538832 (for SRP): Entered as 3 strips at $2180 per strip, resulting in a $196,200 charge for the month in CARP (true financial impact was -$65,400).  
Typically, I provide you with a report detailing the exact dollar amount you should expect to see flow through to your PMA’s based on the changes I am making in CARP. You then see the change in DPR reflected in your PMA report from Risk. When these April 2024 deals hit Settlements, we realized that CARP was calculating each of the two deals at three times their monthly value, which, since these are purchases, resulted in a negative threefold impact to your books.  
When the above positive DPR impacts did not show up in your April 2024 PMA's, we began investigating why these adjustments were missing. Here is a summary of the Risk-Settlements process: Risk values each deal on the day of liquidation. Any intra-month deal changes, even those after the day of flow, are trued up by Risk and posted as DPR adjustments. Any changes made after month-end are recognized by Settlements as a DPR variance and reported to Risk, and this will be reflected as a DPR impact in your PMA report.  
So, the question became: For these two deals, when I zeroed out two of the three strips to correct for the time change, why didn’t Settlements recognize a positive dollar amount back to your books for those two strips? Houston Settlements investigated and found that these deals were originally assigned a DPR impact of ($66,500) for WAPA and ($65,400) for SRP, matching the true single-month value, even though CARP was showing a ($199,500) and ($196,200) charge due to the three-strips setup. Heather Dunton and I researched this and determined that when Risk flashed these deals for April 2024, they recognized them as single MW-month charges, regardless of the number of strips.  
We discovered that CARP, and as a result UNIFY, was incorrectly multiplying these charges by three, due to reading each strip as a full month, rather than recognizing it as a single MW-month deal with date splits to account for the time change. The IT team in Houston is currently correcting this technical issue.  
For DPR, your books initially recognized a negative impact of ($66,500) for WAPA and ($65,400) for SRP, which is correct. Because your April 2024 DPR was already properly calculated, you will not see a subsequent adjustment or positive DPR in your PMA’s.  
I recognize this is not the positive DPR correction you anticipated, and I apologize for the earlier report and any resulting confusion. However, this process has helped us identify a technical error in CARP that will prevent similar issues in the future and reduce manual clean-up going forward.  
Thanks for your patience while we worked through this. Please let me know if you have any questions.  
Thanks,

Here's how this works in practice:

**The Setup:**
- Company A operates an upstream pipeline
- Company B operates a downstream pipeline  
- Company C is an end-user customer of Company B

**Normal Rule:**
Typically, whoever ships gas on a pipeline must own that gas (the "shipper must have title" rule).

**The Exception in Action:**
1. Company B (downstream pipeline) contracts for capacity on Company A's upstream pipeline
2. Company C (the end-user) owns gas that needs to move through both pipelines to reach them
3. Under this exception:
   - Company B acts as the "shipper" on Company A's upstream pipeline
   - BUT Company C retains ownership/title to the gas throughout the journey
   - Company B never owns the gas, even though they're booking the transportation

**Real-World Example:**
Imagine a natural gas utility in Albuquerque (Company C) that buys gas from producers in West Texas. The gas must travel through:
- An upstream interstate pipeline from the wellhead to the Texas-New Mexico border
- A downstream pipeline from the border to Albuquerque

The downstream pipeline company books capacity on the upstream pipeline to ensure reliable service, but the Albuquerque utility retains ownership of the gas molecules throughout the entire journey. This allows for more efficient capacity management while maintaining clear ownership chains for billing and regulatory purposes.

When the Commission granted Texas Eastern authority to hold capacity on  another pipeline in Texas Eastern Transmission Corporation, 74 FERC P 61,074  (1996), it stated that when a pipeline holds capacity on an upstream  pipeline, the downstream pipeline's customers may hold title to the gas  transported on the upstream pipeline.
The Commission recognized this as one  of the limited exceptions to the shipper must have title rule.
Specifically,  the Commission stated:    The downstream pipeline will not hold title to gas shipped on capacity it has  acquired on an upstream  pipeline.
Rather, shippers on the downstream pipeline will hold title to the  gas on the upstream  pipeline.
We will allow a pipeline to hold the upstream capacity; we will  not, however, allow the pipeline  to hold title to the gas being shipped.
Thus, the downstream pipeline will  be the shipper on the upstream  pipeline, but will not hold title when the gas is being shipped.
This results  in a limited exception to the rule  that a shipper must hold title to gas being shipped.
I believe that if we can address the Commission's other concerns about this  filing, they will grant a similar waiver for this transaction.
You can feel  free to pass this along to your contact at PNM.

text: It is critical to our nation's energy future to achieve robust competition in wholesale power markets in order to ensure that electricity can move most effectively from where it is produced to where it is most needed. A competitive market structure fosters innovation, drives down costs, and promotes the efficient allocation of resources, ultimately benefiting consumers and supporting economic growth. To that end, this Administration will strongly encourage the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to actively exercise jurisdiction over all aspects of electricity transmission in interstate commerce and place all uses of the grid under the same rates, terms, and conditions. This will help to eliminate barriers to entry, prevent undue discrimination, and ensure that all market participants have equal access to the grid. Furthermore, a unified and cohesive regulatory framework will facilitate the integration of renewable energy sources, energy storage, and other emerging technologies, which are essential for reducing our reliance on fossil fuels and mitigating climate change. This jurisdiction must also be extended by Congress to cover non-FERC jurisdictional power authorities, such as municipal utilities and cooperatives, to ensure that all entities operating in the wholesale market are subject to the same rules and regulations. By promoting a level playing field and encouraging competition, we can create a more efficient, reliable, and sustainable energy system that supports the needs of all Americans. Additionally, the extension of FERC's jurisdiction will also help to address issues related to grid resilience, cybersecurity, and energy infrastructure development, which are critical to maintaining the integrity and security of our energy system. Overall, a comprehensive and unified approach to regulating wholesale power markets is essential for achieving our nation's energy goals and ensuring a bright and sustainable energy future.

Tim, I strongly believe we need to move forward with this business—but only if the following conditions are met, because the consequences of getting this wrong are substantial. First, we must ensure that we are being fully and fairly compensated for both the financing and the significant underlying commodity risk. This isn’t just about hitting a number; it’s about protecting the firm from exposures that could have real and lasting impacts if mishandled. Second, it’s critical that the paper we hold is top quality—anything less introduces unacceptable vulnerability to our balance sheet. Third, we cannot afford to gamble on counterparties; we must restrict ourselves to dealing only with solid credits and demand a risk-adjusted cost of capital that accurately reflects the true risks of the underlying financing. Fourth, our ability to syndicate the capital or funds flow, should the need arise to manage liquidity, is not just a preference but a lifeline—without that flexibility, we put our entire position, and possibly our reputation, in jeopardy. Finally, it’s essential that RAC is not just informed but truly comfortable we are meeting these thresholds, since their support will be crucial if the unexpected should happen. Any transaction with embedded financing or $5M or more must be DASHED immediately—there is too much at stake to take any shortcuts. 

David, Joe, and Mark will be your vital partners as you navigate these risks; please coordinate closely with them to ensure we are not missing anything. If we manage these issues rigorously and price the risk appropriately, I believe this strategy can work. But let’s be clear—if we get this wrong, there is no cushion. The stakes are simply too high for anything less than full vigilance.

Regards

Endurance, Encouragement, Hope and Bring Home Good Fruit  I heard these words today in our Homily at church.
They seemed to jump out at me with the current situation we have all been faced with at Enron.
You have endured through a tremendous storm.
Although your colleagues have disappeared leaving you to hold the bag, although you are at the center of intense criticism and accusations from investors, shareholders and employees and although the media has been brutal, you have endured.
Your endurance, I believe, gives us the endurance, the encouragement and the hope that Enron will stabilize and be as strong as it ever was and with a much stronger foundation.
Turmoil serves only to strengthen and bring a community together.
It was true on September 11th and it can be true at Enron.
We have been shaken, but we cannot give up.
With hope anything is possible.
Enron has been my home for 20 years.
I was there when we became Enron.
The last week was extremely difficult for all. Let me show you how these words work in real life:

For example, after all the stress at work, one small thing finally hit me hard. I came in to work out on Friday morning at 5:30 a.m. and the Body Shop—our company gym—was closed. There was a note on the front door, "the Body Shop would be shutting down at 7:30 p.m. Thursday evening". Even though it might seem small compared to everything else, that was the moment it all caught up with me. I had been so strong up to this point, but after I found a place to shower, I just broke down and cried for two hours. All the events finally became too much.

But here’s where those words come alive: I found encouragement from my friends and coworkers who reached out to check on me and offered support. Their hope for the future rubbed off on me. By hanging on and not giving up, by showing up and supporting one another, we continue to bring home good fruit, just by making it through each day together despite everything.

I am blessed "for the moment", I still have a job.
I believe I would be blessed even if I didn't have a job.
I have not given up.
As long as we have you and "you can endure", I know we will all make it through this storm.
May God Bless You  Nelda Shealy

Hi Mum! 
As Ann and I left the theater after watching "Mr. Ripley", the sound of the city outside was a jarring contrast to the eerie silence of the film's final scene, which still lingered in my mind. The smell of freshly popped popcorn wafted through the air, but my appetite was suppressed by the unsettling thoughts that plagued me. I lay awake last night, the soft hum of the air conditioner and the occasional hoot of a distant owl outside my window unable to lull me into a peaceful sleep, as I wondered how the main character could have dealt with his dilemma on the boat. The rough texture of the theater's seats and the faint taste of salt from the popcorn still lingered on my skin and tongue, a reminder of the immersive experience I had just had. 
I think I need to go to the movies more often; perhaps it will help me avoid this blurring of film and reality, which can be as disorienting as walking out of a dark theater into the bright sunlight. My tendency is to really get involved when I see them on the big screen, the large format and surround sound enveloping me in the world of the film! 
Might be going to San Francisco next week, where I hope to stroll across the Golden Gate Bridge, feeling the cool mist of the Pacific Ocean on my face and listening to the sound of the seagulls overhead. I'd really like to go, to experience the vibrant sights and sounds of the city. We'll see. 
Probably I will come to Austin on Saturday, where the warm sunshine and gentle breeze will be a welcome respite from the hustle and bustle of the city, but I've not heard from the landscaper yet. I doubt they will be working on the weekend though, and I'm looking forward to a relaxing day surrounded by the sweet scent of blooming flowers and the soft texture of freshly cut grass. 
Hope you're having pretty weather as we have in Houston today, with the sun shining brightly in the sky and a gentle rustle of leaves in the trees. 
Love,

I have had several conversations with EPNG about the possibility of ENA turning back capacity to satisfy two key needs: 1) requests for new capacity in the Power Up 2000 project and 2) any possible capacity that EPNG may need to provide to satisfy incremental needs of full requirements customers as they convert billing determinants to Contract Demand quantities.

**Current Situation and Timing Constraints**

The Power Up 2000 deadline is noon, Thursday, August 2, 2001. However, EPNG did not provide for turn back in the posting that is currently on the capacity system. While we do not know how EPNG will be forced to resolve their capacity issues in the receipt point allocation proceeding, I believe that taking proactive steps now can help preserve our position.

**Our Capacity Holdings and Strategic Considerations**

We have approximately 54,000 of Block I and III capacity and 200,000 of Block III capacity. Notably, the Block II capacity is subject to PG&E recall - PG&E paid approximately $58 million for those recall rights in a settlement. This raises an interesting question: Could EPNG pay a negotiated sum of money for the remaining value of the recall rights to fund the needs of full requirement customers? I have to believe this option would be cheaper than adding new capacity.

**Recommended Action**

In order to preserve our position under either scenario, should I send a formal letter to Al Clark stating our desire to turn the capacity back? I believe that a letter can help us maintain flexibility regardless of how EPNG ultimately resolves their capacity issues.

Leslie - could you help me with the letter?

Many thanks!
Stephanie

Dear Bill,  Thank you for your offer to assist us with our modeling efforts.
I hope that we can share our analysis with you in return.
Below are some questions that we would like to understand in order to better model the ammonia industry.
In our model, we have divided the industry into production, consumption, and storage.
Storage, in particular, is a concern for us because we have very little understanding of the total storage capacity.
How much storage exists in the fields and how much is held by dealers?
Additionally, consumption is quite complex.
We are unsure how to interpret the logistics behind what truly drives consumption.
I know that corn requires more nitrogen than any other crop.
However, I am uncertain what other factors influence the decision to use ammonia as a fertilizer.
How price elastic is the consumption, among other things.
To organize the questions, I would like to summarize them as follows:  How much ammonia storage exists in the US?
How is storage distributed among producers, dealers, and farmers?
From the farmers' perspective, what are the most important decision factors for using ammonia, and in what quantities?
From the manufacturer's perspective, what factors are considered when starting production, and what factors come into play when shutting production down?
I assume it is not solely the price differential between ammonia and natural gas.
Bill, I think it might be easier to discuss these questions directly, as there may not be straightforward answers to any of them.
I will call you in the afternoon, but please feel free to call me at 713-345-1763.

We experienced issues with a few websites on Saturday evening and Sunday afternoon. Unfortunately, I was not available to address the problem at that time. Upon returning home on Sunday evening, I investigated and found that the following data cycles were not scraped: 
- 05/19/2001: Kern Cycles 2 and 4, Transco Cycle 2
- 05/20/2001: KM Cycle 2, Transcolorado Cycle 2, Kern Cycle 3, Northwest Cycle 6
I have reset all the jobs, but I suspect that data loss has occurred for these cycles. The 1line Williams site, a known problem source, is likely responsible for the misses in Northwest, Kern, and Transco. This site is still experiencing issues, so it should be monitored over the next couple of days. When I attempted to access it, I encountered various errors and noticed a different site layout, which could potentially affect the page we extract data from. Currently, "capture" jobs for Kern, Northwest, and Transco are failing due to "Internal Server Errors." Hopefully, this is a temporary issue and the sites will stabilize soon. On a positive note, the Jaguar system functioned as expected, retrying the jobs until they seemed futile and then sending reports to notify us of the problems.
source_text:
We appeared to have some problems with a couple of web sites on Saturday evening / Sunday afternoon.
Unfortunately, I was not home at that time to be able to reset them.
Upon returning home this evening (Sunday), I took a look and the following cycles did not get scraped:  05/19/2001 Kern, Cycles 2 & 4 Transco Cycle 2  05/20/2001 KM (Points R & D, Segments) Cycle 2 Transcolorado (R & D, Segments) Cycle 2 Kern, Cycle 3 Northwest, Cycle 6  I have reset all of the jobs...unfortunately, I suspect there is data loss for the above cycles.
One of our "old friends", the 1line Williams site, is definately the cause for the Northwest, Kern and Transco misses.
This site still appears to be having problems, so it should be checked for the next couple of days.
When trying to go to it tonight, I received various errors, and the general site layout appeared different since the last time I looked (this means they could potentially change the layout of the page we get data from as well).
As I write this, "capture" jobs for Kern, Northwest, and Transco are failing due to "Internal Server Errors".
Hopefully, this is a short-term problem, and these sites will stabilize soon.
The bright side of this story is that the Jaguar system did exactly what it was supposed to do when these problems occur...it retried until the job attempts seemed fruitless, then it sent pages to report the problems.
Chris

Bill,

As per our conversation today, I am sending you an outline of what we intend to be doing in Ercot and in particular on the real-time desk.

**Market Structure and Fundamentals**
For 2002 Ercot is split into 4 zones with TCRs between 3 of the zones. The zones are fairly diverse from a supply/demand perspective. Ercot has an average load of 38,000 MW, a peak of 57,000 MW with a breakdown of 30% industrial, 30% commercial and 40% residential.

**Business Development and Timeline**
There are already several successful aggregators that are looking to pass on their wholesale risk to a credit-worthy QSE (Qualified Scheduling Entity). Our expectation is that we will be a fully qualified QSE by mid-March with the APX covering us up to that point. Additionally, there are more than 10 industrial loads with greater than 150 MW concentrated at single meters offering good opportunities for real-time optimization. Our intent is to secure one of these within the next 2 months.

**Products and Market Operations**
Our initial on-line products will include a bal day and next day financial product. (There is no day ahead settlement in this market). The initial job opportunity will involve an analysis of the real-time market as it stands today with a view to trading around our information. This will also drive which specific assets we approach to manage.

**Competitive Advantages**
I have included some price history to show the hourly volatility and a business plan to show the scope of the opportunity. In addition, we have very solid analytics that use power flow simulations to map out expected outcomes in the real-time market. Furthermore, as we are loosely combining our Texas gas and Ercot power desks our information flow will be superior and I believe we will have all the tools needed for a successful real-time operation.

Let me know if you have any further questions.

Thanks,

When we conduct emissions testing at C/S No. 3, Luepp, it is important to consider both the potential benefits and drawbacks.

A key benefit is the valuable information that Steve and the team will collect during the testing, which seems to be a very useful tool. Additionally, this facility does not currently have specific emission limits associated with its permit. There is also a possibility of reducing emissions fees if this investigation demonstrates that actual emissions from the units are significantly lower than what was previously stated in the permit application.

On the other hand, a potential downside is that the data we gather may indicate that the emissions fees we have paid to date have underestimated the actual emissions submitted in our permit application, and we would likely be required to pay the difference covering the period from 1996 to the present. There is also a risk of enforcement action from local authorities.

I mention these to ensure everyone is aware of both the positive and negative possibilities of carrying out this study. When we submitted emission estimates in the permit application, we included a defensible margin to account for variations in temperature, humidity, engine age, and maintenance conditions.

Finally, we still do not know exactly what emissions these three units produce, as they have never been tested before. This uncertainty itself is a key reason to move forward with testing, so we can avoid situations similar to what occurred at Atoka No. 3 several months ago.

Summary: Upon becoming a member of the New England Power Pool (NEPOOL), EESI opted to fulfill the Financial Assurance Policy requirement by issuing Performance Bond(s) through Fireman's Fund Insurance Company, which initially provided a Performance Bond in the amount of $8,000,000. On October 12, 2001, EESI received a letter from ISO New England, dated October 10, 2001, stating that the current Performance Bond was insufficient and that an increase to $11,703,018.75 was necessary to cover EESI's current activity level.

Through subsequent telephone conversations with ISO New England, EESI was informed that to avoid a Financial Assurance Default, the matter needed to be resolved within ten days of the date of the October 10, 2001 letter, which was October 19, 2001. By October 16, 2001, EESI had requested an increase in the NEPOOL Performance Bond to $20,000,000; however, the company encountered delays in working with the bond issuer.

On October 19, 2001, EESI's Credit Department personnel faxed a copy of the request to the bond company for revisions to the Performance Bond to ISO New England personnel, indicating that EESI was working diligently to resolve the matter. Despite these efforts, EESI was unable to comply with the October 19, 2001 deadline to resolve the Financial Assurance Default due to delays with the bond company.

Dear Uncle Ken and Aunt Linda,

I hope this letter finds you both doing well despite the challenging circumstances you're currently facing. I want to start by saying how sorry I am for everything that's been happening to you both. My heart goes out to you, and I hope God will provide you with the strength and guidance you need to navigate these difficult times.

I've been thinking about you constantly, Uncle Ken, and the struggles your company is facing. I can only imagine how tough it must be for you, and I want you to know that I'm praying for you every day. I hope God will help you find a way to overcome the obstacles and come out even stronger on the other side.

I've wanted to call you so many times to offer my support and listen to your concerns, but I didn't want to distract you from the valuable time you need to focus on resolving the issues at hand. I know how precious your time is, and I didn't want to add to your stress.

Recently, my Political Science teacher discussed the Enron scandal in class, and I immediately thought of you, Uncle Ken. I was the only one in the class who knew about Enron and its current situation, so I raised my hand to share my knowledge. It was interesting to see how the concepts we're learning in class are applicable to real-life situations like yours. I also used Enron as an example in my trial essay for my writing class, and I hope you don't mind that I drew from your experience to illustrate my points.

On a more personal note, Aunt Linda, I wanted to share some exciting news with you. I've started dating someone new, his name is Zeke, and we've been together for over a month and two weeks now. He's an amazing person, and I think you'll really like him. When I get a chance, I'll send you a picture of him so you can see for yourself.

I hope all is well with both of you, despite the challenges you're facing. I want you to know that I'm thinking of you always and sending all my love. I miss you both so much, and I look forward to the day when we can catch up in person.

Take care of yourselves, and don't hesitate to reach out if you need anything. God bless you both, and I'll be praying for your well-being every day.

With all my love and best wishes,
Love

**Main Issue: F&J Law Firm Conflict of Interest and Waiver Agreement**

Bob and I just spoke with Steve Susman about F&J's proposed ethical waiver. Here are the key points:

**Susman's Position:**
1. F&J cannot simply return our files and represent Arthur Anderson due to the "hot potato" rule
2. He doesn't object to F&J representing potentially adverse parties in his cases
3. He rejects F&J's broad advance waiver proposal as ineffective, but would agree to specific waivers once we know who F&J wants to represent
4. He recognizes we may need to accept unfavorable terms to secure F&J for the new Mariner matter

**Our Internal Positions:**
- Bob: Get the best deal possible, but accept F&J's terms if they won't budge
- Britt: Certain changes are essential:
  - Only current F&J-represented Enron entities should sign (not Enron Corp. binding all entities)
  - Remove language about post-Dynegy merger agreements
  - Will accept the advance waiver language if these changes are made

**Next Steps:**
Time is critical - Mariner needs a decision today. I'm prepared to contact Dutton immediately to negotiate these terms and send a proposed draft if he agrees in principle.

Please advise how to proceed.

Britt
source_text:
Bob and I just spoke with Steve Susman.
I tried to mention the points you asked.
Here are his comments:  	1.
F&J probably could not simply send us our files back and put itself in a position to be adverse to us with Arthur Anderson.
Susman believes that there is a "hot potato" rule that prevents F&J from doing so.
2.
That being said, Susman doesn't care if F&J represents Arthur Anderson or anyone else potentially adverse to us in the actions he is handling.
3.
Susman would not, however, agree to a broad advance ethical waiver, as proposed by F&J.
He does not believe such waivers are effective.
Susman would agree to a waiver once we were advised who F&J wanted to represent.
I don't know whether F&J would agree to this or not.
4.
Susman recognizes that we cannot force F&J to take on the new Mariner matter, and that this is ultimately a risk/benefit decision for us to make, and that we may have to agree to terms that we otherwise wouldn't agree to.
Parenthetically, I have received no comments on F&J's proposed waiver letter.
Under the circumstances, from his standpoint, Bob is inclined for us to get the best deal on the waiver letter that we can with F&J, but that if F&J won't budge, that we take something along the lines of what they have given us (Bob, let me know if I have mischaracterized your thoughts).
From my standpoint, I unfortunately think there are some parts of the letter that we must have changed.
This would be to the extent that the letter purports to have Enron Corp. agree to bind all the Enron entities, and to the extent that it involves Enron's agreement to what will happen after the Dynegy merger (as I set out in my earlier e-mail).
My recommendation would be, as set forth in my earlier e-mail, that only the Enron entities currently being represented by F&J sign it and be bound by it, and to remove the language regarding what Enron would agree to after the Dynegy merger.
I also find the advance ethical waiver language repugnant, but could agree to it if the other modifications mentioned could be made.
I do not know whether F&J would be willing to make these changes or not.
Our biggest problem right now is time-management.
I know that Mariner wanted to make a decision by today as to who to use.
I am willing to confer with Dutton ASAP to see what F&J would agree to, and if he can agree in principle, to send him a proposed draft agreement.
I believe he is out of the office but is checking his voice-mail.
Please let me know what you want me to do.
Britt

Ken, I can't begin to tell you how much I admire you.

I still trust you, I still believe in you, I still think you are making the right decisions for the future of this company.

Do you know why?

Because I absolutely love the Enron that you built.

Enron believed in me when no one else would. When I was just a divorced mother of two young children, struggling to make ends meet, Enron saw potential where others saw only limitations.

Enron took a chance on me when I had nothing more than a community college degree and a determination to succeed. While other companies passed me over for positions, Enron opened its doors and gave me the opportunity to prove myself.

Enron made me into what I am today. The company didn't just give me a job – it gave me a career, a future, and the financial security I never thought possible for someone like me.

I'm a single mom that started in the back office seven years ago, processing invoices and filing paperwork for twelve dollars an hour. Through Enron's mentorship programs and internal promotion policies, I worked my way up onto the Weather Derivatives Desk, where I learned to analyze complex meteorological data and develop trading strategies around temperature fluctuations and seasonal patterns. From there, I earned my securities license and was promoted to the Natural Gas Trading Floor in Energy Risk Management, where I now manage a portfolio worth millions of dollars and oversee risk assessment for our Gulf Coast operations.

Where else could anyone get these sort of opportunities? Where else could a single mother with no connections, no advanced degree, and no Wall Street pedigree rise from a back-office clerk to a senior risk management position in less than a decade?

NO-WHERE.

Enron didn't care that I didn't go to Harvard or Wharton. They cared about my work ethic, my analytical mind, and my hunger to learn. They invested in training programs, sent me to conferences in Chicago and New York, and paired me with mentors who believed in my potential. They promoted based on merit, not politics or connections.

I'm so proud of this company. I'm proud of the innovative energy solutions we've developed, the market-making role we've played in deregulation, and the entrepreneurial spirit that drives everything we do. I'm proud to tell people I work for Enron.

I know that it will rise from the ashes and be reborn into something new. Just as this company transformed the energy industry, it will transform itself. The vision, the innovation, the commitment to excellence – these core values that built Enron will carry us through this difficult time.

Warmest regards,

Mr. Lay: I would like to take this opportunity to thank you, from the bottom of my heart, for all the hard work you are trying to do, and continue to try to do, on behalf of those of us who will always be proud to call Enron 'home'.
I joined Enron a short 11 months ago, and moved from the New Hampshire Public Utilities Commission to do so, and will likely never regret taking the leap.
I have learned so much of value here, have broadened my horizons by orders of magnitude, and worked with so many top quality people from around the world, that I cannot help but feel better for the experience.
I have enjoyed professional success and satisfaction beyond my wildest dreams with Enron, and will always carry the confidence of having succeeded amongst the best there are in the global business community.
I cannot help but feel terrible that so many wish to lay blame where it does not belong, but I can only assume that in times of crisis, laying blame may soothe nerves and provide some comfort.
Know that there are still many at Enron who admire the enormity of what you have done for energy markets worldwide, and have never doubted your integrity.
As I, like many others, inevitably move on in these coming weeks and months, I will leave with mainly good memories, and of course, the regret that such an awesome organism like Enron could not survive forever.
My prayers and thoughts are with you as you work so hard at preserving our core businesses, and again, thank you for giving me the opportunity to have been a part of this global team.

Utilities Biweekly Report
A news service for energy professionals
October 17, 2001

To Remove, Substitute or Add an email address to our list, please send brief message to msid@ieee.org

**REGULATORY ACTIONS**

FERC Rejects Reasons for Suppliers Higher Prices

In an order issued on October 5, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) rejected the cost justifications of several power suppliers that sold wholesale electricity above the proxy market-clearing price during July 2001. The electricity had been sold into the California Independent System Operator (CA-ISO) and Western Systems Coordinating Council (WSCC).

FERC said that the justifications from Dynegy, Reliant Energy, Mirant, and Williams Energy were "either untimely filed and/or unsupported" and has ordered refunds on those transactions. The four suppliers submitted their cost justifications in compliance with FERC's April 26 order that established price mitigation for sales into the CA-ISO's spot markets starting in late May. That order required power suppliers and generators who submitted bids above the market-clearing price to file a justification for the higher prices within seven days of the end of the month in which the sale occurred.

FERC did not disclose how much money would be refunded since the four companies requested that the matter be treated confidentially. In a separate but related case, FERC Administrative Law Judge Bruce Birchman has until March 8 to issue a report on whether California is entitled to refunds of nearly $9 billion for wholesale power purchases when prices skyrocketed in the past year. The report's recommendations will be considered by FERC commissioners for further action.

**NUCLEAR SAFETY CONCERNS**

Nuclear Plant Had Long List of Failings

Inexperience, sloppy work habits and poor maintenance increased the chances of dangerous accidents at the Bruce nuclear power station in Ontario, the world's largest atomic facility, according to a secret report obtained by The Globe and Mail.

The report was compiled in 1998 by a group of highly trained, independent nuclear experts from the World Association of Nuclear Operators (WANO), an industry advisory group based in Atlanta. It was given to Ontario Power Generation, the provincially owned utility, the following year.

**Operational Safety Issues**

Among the report's key findings regarding operational practices:
- Some operators were unaware of such important topics as the time it would take for water in reactors to begin boiling away if flows of cooling water were blocked
- Nuclear-plant operators disconnected warning alarms they found too noisy

This morning I raised a concern regarding TW's sale of excess fuel at downstream points.
Here's the problem: the tariff requires shippers to tender fuel to us at their receipt points.
With rare exceptions, those receipt points are not at the California border.
Pipeline regulations mandate that companies unbundle transportation from storage.
They also require that pipelines that make gas sales do so at the furthest upstream point on their pipeline.
That latter requirement means that if a pipeline buys gas at point "x", it should resell the gas at point "x" and not haul the gas to point "y" and then sell it there as a delivered (i.e., bundled) product.
My concern this morning was that our receipt of fuel gas in the San Juan or Permian regions and shipment of that gas to the California border for sale arguably violates the unbundling requirement (because the California border sale is a bundled combination of the sale and the transportation of the gas to the downstream location) or the "furthest upstream point" requirement or both.
Susan and my recollection was that when ECS wanted to receive the Gallup fuel deliveries at a point other than Permian pool, we made them sign a transport contract to move the gas to where they wanted it.
I haven't confirmed that recollection but I am recalling that we told Courtney that we couldn't just move our fuel gas around wherever we wanted it--we needed someone to pay us to transport it.

To make delicious chicken tacos, you'll need the following ingredients: one package of chicken breasts (containing four skinless and boneless breasts), a package of chicken taco seasoning, four to five tomatillos, one small onion, one jalapeno pepper, three to four cloves of garlic, and five sprigs of cilantro. You'll also need salt and pepper to taste. For toppings, consider using cheese, onion, tomatoes, lettuce, sour cream, and picante sauce.

Start by boiling the chicken in water along with the taco seasoning, onion, and bell peppers. After about 20-25 minutes, or once the chicken is cooked through, remove it from the water and shred it in a skillet. 

In a blender, combine the tomatillos, onion, jalapeno pepper, garlic, cilantro, and half a cup of the chicken broth. Blend the mixture until it's well combined. Then, pour the vegetable mixture into the skillet with the shredded chicken and add the chicken taco seasoning. Mix everything together and let it simmer over low heat for 20 minutes.

Finally, serve the chicken mixture in tortillas and offer your choice of toppings, such as cheese, onion, tomatoes, lettuce, sour cream, and picante sauce.

1. Term: What terms are we willing to accept?
2. Availability: We require a single computation for availability, regardless of the power source (market or facility). Is "forced outage" the correct concept, given our desire for discretion and the application of liquidated damages (LD) structure even when power comes from the market? Note VEPCO's insertion of a new default event under 7.1 for failure to deliver energy when the facility is not in a forced outage. Is the liquidated damages language still acceptable? LDs should apply regardless of the scheduled power source, with no cost of cover for market power.
3. Our position is that Contract Capacity is set at contract signing and adjusted (if necessary) based on performance tests, but not subject to adjustment thereafter. The same applies to the demand charge. What is the correct Capacity number? Is there a benefit to Enron in having a correction curve exhibit?
4. Failure to complete the facility has been suggested as a termination event. Is the September deadline sufficient?
5. We need the flexibility to supply power from either or both sources (market and facility) during a day, but this does not grant us the right to change the schedule after it has been set.
6. Note the revised Start Up definition (as suggested by VEPCO) and its application. We currently reject the 50% requirement, subject to further explanation.
7. The construction of the facility is now mandatory (2.3).
8. We need to define commercial operation.
9. Confirm that Enron has adequate protection from interconnection failures or delays.
10. Day-ahead scheduling (3.4): Are we ready to commit to this?
11. What is the agreed-upon number of start-ups (2.3e)?
12. Force majeure: Ensure consistency with the interconnection agreement and provide relief for certain equipment failures. Is the concept logically developed throughout the document? Note the distinction between market and facility power in the force majeure language.
13. Dispute resolution: Should we opt for arbitration or litigation/venue? Should we specify Virginia law?
14. Change in law: Should we counter with a Change in Law (CIL) as a termination event?
15. Exhibit A: Heather is currently working on this.
