Dear Valued Customer,

We are writing to provide an important update regarding the upcoming unbundling of gas services for SoCalGas customers, a move mandated by the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) to foster greater competition and customer choice in the natural gas market.

**What is Unbundling?**
Currently, SoCalGas provides both the natural gas commodity and its delivery to your home or business. Unbundling means these two services will be separated. SoCalGas will continue to be your trusted provider for the safe and reliable delivery of natural gas through our pipelines. However, you will soon have the option to choose your natural gas supplier (the source of the gas itself) from a list of approved third-party providers, similar to how electricity choice programs operate in some areas.

**Key Aspects of the Plan:**
*   **Customer Choice:** You will gain the ability to select an independent gas supplier, potentially offering different pricing structures, renewable gas options, or other benefits.
*   **Continued Reliability:** SoCalGas will remain responsible for maintaining the gas pipeline infrastructure, responding to emergencies, and ensuring the continued safe and reliable delivery of gas to your meter, regardless of your chosen supplier.
*   **Bill Changes:** Your monthly bill will likely reflect separate charges for gas delivery (from SoCalGas) and gas commodity (from your chosen supplier, or SoCalGas if you opt not to switch).

**Proposed Timeline:**
While the specific dates are still being finalized and are subject to regulatory approvals, we anticipate a phased rollout of the unbundling program. Initial pilot programs or informational campaigns are expected to begin in **late 2024**, with full implementation and customer choice options becoming available across our service territory in **2025**. We are committed to providing ample notice and resources to help you understand your options.

**What You Need To Do:**
At this time, no immediate action is required from you. We encourage you to:
*   **Stay Informed:** We will be launching a dedicated section on our website (SoCalGas.com/Unbundling) and will send further communications with more detailed information, including a list of approved suppliers and instructions on how to make an informed choice.
*   **Review Your Usage:** Understanding your current gas consumption can help you evaluate future offers from suppliers.

Our goal is to ensure a smooth transition and empower you with more choices for your natural gas service. We appreciate your patience and cooperation as we implement these important changes.

Sincerely,

The SoCalGas Team

Guys, some of you may have noticed a discrepancy in today's reports: while a meter's flow value for 5/1/2000 is visible, the MDT column shows "na" on the daily report. "na" also appears in the historical report for the May average.

This can be confusing (I was confused initially myself, even as the program's author!). You might wonder why the average isn't shown as today's value, especially when there's only one day's data available.

The simple answer is that these values are pulled from different cycles. The programming logic is designed to grab the flow value from the *latest successful cycle*, but it *always* uses the *last cycle* when calculating averages. This situation occurs when the last cycle is not yet available at the time the report is generated.

Fortunately, this only happens on the first day of each month. Please help explain this "discrepancy" to anyone who might raise questions about it.

Curricular Review Task Force (CRTF) Report # 9 (October 1, 2001)  The Curriculum Review Task Force held its first meeting for the academic year on August 23, 2001.
We reviewed the work done last May to tie up loose ends and to plan the work for the year.
During the intensive work sessions in the last week of May, the eight faculty members of the Task Force (including the Chair) had made detailed presentations to our group on eight topics related to the Curriculum Review (Please see my last report for details).
It was decided that these members would write a summary of their presentations, including their cited references, and circulate them to the other members of the Task Force.
After reviewing these summaries, and remembering the strategic curricular initiatives collectively decided on by our faculty and staff during the Purser-Gans Conference, each Task Force member was asked to come up with five Educational Goals which would guide our future work.
Meanwhile, it had been decided in consultation with the Faculty Senate that the Fall Faculty/Staff Conference would focus on the Curricular Review.
The Task Force had decided last May that the first two curricular initiatives to be considered are (1) Reinvestment in Pedagogy and (2) Communication Across the Curriculum.
These two topics became the key themes for the Faculty/Staff Conference.
The Task Force met with the Conference Planning Group on August 20 and it was agreed that the small group discussions will be led by seven Task Force members.
The Faculty Conference held on August 23 was very productive in providing valuable input for the work of the Task Force.
In a general sense the Conference gave a vote of confidence for the work and approach of the CRTF.
We have taken detailed notes of the discussions in the small groups and the plenary session.
On September 12th and 19th, the Task Force held intensive work sessions in the Boone House from 5:30 to 9:00 p.m. Each member, as agreed earlier, brought a list of five Educational Goals and after a lengthy discussion we have arrived at six educational goals and a list of operational ends for each of them.
These goals focus on the competencies to be developed by our students and the learning outcomes of our academic program.
After these are finalized, we will arrange an open meeting to discuss them with our faculty.
On September 24, the Task Force met with the Assessment Committee and Dr. Susan Holm, Chair of the MFL department.
The Assessment Committee discussed with us its plans and the list of eight Assessment Review Questions prepared by the Committee.
Dr. Holm discussed the role of foreign language learning in the liberal arts education, the recent changes in MFL majors/minors/concentration and her department=s plans for further changes.
The details of these discussions will be available in our minutes which will be posted in the public folders later this week.
To access this folder, please go to Public Folders, All Public Folders, Documents, College, Curricular Review Task Force.
We are planning to meet with other departments in the near future.
Thanks.
Raj Ambrose, Chair Curriculum Review Task Force.

The following items were discussed in this week's ETS and Corporate Change Control Items:

Sept. 24 - From 12:00 a.m. through 10/07 at 11:45 p.m., Enron Network Services is implementing a moratorium on all network changes one week prior through one week after the first move of users to Enron Center South. This moratorium will probably be limited to routing changes, no new networks, no changes to existing networks, etc. No impact to ETS networks is expected.

Oct. 5 - From 9:00 - 11:00 p.m., Enron Network Services will split the two 8 port gig channels from ECS to ECN into four 4 port gig channels. This change will fully mesh the ECS core. No impact is expected.

No impact to ETS is expected.

**EDI and Unix System Updates:**

Oct. 4 - From 9:00 a.m. - 6:00 p.m., the EDI team will replace the backup EDI server located in Omaha. The existing server will be de-commissioned and the new server will take over the DNS and IP address of the old server. No impact is expected as this server is used for disaster recovery.

Oct. 4 - From 11:00 p.m. through 10/5 at 2:00 a.m., the Unix team will rename the edinet.enron.com and ecnet.enron.com systems. During last Saturday's EDI change, the DNS entries were changed but the actual servers were not changed to reflect their new names. They will also install patches to the machines during the maintenance. This change will result in a total disruption of service to EDI Web access only. EDI will not be affected.

**Messaging and Communication Systems:**

Oct. 5 - From 9:00 p.m. through 10/6 at 1:00 a.m., the Messaging team will reboot all Corp and EI Notes servers. No impact to ETS users is expected.

**Application and Database Maintenance:**

Oct. 5 - From 4:00 - 6:00 p.m., the Monitoring group will bring up the new ITContacts site and disable the old. We are currently not using this site but there are plans to access it in the future. No impact is expected.

Oct. 5 - From 7:00 - 8:00 p.m., the Corp server team will perform maintenance on the HR-DB-4 server to add more disk space. This change will result in a disruption of service to all HR Global applications including eHRonline, GCS, GIS, expertfinder, etc.

Drew, we've encountered a significant claim from our consultant, Mark Baldwin of IGS. He's demanding an incentive fee for the Gallup Expansion agreement, a dispute that could cost us up to $200,000 and requires careful handling to protect our interests and, ideally, preserve our working relationship. Here’s the situation:

Our consulting agreement with IGS (which has now terminated) provided for a flat fee, plus an incentive fee calculated using the net present value of any contract "identified by IGS" and entered into during the term of the consulting agreement.
During the term of the agreement, TW entered into its Gallup Expansion agreement with Southern.
IGS is now claiming it brought in the deal and so is entitled to an incentive fee.
While it is undisputed that Mark discussed the deal with Southern, Southern was also on Lorraine's list of shippers to contact for Gallup Expansion capacity.
Also, the capacity was posted for all to see.
So, while Mark can certainly claim he "identified" the deal, he was not alone in doing so.
Steve is going to call Mark in response to his letter (after he talks to Lorraine to verify facts).
Our thinking is that if we offer IGS some money they will be happy.
We would really like to preserve what has been a good working relationship with this consultant.
On the other hand, I think we could probably take the position that they are not entitled to any incentive fee.
However, since the contract is silent as to whether IGS has to be the only party bringing in the deal in order to qualify for the incentive fee, this position is not as strong as I'd like it to be, and IGS might sue TW.
The amount in dispute could be as much as $200,000, depending on what rate we use in calculating net present value.
If you have any problem with our offering to pay part of the incentive fee to IGS, let me know.
I think it will be very important for Steve not to admit that Mark helped in any way in getting the deal -- just in case they do

Subject: Update on Assembly "Edison MOU" Proposal and Pending Legislative Action

Dear Colleagues,

I hope this message finds you well. I wanted to provide you with an important update regarding the Edison Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) proposal currently under consideration by the Assembly.

As of today's date, the Edison MOU has successfully passed through the initial committee review phase with a favorable recommendation. The proposal, which outlines the framework for enhanced cooperation between our municipal utilities and Edison Electric Company, received bipartisan support during yesterday's session.

Key developments include:

• The Finance Subcommittee has approved the budgetary allocations outlined in Section 4.2 of the MOU
• Legal review has been completed with minor language modifications recommended
• Public comment period has been extended through the end of this month to ensure adequate stakeholder input
• Three additional co-sponsors have joined the initiative

Pending legislative action items:
- Full Assembly floor vote scheduled for the first week of next month
- Senate referral expected immediately following Assembly passage
- Governor's office has indicated preliminary support pending final review

I will continue to monitor the progress closely and will provide updates as significant developments occur. Please feel free to reach out if you have any questions or require additional details regarding specific aspects of the proposal.

Best regards,

[Your Name]
Legislative Affairs Coordinator

Adding to Kristin's update, here's the summary of a meeting that just occured  with Assembly leadership staff and industry on the Assembly's latest version  of an "Edison MOU":  The Speaker's staffer said that if he had to bet at this time, he would bet  that the Assembly would not convene on Friday.
He also said that, if it doesn't happen on Friday, nothing will happen until  they get back from recess on the 20th of August.
The Assembly will let folks know by tonight or first thing tomorrow whether  they intend to move forward with a vote on Friday or recess.
From the most recent proposal released today by the Assembly leadership, it  appears that the centrist Democrats are prevailing.
The proposal: Retains Direct Access (though they said that they are continuing to be  pressured by the Treasurer, who wants DA suspended due to the bond issuance) Places 80% of Edison's past debt with large customers (leaving 20% with small  customers, which business customers or strenuously opposing).
Eliminates all references to any purchase, or option to purchase, Edison's  transmission.
(They said there simply ain't the votes to buy, or consider  buying, Edison's transmission in the Assembly) Maintains the Senate provision, which would pay the banks, pay the QFs, but  place with Edison the risk of figuring out how to pay the $1billion owed to  suppliers.
(Even the munis are begining to complain about those provisions.)
Creates a tradeable, renewable portfolio standard (conceptually similar to  the one created in Texas).
The new bill is created by 1) amending SB78 and 2) gutting a different bill  passed from the Senate to the Assembly, SB39, and replacing it with the new  version of 82XX.
The two would go together to create the Assembly's newest  proposal.
If this bill gets voted out of the Assembly, it will likely have a difficult  time getting the votes necessary to pass in the Senate, since the Senate has  considered and rejected several provisions currently included in the Assembly  version.
Will report back on whether the Assembly's going forward or adjourning for  recess as soon as we hear.
Best,

This ensures we meet our environmental obligations and offset our project's impact. 3) We'll present the findings from surveys conducted where the Rogas project will be built, demonstrating our due diligence in checking for sensitive areas.

Permission to lay the Rogas pipeline above ground was approved by the Office of the State Fire Marshall, Pipeline Safety Division. This allows us a specific construction method. We've applied for construction approval from 8 city, county, state, and federal agencies for the 9-mile system of three pipelines. This is the only agency approval received so far, highlighting the multi-layered permit process.

We secured environmental acre credits from Aera for the Rogas pipeline construction. Aera, an oil company, has large land holdings from which we could purchase these offsets. Given the tight project timeline and the risk of not getting credits fast enough from Fish & Game, EOTT bought Aera credits to guarantee we had the necessary environmental offsets for the Rogas project. This was a major win, as it streamlines a significant permitting hurdle.

The initial draft of the baseline noise survey for the new turbine installations in Arizona was received. We'll need to make changes because the contractor made errors and assumptions that don't accurately reflect the noise reduction measures Transwestern will implement.

The Navajo Nation has requested an onsite survey at compressor stations 3 and 4 on the reservation to check for endangered plants and animals and any historical or cultural sites. A contractor has been notified, and these surveys will be completed by 3/12.

The key F-1 environmental report for the federal FERC permit application will be submitted to Donna by this Friday. Air permit applications for compressor stations 1 and 2 have been started. A meeting with the EPA in San Francisco is set for 3/20 to discuss how to get air permits for our facilities on the reservation, a complex process involving multiple jurisdictions. After this meeting, we expect to submit applications to both the Navajo air permitting agency and the EPA within a week. Air permits are generally expected within 5-7 months after submission.

During a conference call this week, a proposal was submitted to remove the existing backup generators and replace them with two new, more efficient units at each location. This upgrade will delay air application submittal by 3-4 days, assuming no major issues arise. A key decision point is that one of the new generators might possibly be a wind turbine, which would be a significant step towards renewable energy for these facilities.

Dear ST_SW Traders,  

FYI - There was a cut on deal # 622350.1 on June 2, 2001 for HE 11. It was a real time cut that reduced the schedule from 40 MW to 25 MW, representing a significant 37.5% reduction in our planned delivery.

Mirant is at fault for the cut. Our up-stream is PAC, and the original transmission path was from PAC through Mirant to WAPA. The cut occurred during peak operating hours when transmission capacity is most valuable and alternative arrangements are difficult to secure on short notice.

We originally thought that this got booked out between Mirant and WAPA, but when I spoke with Kathy yesterday, she informed me that there was no bookout and that they want to cut the schedule. This creates additional complexity as we cannot simply transfer the obligation but must actually reduce our delivery commitment.

The people involved during the cut were Geir at EPMI (representing our trading desk), Bob at PAC (our upstream transmission provider), Emily at Mirant (the party causing the curtailment), and Jackie for WAPA (Jackie is a control area dispatcher, so she cannot do bookouts for WAPA, hence there was no bookout). I have documented timestamps and communication records from all parties involved to support our position that Mirant initiated and is responsible for this curtailment.

We have agreed that to cut the schedule will be the best for now given the operational constraints and the inability to arrange alternative transmission on such short notice. However, this decision was made under duress due to real-time operating conditions, not as a voluntary commercial decision on our part.

They do not plan on charging us liquidated damages (she's checking with her boss to make sure), which is appropriate given that Mirant caused the curtailment. I have requested written confirmation of this commitment to avoid any future disputes. Additionally, I have preserved all communication records and OASIS transmission data showing the curtailment originated from Mirant's system constraints.

We will just reduce the schedules to 25 MW for HE 11. This will result in a 15 MW shortfall that we may need to replace in the spot market if our counterparty requires delivery. The financial impact could be significant depending on real-time pricing during HE 11.

It is up to you if you want to charge liquidated damages to Mirant for the spread, but I recommend we pursue this given their clear responsibility for the curtailment and the market disruption it has caused. We have strong documentation supporting our case, including the timeline of events, communication records, and confirmation that the curtailment originated from Mirant's operational decisions rather than any force majeure event.

Just wanted to let you know and get your input on how aggressively we should pursue compensation for this curtailment and whether we should implement additional safeguards for future transactions involving Mirant as an intermediary transmission provider.

Virginia

On November 14, 2001, SCE filed an advice to establish the ratemaking necessary to implement a number of regulatory components included in its October 2nd Settlement with the Commission   The settlement agreement described the operation a new account termed the PROACT that the Commission will establish by order.
The advice letter provides the structure and operation of the PROACT, The beginning balance of the PROACT will consists of the unrecovered procurement related obligation as of September 1, 2001.
Beginning on Sept. 1, on a monthly basis, the following amounts will be recorded in the PROACT: (1) SCE's Surplus (recorded revenues minus recoverable costs); (2) all refunds related to procurement related liabilities; (3) securitization proceeds, (4) interest expense.
The advice letter provides a detailed explanation as to how SCE's surplus and recoverable costs will be calculated.
In addition, the advice letter addresses settlement rates.
SCE notes that, under the Settlement, the Commission agreed to maintain electric retail rates for retail customers at no less than the Settlement Rates during the Repayment Period.
Settlement Rates are defined in the Settlement as " gross electric retail rates (including surcharges)".

Dear Vince,

Arthur Warga and I have been developing the curriculum for several educational programs that will be offered by the Energy Markets Institute, which we discussed with you this summer.

I am attaching tentative curricula for two key programs we are planning: (1) a graduate certificate in Energy Finance, and (2) a 5-year BBA/MS program in Energy Finance.

The main idea is to establish rigorous academic pathways that will build expertise for both new and experienced professionals in the energy industry. 

The graduate certificate is a 5-course, for-credit program designed for individuals who already have a background in finance, economics, statistics, and mathematics. This program covers accounting issues specific to the energy sector, the fundamentals of energy sources and the organization and regulation of the energy industry, forecasting and time-series econometric methods, the basics of financial engineering and derivatives, real-options and project analysis as they apply to energy, and energy derivatives and risk management.

The 5-year BBA/MS program is more ambitious and is intended to provide a comprehensive and rigorous foundation for future energy industry leaders and managers. In the undergraduate portion, students will take demanding courses in mathematics, probability and statistics, economics, chemistry, physics, accounting, and finance. This program is designed to be “elite” and highly challenging, requiring students to excel in a broad range of subjects. The fifth (graduate) year is focused on the Energy Finance certificate and additional advanced courses in finance and accounting.

Your feedback, even at a broad level, would be extremely helpful as we further develop these programs and select appropriate courses.

We believe these programs could become the foundation of the Institute’s educational activities. Our next step would be to design more specialized, shorter-duration programs for professionals already facing complex challenges in the industry.

We are currently setting up the Institute and developing its governance and administrative structure, and I will provide you with more details soon.

Subject: Urgent Concern: Threat of Re-Regulation in Power Markets

Dear [Relevant Stakeholders/Team/Recipients],

I am writing to address a significant and growing concern regarding the potential for re-regulation within our power markets. This discourse, if materialized into policy, poses a substantial threat to the stability, innovation, and investment climate of the entire energy sector.

The possibility of shifting away from the market-based mechanisms that have driven efficiency, fostered competition, and incentivized critical infrastructure investment for decades is deeply troubling. A return to heavily regulated structures, whether through price caps, guaranteed returns, or other interventions, risks undermining the very foundations that have supported grid reliability and propelled the transition to cleaner energy.

The potential negative impacts of such re-regulation are far-reaching:
*   **Deterrence of Investment:** Uncertainty and reduced profit potential will significantly chill private capital investment, particularly in much-needed renewable energy projects, grid modernization, and new generation capacity.
*   **Stifled Innovation:** Market signals are crucial for driving technological advancements. Re-regulation often removes these incentives, slowing progress in efficiency, storage, and demand-side management.
*   **Reduced Efficiency & Higher Costs:** Historical evidence suggests that re-regulated markets can lead to less efficient resource allocation, increased operational costs, and ultimately, higher long-term prices for consumers due to a lack of competitive pressure.
*   **Compromised Reliability:** Underinvestment and a loss of market-driven flexibility can jeopardize grid stability and energy security, especially during peak demand or extreme weather events.

It is imperative that we actively monitor these developments and engage with policymakers to articulate the critical role well-designed, competitive power markets play in delivering affordable, reliable, and sustainable energy. We must emphasize the unintended consequences of re-regulation and advocate for solutions that strengthen, rather than dismantle, the market structures that have proven beneficial.

We believe that a clear, consistent commitment to market-based principles, coupled with targeted and effective regulatory oversight, remains the optimal path forward for a robust and resilient power sector.

Sincerely,

[Your Name/Organization]

As you have probably observed, power markets have been severely tested this  summer.
There are many underlying causes (demand growth driven by a strong  economy, failure of regulators to quickly grant applications for new  generation, inadequate access to the grid, rate regulation which continues to  insulate end users from real time price signals, etc.).
But, the soundbite  on these troubles has been that deregulation has led to problems on the  grid.
The knee jerk policy response has been price caps and other threats of  re-regulation.
At the upcoming advisory council meeting, Ken and I were hoping that the two  of you could discuss the issue and help put it in perspective:  How great of a threat is re-regulation.
How might we respond.
How likely is this issue to play a significant role in election politics?

In the U.S., this distinction enables us to treat IOUs as general corporates. Thus, we negotiate our standard ISDA Master with an IOU, except that we add an Additional Termination Event to prevent the IOU from taking an adverse stance in its state public utility commission proceedings. A copy of that Additional Termination Event is attached for your review. Our approach with respect to municipals is dramatically different. When negotiating an ISDA Master with municipals, we use a Schedule modeled after the 1992 U.S. Municipal Counterparty Schedule, having additional reps, the added concept of "Incipient Illegality" and an enforceability opinion. A copy of that Schedule is also attached for your reference. We would like to understand whether this distinction also exists in Canada, and if so, in all Canadian provinces, and whether there is a distinction when a municipal is an investor in an IOU (as we understand that the government may assist a utility to emerge from bankruptcy). In that regard, would you recommend that ENA use distinct ISDA Schedules for these types of entities and/or would you recommend specific changes to our format?

Jim: Here's the DG stuff from the Hertzberg letter

***************************************************************************

8 Key Barriers to the Development of Distributed Generation and Proposals to Remove the Barriers

Barrier: Excessive and Unnecessary Utility Stand-by Charges

**Solution**

The executive orders issued by the Governor on February 14th took a step in the right direction, but tragically, they fall heartbreakingly short of what’s truly needed to protect California from looming disaster. Utility stand-by charges have always been designed by the utilities to protect their ironclad monopoly, squeezing customers for every last penny, even as our communities tremble at the threat of power shortfalls. These oppressive charges must be eliminated for all distributed generation applications if we’re serious about saving thousands—maybe millions—from sitting in the dark and heat this summer.

There is absolutely no justification for limiting the elimination of these charges to generation facilities under 1MW. Every hour we let these arbitrary limits stand, we prolong California's agony—stretching out the time it will take to close the alarming, dangerous gap between supply and demand, and we leave our neighborhoods and businesses exposed to the crippling risk of blackouts.

The vital provisions of SB27X that would have eliminated stand-by charges were stripped out, gutting efforts to spark the near-term development of distributed generation—perhaps our only hope to confront the severe, frightening supply-demand imbalance tearing at the heart of California. If we fail to act, we risk betraying the trust and wellbeing of millions who rely on us to keep their lights on and their families safe.

The language eliminating stand-by charges must be re-inserted into SB27X and strengthened to remove **all** size caps—because every megawatt of distributed generation could mean the difference between safety and suffering.

Barrier: Excessive Delays and Costs Related to Interconnecting Facilities with Investor-Owned and Municipal Utilities

**Solution:**

The Governor’s executive order on interconnection, D-26-01, gestures toward hope by requiring utilities to complete interconnection studies within 7 days. But real change demands more. California must ensure this lifeline applies to every generation facility—especially distributed ones—because every day of delay puts us closer to an unforgivable crisis.

But even bold executive orders cannot overcome the crushing financial conflicts utilities face when connecting generation facilities. The self-interest of these utilities is simply too powerful, blocking urgently needed solutions while California waits in the shadow of potential catastrophe.

To truly protect its people, California must seize control of interconnection from the utilities and place it with the California ISO—unlocking hope through decisive amendments to SB27X.

Barrier: Permitting and Air Quality Issues

Developers of distributed (i.e., “on-site”) generation of 50 MWs or greater become ensnared in suffocating, bureaucratic obstacles—forced to undergo the same punishing certification process as large-scale generation and facing an avalanche of impediments that can crush progress.

**Solution:**

California must guarantee that the Governor’s executive orders (D-22-01 thru D-26-01) to expedite plant siting and maximize plant output are applied equitably to distributed generation facilities of all sizes. Failing to do so perpetuates injustice upon the innovators and families who need these solutions most.

Moreover, even smaller distributed generation projects—under 50 MWs—face relentless local opposition. We cannot allow parochial interests to block projects that could be the key to keeping our hospitals running, our children safe, and our communities thriving during a statewide crisis.

Simple amendments to SB27X could turn the tide—empowering the state to override those who would hold all of California hostage to narrow self-interest, and deliver on the promise of reliable, safe, and modern energy for every Californian, before it’s too late.

Summary of RTO-Related Events for the Week of September 10, 2001
(A week that, it turns out, had some *other* major news brewing!)
***************************************************************************************
Monday, September 10
The week kicked off with the FERC Administrative Law Judge for the Southeast dropping her report on the SERTO mediation process. Ah, simpler times!

Tuesday, September 11
Steve Kean was all set to speak with select reporters, ready to enlighten them with Enron's interpretation of the oh-so-important SERTO report. Meanwhile, the House Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality had a hearing lined up on Electric Transmission Policy. Clearly, everyone was focused on energy regulation... for about an hour. Little did they know, the day had far bigger plans.

Wednesday, September 12
Newly-appointed FERC Chairman, Pat Wood, was still planning to preside over his very first meeting at FERC and lay out his FERC business policy. We can only imagine how quickly that detailed agenda was, shall we say, *re-prioritized*.

Thursday, September 13
Enron, ever the dedicated networker, was still planning a breakfast for the Republican Governors Association in Houston, with Ken Lay scheduled to charmingly speak on RTOs. Simultaneously, the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources aimed to markup Senator Bingaman's draft energy legislation. A valiant effort to keep the trains running on time.

Friday, September 14
The House Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality had another hearing on the books regarding Electric Transmission Policy. And Enron, bless their ambitious hearts, was still gearing up to file protests/comments for the ARTO and MISO compliance filings, pushing hard for that single Midwest RTO. They even had a "Show Cause Order" ready, essentially telling utilities to join FERC-approved RTOs or face some serious "repurcussions" (like losing market-based rates!). Because even after a week that fundamentally changed the world, the call for RTO compliance, apparently, had to go on.

Subject: Commission Policy on Reverse Open Seasons for Pipeline Expansion Projects

Dear [Recipient],

I am writing to provide clarification on the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's policy regarding reverse open seasons for natural gas pipeline expansion projects.

Under current Commission policy, interstate natural gas pipelines may utilize reverse open seasons as an alternative method for soliciting shipper commitments for expansion projects. Unlike traditional open seasons where pipelines first design capacity and then seek commitments, reverse open seasons allow pipelines to gauge market demand before finalizing project scope and design.

Key policy elements include:

• Reverse open seasons must provide fair and equal opportunity for all potential shippers to participate
• Pipelines must clearly communicate the preliminary nature of project parameters during the reverse open season process
• Following the reverse open season, pipelines must conduct a traditional open season if proceeding with the project
• All non-discriminatory practices applicable to standard open seasons apply to reverse open seasons
• The Commission will evaluate the entire open season process, including both phases, when reviewing certificate applications

The Commission views reverse open seasons as potentially beneficial for market efficiency, as they can help ensure proposed projects align with actual market demand while reducing the risk of overbuilding infrastructure.

Pipeline companies considering this approach should ensure full compliance with the Commission's open season requirements and maintain detailed documentation of all communications and commitments made during both the reverse and traditional open season phases.

Please contact our office if you require additional guidance on this matter.

Sincerely,
[Name]
[Title]
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
source_text:
Here is the Commission's basic policy on reverse open seasons.
I've asked Randy Rich to look into the other aspects of your questions, which we'll discuss shortly.
The Commission has a two-step process for determining whether the market finds an expansion project economically viable.
The first step, which occurs prior to the certificate application, is for the pipeline to conduct an open season in which existing customers are given an opportunity to permanently relinquish their capacity.
This first step ensures that a pipeline will not expand capacity if the demand for that capacity can be filled by existing shippers relinquishing their capacity.
The second step is that the expansion shippers must be willing to purchase capacity at a rate that pays the full costs of the project, without subsidy from existing shippers through rolled-in pricing.
The reverse open season requirement (i.e., the requirement that a pipeline give customers the opportunity to turn back capacity) is established Commission policy.
It was stated in the Commission's Pricing Policy for New and Existing Facilities Constructed by Interstate Natural Gas Pipelines, 71 FERC P61,241 at p. 61,917 (1995), reh'g denied, 75 FERC P61,105, and later reiterated in Certification on New interstate Natural Gas Pipeline Facilities (Certificate Policy Statement), 88 FERC P61,227 (1999), order clarifying statement of policy, 90 FERC P61,128, order further clarifying statement of policy, 92 FERC P61,094 (2000).
My research has indicated that the Commission has provided few specifics on how a reverse open season is to be conducted.
This probably allows pipelines considerable discretion in how they conduct their solicitations of turnback.
General Commission policy would probably require only that shippers be given adequate notice of and opportunity to respond to the reverse open season.
If the procedure used by El Paso for soliciting turnback becomes an issue, please let me know and let's discuss it.
I'll be up in a few minutes for our call to Randy.

Christine, I rarely write love notes anymore.
17 years ago it was commonplace, even a daily event.
What happened to that guy?
I could have been a cartoonist in another life.
I am here at 35,000 feet, 2,000 miles from Bangkok, Thailand, flying by China, soon to be over the Philippines, and pondering our lives.
You said something very interesting to me on the phone as I was getting on the bus to the airport.
You said that you would love to have 6 hours on the airplane by yourself.
I can certainly understand that.
I seem to have a lot of that on this trip.
I am sitting here on the plane, a little tipsy after a couple glasses of wine, and my mind turns to you and the kids.
I wish I could be there now to see the kids all dressed up in their costumes ready to go out trick or treating.
I bet they look great.
As I sit here and feel a little sorry for myself, I come back to reality and realize just how lucky we really are.
I turned to Ken Rice at the ceremony yesterday and said, "What is an Okie and a boy from Nebraska doing at a Japanese barrel ceremony with Thomas Foley, former Speaker of the House, breaking a barrel of sake in front of 300 Japanese executives and TV cameras?"
The Prime Minister of Japan didn't show up and apparently it is expected that he is out of a job on a no confidence vote last night.
(Really bad luck for Enron here) I would have liked to have met him.
Actually, the ceremony was impressive and I imagine that they will have some funny pictures from it.
You should see me in a Happy coat.
I'll explain when I get home.
Can you imagine sitting in our home, right after Michael was born, and even imagining what our lives are like today?
We are so blessed.
Even more than that, I am so blessed to have you.
I was writing in my journal on the trip over, you know my journal - that project that I have dedicated a big part of my life to and that you have never read, reflecting on our lives and wondering why God let me find you so many years ago.
I must have been a priest in a former life.
Anyway, I just wanted to say I love you and there aren't any phones on this airplane.
Thai Airlines, go figure.
So I am calling you via email.
Although I am not sure when I will get the opportunity to actually send this over the internet.
I love you and miss you very much.
Eternally, Michael See you soon and in time for soccer.
xxxxxooooo

As a critical reminder, stemming from both environmental stewardship and regulatory compliance, the state of Texas requires all releases of natural gas greater than 119 mscf to the atmosphere (in a 24-hour period) to be meticulously reported to the Regional Offices of the TNRCC. This is not merely a formality; it reflects a commitment to tracking significant industrial emissions.

These reportable releases encompass a range of operational events, from the sudden, urgent venting of Emergency Shut Downs (ESD's) and the routine but substantial emissions during startups and shutdowns, to the often dramatic events of pipeline ruptures and necessary maintenance activities that release gas.

Should any of these activities—be it an unexpected upset or a planned operational procedure—result in a natural gas release exceeding 119 mscf, a written notification, typically a fax, must reach the Regional Office of the TNRCC within strict timeframes. For unanticipated upsets, where a sudden malfunction or accident occurs, this notification is due within 24 hours after the discovery of the upset, prompting immediate action from the field. For planned maintenance, startups, or shutdowns, the notification requires foresight, needing to be submitted 10 days prior to the expected exceedance.

This important reminder is now being circulated to all ET&S teams within Texas because, during the last two Northern Natural Gas compressor station inspections, TNRCC officials arrived with a clear focus. I understand that I haven't been the best at expressing myself or really listening to what you need. I know I've shut down during arguments instead of working through them with you, and I can see how frustrating and hurtful that must have been.

Greg,  As you asked, I have taken a quick look at Global Crossing.
I think it is a close call, but they certainly have a decent shot of making it (by "making it" I mean the equity will have value and the company will not be restructured through bankruptcy).
Their assets, customers, and cash might marginally outweigh the debt load that the company has.
Most importantly, they definitely have a currency (Global Crossing stock) that has more value than anything in EBS.
If there is a potential deal to contribute assets of EBS into Global Crossing in exchange for equity, then I would recommend pursuing it even if it means contributing up to $100 million in cash to get it done.
However, I would make sure that Enron has no more contingent liabilities, consolidated burn or cash commitments.
The real question is will Global Crossing want what we have at any price.
I suspect that once they perform due diligence, they will "run away" (just as the knights did when faced with the killer rabbit in Monte Python's Search for the Holy Grail).
Thanks,

And to avoid interest and                            penalties, you'll generally need to pay any taxes  owed by April 16.
April 16 is also the deadline for making IRA  contributions for 2000 returns and for making the first                            installment of quarterly estimated taxes for 2001.
Filing extension: If you'd like more time to file  your return, getting a filing extension is simple.
In fact,                            the IRS has expanded the options this year for  obtaining a filing extension.
You can now do it by                            phone, computer or mail.

Dear [Recipient Name],

I hope this email finds you well.

As I approach the ten-month mark in my role as Business Controller, I wanted to take a moment to reflect on the significant progress we've made in building out the mid and back office infrastructure for EIM. It has been an incredibly productive period, and I am proud of the foundational work accomplished, including:

*   **Establishing robust financial processes:** Successfully designed and implemented key operational workflows for EIM, ensuring greater efficiency and control.
*   **Enhancing reporting and analytics:** Developed comprehensive reporting frameworks that have significantly improved visibility and decision-making capabilities for our EIM initiatives.
*   **Strengthening internal controls:** Integrated new control mechanisms and compliance protocols, fortifying the financial integrity of our EIM operations.
*   **Building foundational infrastructure:** Played a pivotal role in creating the scalable financial infrastructure necessary to support EIM's rapid growth and future expansion.

Looking ahead, I am eager to discuss my career trajectory within the company and explore how my skills and experience can continue to contribute to our strategic goals in new and impactful ways. I am particularly interested in understanding any emerging opportunities that align with my professional growth aspirations.

As I look back on the ten months that I have been the Business Controller for EIM and challenged to build the mid and back office infrastructure, the most significant accomplishments are:  Systems - Tactical systems have been implemented to bridge the business while strategic systems are developed.
Financial and physical confirmations (with the exception of Lumber) have been predominantly automated.
Financial settlements has been automated.
Implemented modified versions of LISA to handle physical movements and settlements.
Bridges have been built to SAP and Credit Aggregation systems.
People - Ten months ago, the mid and back office had three employees, with the remaining efforts supported by Global Markets.
Today, we have an enthusiastic, energetic team of 41 employees.
The team includes our London office also.
We continue to recruit for additional positions.
Processes and Controls - Many processes and controls have been developed to ensure accurate and timely reporting of P&L and positions, confirmations and settlements.
Some of these tools include: Pulp and Paper Deal Ticket (Access Database) - Ten months ago, deal tickets were generated through an Excel template and no master copy or controls were in place.
Today, traders, Risk, Confirms, Settlements, Credit, Logistics, etc.
can view the deal tickets in a controlled and timely manner.
LISA/TAGG Reconciliation (Access Database) - When the onset of physical business and the implementation of LISA systems, physical transactions for all commodities (except lumber) are entered into 2 systems - LISA and TAGG.
This tool provides a reconciliation tool that allows the Risk system and the logistics/settlements systems to stay in sync.
Trader Training Tools - Two different presentations have been developed and presented to the EIM trading community to help the traders (mostly new to Enron) understand the roles and responsibilities of traders, segregation of duties and the processes within Commercial Support functions such as Credit, Tax, Legal, Operations, Logistics, etc.
Sally, I hope this will give the flavor of the focused efforts.
Additionally, as I have had a few hours to reflect on our conversation, I would like to follow-up with an additional meeting.
I need just a bit more clarity around the EIM role, but more so, I want to move forward to discuss the new role and in your view, how I can still accomplish the successes that coincide with my personal goals.
If you have time tomorrow afternonn, I would really appreciate 30 minutes.
Thanks for your support.
It means alot to me.
Brenda

From time to time there have been discussions in the TIE list criticizing Con Edison for its involvement in out-of-merit actions, implying that it is inappropriate for Con Edison control room operators to make such requests.
In its recent order on the Revised Local Mitigation Measures, FERC, in response to allegations made by Orion, ordered the NYISO to take responsibility for out-of-merit.
The Con Edison system has the world's most concentrated use of energy for residential and commercial purposes.
It is also a highly transmission-constrained area where transfer limitations under normal and second contingency conditions require certain minimum generation levels within specific load pockets to assure reliability under existing reliability rules.
One of the main functions of the Con Edison control center is to be vigilant of system conditions at all times and prevent the system from reaching an unreliable operating state.
When such conditions are imminent, the Con Edison operator so advises the NYISO.
Some parties have said that Con Edison operators should never make out-of-merit requests.
Con Edison operators would be acting irresponsibly if they were to detect an imminent unreliable operating condition and just sit back and not inform the NYISO of the potential danger.
Con Edison operators have been trained to focus on operating the New York City system.
The NYISO operators have a much wider state-wide focus.
It is entirely appropriate for both a transmission owner (TO) and NYISO operators to work cooperatively in maintaining reliability with the clear understanding that under the FERC-approved tariff, it is the NYISO that has sole responsibility for reliability.
I would like to clarify that all involvement by Con Edison operators in out-of-merit actions are based on the following  FERC-approved process in which the NYISO, and not the TO operator, has sole responsibility for these actions.
The NYISO FERC Electric Tariff, Section 5.4,  Operations Under Adverse Conditions states in essence that: 		*	The NYISO shall operate the system in accordance with Reliability Rules, including local rules 		*	The NYISO will do this, among other measures, by adjusting generator output levels 		*	The NYISO has sole responsibility for declaring that Adverse Conditions are imminent 		*	Activation of these actions shall involve a two-step process 			1.
The TO involved will advise the NYISO that an Adverse Condition is imminent and recommend action 			2.
The NYISO activates the appropriate procedures 		*	Records of the activation of such procedures shall be maintained by both the TO and the NYISO  Having stated the above, let me also say that Con Edison has been working with NYISO operations to minimize the occurrences of conditions that require Con Edison operators to request actions that result in OOM operations.
Con Edison supports current efforts by the NYISO to manage load pocket reliability events in a way that SCD can be used to maintain reliability with in-merit generation.
In effect, the FERC recent order does not require any change from present practice which is, and has always been, in compliance with Section 5.4 of the NYISO FERC Electric Tariff, and in compliance with FERC's recent order: the NYISO is solely responsible for out-of-merit actions.

Con Edison operators have been trained to focus on operating the New York City system.
The NYISO operators have a much wider state-wide focus.
It is entirely appropriate for both a transmission owner (TO) and NYISO operators to work cooperatively in maintaining reliability with the clear understanding that under the FERC-approved tariff, it is the NYISO that has sole responsibility for reliability.
I would like to clarify that all involvement by Con Edison operators in out-of-merit actions are based on the following  FERC-approved process in which the NYISO, and not the TO operator, has sole responsibility for these actions.
The NYISO FERC Electric Tariff, Section 5.4,  Operations Under Adverse Conditions states in essence that: 		*	The NYISO shall operate the system in accordance with Reliability Rules, including local rules 		*	The NYISO will do this, among other measures, by adjusting generator output levels 		*	The NYISO has sole responsibility for declaring that Adverse Conditions are imminent 		*	Activation of these actions shall involve a two-step process 			1.
The TO involved will advise the NYISO that an Adverse Condition is imminent and recommend action 			2.
The NYISO activates the appropriate procedures 		*	Records of the activation of such procedures shall be maintained by both the TO and the NYISO  Having stated the above, let me also say that Con Edison has been working with NYISO operations to minimize the occurrences of conditions that require Con Edison operators to request actions that result in OOM operations.
Con Edison supports current efforts by the NYISO to manage load pocket reliability events in a way that SCD can be used to maintain reliability with in-merit generation.
In effect, the FERC recent order does not require any change from present practice which is, and has always been, in compliance with Section 5.4 of the NYISO FERC Electric Tariff, and in compliance with FERC's recent order: the NYISO is solely responsible for out-of-merit actions.

In lieu of sending out multiple letters and then aggregating the exposures for set off purposes, I thought it would be more understandable if we put all the matters in one letter. This would avoid confusion and duplication, especially since several positions across different commodity desks—such as Natural Gas West Desk, Power Northwest Desk, and Crude Oil Derivatives Group—are affected by the same event of default and closeout.

For each product line, I thought we could attach all the relevant information (I'm not sure if this is making it too easy for the court but it seems like the right thing to do). For instance, for the Power positions, we would include transaction data for the terminated May-July 2002 monthly swaps and confirmations for the Pacific Northwest Balancing Market positions. For Gas, we could attach positions relating to the California border basis swaps and all relevant confirmations executed, for example, on February 10, 2001. For each product line, supporting details reflecting the specific transactions, quantities, strike prices, and settlement periods should be included.

Each commodity line then would assemble the following and attach as an Appendix to the letter: 
1. Copy of Master Contract or applicable GTC, such as the 1992 ISDA Master Agreement between Enron North America Corp. and PG&E Energy Trading, including all relevant schedules and amendments.
2. Copy of transaction confirmations, e.g., the executed confirmation for the July 2002 Henry Hub Natural Gas swap, the signed power strip deal dated April 15, 2001, etc.
3. Copy of termination notice sent to PG&E, such as the notice dated September 14, 2001, referencing section 6(a) of the Master Agreement.
4. Chart summarizing key commercial terms of transaction(s)—for example, product (Natural Gas), volume (10,000 MMBtu/day), price ($4.12/MMBtu), delivery point (SoCal Border), term (May-July 2002).
5. Chart summarizing unpaid receivables and invoices for same, detailing outstanding amounts on each trade, including invoice numbers, dates, and aging.
6. Chart setting forth termination payment calculation for each terminated trade, including market value as of closeout, amounts due under each transaction, and net amount payable following set-off.
7. Paragraph describing methodology used to determine termination payment valuation (eg - 4 quotes secured, threw out high and low and averaged middle), specifying, for example, that independent market quotes for the relevant product and date (e.g., NYMEX settlement prices, Broker quotes from tradition Energy and Amerex) were obtained at 10:30 am CT on the date of termination.
8. List showing quotes secured (entity, person, time and amount) and, to the extent available, written confirmation of such quote, e.g., "Amerex, John Smith, 10:35 am CST, $4.05/MMBtu, attached broker confirmation email."

I will be out of the office the rest of this week but will organize a call for early next week in order to finalize the PG&E package.

Thanks for all your help.

vivify (VIV-i-FY) verb tr.
1.
To endow with life; animate, as if breathing into a work the crackling of autumn leaves underfoot, the scent of rain-soaked earth, or the vivid splash of crimson against rough canvas.
2.
To impart vitality or liveliness—a sudden burst of laughter echoing in a silent room, the tang of citrus on the tongue, or the bright flaring colors of sunrise on chilly skin.
[From Latin vivus (alive) via Late Latin vivificare.]
"Yet how could artists vivify culture with `sympathies and admirations' if they felt out of step with their place and time, their senses dulled to the pungent ink, coarse fibers, and distant hum of city streets?"
Jackson Lears, The Golden Age, The New Republic (Washington), Aug 21, 2000.

............................................................................
I am no more humble than my talents require.
-Oscar Levant, composer

Subject: Legal Hold Notification - Documents Related to Lawsuits Against Enron and Broadband Services Division

Dear [Recipient Name/Legal Counsel/Custodian],

This email serves as a formal notification of a legal hold on all documents and electronically stored information (ESI) related to lawsuits, investigations, and potential claims against Enron and its Broadband Services Division. This legal hold is effective immediately.

You are required to preserve all information, regardless of format (e.g., electronic files, emails, physical documents, presentations, databases, instant messages, voicemails, drafts, notes, calendars, expense reports), that may be relevant to these matters. This includes, but is not limited to, documents concerning:

*   The formation, operations, and financial performance of Enron's Broadband Services Division.
*   Decisions, strategies, and communications related to the development, marketing, and accounting of broadband services.
*   Any agreements, contracts, or partnerships involving the Broadband Services Division.
*   Financial statements, audit reports, and internal communications regarding the financial health and reporting of Enron and its divisions.
*   Employee compensation, severance, and stock options.
*   Communications with auditors, legal counsel, and regulatory bodies.
*   Any internal or external investigations, complaints, or allegations related to Enron or its Broadband Services Division.

**Key Requirements:**

1.  **Do Not Delete:** Cease all routine destruction or deletion of any relevant documents or ESI.
2.  **Preserve:** Ensure the preservation of all existing relevant documents and ESI, including any drafts or non-final versions.
3.  **Identify:** Begin identifying all potential sources of relevant information under your control.
4.  **No Alteration:** Do not alter, modify, or convert any relevant documents or ESI.
5.  **New Information:** Preserve any new information created from this point forward that relates to these matters.

If you have already deleted or destroyed any potentially relevant documents or ESI, please report this immediately to [Name/Department, e.g., Legal Department] with details of what was deleted and when.

We understand this may involve a significant effort. Your cooperation in preserving this information is critical to our legal defense and compliance obligations. Further instructions regarding collection and review may follow.

Please direct any questions regarding this legal hold to [Name/Department, e.g., Legal Department] at [Email Address] or [Phone Number].

Sincerely,

[Your Name/Legal Department]
[Your Title/Company]

Some of the litigation claims relate to the performance of the Broadband Services Division.
Enron has employed counsel and they will represent Enron and its interests in the litigation.
Under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act, we are required to preserve documents that might be used in the litigation.
Accordingly, our normal document destruction policies are suspended immediately and shall remain suspended until further notice.

Subject: FERC Order on Southeast RTOs: Proposals Rejected, Mediation Set

Dear Team,

FERC issued its anticipated order today on the competing Southeast RTO proposals, rejecting both the GridSouth and SeTrans filings while establishing a mediation process to move forward.

Key points from the order:

• Both proposals deemed insufficient to meet FERC's RTO requirements under Order 2000
• Concerns raised about market design, governance structure, and transmission planning processes
• FERC has appointed Judge Carmen Cintron as mediator for 90-day settlement discussions
• All Southeast utilities must participate in mediation process beginning January 15th
• If mediation fails, FERC will impose its own RTO structure for the region

The Commission emphasized that Southeast RTO formation remains a priority and warned that continued delays will result in mandatory federal intervention. Commissioner Massey dissented, arguing the agency should have accepted the GridSouth proposal with modifications.

Next steps:
- Preparing for mandatory mediation participation
- Reviewing order for potential rehearing grounds
- Coordinating with legal counsel on strategy

We'll schedule a team call for tomorrow at 2 PM to discuss implications and develop our mediation approach.

Best regards,
[Name]

I chatted with Patti today and she's giving us the thumbs up on our user-friendly approach.

Just some food for thought - I'm sure we'll cook up plenty more questions as we go.

Thanks!

This project would necessitate a dedicated gas bypass pipeline, approximately 20 miles in length, to connect directly to the main interstate transmission lines serving the Albuquerque metropolitan area, ensuring a reliable and independent fuel supply.

Kevin, you should be getting a priority call from a contact I spoke with today – a Project Development Manager from Portland whose name momentarily escapes me, though I've jotted it down somewhere. He had received my contact information directly from Thome, who apparently mentioned our firm's expertise in regional energy infrastructure. This individual called to inform me that ENA, a firm we've tracked, is expressing significant interest in pitching either PNM, the primary utility, or a lesser-known independent power producer referred to only as "Delta Energy Solutions," on a substantial development or expansion of an existing gas-fired power plant located specifically in the southern industrial quadrant of Albuquerque, near the Mesa del Sol development zone. Their focus appears to be on adding significant capacity, potentially another 200-300MW block. Based on his rather vague descriptions and lack of concrete specifics, it didn't sound to me like ENA was very far along in their diligence or had secured any firm commitments. Their inquiries seemed to be at a very preliminary 'market sounding' stage.

I thought it was a little curious, and somewhat coincidental, that ENA is expressing such acute interest in new generation capacity in Albuquerque all of a sudden, especially considering the recent shifts in regional power demand and transmission constraints that we've been analyzing.

On the Tino front, he called back later in the afternoon to apologize profusely for the delay in following up after their significant DOE meeting last week, explaining that the post-meeting debriefings had been extensive. He reported that the meeting regarding their innovative energy storage and grid stabilization proposal went exceptionally well. He relayed that the Department of Energy is now actively considering their revised offer – specifically, a long-term power purchase agreement structured at $.085/Kwh for base load, with an added incentive for all surplus power sold beyond their contracted amount, structured as a 50/50 revenue sharing arrangement after accounting for operational expenses. This represents a potentially lucrative partnership for them, contingent on final DOE approval, which he anticipates within the next 30-45 days.
Tino

California:  CA Legislature.
On Monday Jan. 7th the legislature recovenced and Gov.
Davis delivered his State of the State Address on Tuesday.
Davis focused on the projected $12.5 billion budget shortfall and increased education spending.
Gov.
Davis pledged he will not advocate increasing taxes and his proposed budget for closing the gap will include a combination of cutbacks, deferred spending, internal borrowing and accelerated revenue.
On Thursday, Assemblyman Herb Wesson, Jr. was elected as Speaker of the Assembly.
Assemblyman Wesson is a Culver City Democrat.
Also on Thursday, Gov.
Davis submitted his balanced budget without tax increases.
Key and controversial provisions to cover the shortfall included borrowing from teacher and state worker pension funds, cashing in on future year revenues from the tobacco settlement and spending cuts of $5.2 billion largely from health and welfare programs.
I99-07-003  SoCalGas Unbundling.
On Jan. 9th SoCalGas held a customer meeting to review their proposed unbundling implementation plan.
This plan will be filed with the CPUC on Jan 17th.
Other key dates included the beginning of the open season for the backbone receipt point capacity which will be held in three phases beginning May 29, 2002, with the third phase ending June 21, 2002 and implementation of transportation under the plan to begin July 1, 2002.
The Core customers were reserved capacity of 313 mmcf/d at Needles.
The remaining capacity of 487.5 mmcf/d will be placed in the open season for bids.
I00-11-002  Adequacy of SoCal Capacity.
On Monday, the CPUC issued an ALJ ruling requesting parties to submit briefs on the implications of the Unbundling Decision to this proceeding.
Briefs are due January 30, 2002.
Additionally, in the Commissions Infratstructure Report issued last week they cite this system adequacy proceeding as the forum for addressing potential system constraints at two transmission locations (ie San Joaquin and Imperial Valleys).
PG&E Plan of Reorganization.
Along with Enron Corp and Marketing, participated in a conference call regarding PG&E's Plan of Reorganization as related to establishing their backbone system as an InTERstate, open access pipeline.
PG&E is seeking approval of its plan by the Debtors Committee and FERC by mid-2002.
They filed a Section 7(c) Application on Nov. 30, 2001 to establish this interstate company given a temporary name of GTRAN.
During this "transition" period current rates remain in effect.
Their plan is to make a Section 4 filing after receiving FERC approval of the current filing.
PG&E requested that Enron and Transwestern file in support of the plan.
No committment was made as we are continuing to evaluate our position.
Interventions are due January 29, 2002.

Subject: Enron Senior Management’s Deception and Betrayal of Employees and Shareholders

Dear Stakeholders,

The catastrophic collapse of Enron serves as a permanent and painful reminder of the profound betrayal perpetrated by its senior management against its own employees and shareholders. This was not merely a business failure; it was a deliberate act of deception that shattered countless lives and eroded public trust in corporate governance.

For the dedicated employees of Enron, the betrayal was particularly egregious. They were not only encouraged but often implicitly pressured to invest their life savings and retirement funds into company stock, believing in the leadership's optimistic pronouncements. While senior executives were quietly divesting their shares and manipulating financial statements to create an illusion of prosperity, thousands of employees were losing their jobs, their pensions, and their entire life savings. Their loyalty was met with calculated duplicity, and their financial security was sacrificed for the personal gain and maintaining the false image of a select few at the top.

Shareholders, both institutional and individual, faced a similar, devastating betrayal. They invested their hard-earned capital based on meticulously fabricated financial reports and misleading information designed to inflate Enron’s stock price. Senior management engineered complex off-balance-sheet entities and engaged in aggressive accounting practices, such as the abuse of mark-to-market accounting, to hide massive debts, conceal financial risks, and create a false impression of robust profitability. These elaborate schemes were designed to deliberately misrepresent the company's true financial health, leading investors to make decisions based on fraudulent data. The inevitable implosion wiped out billions in shareholder value, demonstrating a profound disregard for fiduciary responsibility and ethical conduct.

The actions of Enron’s senior executives represented a systemic failure of ethics and a cynical exploitation of their positions. Their primary focus was on personal enrichment and maintaining an illusion of success, rather than on their fundamental duties to protect the interests of their employees and investors. The Enron scandal stands as a stark warning about the catastrophic consequences when corporate power is wielded without integrity, transparency, and accountability.

Sincerely,

Subject: FERC Writing Handbook: Part II

Dear Team,

I am pleased to share Part II of the FERC Writing Handbook. This section builds on the foundational guidelines provided in Part I, focusing on clarity, consistency, and best practices for regulatory correspondence. Please review the attached document and adhere to these standards in all future communications.

If you have any questions or would like to suggest additional topics, feel free to reach out.

Best regards,  
[Your Name]
source_text:
Part II:  FERC Writing Handbook  1.
"WHEREFORE, PREMISES CONSIDERED" adds a note of authority to your  pleadings.
In fact, some administrative law judges will throw your pleading  into the special incinerator marked "Nonconforming Pleadings" (located on the  west side of the FERC building) unless such language is present.
2.
Pronouns should be used sparingly, if at all.
With few exceptions,  parties must always be named to avoid confusion, even if it means the name of  the party will appear several times in one sentence.
3.
The verb "request" may not be used without the word "to."
Example:   "Pipeline X respectfully requests the Commission to grant its motion."
4.
"In regards to" or "vis-a-via" sound more intelligent than "about" or  "concerning."
5.
If you are not sure you've conveyed an important point effectively,  repeat the statement verbatim at various other points in your pleading for  emphasis.
Additionally, repeating a contractual provision several times in a  contract will give your client greater rights than if you only include the  provision once.
6.
Always recite the entire history of the proceeding in your pleading  before stating the purpose of your pleading.
No FERC staffer ever remembers  what happens, and the added pages will make your pleading really impressive.
7.
When in doubt, insert more commas.

Subject: Long-Dated Commodity Derivatives Transaction Setup and ISDA Documentation Requirements

Dear [Recipient Name],

I hope this message finds you well.

I am writing to outline the steps and documentation requirements for setting up a long-dated commodity derivatives transaction.

Before executing any such trades, please ensure that an ISDA Master Agreement is in place between both counterparties. In addition to the ISDA, the following supporting documentation may be required:
- Schedule to the ISDA Master Agreement tailored to cover specific commodity provisions and any credit support arrangements (CSA), if applicable.
- Confirmation templates reflecting key economic terms, including trade date, notional amount, settlement provisions, pricing methodology, and maturity date.
- Additional commodity annexes or definitions (such as the 2005 ISDA Commodity Definitions), depending on the specific commodity and transaction structure.
- KYC/AML documentation and any required regulatory representations or protocols (e.g., Dodd-Frank, EMIR).

Please note that since these are long-dated transactions, close attention should be paid to credit exposure, collateral requirements, and any bespoke terms covering termination events or early unwind provisions.

Let me know if you need further details or assistance coordinating with legal or operations.

Best regards,

[Your Name]  
[Your Position]  
[Your Company]

As you have heard, Dynegy is terminating the merger agreement today.
Among other things, this means we are now free to pursue other alternatives - which we are actively doing.
As a consequence of uncertainty about the deal - and now Dynegy's announcement - Enron's debt was downgraded to below investment grade levels today by S&P, Moody's and Fitch.
In response to this action, we have initiated a plan to protect value in our core trading and other energy businesses.
At the same time, we are nearing the completion of the business review process announced last week.
Once this process is complete, we will be conducting a comprehensive restructuring of our business.
Regrettably, but unavoidably, this will include the sale of non-core assets and the implementation of a comprehensive cost saving plan, including layoffs.
We are taking these actions to focus our resources on preserving the value of our core businesses, retaining our employees who are key to our future success, and maintaining relationships with our trading counterparties.
This must be our priority to establish a more solid footing for the rest of Enron.
I know you have serious concerns about what this all means for you.
Although, there are no guarantees, you should know that we are still in this fight and remain absolutely committed to protecting the value of the ongoing businesses of Enron.
All I can ask is that we all be supportive of each other, stay focused on our work as best we can, and stick together while we work to overcome these latest challenges.
Even six or so weeks ago, none of us could have imagined that we would be where we are today.
We will not recover in six weeks what we have lost, but we will work to stabilize and then rebuild this great company.
As always, I appreciate the extraordinary contributions each of you make.
Thank you.
Ken

As you may remember, York initiated two summonses against Enron and Eric Holzer in two distinct lawsuits related to the parties' transactions in the paper market.

Both summonses (permitted under Pennsylvania law) contained no details regarding York's allegations against Enron or Mr. Holzer.

The Enron defendants transferred their cases to federal court.

Dechert serves as outside counsel for the Enron defendants.

We have now obtained York's complaint outlining its allegations against Enron and Mr. Holzer.

In summary, York alleges that Enron recruited Holzer from York to misappropriate York's client base and then, violating the parties' agreement and industry standards, proceeded to take customers from York.

More specifically, York contends that it only released Holzer from his non-compete agreement with York because both Holzer and Enron assured them: that they would respect the purportedly established paper industry practice that prevents competitors from taking each other's clients by selling paper directly to those clients, and that York would receive new business from Enron.

York maintains that Holzer obtained confidential and proprietary information from York upon his departure, provided this information to Enron, and that Enron and Holzer utilized this information to improperly take York's customers.

York has brought the following claims against Enron and Holzer: 1. Misappropriation of trade secrets, 2. Breach of contract (multiple counts), 3. Tortious interference with contractual relations, 4. Tortious interference with prospective contractual relations, 5. Fraudulent inducement, 6. Unfair competition, and 7. Civil conspiracy.

My preliminary assessment suggests that York should be more concerned about having anti-solicitation agreements with competitors than Enron should be about predatory pricing allegations; however, I lack sufficient factual knowledge to form a definitive opinion on the case.

We are currently gathering additional information about these allegations and I will provide another update once we have consulted with our team.

Meanwhile, please contact me with any questions or comments.

I have a concern about Enron's forward-looking exposure associated with legacy deals (deals that existed during the June 2000 through the May 2001 price shock). 

To illustrate, imagine a small bakery on Main Street—one of Enron's legacy customers—whose owner, Mrs. Lopez, signed a deal in early 2000. Business was good until the energy price shocks hit, biting into her profits and making each month's bill a nervy surprise. She trusted that when her contract ended, so would her obligations.

But my concern is that, if Edison gets its way, all customers will pay for Edison's under-recovery from June 2000 through January 2001 plus CDWR spot market purchases during 2001. This would take the form of a surcharge on future bills. 

Even long after Mrs. Lopez has finished her morning pastries and sold her last muffin under our contract, Enron could still be on the hook for these future charges associated with past under-collections—even beyond the term of our legacy deals. For example, if a deal ends in March 2002, we could be on the hook for surcharges that a legacy customer like Mrs. Lopez would receive on her bill after that date, provided the surcharge pertained to costs incurred by the utility during the time that the legacy customer was ours. 

So, like Mrs. Lopez, who thinks she’s finally free from the unpredictability of past energy price spikes, Enron too might find herself haunted by the echoes of old deals, long after the kitchen lights have gone out.

- Legal and Compliance Support
- Facilities Management

Effective August 15, 2001, Market Participants will see two new billing codes on their advisory statements:

**1. Hourly Code Activation:**
While Code 238 has previously existed in the hourly advisory statement as a null value, it will now be activated as 'Hrly LRR DAM Contract Bal Pmnt $'. This code reflects dollars paid to a generator for DAM Contract Balancing that is Out-of-Merit for LRR. Code 239 will reflect dollars paid to a generator for DAM Contract Balancing and is not Out-of-Merit for LRR. The combined sum of Codes 238 and 239 will be reflected in Code 313, which can be found under the "Power Supplier" section of the daily advisory statement.

**2. New Daily Code:**
Code 314, designated 'ELR DAM Contract Balancing Payment $', is a new addition that did not exist on the daily CSV file before. There is no corresponding hourly code for ELR DAM Contract Balancing, as it is processed as a daily, not hourly, settlement.

Funds for both Code 313 and Code 314 will be collected from Load Serving Entities (LSEs) via residual adjustment codes 611 (hourly) and 813 (daily).

These new billing codes, along with other updates, will be reflected in Version 14 of the Data Dictionary. Additionally, Version 7 of the Billing Code Mapping will be available. Both documents can be found on the NYISO website under the 'Grid Accounting & Settlements' section, consistent with prior versions.
