Dear Mr. Lay,

Yesterday, I went home along with the other 3,999 employees who lost their jobs at Enron. Even though we had weeks to prepare for the worst, the reality of the layoffs hit me hard. I cried a great deal—not only because of the uncertainty about my future, but also for the loss of the relationships and friendships I built over the five years I spent at Enron.

The hardest part of yesterday was saying goodbye to my friends and co-workers. We’ve all resolved to stay in touch, and I hope we will all find a way to pick up the pieces and carry on with our lives.

I appreciate the efforts that were made to secure us some severance, but as you know, we gave so much of ourselves to the company and lost so much in return. I’m sure I’m not alone in urging you and Enron’s management to continue pushing for additional severance for those of us who lost our jobs.

This is a difficult time to be looking for work, as Continental, Compaq, and now Enron have all downsized—and the holidays are upon us. I know you have probably received many messages like this in the past few weeks, but I hope you will continue to do the right thing for the employees.

We need additional severance to ensure there is food on our tables and roofs over our heads until we can land on our feet after this free fall. I will never regret my five years at Enron—they will always be an important part of my past.

Thank you for your consideration of this request.

Sincerely,

Note:   Update on ammonia plant operations.
Check out the economics in the last paragrph.
LB Ammonia Industry Finally Approaches Full Production  Plummeting gas prices have prompted a large number of idled ammonia producers to restart operations this month, after lengthy downtime due to last winter's record gas price increases.
Houston-based Industrialinfo.com, which tracks manufacturing, said most of the Gulf Coast and Midcontinent plants are at partial or full capacity.
An ammonia industry expert at Duke Energy said there has been a 20% increase in ammonia production (222,000 tons of ammonia) since August, representing about 7.6 Bcf of gas demand (34 MMBtu per ton of ammonia).
There was a doubling of ammonia productive capacity in Louisiana alone.
"We think just about every plant in the U.S. is back on or in the process of coming back up right now," he said.
"Obviously they are not going to be running full out, but every plant is coming back up."
A year ago, ammonia producers were rocked by soaring natural gas prices, which reached $10/MMBtu, up from a historical average of $2.
Combined with product overcapacity, the rising costs caused a wave of plant shutdowns across the country.
Louisiana was particularly hard hit, with five out of eight ammonia plants idled during the summer.
Arkansas, Georgia and Texas were among other ammonia producing states affected.
The recent decline in gas prices and inventory, however, has sparked some ammonia producers into ramping up production.
Triad Nitrogen and PCS Nitrogen both resumed full production in September at their respective plants in Donaldsonville and Geismar, LA, Industrial Information reported.
Terra Industries restarted a Verdigris, OK, plant after an extended shutdown and is expected to bring its Blytheville, AK, plant online sometime this month.
Koch Industries and IMC Agrico, with plants in Sterlington, Donaldsonville, Convent and Uncle Sam, LA, are now operating at partial capacity.
Other ammonia manufacturers are waiting to see if natural gas prices remain stable before resuming production.
DuPont in Beaumont, TX, Borden Chemical in Geismar, LA, and PCS in Augusta, GA, remain idled.
"It looks as if these guys are going to make money running their plants all winter," the Duke Energy ammonia industry expert said.
"They are making less and less money as gas prices rise and ammonia prices fall.
I see them at the closest to break-even by February where gas is averaging about $2.85.
"Last year the domestic producer margin was only about $3/ton," he said.
"They pretty much broke even in terms of gas costs on average.
This year they are probably going to make $20-25/ton of production.
At $2.80/MMBtu for gas and 34 MMBtu of gas per ton of production, plus $25/ton of additional costs, it will cost them about $120/ton for ammonia production.
In New Orleans they will probably cover that for most of the season."

Subject: Important Computer Security Tips and Precautions

Dear Team,

I hope this email finds you well. As cyber threats continue to evolve, I wanted to share some essential security practices to help protect both your personal and work computers.

**Key Security Measures:**

• **Keep software updated** - Enable automatic updates for your operating system, antivirus software, and applications
• **Use strong, unique passwords** - Create complex passwords with at least 12 characters and use a different password for each account
• **Enable two-factor authentication** - Add this extra security layer to your important accounts whenever possible
• **Be cautious with email attachments** - Never open attachments or click links from unknown senders
• **Backup your data regularly** - Store important files in multiple locations, including cloud storage or external drives
• **Use reputable antivirus software** - Keep it running and perform regular system scans
• **Secure your Wi-Fi** - Use WPA3 encryption and avoid public Wi-Fi for sensitive activities
• **Be selective with downloads** - Only download software from official websites and trusted sources

**Red Flags to Watch For:**
- Unexpected pop-ups or system slowdowns
- Unfamiliar programs running on startup
- Suspicious emails requesting personal information
- Unusual network activity

If you notice any suspicious activity or have security concerns, please report them immediately to our IT department.

Stay vigilant and stay safe online.

Best regards,
[Your Name]

Subject: Warm Holiday Wishes and Updates

Dear Friends,

As the holiday season approaches, I wanted to take a moment to catch up and share some updates from our corner of the world.

This year has been a whirlwind of changes at work. Our company recently launched a new product line, and it’s been wonderful to see the positive response from customers. The team has grown as well, bringing in new faces and lots of fresh energy.

On a more somber note, we were saddened by the passing of our longtime colleague and friend, John. His presence in the office will be deeply missed, and we’re grateful for the years of dedication and warmth he shared with all of us.

Preparations for the holidays are in full swing at home. The kids helped decorate the tree last weekend (with more ornaments clustered at eye-level than anywhere else!), and we’re looking forward to baking our traditional gingerbread cookies.

Family-wise, June started high school this fall, and Ethan has taken up soccer with great enthusiasm. We’re planning a quiet family gathering this year but hope to see many of you soon.

Wishing you a peaceful holiday and a joyful New Year. Please keep in touch and let us know how you’re doing.

Warmest regards,

Dear Fellow Americans,

Our hearts are heavy with grief and profound sadness following the horrific terrorist attack that has struck our nation. We are grappling with the senseless violence that has claimed innocent lives and brought immeasurable pain to so many families. Our deepest condolences go out to all those who have lost loved ones, and our thoughts are with the injured and those working tirelessly on the front lines.

This cowardly act of terror is an attack on our shared values, our peace, and our way of life. It seeks to sow fear and division among us, but we will not let it succeed. In moments of such profound tragedy, it is more vital than ever that we stand together, united in our resolve against hatred and extremism.

America has always been defined by its strength, resilience, and the unwavering spirit of its people. We have faced adversity before, and we have always emerged stronger, more determined, and more united. We will mourn, we will heal, and we will rebuild. We will continue to uphold the principles of freedom, democracy, and justice that are the bedrock of our nation.

Let us support one another, offer comfort to those in need, and remember the enduring power of community. Our collective strength is our greatest defense.

With deepest sorrow and unwavering hope,

[Your Name/Organization Name]

<<MF May 1st 2001.pdf>> 			Good Tuesday Morning - Comments From The Local Guys!

The National Association of Purchasing Managers report for April this morning was essentially unchanged versus March. The actual number was 43.2, compared to March's reading of 43.1, representing a marginal 0.1 point increase. Any number below 50 indicates that the manufacturing sector is still contracting, and this marks the ninth consecutive month that the index has remained below this critical threshold. So, while this contraction is still in effect, it does seem as if the inventory drawdown is continuing apace, which is a positive development for future manufacturing recovery. The employment component of the index fell to 43.8 from 44.1, while the new orders index improved slightly to 47.2 from 46.8, suggesting potential stabilization in demand patterns.

Interest rate movements continue to reflect economic uncertainty. The 30-year US T-Bond yield is 5.72%, down from 5.85% just two weeks ago. The 10-year yield is 5.28%, representing a 12 basis point decline from the previous month. The 5-year is trading at 4.83%, maintaining its position in the lower end of the recent trading range. This yield curve flattening suggests growing market expectations for Federal Reserve interest rate cuts in response to the economic slowdown. Fed funds futures are now pricing in a 75% probability of at least one rate cut by the June FOMC meeting.

Energy markets remain volatile amid global supply concerns and weakening demand signals. Spot crude oil is trading at $28.85 p/b, down $1.20 from last week's close, as OPEC production cuts continue to compete with demand destruction from the manufacturing slowdown. Natural Gas - Henry Hub - is trading at $4.70 p/mcf, up significantly from the $3.85 level seen in early April, driven by late-season heating demand and lower than expected storage injection rates. Weather forecasts calling for below-normal temperatures in the Northeast through mid-May are providing additional support to natural gas prices.

AD Time: New Federal Insider-Trading Rule (Rule 10b5-1) have been adopted by the SEC under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, effective as of April 15th, 2001. This rule greatly enhances an insider's/employee's ability to trade his/her corporate shares during blackout periods, addressing a long-standing concern among corporate executives and employees who previously faced significant restrictions on their ability to manage personal portfolios. 

Previously, without the protection of this new SEC rule, employees and insiders could safely trade only outside of designated blackout windows, typically creating concentrated trading periods that could impact stock prices and limit portfolio management flexibility. These blackout periods often lasted 6-8 weeks around earnings announcements and other material corporate events, effectively preventing insiders from executing normal investment strategies for significant portions of the year.

Under this new rule, insiders/employees may have the ability to purchase and sell their corporate shares even during blackout periods if a written plan was established and in force when the insider/employee was not in possession of material, non-public information. The plan must specify the amount, pricing, and timing of transactions, and cannot be modified during blackout periods. Additionally, there must be a "cooling off" period of at least 30 days between plan establishment and the first transaction under the plan.

The new rule contains other restrictions and should be reviewed carefully, including requirements for good faith establishment of plans, prohibition of multiple overlapping plans, and specific documentation requirements that must be maintained for SEC examination purposes. Plans must also include safeguards to prevent abuse and ensure compliance with existing anti-fraud provisions.

Lehman Brothers has established a turn-key plan that takes into account the regulatory procedures for establishing such a plan, including legal review, documentation preparation, and ongoing compliance monitoring. Our Corporate Services team has already assisted over 200 executives in establishing compliant 10b5-1 plans since the rule's adoption.

Please email us or call us for more information.

Lehman Brothers' Research.

First, we must terminate the OBA by giving 30 days' notice to Burlington. Paragraph 13 of the 6/1/94 OBA with Burlington (as successor in interest to Meridian) provides that either party may terminate the OBA "at the end of the primary term, or thereafter by providing thirty (30) days prior written notice" to Burlington. Next, on the effective termination date of the OBA, we can terminate the interconnect agreement by giving 30 days' notice to Burlington. Importantly, the paragraph also provides that the agreement "may be terminated by either party upon thirty (30) days prior written notice in the event the OBA between the parties is terminated."

As we've already discussed, termination of the agreement is an extreme measure from a customer relations standpoint, and we probably need to weigh our other options first.

Subject: Supporting Texas Coast Conservation Through the Saltwater Conservation Association

Dear [Recipient],

I wanted to share information about the important conservation work being done along our Texas coast by the Saltwater Conservation Association of Texas (SCAT).

SCAT is a leading non-profit organization dedicated to preserving and enhancing marine resources and coastal habitats throughout Texas. For over four decades, they have been at the forefront of efforts to protect our state's valuable saltwater fisheries and coastal ecosystems.

Key conservation initiatives include:

**Habitat Restoration**: SCAT actively supports oyster reef restoration, seagrass bed protection, and coastal marsh preservation projects that serve as critical nursery areas for marine life.

**Water Quality Protection**: The organization advocates for policies that reduce pollution runoff and maintain the health of our bays and estuaries.

**Fisheries Management**: SCAT works with state agencies to establish science-based fishing regulations that ensure sustainable fish populations for future generations.

**Education and Outreach**: Through their youth programs and public awareness campaigns, SCAT teaches proper conservation practices and stewardship ethics to anglers and coastal communities.

**Advocacy**: The organization actively lobbies for legislation that protects coastal resources and promotes responsible coastal development.

Recent successes include supporting red drum population recovery, advocating for stricter water quality standards, and helping establish new marine protected areas along the Texas coast.

The Texas coast faces ongoing challenges from development pressure, climate change, and water quality issues. Organizations like SCAT play a vital role in ensuring these precious resources remain healthy and productive for future generations of Texans.

To learn more about their work or get involved, visit their website or consider supporting their conservation efforts.

Best regards,
[Your Name]

Fellas:   Enjoyed the weekend with you all immensely.
I  think Travis and Don Jr. are my new benchmarks for late night longevity, and  Don.
Sr. is my new benchmark for marksmanship from a seated position.
I want to make you all aware of a new organization  that I have helped start up.
The Saltwater Conservation Association of  Texas was founded to give Texans a new conservation resource that is dedicated  solely to the coast of Texas.
We are a 501 (c) 3, non-profit, and we have no paid  staff.
Our goal for the next 3-5 years is to assist TPWD in their effort  to retire as many commercial shrimping licenses as possible, as Texas shrimpers  now accumulate around 80 million pounds of bycatch annually.
This bycatch  includes an incredible amount of flounder and croaker, not to mention numerous  forage fish for trout and reds.
We are an authorized agent of TPWD, whereby we can  solicit bids from shrimpers, purchase their license, and then hand it over to  TPWD.
The program is intended to target bay shrimping (not bait shrimping)  as the bay shrimpers drag their nets for hours on end, whereas the bait  shrimpers usually only drag for around 20 minutes or so.
To make a long  story short, the effect of thousands of chains dragging across the bays on a  daily basis is not good for the ecosystem.
I hope you will all consider becoming a Founding  Father.
If not, then any level of sponsorship is certainly  appreciated.
Details of our organization and sponsorship levels can be  found at our website - www.scatexas.org  -  or you can call direct at 512-392-1256.
You can join online or print an  application and mail it in.
Thanks for your consideration, and once again I  really enjoyed the weekend with you all.
Take care.
Sincerely,

NOTHING of importance was discussed  during our entire meal and it was only when I brought things up as we were  leaving that any actual talking occurred.
Here are the basics...  - There is definitely no "us" anymore...and I quote "sometimes these things  just fade out" - There is much I didn't know about him and I am sure even more that I still  don't - Case in point...He was MARRIED before (yes, you read correctly married) - Turns out he's been divorced about three years, it didn't end well and he  hasn't had a relationship that has lasted beyond       2 mos.
in those three  years (even though, by his own admission, he has dated a lot) - Can you say  issues?
- He told me "I know this sounds so trite, but this really has nothing to do  with you, it's all me."
Of course I agreed with him saying "I know it's you  Ted, I don't have any problems."
(He got a chuckle out of that one) - I told him about my frustrations and disappointment with how he had handled  things and he apologised (evidently Kevin told him about our exchange at  Steak Night) and I also let him know how much I appreciated his handling of  things in the beginning - I said I really hated animosity and hard feelings and that as long as he  hadn't done anything truly horrible to me (i.e.
murder a family member, etc.)
I would really like to leave things on a good note...He agreed.
- He said I was a fantastic girl and that he still enjoyed hanging out and  talking with me (although I don't see us doing a lot of that)  So all in all I walked away with three very important things 1.
A lightened  load (I got everything of my chest that I wanted to and needed to) 2.
My  dignity (I handled it just as I'd hoped...with composure and wit) 3.
A  clearer since of Ted as a person (He definitely has a lot of issues in his  life he has not completely dealt with yet, and who knows if he ever will?)
Anyway, I'm okay with everything and surprisingly feel pretty good.
I'll  talk to you soon.
Susan  By the way, I told him about the shirt idea (he thought it was funny, and  maybe just a little harsh)

Subject: Colorado PUC Proposed Amendments to Gas Utility Price Risk Management Rules

Dear Stakeholders,

We are writing to inform you of the Colorado Public Utilities Commission (PUC)'s recently proposed amendments to the rules governing price risk management for gas utilities operating within the state.

These proposed amendments aim to refine and potentially enhance the current regulatory framework for how gas utilities manage the price volatility of natural gas. The PUC's objective is to further ensure consumer protection, promote greater stability in natural gas costs, and encourage sound risk management practices among utilities.

We encourage all interested parties, including gas utilities, consumer advocates, and industry stakeholders, to carefully review the detailed proposed rule changes. The PUC will be conducting proceedings to gather feedback, and there will be opportunities to submit comments and participate in public hearings.

Further details regarding the specific proposed changes, along with instructions on how to submit comments and participate in upcoming workshops or hearings, can be found on the Colorado PUC's official website under the relevant docket number. Your engagement in this process is vital to ensuring a comprehensive and effective outcome.

Sincerely,

[Your Name/Organization Name]

Subject: Proposed Standardization of Contract Provisions to Mitigate Non-Market Risks in California Trading Operations

Dear Team,

As part of our ongoing efforts to strengthen risk management within Enron’s California trading operations, I am proposing the development and implementation of standardized contract provisions aimed at reducing our exposure to non-market risks. These risks—including counterparty default, regulatory uncertainties, and operational ambiguities—can materially impact both the profitability and compliance profile of our activities.

Standardizing key contractual terms across trading agreements will help ensure greater consistency, clarity, and enforceability. Proposed areas for standardization include:

- Credit support and collateral requirements  
- Force majeure and regulatory change clauses  
- Dispute resolution mechanisms  
- Standard settlement cycles and delivery terms  
- Early termination and default provisions  

By adopting a consistent approach, we will be better equipped to manage uncertainties, streamline negotiations, and respond quickly to regulatory developments in the California market.

I welcome your feedback and suggestions on the proposed areas of standardization and invite you to participate in a working group to define the specific provisions to be adopted. Please respond by [date] with your interest and any initial comments.

Thank you for your attention and cooperation as we work to further fortify our risk management framework.

Best regards,

[Your Name]

Enron North America

Status report of integration testing from Wednesday, Jan. 23rd

Beginning:
On Wednesday, January 23rd, integration testing was conducted with 16 gas/power transaction types. The overall environment was stable, with no infrastructure or major application issues reported. Unlike previous rounds, this test involved a broader range of gas transaction types and used a baseline with all non-essential Netco data removed in preparation for Netco’s go-live.

Middle:
During today's test, several data setup-related issues arose, resulting in downtime. These included missing EOL-Dynegy information, TGP address details, bad credit counterparties/contracts, and database issues with data synchronization/replication. Most of these issues were due to the extensive cleanup and removal of unnecessary data. The deferred start time (from 12:00 pm to 2:00 pm) and the data setup/sync complications prevented completion of all downstream processes, most notably Settlements, Confirmations, and SAP.

End:
The remaining open issues are being addressed Wednesday night. Testing will continue into Thursday, and testers with outstanding tasks are requested to complete script execution during both the morning and afternoon shifts, as some will be unavailable due to UBS offsite meetings. Testing activities will be balanced accordingly. The bridgeline will remain active from 9:00 am to 5:00 pm for communication and status updates. This recap summarizes where testing left off for both Netco and EOL entry.

PG&E will announce via press release very early next week an open season on Redwood, Baja and Silverado.
It comes in direct response to recent announcements of expansions into California by pipelines.
The bid protocols will be structured similar to original open season from the original Gas Accord.
The open season will start on June 1 and end on July 31.
Capacity will be available starting 1.1.03.
Bidders will be able to bid up to 30 years (PG&E states that that's what generators want).
Accompanying the announcement will be another announcement that PG&E will expand Redwood by 200mmcf/day, which they hope to have available by 1.1.03, or some time during Q103.
About 2-4 weeks after the open season begins, PG&E will file its proposed "Gas Accord II,"  (the first one expires end of 02).
As part of that filing, PG&E will offer its proposed ratemaking treatment for the next five years (beginning 1.1.03).
PG&E will not include in the open season 1) core capacity and 2) certain EAD contracts that extend beyond the Gas Accord 1 end date.
In addition, PG&E will hold back an additional 20% (after excluding core and EAD), to be "open-seasoned" at some "future" date.
The capacity to be auctioned is: 1) 900 mmcf/day on Redwood, 2) 245 (annual) on Baja, plus an additional 200/day in summer on Baja, 3) 155 on Silverado.
How PG&E will market the 20% they intend to hold back, and when they might auction it off in the future will be discussed in PG&E's Gas Accord II filing.
No single company will be awarded more than 30% of the capacity on any specific path in the primary open season (though firms can bid whatever level of capacity they choose).
Please forwad along to anyone else who might be interested.
If you have any questions, just holler.
Best,

A man, weary from a long week, boarded an airplane and found his designated window seat. As he settled into the surprisingly plush upholstery, he glanced up the aisle. His breath hitched for a moment. A woman, stunning in a way that made the cabin lights seem to dim around her, was gracefully making her way through the narrow passage. Her hair, the color of rich mahogany, framed a face that was both elegant and inviting. His heart gave a hopeful flutter as he soon realized she was heading straight toward his row. Lo and behold, she took the aisle seat right beside his, a faint scent of jasmine accompanying her.

Eager, perhaps too eager, to strike up a conversation with this captivating stranger, he blurted out, "Business trip or vacation?"

She turned her head, a captivating smile playing on her lips, and her eyes sparkled as she said, "Business, actually. I'm going to the annual Nymphomaniac Convention in Chicago."

He felt a sudden, visceral jolt, a mixture of shock and profound interest. His carefully constructed composure threatened to crumble as he swallowed hard. Here was the most gorgeous woman he had ever seen, radiating an almost ethereal beauty, sitting next to him, and she was on her way to a meeting for... *nymphomaniacs*! His mind raced, a thousand inappropriate questions bubbling to the surface, but he forced them down, struggling to maintain any semblance of polite conversation. He took a deep breath and, striving for a casual tone he didn't feel, calmly asked, "What's your business role at this convention?"

"Lecturer," she responded, her voice smooth and confident. "I use my experience to debunk some of the popular myths about sexuality."

His curiosity, now fully piqued beyond anything he'd ever imagined, overwhelmed his earlier shock. "Really," he pressed, leaning forward slightly, "what myths are those?"

"Well," she explained, leaning back comfortably, "one popular myth is that African American men are the most well endowed, when in fact, scientific studies have shown it's the Native American Indian who is most likely to possess that trait. Another popular myth is that French men are the best lovers, when actually it is the men of Jewish descent. We have, however," she paused, a slight mischievous glint in her eye, "found that the best potential lover in all categories, combining passion, stamina, and skill, is often the Southern redneck."

A sudden blush crept up her neck, and she looked down, a little self-conscious. "I'm sorry," she said, her voice softer, "I shouldn't really be discussing this with you. We've only just met, and I don't even know your name."

A slow, knowing smile spread across the man's face, his eyes twinkling as he extended a hand. "The name's Tonto," he said, his voice a low rumble. "Tonto Goldstein, but my friends, they just call me Bubba."

Mark,  The following are my responses to Phillip's changes in our letter  agreement:  1.
1st Sentence of Second Paragraph - Strike of reference to Section 3.3 and  reference to Appendix 1 - ENA's right to decrease confirmed volumes and  Phillips' rights to release the gas are clearly set out in Section 3.3.
The  "Operations/Delivery Scheduling Procedures" only are the method by which this  is effected.
This change needs to be removed.
2.
1st Sentence of Second Paragraph  - The remainder of the changes to the  1st Sentence except for the strike of Seller's Daily Deliverability are OK.
Seller's Daily Deliverability needs to remain as this is the correct  terminology under the Purchase Agreement.
All we are doing here is effecting  the provisions of the Purchase Agreement to which both parties have already  agreed.

The added sentence at the end of the second paragraph - This needs to be  stricken.

However,  the term rights ENA  "may" have needs to be stricken.
ENA's position is that we have the right to  recall the gas as long as it hasn't been released longer than 120 days.
If you wish to discuss these comments or would like me to discuss these with  Phillips, I would be happy to do so.

Hi Steve and Bob, Happy New Year!!
Steve, based on our meeting in Houston, I met with our engineering and operations folks to discuss the possibility of putting together a new firm (or limited firm) Park N Ride storage service on the pipeline project.
Everyone agreed it is likely doable under certain conditions not the least of which is FERC approval.
The question I have for you is: how much volume and for how long a period?
For example, on any given day, assuming there is no Copper Eagle storage available, it will likely be easier to borrow (ride) gas off the system than to park gas on it.
I think this was your greater concern.
In your ideal world, how much volume would you like to be able to pull off Sun Devil say if your MDQ was 100,000?
Would you want an additional 25,000/day, more or less?
and for how long?
Also, how much would you want to Park on the system and for how long?
For purposes of evaluation, assume the cost would be significantly less than a storage option.
If you give me some parameters, we will build a service offering that meets your needs as close as possible.
I will be out of the office on Friday 1/4 but look forward to hearing from you early next week.
Best Regards,

Dennis has a meeting lined up with DOE decisionmakers on the 25th.
He is going to pitch the project as an approximately 100 mw power plant, to be owned by DOE, with the gas pipeline owned by Dennis and/or third parties.

How did he do it?
Very easy: they ran the power plant economics using about a $2.00 gas cost instead of current, real world prices.

Subject: Review of Adapting AE’s Snow and Water Forecasting Model for Year-Round Use and Integration with Power Plant Data

Dear Team,

I am writing to provide an update on our review of adapting AE’s snow and water forecasting model for year-round application and integration with power plant data.

Our initial analysis indicates that while the current model performs well during the winter and snowmelt seasons, there are opportunities to enhance its performance for all-season utility. This would involve expanding meteorological inputs to account for rainfall and evaporation patterns during spring, summer, and fall. Modifying the model’s temporal resolution and hydrologic process representation may also be required to improve accuracy outside of the snowmelt period.

Integration with power plant operational data is technically feasible. By linking real-time water forecasts with plant intake, discharge, and cooling system metrics, we can establish a dynamic feedback loop to inform ongoing operational decisions. Preliminary steps include mapping model output parameters to plant-specific data needs and adjusting data interfaces for automated exchange.

We recommend a pilot phase focused on a single site to refine the integration process and validate all-season forecasting accuracy before scaling up. Additional efforts should include collaboration with the AE model development team to ensure updates are in alignment with their long-term roadmap.

Please let me know if you have any questions or would like to discuss the next steps in more detail.

Best regards,  
[Your Name]

Last year, gray rain streaked the office windows as we gathered in a cramped conference room, spreadsheets spread across the table, to hammer out the details: money was to be set aside in reserves to cover the net amount needed to resolve lingering issues with Transco, BUG, LILCO, and Enron. The discussions stretched into the evening, fluorescent lights buzzing overhead, and the total dollars required came to approximately $4.25 million.

A large portion—$3.55 million—was earmarked specifically for the Transco historical imbalance resolution. The rest, we noted on the whiteboard smudged with old calculations, would cover the BUG and LILCO accounting issues that Keyspan brought to our attention the previous spring.

In his office lined with neatly labeled binders, Bob Hall meticulously reserved $3.5 million in his area for the Transco resolution. The remaining $50,000 for Transco, along with approximately $700,000 in additional funds for the lingering accounting issues, were supposed to be reserved last year under "The Office of the Chairman." Files exchanged hands; Sally Beck and Janet Dietrich arranged for this entire sum to be set aside at the "Chairman" level, reasoning that these funds were needed to correct an old accounting error—one that should never have impacted the East Desk P&L.

Stacks of forms and internal memos outlined the arrangement: the reserve would remain untouched until settlement payments were made by Enron.

But, as with most stories, there’s some good news and some bad news.

First, the bad news: After a great deal of investigation—tracing paper trails, combing through digital ledgers—it appears that there currently is no reserve at the "Office of the Chairman" for these additional funds. The spreadsheet cells come up empty, and no entry marks the funds' existence.

Now, the good news: Georgeanne has agreed, with determined calm in her voice beneath the office's humming HVAC, to take the necessary steps to ensure money is available so we can quickly resolve these issues with Keyspan and Transco.

If you have questions, feel free to give me a call.

Ruth x31667

Subject: Review of Turnkey Construction Contract Draft - Key Areas for Discussion

Dear Team,

I've completed an initial review of the draft turnkey construction contract and have identified several critical areas that require further discussion and potential revision. My focus was particularly on the following provisions:

1.  **Liquidated Damages:** The current wording regarding liquidated damages warrants a thorough review to ensure it accurately reflects potential losses, is reasonable, and enforceable. We need to confirm the daily rate and the cap align with our risk assessment and project financial model.

2.  **Force Majeure Clause:** The scope and definitions within the force majeure clause need to be carefully examined. We should ensure it provides adequate protection against unforeseen events, clearly outlines notification procedures, and specifies the impact on project timelines and costs without being overly broad or restrictive.

3.  **Permitting Responsibilities:** The draft's allocation of permitting responsibilities appears to place a significant burden on our side. We need to clarify which party is accountable for obtaining specific permits, licenses, and approvals, especially those that are complex or have long lead times, to prevent project delays and cost overruns.

4.  **Utility Coordination Provisions:** The provisions related to utility coordination are critical for project execution. We must ensure there is a clear understanding of the responsibilities for identification, relocation, connection, and costs associated with existing and new utilities. Any ambiguities here could lead to substantial delays and disputes.

I propose we schedule a meeting next week to discuss these points in detail and work towards refining these sections to protect our interests and ensure a smooth project execution. Please let me know your availability.

Best regards,

[Your Name]
[Your Title]

Hi Jewel,

Sorry, I was not available to visit with you when you called the other day. Things have been extremely busy around here recently, with several key projects reaching critical deadlines and an increase in market activity, which often means our days extend well beyond normal hours. Plus, as you know, our open-plan office environment provides very little room for private or in-depth conversations without interruption, which makes it challenging to truly focus when someone calls.

In answer to your question, regarding special requirements for a gas scheduler role, the landscape has significantly shifted. Back in the day, the industry would indeed have been strictly looking for candidates with actual, hands-on pipeline scheduling experience. However, the dynamics have changed considerably. Anymore, the *liquidity* – meaning the available pool of highly experienced and qualified gas schedulers – is surprisingly low across the industry. This shortage stems from a combination of factors, including an aging workforce, the specialized nature of the role, and the rapid evolution of market complexities and data analysis demands. Because of this, companies are now much more open to considering most people who possess a strong analytical or coordinative type background. This typically means individuals who can demonstrate excellent problem-solving skills, an aptitude for data interpretation, strong organizational abilities, and a knack for managing complex logistics and communications, even if it's not directly in energy. I truly think it's one of those strategic roles where once you "get your foot in the door" and demonstrate your capabilities, you can gain invaluable industry-specific knowledge and build a foundational network, opening up opportunities to move onward and upward into various other areas like trading support, operations management, or even market analysis.

Just be aware, that if you were to become a gas scheduler, it's not a typical 9-to-5 job. It may require working on weekends and late nights from time to time. This is primarily due to the 24/7 nature of energy markets, where pipelines operate continuously, and nomination deadlines, unexpected operational issues (like a compressor station outage), or sudden market changes can occur at any hour, requiring immediate attention to ensure reliable gas flow and compliance. The critical importance of maintaining supply and demand balance means schedulers often need to be on call or work extended hours to react to these dynamic circumstances.

As far as the next step, I would strongly suggest that you just simply send a direct e-mail to George Smith, who is the Manager of Logistics on the Central Desk, and ask him if he has time to visit with you for an informational chat. This proactive approach by simply expressing a genuine interest in the role demonstrates initiative and personal drive, qualities that are highly valued in our field and often set candidates apart. During this conversation, you can aim to learn what his specific expectations are of a successful scheduler, perhaps asking about the key challenges of the role, what a typical day might entail, or the most critical skills needed to excel. Equally important, you should also try to understand what you can expect to learn from him and the team, and what the growth trajectory might look like within the department or company. I believe this direct, information-gathering first step is crucial for both you and him to gauge mutual fit and for you to gain a clearer understanding of the role's demands and rewards.

Also, it's worth noting that if George is interested in your profile, but does not have a position currently open on his team, then he is very likely to pass on your name to some of the other managers within logistics or related departments. They're actually pretty good about inter-departmental collaboration and sharing promising candidates, especially given the ongoing need for talent across the organization. An internal referral like that often carries significant weight and can open doors that a cold application might not. To help you along, I'll definitely mention to George that you may be giving him a call in the coming days.

Please don't hesitate to let me know if you have any further questions, or if you'd like to visit some more to discuss this or anything else. I'm happy to help.

Take care!

Subject: Risks Associated with Discounted Contract Rates and Assignment Clauses

Dear Team,

This email addresses a crucial area of risk related to our discounted contract rates, specifically in the context of contract assignment.

It's important to recognize that many of our discounted rates are often granted based on specific criteria such as:
*   The volume or long-term commitment of the original client.
*   A particular project scope or relationship.
*   Strategic partnerships or market entry considerations.
*   The original client's financial standing or operational context.

When a contract containing a discounted rate is subsequently assigned to a different entity, the fundamental basis for that original discount may no longer hold true. The assignee may not meet the criteria that qualified the original party for the special rate.

The primary risks arising from this situation include:

1.  **Loss of Discount and Rate Reversion:** The most immediate risk is that the discount may be deemed invalid upon assignment. This would mean the assignee would then be subject to our standard, higher rates, potentially leading to unexpected cost increases for them.
2.  **Budget Overruns for Assignee:** If the assignee was unaware that the discounted rate was contingent on the original party, they might have budgeted based on the lower rate, leading to significant financial discrepancies post-assignment.
3.  **Contractual Disputes:** Ambiguity in contract language regarding the persistence of discounts upon assignment can lead to disputes, negotiations, and potential legal challenges, consuming valuable time and resources.
4.  **Reputational Damage:** Surprising an assignee with higher rates post-transfer can strain relationships and damage our reputation for transparency and reliable pricing.
5.  **Operational Inefficiencies:** The need to re-negotiate terms or clarify pricing can disrupt project timelines and administrative processes.

To mitigate these risks, it is imperative that we:
*   **Clearly define discount conditions:** Ensure our contracts explicitly state the conditions under which discounts are granted and, crucially, whether these discounts are contingent on the original contracting party or project.
*   **Address assignment in pricing clauses:** Include specific language within our assignment clauses detailing what happens to discounted rates upon transfer – e.g., if the discount terminates, if rates revert to standard, or if a re-negotiation is triggered.
*   **Conduct due diligence:** When reviewing potential assignments, thoroughly assess the impact on our pricing and communicate any changes proactively to all involved parties.

I encourage everyone involved in contract drafting, negotiation, and management to pay close attention to these details. Let's ensure our contracts are robust and transparent, protecting both our interests and those of our partners.

Please reach out if you have any questions or would like to discuss this further.

Best regards,

For a Gas daily swap deal, its gamma, vega, theta, rho, drift, 2nd order should be zero.
The change between today and prior day comes from forward value of new deals, changed value of old deals, curve shift of old deals, and liquidation of old deals.
We can put it in a simplified formula,   Today Value - Prior Day Value = New deals + Changed Deals + Curve Shift - Liquidation of old deals   If you look at the gas top page, its liquidation actually includes both existing deals and new deals.

Europe.
These margins are based on PIRA's proprietary crude yields, and represent industry or "swing" refinery margins.
The added margins are "cracking" and "hydroskimming" for Urals crude in the Mediterranean, and "cracking" and "topping" margins for Dubai crude in Singapore.
The $/Bbl margins represent incremental cash operating margins, which equal gross product worth, less delivered crude cost, less variable refining operating costs.
Margins are calculated and plotted for each day that prices are available.
PIRA will continue to publish margin charts every Monday afternoon at www.pira.com.

Subject: I Did It! MS150 Ride Complete - Thank You!

Hi everyone,

I’m excited to share that I completed the MS150 ride! It was a challenging but incredibly rewarding experience, and I couldn't have done it without your support and encouragement.

Thank you so much for your generous donations, cheering me on, and believing in this cause. Your support not only motivated me to cross the finish line but also helps make a real difference in the fight against MS.

I’m grateful to have you in my corner!

With appreciation,  
[Your Name]
source_text:
I finished the ride!
I again want to say again to all of you for supporting my ride.
Your donation is for a good cause.
Finally, your cancelled check to the National MS Society will serve as your tax receipt.
Please send me an email if you have any questions.
Below is my story if you wish to read more.
=======================================  Prologue  Should I do it or not?
This was a question that had to be answered.....and soon.
This question had been lurking in the back of my mind since I'd already seen some gnarly bike crashes before and I've heard all the nasty stories about them.
So I was basically reluctant to do so, but I was obviously curious about it and so I had mixed feeling altogether.
I jumped on the internet for some perspective and discovered the pros and cons.
I figured, if I did happen to be involved in a pile-up, then I'd be sorry.
In the end, I did it.
In the tradition of cycling, I decided to shave my legs!
Day One - 100 miles  My alarm sounded off at 4:30 and I jumped out of bed, quickly dressed, and threw my gear into my Jeep and hit the road.
The MS150 ride started at 7am.
And with 10,000 riders participating, my goal was to avoid as much traffic as possible.
Thankfully, the team I rode with (Sun & Ski Sport) started in the number two position.
bp, the corporate sponsor, started off the race.
It should be noted that my ride started at Tully Stadium (Dairy Ashford/I-10) as opposed to Rhodes Stadium (located in Katy) and so an extra 15 miles were immediately tacked on.
From my POV, this day's ride was no different from any other I did in the preceding weeks other than the fact that it was longer by about 40 miles.
After the start and once the crowd thinned out, I got into my groove (after pulling over for a quick relief stop) and stayed within my own and kept a moderate speed with a high cadence.
The sun was above the clouds, but while en route a large, dark menacing cloud seemed to head my direction, but thankfully it amounted to nothing and the cloud cover remained most of the day.

Subject: On Trust, Vulnerability, and Wise Discernment in Our Connections

Hi everyone,

Today, I wanted to reflect on a nuanced but crucial aspect of our human connections: the intricate interplay of trust, vulnerability, and the importance of cautious discernment. Navigating relationships is a delicate dance, requiring both an open heart and a watchful mind.

Trust is the bedrock of any meaningful relationship. It’s the quiet confidence that another person will act with good intentions towards us, respect our boundaries, and be there when it counts. Trust isn't given freely or instantly; it's built brick by brick through consistent actions, reliability, and shared experiences. It allows us to feel safe enough to truly be ourselves.

And it’s this sense of safety that enables vulnerability – the willingness to expose our true selves, our fears, our hopes, and our imperfections to another. Vulnerability is the gateway to deep intimacy and authentic connection. It’s an act of immense courage, as it requires us to drop our guards and risk potential hurt for the sake of profound belonging. Without it, relationships remain superficial.

However, the very act of being vulnerable necessitates careful discernment. While opening up is essential, it shouldn't be indiscriminate. Cautious discernment means taking the time to observe, listen, and assess if someone has earned the privilege of your vulnerability. It means looking for consistency between their words and actions, assessing their empathy, their respect for others, and their reciprocity in the relationship. It's not about suspicion, but rather about self-preservation and wisely investing your emotional energy in those who prove themselves worthy and safe over time.

Ultimately, building strong, healthy relationships involves finding this delicate balance: daring to trust and be vulnerable, but always with an undercurrent of mindful awareness. It’s about building wisely, protecting your heart, and choosing to open up to those who honor the gift of your authentic self.

Warmly,

[Your Name]

While I don't truly fear you becoming a bitter individual as a result of  these negative experiences, I do feel the highlighted section below is now  more appropriate than ever.
One must keep their eyes open and use all of the wisdom they possess when  they trust.
Just as I suggested that positive experiences can cause one's  level of trust to grow exponentially, negative experiences can cause  irreparable harm.
If you trust blindly or too willingly and that trust is  violated it colours every aspect of your life.
There are too many people in  this world that have become bitter and cynical, not because they were born  that way but, because they handed out trust haphazardly and too many times  that trust was thrown back in their face.
I don't mean to suggest from the  above that one should live in a day-to-day mind-set of distrust but rather  that they must really look at people and all the aspects which they posses.
I have come to the conclusion that if you spend most of your time observing  and listening to people rather than always taking the lead you will learn a  great deal more about them and their character.
The smallest acts and  statements can in fact say the most, so always be observant.
(This includes  listening to what others have to say and paying attention to the opinions of  people whom you respect.)
To that end I have one last comment...I am constantly amazed and periodically  reminded what fragile creatures we humans are.
That beyond the hype and  self-grandizing the basic components of ourselves (our experiences, fears,  cares, concerns, needs etc.)
cannot be completely disregarded and will always  be a part of us.

Subject: ISDA Event of Default Termination - Opportunistic Delays When Declaring Termination Dates

Dear Team,

Following the recent Event of Default concerning [Counterparty Name/Specific ISDA Agreement], we are now at a critical juncture regarding the exercise of our termination rights under the ISDA Master Agreement. While the immediate impulse might be to declare an Early Termination Date without delay, it's crucial to consider the strategic advantages of an *opportunistic delay* in this declaration.

Delaying the declaration of the Early Termination Date can provide significant tactical benefits. This period allows us to closely monitor market conditions for the underlying transactions, potentially waiting for more favorable pricing for replacement trades or for the defaulting party's position to further deteriorate, thereby improving our net recovery calculation. It also creates valuable time for us to gather additional information, assess the full scope of the counterparty's financial distress, and evaluate any potential cross-defaults or related claims.

Furthermore, a controlled delay can enhance our negotiation leverage. It keeps the counterparty on the hook, providing an opportunity to extract concessions, negotiate a more advantageous settlement, or secure additional collateral before committing to a final termination. This strategic pause also facilitates coordination with other affected creditors, if applicable, allowing for a more unified and impactful response. The careful timing can also allow for a more thorough legal and operational readiness for the full close-out process.

While the right to terminate exists, the timing of its exercise can significantly impact our financial outcome. A calculated delay is not inaction but a deliberate strategy to maximize our position. We should carefully weigh the ongoing risks against the potential for an improved recovery before setting a definitive termination date.

Let's discuss the specific market conditions and our negotiation strategy before proceeding.

Best regards,

[Your Name/Team]

A jeweler watched as a huge truck pulled up in front of his store. The back opened, and an elephant walked out. It broke one of the windows with its tusk and then, using its trunk like a vacuum cleaner, sucked up all the jewelry. The elephant then got back in the truck, which quickly disappeared out of sight.

When the jeweler finally regained his senses, he called the police. Detectives arrived, and he told them the whole story.

"Could you describe the elephant?" one of the officers asked.

"An elephant is an elephant," he replied. "You’ve seen one, you’ve seen them all. What do you mean, 'describe' him?"

"Well," said the policeman, "there are two types of elephants: African and Indian. The Indian elephant has smaller ears and isn’t as large as the African elephant."

"I can’t help you," said the frustrated jeweler. "He had a stocking pulled over his head."
